Round 1068.decision_summary:
What closes MM2, measured rather than asserted — and the trap that closing it
badly would walk into.

Two reads have sat outside every sweep this arc runs. The play-break census
names them in an assertion of its own — `validate-disclosure-leak` and
`validate-render-fidelity` — as "the reads this corpus cannot ask without
inventing an argument", and Round 1051, which halved that list, wrote down why
these two survived it: what they need is a FILE, and no vocabulary can supply a
file. The debt ledger has carried them as MM2 ever since with one sentence — a
fixture closes it — and a sentence is not a design.

SO THE READ WAS ASKED BY HAND. `validate-render-fidelity --against <store>
--world main` answers. Its `reextracted_facts` is the fact count of the file
handed to `--against`, and nothing else in the report comes from the authored
store except the CANON ORDER it composes and the branch registry it checks the
world against. The law is: every fact in the re-extracted store is placed by its
`canon_from` against the world's composed order — on the path, off the path (a
node this world does not walk), or unplaced (no node at all) — and a fact at a
maximal node means the telling reached its terminal.

THAT IS WHY THE FIXTURE IS THE BASELINE CORPUS STORE, and why this is not
circular. The population's 108 ROAD EDITS move the composed order; the fixture
does not move with them. A road edit that drops a scene from a world's path
turns every re-extracted fact placed there from on-path into off-path, and the
answer moves. The second value this read has never had is already in the
population — what is missing is only the file to compare against.

AND THE TRAP IS THE OBVIOUS FIXTURE. Handed the SPEC workspace store, the verb
answers `reextracted_facts: 0` — that store holds no narrative facts — and 0
re-extracted facts is a clean fidelity report: no off-path, no unplaced, exit 0.
Handed the corrupted store itself, it would compare a thing to itself and answer
clean forever. Either way the read becomes askable and inert, which is worse
than unaskable: an unasked read is a hole the census PRINTS, and an inert one is
a green cell. So the round that closes this owes two assertions beyond the
wiring: that the fixture's fact count is not zero, and that at least one
corruption in the population moves this read's answer.

THE SEAM IS ONE SIGNATURE. `values_for(flag, store)` answers with values read out
of the store, which is exactly why it cannot answer `--against`: the value is a
PATH, and a path is a fact about where the walk put things rather than about
what the corpus declares. Closing MM2 means giving that function the baseline
store's path and returning it for `--against` — after which the panel's existing
machinery supplies the rest, since `--telling`, `--world` and `--truth-frame`
already resolve from the corpus's own vocabulary (that is what Round 1051 left
standing when it removed the other two verbs from this list).

WHAT MOVES WHEN IT LANDS: the census's `unaskable` assertion, which today names
exactly these two verbs, and every count in the three walks that divides by the
number of reads asked. That constant churn is the reason this is a design and
not a half-finished edit at the end of a session.
changes_bullets: No code. This round is the design for MM2, written as a self-contained entry so the round that implements it does not have to re-derive what was measured here: the fixture is the baseline corpus store on disk, the second value comes from the population's road edits moving the composed order, the seam is `values_for`'s missing path context, and the two assertions the wiring owes are a non-zero fixture and one corruption that moves the answer.
verification_bullets: The read was RUN, not read about: `validate-render-fidelity --against docs/.atomic/workspace.atomic.json --world main --json` answers `{"world":"main","reextracted_facts":0,"off_path":[],"unplaced":[],"reached_terminal":false}`. That is the trap this design names — the spec workspace holds no narrative facts, so the answer is a clean report about nothing.

The law was read at its source rather than inferred from the flag names: `render_fidelity` in `crates/mnemosyne-validate/src/disclosure.rs` counts `reextracted.narrative_facts.len()` and classifies each of them by `canon_from` against the world's composed order. The authored store reaches this report only through that order and the branch registry.

The absent-file case is already closed and did not need this round: `load_named_store` refuses a path that does not exist, with the reason spelled out — an absent store would load as an empty one, and an answer about nothing reads exactly like an answer that found nothing.

What is NOT verified: that `validate-disclosure-leak` answers once its file exists. Its other three flags resolve from the corpus vocabulary by the census's own measurement, but the verb has not been run here, and the round that closes MM2 is where that gets measured rather than assumed.
carry_forward_bullets: MM2 IS NOW A DESCRIBED EDIT AND NOT A SENTENCE, which makes it the next round's work rather than the ledger's: give `values_for` the baseline store's path, return it for `--against`, and assert the two things that keep the closure from being empty. Its cost is not the wiring but the constants — the census's `unaskable` list is asserted by name today, and the three walks divide by how many reads were asked.

The trap generalises past this pair and is worth carrying as a rule: making an unaskable read askable is only progress if the read's answer can MOVE. Round 1069.decision_summary:
A gate that resolved its own tree from its own location, and the round that
named this failure before committing it.

Round 1066 gave the pre-commit hook one definition of the separate-workspace
checks by having it call the script CI runs. That push turned `main` red. The
hook's own smoke test builds a fixture repository with a synthetic separate
workspace and runs THIS repository's real hook over it — and two assumptions
broke at once. The hook looked for the script relative to its WORKING DIRECTORY,
which in that test is the fixture, where no such script exists. And the script
resolved the tree to check from its own `$BASH_SOURCE`, so even when found it
would have walked this checkout rather than the caller's.

Both are the same mistake in two places: a tool that is handed a tree and looks
somewhere else for it. So the script takes the WORKING DIRECTORY as the tree
under check — which is where a git hook starts and where CI runs it — and says
so out loud when that directory holds no `Cargo.toml`, rather than walking a
tree nobody asked about. And the hook resolves the script from its own path, so
it is found however the hook was invoked, and REFUSES THE COMMIT if it is not
there: a gate that quietly disappears when its script is out of reach is a gate
that stops existing without saying so.

THE TEST WAS ASSERTING A SENTENCE, and that is why it caught this. Its literal
expectation was the old copy's wording; what it is FOR is that the rejection
names the workspace. It now asserts both that and the gate the message came
from, so a future round that quietly re-copies those two commands into the hook
fails here rather than in CI.

AND THE REASON THIS REACHED CI AT ALL IS THIS SESSION'S OWN NAMED DEBT. The last
full workspace run before the push was taken BEFORE the hook changed — the same
shape this session filed one round earlier as XX14, evidence collected on a tree
that is not the tree that shipped. A hook change is a `crates/` test's subject
here, which is exactly the kind of coupling a person does not feel. The rule the
next round inherits: the suite runs on the tree that is about to be pushed, and
"nothing in `crates/` changed" is not a reason to skip it.
changes_bullets: `scripts/check-side-workspaces.sh`: the tree under check is the working directory, not the script's own location, and a directory with no root `Cargo.toml` is refused with the reason. A hook may run this repository's script over another tree; its own smoke test does exactly that.

`.githooks/pre-commit`: the gate script is resolved from the hook's own path rather than the working directory, and a missing one REJECTS the commit with where it looked instead of silently skipping the gate.

`crates/mnemosyne-cli/tests/git_hooks_smoke.rs`: the rejection assertion follows the message to its new home and adds the half that was missing — that the message came from the shared gate, so re-copying its commands into the hook fails this test rather than CI.
verification_bullets: The failure was read from the run rather than guessed: run 31135073034 on `a166084`, job `validate` FAILED with one annotation and `pre_commit_gates_a_separate_in_repo_workspace_the_root_gates_miss` panicking at `git_hooks_smoke.rs:485`. The other two jobs were green — `separate in-repo workspaces` succeeded in 12m52s against the 60-minute budget Round 1067 set, which is that budget's first real measurement.

`cargo test -p mnemosyne-cli --test git_hooks_smoke` is 10 passed / 0 failed here, and the whole workspace is 1779 passed / 0 failed over 152 targets ON THE TREE BEING COMMITTED — which is the discipline this round exists to restore.

Both directions of the working-directory rule were run: from the repository root the gate reports `checked 4 … skipped 0`; from `/tmp` it refuses with `/tmp has no Cargo.toml — run this from the root of the tree to check`.
`shellcheck` on the script and the hook exits 0.
carry_forward_bullets: THE CI RUN THIS FIXES WAS ALSO THE FIRST TO BUILD `bench`, and it passed: `separate in-repo workspaces` succeeded in 12 minutes 52 seconds, with `studio` skipped for the machine-derived reason printed in full — eight `../../pinion/crates/*` paths that no checkout of this repository contains. That closes the two things Round 1063 and Round 1065 could only carry as unverified, and it says the 60-minute budget has room rather than that it was needed.

The lesson is a rule and belongs where rules live: run the suite on the tree being pushed. This session filed that shape as a limit one round before walking into it, and the walk cost a red `main` and a round to undo.
The other open debts are untouched and still ranked: MM2 (designed in Round 1068, wiring plus two assertions), XX1, XX2 (three walks over one population, 14m21s going to 21m6s in CI), XX3, ZZ2.

Round 1071.decision_summary:
One sweep, three laws — and the reason it was three was the file layout.

Round 1061 recorded XX2 as a tidiness debt: three walks build the same 312-store
population and ask the same panel three times over. The run this session's push
started made it something else. The `validate` job took 26m45s of a 30-minute
budget — 14m21s at Round 1060, 21m6s at Round 1061, 26m45s now — and the same
suite measured the three walks at 220.53s, 191.08s and 139.94s. That is 9m12s,
the dominant term, and every future widening of the population multiplies it by
three. Two more rounds of the same growth turn the gate red, and the round
waiting behind this one (MM2) ADDS panel probes to every store in the
population.

WHY IT WAS BUILT THREE TIMES IS NOT A DECISION ANYONE MADE. A file under
`tests/` is a separate integration-test BINARY, and separate binaries are
separate processes: they can share a definition, which is what `common` already
is, but they cannot share a computation. The three walks each called the same
shared builders and each paid for them. So the three files are now three MODULES
of one binary, `authoring_surface`, and `common::sweep()` builds the corpus, the
panel and every trial ONCE for the process. Each law keeps its own name, its own
printout and its own assertions — the point is one sweep, not one law.

WHAT SHAPED THE SUBSTRATE WAS A MEASUREMENT, NOT A PREFERENCE. The obvious form
— memoize the parsed panel per trial — does not fit in memory: one panel of this
corpus is most of a megabyte of JSON before parsing, the parsed form is several
times that, and there are 312 of them. So the sweep holds THE BYTES EACH READ
PRINTED, and hands a consumer a parsed copy for the length of its own iteration.
Parsing three times is nothing beside the process launches this removes, and the
held size is PRINTED by the sweep rather than assumed, so a population that
outgrows the choice says so instead of being discovered as an OOM.

MEASURED AFTER: the same command, the same nine tests, 212.31s against 551.55s
— 339.24s off the suite, 61%. (An isolated run while a sibling repo was
compiling read 342.28s; both are here because the machine is shared and the
number moves with it.)

THE PROOF THAT THIS CHANGED NOTHING BUT THE COST is that no pinned number moved.
These three walks pin the census buckets, the CARRIED rows by name, the
subject-agreement backlog, the accounted/unaccounted field lists — dozens of
constants derived from the population. A sweep that had drifted from what the
three built for themselves would have moved one of them. None moved.
changes_bullets: `common::sweep()` — the corpus, the panel, the baseline and every trial, built once per test binary and memoized. A trial holds the corruption and either the write path's REFUSAL or a `Seen`: the bytes each read printed plus the sidecar the import wrote. `Seen::parsed()` hands a consumer a `Panelled` for the length of its own iteration, which is the only form that fits — 312 parsed panels do not. The sweep PRINTS what it holds.

The three walks are three modules of one binary, `tests/authoring_surface.rs`, rather than three files under `tests/`: a file there is a separate BINARY and separate binaries share no computation, which is the whole of why the population was built three times. Each keeps its name, its printout and its pins; what moved is where the population comes from.
The corruption closures gained `Send + Sync` so the memo can be a `OnceLock` — the three `#[test]`s run as threads of one process and the first to ask builds the sweep for all of them.
verification_bullets: THE SAVING IS MEASURED, ON THE SAME NINE TESTS UNDER THE SAME COMMAND. A full `cargo test -p mnemosyne-cli` run before: three binaries at 220.53s + 191.08s + 139.94s = 551.55s. The same command after: one binary at 212.31s. That is 339.24s — 61% — off a suite whose CI job had reached 26m45s of a 30-minute budget.

THE MACHINE IS SHARED AND THE NUMBER MOVES WITH IT, which is why both readings are here rather than the flattering one. An isolated run of the merged binary while a sibling repo was compiling took 342.28s; the 212.31s reading is the full-suite run, the same shape as the 551.55s it is compared against. Neither is a claim about a CI runner, and the honest floor on the saving is what the duplication was: three builds of the population became one.

NO PINNED NUMBER MOVED, which is the whole of the evidence that this changed cost and not measurement. The three walks pin the play-break census (Refused 56 / Caught 81 / Reported 159 / Carried 16 / Inert 0), the CARRIED rows by name, the 74-pair read-agreement backlog with its counts, the accounted and not-a-count-of-names field lists, and the rule verdicts with their authored distributions. All nine tests pass with every constant as it stood.

THE PRINTED COST IS THE SWEEP'S OWN: `sweep: N trial(s), M refused by the write path, X MiB of answer bytes held for the process`. It surfaces exactly where the three walks' own printouts do — on a failing test, or under `--nocapture`; a plain `cargo test` run captures all of it, which was checked rather than assumed. So it is a diagnosis beside the assertion, not a metric anyone watches. The choice it records was measured first and the alternative rejected: one panel of this corpus is 580 KiB of JSON across 31 answers, the full panel is larger, the parsed form is several times that, and 312 of them do not fit.

The removed duplication was real work, not idle time: each of the three built 312 workspaces through the real import path and asked ~68 shipped reads on each — roughly 22,000 process launches per walk, 66,000 across the three, now 22,000.
carry_forward_bullets: MM2 IS THE NEXT ROUND, and it is now affordable. Round 1070 shipped `project-world`, the artifact the panel must ask the corpus to produce before `--against` can be supplied; what remains is running it into the baseline workspace, returning those paths from `values_for`, giving `--truth-frame` the frame vocabulary it has never had, and owning the constant churn. Every probe it adds is paid ONCE now rather than three times.

THE SWEEP IS SHARED WITHIN A BINARY, NEVER ACROSS ONE. Any future law over this population belongs in `authoring_surface` as a fourth module; putting it in its own file under `tests/` silently buys a fourth copy of the population, and nothing in the tree says so except this sentence and the module doc. A gate that would catch it — "no test file outside `authoring_surface` calls `corruptions`" — is describable and was not built.

WHAT THE MEMO COSTS IS PRINTED AND NOT BOUNDED. The sweep reports the answer bytes it holds; it does not refuse to run when they grow. The bound that matters is the machine's, and the honest form of it is the number in the log rather than a constant nobody re-measures.

Round 1072.decision_summary:
MM2 closed: the panel asks the corpus to MAKE the argument it cannot declare.

Two render-acceptance gates have sat outside every population this arc derives
since Round 1051, named in the census's own assertion as "the reads this corpus
cannot ask without inventing an argument". Round 1051 wrote down why they
survived the round that halved that list: what they need is a FILE, and no
vocabulary can supply a file. Round 1068 designed a fixture; Round 1070 ran that
design, refuted it, and shipped the operation the gates actually require. This
round is the seam between them.

THE SEAM WAS NOT A PATH, IT WAS A REQUEST. `values_for` answers with values read
out of the store, which is exactly why it could not answer `--against`: the
value is a file. But it is not a file the corpus HOLDS either — it is the
single-world projection of the corpus, which the corpus must be ASKED to
produce. So `values_for` takes the workspace as well as the store, `panel` asks
`project-world` for one projection per registered world before it derives any
argument, and `--against` is answered with the files that are then there. A
corpus nobody projected supplies no value and its gates stay unaskable, which is
the truth about that corpus rather than a path to nothing.

AND THE FIXTURE IS FROZEN AT THE BASELINE, CARRIED. Every corrupted workspace
receives a COPY of the baseline's projections under the same relative names. The
name is relative on purpose: the panel's argv is reused against 312 stores and
an absolute path into a temp directory would put a different string in the
read's label on every run. The COPY is the whole mechanism — a world's telling
does not change because its road did, and re-projecting the corrupted store
would hand the gate its own answer and report clean forever.

ROUND 1068 ALSO ASSUMED `--truth-frame` ALREADY RESOLVED. It did not: the
vocabulary had no arm for it, so the leak gate had no argv the panel could build
even once its file existed. A truth frame is a frame; it now reads the same
store vocabulary `--frame` does.

own measure of what stands between an authoring slip and the runtime — moved
three rows from REPORTED to CAUGHT: 56 / 81 / 159 / 16 became 56 / 84 / 156 /
16. The three are the fork attachment points, `sc-22/order.from` on each of the
corpus's three forks. Move one and that world's frozen prose is left standing on
a node the world no longer walks; every other shipped read exits 0 and some
reclassify, which is why they sat in REPORTED for twenty rounds. The gate that

if the read's answer can MOVE. A read wired to a fixture it cannot disagree with
turns a hole the census PRINTS into a green cell nobody questions, which is
strictly worse — an unasked read is visible and an inert one is not. Three tests
stand on the shared sweep and discharge it: the gates are on the panel at all,
the fixture they were handed is not empty, and some authorable edit moves what
they say.

Round 1073.decision_summary:
The assertion measured the machine, and the machine said no.

The push that landed Rounds 1070-1072 turned `separate in-repo workspaces` red.
The failure is in `bench`, which this session never touched, and it is one test:
`sled-baseline`'s `many_writers_show_some_conflicts` ran 8 writers over 4 hot
keys for 500 ms and required `total_conflicts > 0`, reading a zero as "CAS
detection broken?". A CI runner produced zero.

IT IS NOT BROKEN, AND THE TEST COULD NEVER HAVE SAID SO. A scheduler that
serialises eight threads produces zero CAS conflicts with a perfectly working
compare-and-swap; contention is an OUTCOME of how the machine happened to
interleave, not a property of the store. The assertion was over the runner, and
it had been passing because the runner had been fast enough — which is the
definition of a test whose green means nothing in particular.

WHAT IT MEANT TO CHECK IS CONSTRUCTIBLE IN ONE THREAD: read a value, move it,
then CAS with the value you read and require the refusal. That is the property —
a stale expected value is rejected, and the refused write does not land — and it
holds on every machine because nothing about it is a race.

The throughput run stays, asserted on what it GUARANTEES: commits happen, every
writer reports, and every attempt is a commit or a conflict, which is the
report's own arithmetic. Conflicts are printed and never required.

WHY THIS IS THE FIX RATHER THAN A RETRY OR AN IGNORE: a retry loop would still
be asking the machine, with a longer question; an `#[ignore]` would delete the
only check that CAS refuses anything. Both leave the property untested. R1069
went red the same way — a suite run on a tree that was not the one pushed — and
the answer there was the same shape: assert the thing that is true rather than
the thing that usually happens.
changes_bullets: `bench/crates/sled-baseline/src/concurrent.rs`: `many_writers_show_some_conflicts` is replaced by two tests that between them cover what it was reaching for. `a_stale_expected_value_is_refused_by_cas` moves a value under a held read and requires the CAS to refuse AND the refused write not to land — single-threaded, so it says the same thing on every machine. `many_writers_commit_and_every_attempt_is_accounted` keeps the eight-writer throughput run and asserts only its guarantees: commits > 0, all eight writers report, and per-writer commits + conflicts equals the reported totals. The conflict count is printed, never required.
verification_bullets: `scripts/check-side-workspaces.sh bench` — the gate CI runs, run whole here: 9 tests in `sled-baseline` green (was 8 with one flaking), fmt and clippy -D warnings clean across the workspace.

THE RUN THAT FOUND IT WAS READ, ANNOTATIONS AND ALL (R893): run `31142269154` on `01cd95b` — MSRV ✓ 49s, `validate` ✓ **12m22s**, `separate in-repo workspaces` ✗ 12m37s with one annotation, `Process completed with exit code 101`, resolving to `-p sled-baseline --lib` and the single assertion above.

AND THE SAME RUN CARRIES THIS SESSION'S HEADLINE MEASUREMENT: `validate` went 26m45s to **12m22s** — 89% of its 30-minute budget down to 41%. Round 1071 shared one sweep across three walks and Round 1072 widened the panel from 68 questions to 79 on top of that; the net is more than half the job's wall clock returned. XX2 was booked as a tidiness debt and was paying for a timeout.
carry_forward_bullets: ⚠ THE BENCH WORKSPACE HAS ONLY EVER RUN IN CI TWICE. Round 1063 put it under a gate, Round 1069's push built it for the first time, and this is the second run — the first to disagree. A test that depends on scheduling is exactly what a workspace nobody ran accumulates, and there is no reason to believe this was the only one; the population of timing-dependent assertions in `bench` has not been swept, only this one instance repaired.

⛳ THE GREEN THAT PRECEDED IT PROVED NOTHING. `many_writers_show_some_conflicts` passed locally and in one CI run before failing in the next, with no code between them touching `bench`. Any assertion whose subject is "did the machine interleave" has that shape, and the honest reading of its history is that it was never evidence.

Round 1074.decision_summary:
The sweep names the target that may build it, and the compiler enforces it.

Round 1071 merged three walks into one binary because three files under
`tests/` are three BINARIES and separate binaries share no computation. It
saved 61% of that suite. Then it wrote down what stood between the tree and a
fourth copy: "nothing in the tree says so except this sentence and the module
doc. A gate that would catch it is describable and was not built." A
describable gate that was not built is undone work, not a limit.

WHAT THE GATE HAD TO BE ABOUT WAS MEASURED FIRST, AND THE CARRY NAMED THE WRONG
THING. It said the hazard was calling `common::corruptions` from another file.
It is not: `authorable_population` — the population's own oracle, and rightly
its own binary since it judges the DERIVATION rather than the surface — calls
`corruptions` five times and the whole binary runs in 4.12s. Deriving the edits
is nearly free. What costs is APPLYING 312 of them and asking every advertised
read about each, which is `sweep()`, and the memoization that makes it cheap is
a `OnceLock` — per PROCESS. So a second binary calling `sweep()` shares
absolutely nothing; it pays the entire 212s again, and the only symptom is that
the suite takes longer. That is the same defect Round 1071 removed, re-entering
by the same door.

SO THE SWEEP LEFT THE SHARED MODULE. `tests/common/` is where a definition
every binary may use belongs; the sweep is a computation exactly one binary may
run, and a single-owner thing in a shared home is a hazard held back by a
comment. It is now `tests/surface/sweep.rs`, which declares its OWNER and
checks it in a `const` — Cargo sets `CARGO_CRATE_NAME` to the test target being
compiled, so "which binary is this being compiled into" is a compile-time fact.
Including the module anywhere else is a BUILD ERROR whose message names the
right move. Not a lint, not a convention, not a scan of source text for a
function name: the fourth population became unbuildable.

MOVING IT OUT FROM UNDER `#![allow(dead_code)]` IMMEDIATELY FOUND DEAD DATA.
That allow is correct where it is — each test binary uses a different part of
the shared module, so unused-there is not unused — but it also covered a struct
only ONE binary ever reads, and the first compile in its new home said
`Sweep::manifests` and `Sweep::held_bytes` are never read. They are the shape
Round 1062 found in the injection harness's `exit_code`: recorded, carried for
the life of the process, consulted by nobody. Both are gone. The manifests
build the trials and the held size is printed by the builder; neither needed a
field, and a law that comes to want one adds it in the round that reads it.

THE GATE'S REFUSING ARM WAS RUN, NOT REASONED ABOUT. A `const` assertion that
holds proves only its true side — a predicate answering `true` for every name
would satisfy it identically — so the false side was put to the compiler by
adding the module to `authorable_population` and building: E0080, with the
message. And because that arm can never fire in a green tree, a `#[test]` holds
the predicate to refusing the names it must refuse, including a prefix and a
suffix of the owner's own name, and asserts the true side against the REAL
`CARGO_CRATE_NAME` rather than a literal, so a rename cannot leave the gate
guarding nothing.
changes_bullets: `tests/surface/sweep.rs` — the sweep, `Answer`, `Panelled`, `ask_panel`, `Seen`, `Trial` and `Sweep`, moved out of `tests/common/` because they are a computation with exactly one owner rather than a definition every binary shares. It carries `OWNER = "authoring_surface"`, a `const fn owned_by`, and `const _: () = assert!(owned_by(env!("CARGO_CRATE_NAME")), ...)`: Cargo names the test target it is compiling, so including this module from any other test file fails to BUILD, with a message that names where the new law belongs instead.

`Sweep::manifests` and `Sweep::held_bytes` are removed. They were never read; the shared module's blanket `#![allow(dead_code)]` — correct there, since each binary uses a different part of it — had been hiding that in a struct only one binary reads. The manifests build the trials and the held size is printed by the builder, so neither needed a field.

`sweep::the_sweep_names_the_target_that_may_build_it` asks the predicate the question the `const` cannot: that it REFUSES foreign target names, including a prefix and a suffix of the owner's own, and that its true side holds for the real `CARGO_CRATE_NAME` rather than for a literal.

Round 1075.decision_summary:
The sweep Round 1073 asked for, and the refuter the assertions never had.

Round 1073 repaired one test that measured the machine and said plainly what it
had not done: "there is no reason to believe this was the only one; the
population of timing-dependent assertions in `bench` has not been swept, only
this one instance repaired." That is not a limit. It is a sentence describing
work, which makes it undone work.

THE SWEEP FOUND THE SAME DEFECT UNREPAIRED, IN THE SAME WORDS. `direct-impl`'s
`many_writers_show_some_aborts` ran 8 writers over 4 hot keys for 500 ms and
required `total_aborts > 0`, reading a zero as "race detection broken?" — the
identical assertion over the identical workload with the identical comment, in
the crate next door. Round 1073 fixed sled and did not look sideways.

AND IT FOUND A THIRD SHAPE NOBODY HAD NAMED. Every concurrent test in all three
baselines carried `assert!(report.total_commits > 0, "no commits in 200ms?")`.
That is the same defect one step weaker, and Round 1073 kept it as a guarantee.
It is not one: the writers run `while !stop`, the stop flag is set after the
sleep, and a writer thread the OS has not scheduled by then performs zero
iterations. With one writer and 200 ms on a loaded runner, zero commits is a
legal outcome of a perfectly working store — the same "it had been passing
because the runner had been fast enough" that turned main red.

SO THE RULE LIVES IN ONE PLACE AND IS SHORT. All three baselines already depend
on `workload-gen`, so the thing they must agree about needed no new crate:
`contention::WriterRun::assert_guarantees` holds a run to what is true whatever
the scheduler did — every requested writer reported, the per-writer rows sum to
the totals, the run took at least as long as it was asked to — and to nothing
else. Each backend maps its own report onto it, which is where that mapping
belongs, because only that type knows which of its counters is the contention
one (`total_conflicts` for sled and LMDB, `total_aborts` for an optimistic
transaction).

WHAT THE PROPERTIES WERE REACHING FOR IS CONSTRUCTIBLE IN ONE THREAD, and that
is where they are asserted now: for RocksDB, read a key for update, let a
committed transaction move it, and require the commit to be refused and the
refused write not to have landed; for LMDB, that a committed write is what the
next read returns. Neither involves a timer or a second thread, so neither can
be answered by the machine.

THE PART THAT MAKES THIS MORE THAN THREE REPAIRS is that every backend asks
`assert_guarantees` of a run with ONE writer as well as of the contended run. A
single writer is the limiting case of the schedule a loaded machine is allowed
to produce — no overlap at all, so every contention counter is deterministically
zero. Any future claim that needs writers to collide dies there, in every
backend, in the round it is written, instead of on whichever CI runner is slow
enough first. That refuter is what the original assertions never had, and its
absence is the whole reason they survived a local green, a CI green, and then
failed.
changes_bullets: `workload-gen::contention` — `WriterRun` and `assert_guarantees`, THE one definition of what a run of concurrent writers supports whatever the scheduler did: every requested writer reported, the per-writer rows sum to the totals, the run took at least as long as it was asked to. Nothing about a commit or a collision having happened is on the list, and the module says why. It lives in `workload-gen` because all three baselines already depend on it, so the rule needed no new crate and has no second copy to drift from.

Each backend maps its own report onto the rule (`ThroughputReport::writer_run` / `AbortRateReport::writer_run`), which puts the "which counter is the contention one" decision in the type that knows: `total_conflicts` for sled and LMDB, `total_aborts` for RocksDB's optimistic transactions.

`direct-impl::many_writers_show_some_aborts` is gone and its property is asserted deterministically: `a_read_that_moved_underneath_is_refused_at_commit` reads a key for update, lets a committed transaction move it, and requires the commit to be refused and the refused write not to have landed. `lmdb-baseline` gains `a_committed_write_is_what_the_next_read_returns`, the single-threaded form of the `total_commits > 0` it used to assert over a timer.

Every baseline now asks `assert_guarantees` of a ONE-WRITER run as well as of the contended one, and `total_commits > 0` is gone from all six tests — reported by `WriterRun::observed`, never required.
verification_bullets: THE REFUTER WAS FIRED, AND WHICH TESTS CAUGHT IT IS THE MEASUREMENT. `assert!(self.contended > 0)` was injected into `assert_guarantees` and the four crates run: 7 red — the solo-writer test in all three baselines, `workload-gen`'s own `a_run_that_never_collided_and_never_committed_is_still_guaranteed`, and two `should_panic` tests that panicked with the injected message instead of their own. The file was restored from a copy taken before the injection, and `grep` for the marker returns 0.

WHAT STAYED GREEN UNDER THE INJECTION IS THE POINT. The CONTENDED runs of sled and direct-impl passed with a contention floor in place, because on a 32-core machine 8 writers over 4 hot keys do collide. That is exactly the state Round 1073's assertion was in for every green it ever produced. Only the no-overlap arm refuses it here, and it refuses it on any machine.

ALL THREE BASELINES AND THE SHARED RULE PASS, on the tree as committed: `cargo test --manifest-path bench/Cargo.toml --workspace --no-fail-fast` = 198 passed / 0 failed over 31 targets (191 before this round: +4 for the shared rule's own tests, +3 net across the baselines).

THE FULL SIDE-WORKSPACE GATE PASSES: `scripts/check-side-workspaces.sh` = checked 4 (bench studio tools/experiment-harness tools/injection-harness), skipped 0, 269 passed / 0 failed over 36 targets, fmt and clippy -D warnings clean. The gate caught this round's own unformatted code before the commit did, which is the R1066 repair working.

THE POPULATION WAS DERIVED, NOT GUESSED. The crates that spawn writer threads are `direct-impl`, `sled-baseline` and `lmdb-baseline`; `schema-bench` matched a first search only because `blob_invalidate_scope(` contains the token, and it has no thread at all. Three files, six tests, all six now asserted only on what a schedule cannot change.
carry_forward_bullets: WHAT THE ONE-WRITER ARM CANNOT REFUTE is an assertion written OUTSIDE `assert_guarantees` — a test that reads `report.total_conflicts` directly and requires it non-zero would not go through the rule, and no arm here sees it. Making that unwritable means the contention counters cannot be a plain public `u64`: they would have to be a type whose accessor names them as observations. The reports are three unrelated structs that serialise to the measurement record, so that is a change to what `bench` PUBLISHES, not only to what it asserts, and it was not made in the round that had no measurement asking for it.

THE THREE BACKENDS SHARE A RULE, NOT A REPORT. `writer_run` is written once per backend because the three reports are three different types with different field names in three independently-built baselines; the shared crate holds the rule and the assertion, which is the part that could drift into disagreement. What is left per-crate is the mapping, and it is four lines each, next to the type it maps.

THE `elapsed_ms >= requested_ms` GUARANTEE IS THE WEAKEST OF THE THREE. It holds because the run sleeps for the requested duration before setting the stop flag and measures from before the spawn, so it is arithmetic rather than scheduling — but it is the one claim here that would become false if the run were ever restructured to stop early, and it would then look like a machine problem rather than a design change.

An account may name a list the answer does not spell — and the walk now says
which of "nothing the answer names" it means.

Round 1057 filed two numbers as a limit of the SEARCH rather than of the read,
in a sentence describing work: "an account here is composed as a UNION of named
lists, and a subset selected by a field's value is not a union of anything.
Teaching the search filtered subsets is the next round's work, and it is not
free: the hypothesis space multiplies by every (list, field, value)."
`report-spec-map` names every section AND that section's `coverage_class`, so
`summary.by_class.informative_exempt` is exactly the sections carrying that
class. A consumer holding the answer can say what the number counts. The walk
could not, and said so as though the read were at fault.

A PLACE IS NO LONGER ALWAYS A FIELD. `Place` is a type rather than a formatted
key because the third component is authored content — a classifier is any scalar
field of a record, so its value can be a `claim` or a `title` holding whatever
words the walk would print around it, and two triples printing alike would be
one key in a scope, each silently taking the other's ids.

THE VOCABULARY IS WHERE THE BOUND BELONGS, AND THAT COST A MEASUREMENT TO LEARN.
Letting classified places into the union search ran the process to 23.9 GiB
resident and 24.2 GiB of swap on a 31 GiB host shared with sibling checkouts,
filled swap to 100%, and finished nothing in 22m33s: `accountings` accumulates
every account it finds, and the count of unions reaching a given size grows with
the vocabulary. The answer it was buying is one nobody can read either — a
number explained by any of a hundred thousand surviving hypotheses is a number
nothing has explained. Cost and precision failed in the same direction, which is
what says the bound is on what an account may SAY, not on how hard the walk
tries: a selection is a whole account or it is not an account.

"ONE CLASS IS NOT A CLASSIFICATION" WAS A RULE HERE FOR ONE RUN AND WAS WRONG:
it is true of one answer and false of a population. A key holding a single value
across the unedited store selects everything it sorts THERE, so proposing it
looks redundant — and it is exactly the description that stops being redundant
when an edit splits the value, which is the only moment this walk asks about.

AND THE INSTRUMENT NOW DISTINGUISHES ITS OWN SILENCE. "NOTHING THE ANSWER NAMES"
was one sentence for two findings: the walk proposed the right account and a
store refuted it (a fact about the READ), or the walk never proposed it (a limit
of THIS SEARCH, saying nothing about the read). Each unaccounted number now
prints what the unedited store SAID, how many accounts were proposed, and how
many named a class. The first run of that found `report-quest-graph
quests[].locators[].scene_ordinal` has had ZERO accounts proposed for it since
Round 1057 — its verdict was never evidence — and that `by_class.normative_gap`
is 0 in the unedited store because no section carries that class, so there is no
place for an account to be made of. A class with no rows is not a place; that is
the rule `accountings` already states for the frame whose view is empty, met
from the other side.

AND THE ROUND SHIPPED A BROKEN REFERENCE THAT NOTHING IN THIS REPOSITORY LOOKS
AT. Renaming the function that says which places the search composes with left
two references to the name it no longer has — one in a `///` doc comment on
`accountings`, one in a plain `//` comment inside `scope_of`. Both are repaired
here, and the reason neither was caught is worth more than the repair: rustdoc's
`broken_intra_doc_links` is the shipped resolver for exactly this question, and
`cargo doc` does not document integration-test targets, so not one of the laws
this arc has built over twenty rounds has ever had its cross-references
resolved by anything. `cargo rustdoc --test <name>` can point that resolver at
them; that gate is the next round's, and it reaches only the `///` half — a
reference inside an ordinary comment is prose, and no tool resolves prose.
changes_bullets: `counted_without_naming.rs` — `Place` is a type, not a formatted key: `Spelled(field)` is what the answer prints, `Classified { field, key, value }` is the ids one field names in the records where another holds one value. `Scope` and `Accounting` are keyed by it, so a place whose printed form collides with another can no longer take its ids.

`classifiers_of` derives the classifying fields from the record itself — every scalar string or boolean, never a number, because using a count to sort the names would let a count excuse itself with another count. `classes_matching` states the one rule: a key taking fewer values than there are ids it sorts is classifying them, and one taking as many is naming them one apiece.

A classified place enters `accountings` as a WHOLE one-place account rather than a term the union search may compose, and the doc comment carries the measurement that bought that bound (23.9 GiB resident, 24.2 GiB swap, nothing finished in 22m33s). `spelled` is what the union search still walks.

`Proposed` splits "nothing the answer names" into its two findings — what the unedited store said, how many accounts were proposed, how many named a class, and the smallest — so a number the search never reached is no longer printed as a number a store refuted.

`ACCOUNTED_FOR_ONLY_BY_A_CLASS` asserts what the wider vocabulary bought, because a wider search makes leaving `NOT_A_COUNT_OF_NAMES` strictly easier and the shrink alone is no evidence: a field is on it when EVERY surviving account names a classified place, in all 93 stores.

Round 1077.decision_summary:
A citation to a Round is gated. A citation to an ITEM was gated by nothing, and
34 of them in shipped source named things that are not there.

Round 255 built the rule that a `Round NNN` written in code must exist in the
ledger, and `validate-code-refs` enforces it on every commit, because an
invented round number is silent corruption of the audit trail — no compiler
catches it and `git blame` chases the wrong rationale. The same sentence is true
word for word of `[`foo`]`. An agent following that link gets nothing, and
nothing anywhere in this repository ever checked.

THE RESOLVER WAS ALREADY SHIPPED AND HAD NEVER BEEN POINTED HERE. rustdoc's
`broken_intra_doc_links` answers exactly this question, and `cargo doc` had
apparently never been run over this workspace: its first run reported 34
unresolved links across the production crates. They are four shapes, and only
the first is a typo:

- NAMES THAT NO LONGER EXIST. `AuditAppender::with_fanout` (the method is
  `with_broadcast_capacity_and_fanout`), `InMemoryAuditBroker::subscriber` (it is
  `subscribe`), `resolve_explicit_cli_path` (nothing by that name anywhere),
  `MAIN_BRANCH` (the constant is `MAIN_BRANCH_ID`). Worst of these:
  `mnemosyne-query`'s module doc advertises the crate's four entry points, and
  TWO of the four — `related_sections` and `workspace_section_id_set` — have not
  existed for rounds. The front page of a crate listed an API by names it does
  not have.
- LINKS ACROSS A DEPENDENCY THAT ISN'T ONE. `mnemosyne-atomic` linked twice to
  `mnemosyne_validate::scan_content_drift`, and both reference definitions had
  drifted into the WRONG doc block on the way — one of them is the entire doc
  comment of the function beneath it.
- A FIELD OR METHOD NAMED WITHOUT ITS TYPE (`edge_costs`, `kind_migration_report`,
  `Line`, `AtomicSnapshot`, `Channel`, `MapFrontierReport`).
- PROSE THAT LOOKED LIKE A LINK: `[early]`, `[late]`, `first_at[world]`,
  `[[publishable_override_ledger]]`, `[`Arc::new(NoopAuditFanout)`]`. Brackets in
  a doc comment are markdown whether or not they were meant as one.

AND THE GATE HAS A CEILING THE WORLD SETS, MEASURED FROM THE ARTIFACT RATHER
THAN ASSUMED. rustdoc cannot see a `#[test]` or a `#[cfg(test)]` item: the
generated documentation for one test target carries `fn.spelled.html`,
`enum.Place.html` and every other private non-test item, and not one page for
any of its thirteen tests. So the 106 integration-test targets are OUT OF THIS
GATE'S REACH — `cargo doc` does not document them, and pointing `cargo rustdoc
--test` at one reports every law-cites-law reference as unresolved, which is
this codebase's dominant idiom and not a defect. Reaching them needs a SECOND
authority beside rustdoc, and the shipped one exists: a test binary's `--list`
is the harness's own answer to "what tests are here". A link is a defect when it
is unresolved AND names nothing on that list. That is the next round, and
Round 1076 — which shipped two references to a function it had renamed, and
found them by reading — is the reason it is worth building.
changes_bullets: `.githooks/pre-commit` Gate 5a and a `validate` CI step run `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items`, beside the clippy gate they share a trigger with. `--document-private-items` because the internals here are documented for an agent reading them, so a link into one is a real reference rather than a leak.

34 unresolved links repaired across 11 crates. Where the item exists the link now names it in full (`AtomicStore::edge_costs`, `mnemosyne_core::AtomicSnapshot`, `crate::types::Line`, `tonic::transport::Channel`, `mnemosyne_validate::continuity::MapFrontierReport`, `mnemosyne_engine::passages_to_parts`); where it was renamed the link now names the real one (`with_broadcast_capacity_and_fanout`, `subscribe`, `related_sections_with_atomic`, `AtomicStore::atomic_section_id_set`); where nothing exists or the crate is not a dependency the link becomes a plain code span, which is what an unlinkable name honestly is.

Two `mnemosyne_validate::scan_content_drift` reference-link definitions are removed rather than requalified: `mnemosyne-atomic` does not depend on `mnemosyne-validate`, so the link could never have resolved, and both definitions had drifted into the doc block of the following item.

No link is left pointing at a `#[test]` or `#[cfg(test)]` item, because rustdoc cannot resolve one: the three in `continuity.rs` and `PlayableProjection::from_report` are plain code spans now, and `from_report`'s says out loud that it is test-only.
verification_bullets: THE GATE WAS FIRED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, which is the only way an empty report
means anything. Injected one link naming nothing (`related_sections_that_do_not_
exist`, substituted with the count asserted at exactly 1): the gate exits 101
with `error: unresolved link` and `could not document mnemosyne-query`. The file
was restored by rewriting the bytes from a copy taken before the injection (a
fresh mtime, never `cp -p`), `cmp` reports byte-identical and the marker count is
0. On the restored tree the same gate exits 0.
34 UNRESOLVED LINKS BEFORE, 0 AFTER, both measured by the gate itself over
`cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items`.
THE CEILING WAS MEASURED FROM THE GENERATED ARTIFACT, not argued. With
`--document-private-items`, `cargo rustdoc -p mnemosyne-cli --test
authoring_surface` emits `fn.spelled.html`, `fn.accountings.html`,
`enum.Place.html`, `struct.Proposed.html` and every other private item of that
target — and zero pages for any of its 13 tests. Pointed at that target the lint
reports 7 unresolved links, every one of them naming a real `#[test]` function
that `--list` on the same target's binary prints. That is the population the
next round's second authority is for.
Full workspace suite, `validate-workspace`, clippy `-D warnings` and `cargo fmt
--check` on the committed tree; the pre-commit hook ran its own copy of the new
gate on the commit that added it.
carry_forward_bullets: UNDONE WORK, NOT A LIMIT — 106 integration-test targets are outside this gate, and the design that reaches them is measured rather than sketched: run `cargo rustdoc -p <pkg> --test <target> -- --document-private-items -D rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links` for every test target `cargo metadata` names, and take the harness's own `--list` on that target as the second authority. A link is a defect when it is unresolved AND names nothing the harness lists; a link that is unresolved but names a real test is what rustdoc structurally cannot see. Round 1076 shipped exactly the first kind and only a reading caught it.

A `#[test]` OR `#[cfg(test)]` ITEM IS INVISIBLE TO RUSTDOC, and no flag changes it — measured from the artifact, not inferred. That is why the gate above needs two authorities rather than a stricter lint, and why re-implementing resolution to reach them would be the second copy of a resolver the toolchain already ships.

`private_intra_doc_links` IS NOT GATED. 59 links resolve only because `--document-private-items` was passed and rustdoc says so each time; without the flag they would break. THE SECOND AUTHORITY, AND WHY IT DOES NOT LOOSEN THE LAW. A `#[test]` function
is expanded away outside test mode, so rustdoc cannot see one no matter what
flags it is given, and this codebase's test prose is written in exactly the
idiom that cites one (7 sites in `authoring_surface`). The gate asks the

WHAT COST TWO MEASUREMENTS TO LEARN, BOTH ABOUT CARGO RATHER THAN ABOUT THIS
REPOSITORY.

- Cargo does not hand a package's own library to the documentation unit of that
  package's INTEGRATION TESTS. The rustdoc command line carries an `--extern`
  for every dependency and none for the crate under test, so 29 of the 106 could
  not resolve their own crate and documented nothing, silently except for `could
  not document`. The missing `--extern` is put back from cargo's own artifact
  record — the crate name is the library target's name in the metadata, the path
  is the `.rmeta` cargo says it produced.
- It DOES hand one to binaries and to examples, and a second `--extern` for the
  same library is `E0464`, "multiple candidates", and documents nothing either.
  Three binaries came back unreached from the run whose repair for the tests was
  working perfectly. Benches and examples sit on OPPOSITE SIDES of that line,
  which no reasoning about "what a target is" would have produced, so
  `tests/gate.rs` puts all four kinds to cargo and reads the command lines it
  builds. If a later cargo changes any of those answers, that test goes red and
  says which.

targets", it is "every target with `test = true`", which includes the library
and the binaries. Selecting that way put binaries into the invocation carrying
the extern repair, where they were E0464 — invisibly, because the other
invocation had already documented them correctly. Every target is now named by
its own selector.

WIDENING IT IS NOT AN EFFORT QUESTION. `scan_coverage` asserts that every `.rs`
under the root is either scanned or excluded — that is why no Rust tree can
drift out — and it says `rust source(s)` because the universe it walks is
filtered to `.rs`. The generalisation is not "walk every file instead": every
file that MENTIONS a round includes `docs/.atomic/workspace.atomic.json`, which
is the ledger itself and cites nothing; it includes `ARCHITECTURE.md` with 55,
`RULEBOOK.md` with 9, and whatever `claudedocs/` holds. Widening the axis
therefore means DECIDING which trees this gate is responsible for across the
whole repository — documentation, design notes, the store — and that is a
decision, not a mechanical change. It is named here rather than made in passing.

tree named in `paths` is read whatever language it holds, and a tree not named
there is not read at all. Both directions, because a path entry that changes no

Round 1081 — a wait ends on a condition,.decision_summary:
In test code, a wait must end on a CONDITION, and the budget that bounds it must be NAMED. `tools/blind-waits` enforces both clauses over every workspace in this repository — the root one on every commit and every push, the six separate ones through `scripts/check-side-workspaces.sh` — and the nine sites the first run found are repaired here rather than carried.

WHY THIS ROUND. Round 1073 turned main red with `conflicts > 0` after running eight writers over four hot keys for 500 milliseconds: an assertion whose subject is how the scheduler interleaved, wearing the clothes of an assertion about the store. Round 1075 swept `bench` and found the same claim in a neighbouring crate under the same comment, plus a third shape (`commits > 0`) in six tests across three baselines. Both rounds recorded that the question had NOT been asked of the root workspace or of `tools/`, and the ledger carried that as AA12 from Round 1075 to here. `bench` has run in CI twice. The root workspace runs on every push.

WHAT ASKING FOUND. Nine sites: four waits that end on a clock and five budgets spelled where nobody reviews them. All nine are in `mnemosyne-server`, and one of the four has no red side at all — `zero_rate_sampling_drops_all_spans` slept 300 milliseconds and then required that the collector had received nothing, so a wait too SHORT does not fail it, it PASSES it, for exactly the reason the test exists to rule out. A hand list assembled by reading `tests/` would have been eight: the ninth is a budget inside a `#[cfg(test)]` module in `src/audit.rs`, and the gate found it on its first run. That is the third consecutive round in which the machine's census beat the author's pattern.

WHY A PARSER. The difference between a `sleep` that IS the synchronisation and a `sleep` that is the retry step of a poll is the entire law, and no text pattern sees it; neither can one tell test code from shipped code, where waiting is behaviour rather than a claim. The gate walks the same syntax tree the compiler reads (`syn`), takes its file census from `cargo metadata`, and lands every `.rs` under the workspace root in exactly one bucket — scanned, owned by a nested workspace, or under `target/` — so a tree nobody's list mentions cannot pass unexamined. It REPORTS ITS REACH and REFUSES (exit 2, distinct from exit 1) when the reach is empty or partial: an empty finding list is what a clean workspace looks like and what a workspace nobody opened looks like, which Round 1078 produced while believing the first.

THE REPAIRS ARE PROPERTIES, NOT LONGER SLEEPS. Three of the four blind waits are gone entirely, replaced by `common::quiesce`, which drives the traced system to rest: join the server (every handler future dropped, every span closed and queued), then shut the tracer provider down, which blocks until the collector has ANSWERED the flush. After it the collector holds everything it will ever hold, so there is nothing left to wait for. The fourth retries the rotated-identity handshake until it succeeds. The `src/audit.rs` budget did not need naming — it needed deleting: `AuditAppender::write` publishes to the broadcast channel inside the same synchronous call that does the durable put, so `try_recv` asserts the STRONGER property that the record is already in the subscriber's buffer when the append returns.

AND THE TESTS THE SUITE COMPILES TO NOTHING. `mnemosyne-server` declares `default = []`; its TLS and OTLP test files open with `#![cfg(feature = ...)]`. Under `cargo test --workspace`, which is what CI has run since Round 583, SIX integration test targets report `running 0 tests` — nine tests that have never run in CI, and four of this round's blind waits lived in them. A 50ms sleep called a "tiny grace" survives indefinitely when nothing executes it. carry_forward_bullets: THE GATE JUDGES THE SHAPE OF A WAIT, NOT WHAT ITS CONDITION IS ABOUT. `while Instant::now() < deadline { }` ends on a condition and names no budget at the site, so it satisfies both clauses while being a blind wait with extra steps. Telling "a condition about the system under test" from "a condition about the clock" is a semantic question, and no parser answers it — the loop that IS lawful (`tools/injection-harness`'s `until`) has exactly that head, with the real condition inside. Nothing in any of the seven workspaces has the degenerate shape; if one appears, it will be found by a reader, not by this.

NAMING A BUDGET IS NOT CHECKING IT. `const LIVENESS: Duration = Duration::from_millis(1)` passes clause two. That is deliberate rather than unfinished: a floor would be a number nobody measured, which is the thing clause two exists to stop. What naming buys is that the number is ONE decision with a comment beside it instead of five spread across five files, and a reviewer can find it. Judging the magnitude would need const evaluation across files (`common::LIVENESS` is resolved by the compiler, not by this walk) AND a constant to compare against that no measurement supports.

THE LAW READS RUST. A wait written in a shell script — `scripts/` has four, and the hook smoke test drives real `git` — is outside it, and extending the parser means a second grammar with its own notion of "loop" and "condition". This is a declared boundary of the corpus, not a claim that those trees are clean.

That measurement covers today's tree; it does not promise that a feature added to another crate tomorrow will be noticed, because what would notice is a gate over "every crate's non-default features", and nothing here builds one.

It is pinned by a test rather than by a comment: if that stopped holding, `resource_attributes_and_full_sampling_emit_to_collector` goes red, which is the same run that keeps the zero-rate test non-vacuous. A version bump that changes it produces a red, not a silence.

Round 1081 — a wait ends on a condition,.publishable_decision_summary:
In test code, a wait must end on a CONDITION, and the budget that bounds it must be NAMED. `tools/blind-waits` enforces both clauses over every workspace in this repository — the root one on every commit and every push, the six separate ones through `scripts/check-side-workspaces.sh` — and the nine sites the first run found are repaired here rather than carried.

WHY THIS ROUND. Round 1073 turned main red with `conflicts > 0` after running eight writers over four hot keys for 500 milliseconds: an assertion whose subject is how the scheduler interleaved, wearing the clothes of an assertion about the store. Round 1075 swept `bench` and found the same claim in a neighbouring crate under the same comment, plus a third shape (`commits > 0`) in six tests across three baselines. Both rounds recorded that the question had NOT been asked of the root workspace or of `tools/`, and the ledger carried that as AA12 from Round 1075 to here. `bench` has run in CI twice. The root workspace runs on every push.

WHAT ASKING FOUND. Nine sites: four waits that end on a clock and five budgets spelled where nobody reviews them. All nine are in `mnemosyne-server`, and one of the four has no red side at all — `zero_rate_sampling_drops_all_spans` slept 300 milliseconds and then required that the collector had received nothing, so a wait too SHORT does not fail it, it PASSES it, for exactly the reason the test exists to rule out. A hand list assembled by reading `tests/` would have been eight: the ninth is a budget inside a `#[cfg(test)]` module in `src/audit.rs`, and the gate found it on its first run. That is the third consecutive round in which the machine's census beat the author's pattern.

WHY A PARSER. The difference between a `sleep` that IS the synchronisation and a `sleep` that is the retry step of a poll is the entire law, and no text pattern sees it; neither can one tell test code from shipped code, where waiting is behaviour rather than a claim. The gate walks the same syntax tree the compiler reads (`syn`), takes its file census from `cargo metadata`, and lands every `.rs` under the workspace root in exactly one bucket — scanned, owned by a nested workspace, or under `target/` — so a tree nobody's list mentions cannot pass unexamined. It REPORTS ITS REACH and REFUSES (exit 2, distinct from exit 1) when the reach is empty or partial: an empty finding list is what a clean workspace looks like and what a workspace nobody opened looks like, which Round 1078 produced while believing the first.

THE REPAIRS ARE PROPERTIES, NOT LONGER SLEEPS. Three of the four blind waits are gone entirely, replaced by `common::quiesce`, which drives the traced system to rest: join the server (every handler future dropped, every span closed and queued), then shut the tracer provider down, which blocks until the collector has ANSWERED the flush. After it the collector holds everything it will ever hold, so there is nothing left to wait for. The fourth retries the rotated-identity handshake until it succeeds. The `src/audit.rs` budget did not need naming — it needed deleting: `AuditAppender::write` publishes to the broadcast channel inside the same synchronous call that does the durable put, so `try_recv` asserts the STRONGER property that the record is already in the subscriber's buffer when the append returns.

AND THE TESTS THE SUITE COMPILES TO NOTHING. `mnemosyne-server` declares `default = []`; its TLS and OTLP test files open with `#![cfg(feature = ...)]`. Under `cargo test --workspace`, which is what CI has run since Round 583, SIX integration test targets report `running 0 tests` — nine tests that have never run in CI, and four of this round's blind waits lived in them. A 50ms sleep called a "tiny grace" survives indefinitely when nothing executes it. A new `server-features` job runs `cargo test -p mnemosyne-server --all-features` AND clippy over the same build; the first lint of that build found a `MutexGuard` held across an await.

Round 1083 — ask the lister which worksp.decision_summary:
R1082's feature gate turned this branch red on its first push, and this repairs it: WHICH workspaces can be asked about on a given machine is `scripts/check-side-workspaces.sh --list`'s answer, consumed rather than written a second time.

WHAT HAPPENED. `studio` depends on the sibling `../pinion` checkout by path. That checkout exists on the machine this project is written on and does NOT exist on a GitHub runner, so `cargo metadata --manifest-path studio/Cargo.toml` fails there with "failed to load manifest for dependency `pinion-a11y`". R1082's gate asked every discovered workspace unconditionally and took the failure as its own: three of its four tests panicked and the `validate` job failed. The other four jobs of that run and the whole `evidence-replay` run were green — the defect was one test file's assumption about what is on disk.

THIS WAS A SOLVED PROBLEM TWELVE LINES AWAY. `check-side-workspaces.sh` has carried `missing_siblings` since R1079, which found exactly this: the shell gate had spent three rounds reporting `studio` as unformatted because of files in `../pinion`, and R1079 named the class — "a gate that fails on somebody else's file is a gate that gets ignored". R1082 wrote its own discovery beside that one and inherited none of it. Two implementations of "which workspaces are there and which can we ask about" is the drift R1066 corrected for fmt and clippy by making the hook call the script; the same correction applies here.

SO THE SCRIPT ANSWERS AND THE TEST CONSUMES. `--list` runs discovery and the sibling check and stops, printing `CHECKABLE <ws>` or the existing `SKIP <ws> — <reason>` line for each. The test adds the root workspace (which that script excludes by construction — it exists to reach the ones the root gates never compile), asks only the checkable ones, and PRINTS every skip with its reason. A workspace nobody can ask about is a fact; a fact that does not appear in the output is one nobody can act on.

THE BRANCH THIS MACHINE NEVER TAKES IS PINNED BY A TEST. The SKIP line only appears where a sibling checkout is absent — on a runner, and not here — which is precisely why the first version had no handling for it and why nothing local caught that. The reading of the lister's output is now a pure function with the SKIP string pinned against it, and the script's own SKIP behaviour was demonstrated by pointing it at a throwaway tree whose member names a path dependency outside that tree. Neither proof needed the sibling checkout touched: it belongs to another project and had a session live in it.
changes_bullets: `scripts/check-side-workspaces.sh` — a `--list` flag: discovery plus the sibling check, then stop. Prints `CHECKABLE <ws>` beside the existing `SKIP <ws> — <reason>`, runs no cargo, and is placed after the skip branch so it inherits it rather than restating it.

`crates/mnemosyne-cli/tests/feature_coverage_smoke.rs` — `workspaces()` now runs that lister and returns (askable, skipped-with-reason) instead of walking `git ls-files` itself. The root workspace is added here because the script excludes it by construction. Every skip is printed.

`parse_lister` is a pure function, and `the_lister_is_read_for_what_it_can_and_cannot_be_asked` pins the SKIP branch against the exact string the script prints — the branch this machine cannot take, and therefore the one that shipped unhandled.

`every_tracked_manifest_is_inside_a_workspace_this_gate_asks` counts a manifest under a SKIPPED workspace as accounted for. "Nobody could ask, and here is why" is a different answer from "nobody's list mentions it", and only the second is the failure that test exists for.

The run's other four jobs (`MSRV`, `item citations name items`, `separate in-repo workspaces`, `the server targets the workspace suite compiles to nothing`) were success, as was the whole `evidence-replay` run `31225638939` — so R1081's and R1082's substance held and one file's assumption about the disk did not.

THE LISTER EMITS SKIP — proved by pointing `check-side-workspaces.sh --list` at a throwaway tree holding one workspace whose member declares `path = "../../../../ghost-checkout"`, i.e. outside that tree: `SKIP side — its path dependencies leave this repository and are not on this machine: ../../../../ghost-checkout`. The first attempt at that fixture pointed the path INSIDE the fake root and came back `CHECKABLE`, which is the fixture being wrong rather than the rule — worth recording, because a fixture that does not reach the branch proves nothing about it. The sibling `../pinion` checkout was not touched in either attempt: it belongs to another project and had a session live in it.

Round 1083 — ask the lister which worksp.publishable_decision_summary:
R1082's feature gate turned this branch red on its first push, and this repairs it: WHICH workspaces can be asked about on a given machine is `scripts/check-side-workspaces.sh --list`'s answer, consumed rather than written a second time.

WHAT HAPPENED. `studio` depends on the sibling `../pinion` checkout by path. That checkout exists on the machine this project is written on and does NOT exist on a GitHub runner, so `cargo metadata --manifest-path studio/Cargo.toml` fails there with "failed to load manifest for dependency `pinion-a11y`". R1082's gate asked every discovered workspace unconditionally and took the failure as its own: three of its four tests panicked and the `validate` job failed. The other four jobs of that run and the whole `evidence-replay` run were green — the defect was one test file's assumption about what is on disk.

THIS WAS A SOLVED PROBLEM TWELVE LINES AWAY. `check-side-workspaces.sh` has carried `missing_siblings` since R1079, which found exactly this: the shell gate had spent three rounds reporting `studio` as unformatted because of files in `../pinion`, and R1079 named the class — "a gate that fails on somebody else's file is a gate that gets ignored". R1082 wrote its own discovery beside that one and inherited none of it. Two implementations of "which workspaces are there and which can we ask about" is the drift R1066 corrected for fmt and clippy by making the hook call the script; the same correction applies here.

SO THE SCRIPT ANSWERS AND THE TEST CONSUMES. `--list` runs discovery and the sibling check and stops, printing `CHECKABLE <ws>` or the existing `SKIP <ws> — <reason>` line for each. The test adds the root workspace (which that script excludes by construction — it exists to reach the ones the root gates never compile), asks only the checkable ones, and PRINTS every skip with its reason. A workspace nobody can ask about is a fact; a fact that does not appear in the output is one nobody can act on.

THE BRANCH THIS MACHINE NEVER TAKES IS PINNED BY A TEST. The SKIP line only appears where a sibling checkout is absent — on a runner, and not here — which is precisely why the first version had no handling for it and why nothing local caught that. The reading of the lister's output is now a pure function with the SKIP string pinned against it, and the script's own SKIP behaviour was demonstrated by pointing it at a throwaway tree whose member names a path dependency outside that tree. Neither proof needed the sibling checkout touched: it belongs to another project and had a session live in it.

`parse_lister` is a pure function, and `the_lister_is_read_for_what_it_can_and_cannot_be_asked` pins the SKIP branch against the exact string the script prints — the branch this machine cannot take, and therefore the one that shipped unhandled.

Round 1084 — every test compiled is one.decision_summary:
EVERY TEST THIS REPOSITORY COMPILES IS ONE SOME CI COMMAND RUNS. R1082 closed the level below: every cargo feature declared is compiled by somebody. Compiling is not running — an `--all-features` build keeps passing after every test behind those features is deleted — and this closes that gap with a gate whose two sides are both asked of the machine.

WHY THE OBVIOUS RULE IS NOT A RULE. R1081 found the defect class by hand: six `mnemosyne-server` integration targets printed `running 0 tests` under the workspace suite, nine tests had never run in CI, and four waits that end on a clock had survived inside them because nothing executed them. The instrument was free and printed on every push, and R1082 carried the open question of what to do with it: three binary unittest targets legitimately run zero tests, so "every target runs something" is false, and "every target somebody expected to run does" had no basis for the somebody. The basis is the tree itself. A test function exists because an author wrote it; the rule is that every one of them is executed, and the three quiet binaries hold none.

BOTH SIDES ARE ASKED, NEITHER IS A LIST. POPULATION: for each workspace `scripts/check-side-workspaces.sh --list` says this machine can build, `cargo test --workspace --all-features --no-run`, the test binaries read out of cargo's own `compiler-artifact` records, and each binary's `--list`. RUN: every `cargo test` this repository's workflows and its workspace lister issue, RE-ISSUED with `--list` appended to that command's own harness arguments — so whatever `-p`, `--test`, `--features` or `--ignored` it carries, cargo and libtest resolve them exactly as they do in CI. Nothing about a command is modelled; it is asked.

THE SUBTRACTION THAT MAKES IT MEAN ANYTHING. `--list` prints ignored tests too, measured rather than assumed: a binary with 39 tests and one `#[ignore]` answers 39 to `--list` and 1 to `--list --ignored`. So what a command LISTS is not what it RUNS, and the difference is exactly the ignored ones. A command that itself passes `--ignored` or `--include-ignored` runs what it lists; every other runs its list minus its own ignored list. Without that subtraction, nine of this round's eleven findings would have read as covered.

WHAT IT FOUND, FIRST RUN, ALL REAL. ELEVEN. Nine are Round 252 disablements against a document model Round 400 deleted — eight in `query_subcommand_smoke.rs` asserting on §43, §66 and `docs/DESIGN.md`, plus a `query_api_smoke_placeholder` with an empty body — ignored for 830 rounds, contributing zero, and retired here on the precedent this repository already set when `bench` carried eleven tests reading deleted documents. One is R880's proof that the revision a kit was authored under still builds and still eats the kit's original bytes: ignored for cost, with the command to run it written in its own header, and no job ran that command — so the one unmeasured assumption the whole `[tool] pin` design rests on went back to being unmeasured the day it was measured. It now runs in the `evidence-replay` job, which is where its risk lives (a pinned revision stops building because the world moved, which only a clock finds) and which already has what it needs: full history for `git archive`, a warm registry for old lockfiles. The eleventh is a `​```ignore` doc example in `mnemosyne-build-stamp`, a code sample no compiler had ever read, now `no_run`.

THE HOLE IT FOUND IN ITSELF, BEFORE SHIPPING. Its first run reported a population thirteen short of what `cargo test -- --list` prints. The difference was doc-tests: cargo's artifact record never mentions one, because a doc-test has no test binary. They were missing from the POPULATION and from the RUN set at once — invisible symmetrically, which produces no finding and therefore no evidence of itself. Closed by asking cargo directly with `--doc -- --list`, and it is what found the eleventh. Its first repair then made the gate refuse over three workspaces whose packages have no library, because `cargo test --doc` exits non-zero saying so — a gate rejecting for a reason outside its own law, the shape R1081 shipped and repaired inside its own round. Whether there is a library is now asked of `cargo metadata` before the probe, not read out of an error message cargo is free to reword.

ONE ANSWER TO WHAT CI RUNS. Three gates now ask that question, so the reader is a crate rather than a test module: `tools/ci-plan` owns which workflows exist, how one is parsed, how a shell line becomes a cargo invocation split at the bare `--`, and what the workspace lister says. R1083 is the argument in its sharpest form — a gate that re-derived which workspaces can be asked about turned this branch red on a runner with no sibling checkout — and the lister now also names the suite command it runs for each workspace, written once and read by both the runner and the gate.

POPULATION per askable workspace via `cargo test --workspace --all-features --no-run --message-format=json`, test binaries read off cargo's `compiler-artifact` records, each binary asked with `--list`; RUN per CI `cargo test`, re-issued with `--list` appended to that command's own harness arguments, minus the same command's `--list --ignored` answer unless it selects the ignored ones itself. Exit 0 / 1 / 2 are three answers: the law holds, tests are dark, the gate could not judge.

Only for commands with no target selector (`--test`, `--lib`, `--all-targets`, … all narrow away from doc-tests), and only when `cargo metadata` says the scope has a library — `cargo test --doc` on a bin-only package exits non-zero, and reading that as a refusal is the gate rejecting outside its own law.
