Reach on that run: 2149 tests compiled across 8 workspaces, 2138 run by 11 CI test commands. AFTER the repairs, on the tree this entry ships with: 2140 compiled across 8 workspaces, 2140 run by 12 CI test commands, dark 0, exit 0, in 73.4s fully warm on a 32-core machine. Local numbers; on a runner `studio` is skipped by the lister and both sides lose its one test.

THE GATE FOUND A HOLE IN ITSELF BEFORE IT SHIPPED, and it was found by disagreement rather than by reading: its population for the root workspace came to 1807 where `cargo test --workspace -- --list` prints 1811. Chased rather than assumed — the same 136 binaries listed independently summed to 1798, and the difference was 16 doc-test names and 3 tests added since. Doc-tests have no test binary, so cargo's `compiler-artifact` record never mentions one and they were missing from BOTH sides at once. `cargo test --doc -- --list` closed it, and the eleventh finding is what came out.

ITS FIRST REPAIR THEN REFUSED OVER THREE WORKSPACES — `studio`, `tools/experiment-harness`, `tools/injection-harness` — because `cargo test --doc` exits non-zero on a package with no library. That is the gate rejecting outside its own law (R1081's shape, repaired inside its own round). Whether a scope has a library is now asked of `cargo metadata`, and `a_package_with_no_library_has_no_doc_tests_and_that_is_an_answer` is the fixture that pins it.

THE MECHANISMS ARE NOT VACUOUS — `tools/unrun-tests/injection-sweep.json`, run through `tools/injection-harness`: control 9 passed / 0 failed, then six injections, 6/6 fired, missed 0, target drift 0. Each removes one mechanism: the `#[ignore]` subtraction, the doc-test probe, the library question, `--all-features` in the population, the build refusal, and the inversion of `dark()`. The last two exist because writing the sweep found two computations no test reached, and they now have one.

THE FIXTURES REACH THE BRANCHES A REAL TREE CANNOT BE ASKED TO PRODUCE: a crate carrying one plain test, one `#[ignore]`d test, one behind a feature and one doc example, plus a bin-only crate and a crate that does not compile. Adding an `#[ignore]` to this repository to test the gate would have created the very thing the gate rejects.

THE HEAVY TEST WAS RUN BEFORE THE JOB THAT RUNS IT WAS WRITTEN: `cargo test -p mnemosyne-cli --test pinned_revision_rechecks_evidence_smoke -- --ignored --nocapture` — 1 passed in 9.44s, deriving authoring revision `7d95e68`, building it, and showing today's binary refusing the same bytes. Putting a step into CI without running it once is how a repair turns main red.

ROOT WORKSPACE, whole suite: 154 targets, 1803 passed, 0 failed, 2 ignored — and the 2 are exactly the two `--ignored` tests the `evidence-replay` job now runs. `cargo fmt --all --check` clean, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings` clean, `validate-workspace` T3 reject 0 / warn 0 / info 0, `validate-code-refs` violations total 0, `blind-waits` 200 `.rs` scanned and 6 wait sites none blind or spelled, `item-citations` reached 133/133 targets with 0 defects. Separate workspaces: `check-side-workspaces.sh` checked 7 / skipped 0, exit 0, the new `tools/unrun-tests` among them at 9 passed. The `server-features` job's own two commands run locally: `cargo clippy -p mnemosyne-server --all-features --all-targets -D warnings` clean, `cargo test -p mnemosyne-server --all-features` 81 passed / 0 failed.

CLIPPY FOUND THE DOC REPAIR'S SECOND HALF: turning `​```ignore` into `​```no_run` made something compile the example for the first time, and `needless_doctest_main` rejected its `fn main` wrapper immediately. A sample nothing compiles is a sample nothing has an opinion about.

THE `=` SPELLING WAS CLOSED WHILE THE READER WAS BEING SHARED. R1082 carried `--features=a,b` as unread on purpose, having chosen the loud direction; one reader for three gates makes the two spellings one flag, and `a_shell_line_is_split_where_cargo_stops_and_the_harness_starts` pins both.
carry_forward_bullets: WRITTEN IS NOT COMPILED, AND THAT HALF IS NOT BUILT — undone work, not a limit, and it is the NEXT. This gate's population is what CARGO compiles. A test in a file cargo never compiles — a manifest with `autotests = false`, a `tests/*.rs` no target claims, a workspace outside the lister's answer — is in neither the population nor the run set, so it produces no finding. The second authority that would close it is a `syn` census of every `#[test]` in every tracked `.rs`, compared against the compiled population by module path, which is the same shape R1078 used when it made a test harness's `--list` the second authority for rustdoc. Measured before writing this: no manifest in this repository sets `autotests`, `autobins` or `autobenches`, so the class has no known instance today — which is a statement about today and not about the gate.

A CONFIGURATION NOBODY CAN BUILD IS OUTSIDE THE POPULATION, and this one is the world. The population is `--all-features` per workspace UNION every CI command's own list, which covers a test hidden behind a feature and a test hidden behind `not(feature)` — the second is visible in the default build, which CI runs. What it cannot cover is a test visible only under a combination cargo cannot resolve at once (two features that exclude each other), because enumerating configurations is exponential and there is no single build that sees them all.

A PATH-FILTERED JOB STILL COUNTS AS RUNNING. `evidence-replay` triggers on its own inputs and on a weekly clock, so the two tests it owns are credited as run even though a change to the code under them does not re-run them. Deciding otherwise needs a different law — which changes can affect which test — and that is dependency analysis, not a listing. The workflow's own header argues its filter is tight by construction, and this round takes that argument rather than restating it.

THE GATE IS NOT IN THE PRE-COMMIT HOOK, AND THAT IS A COST JUDGEMENT, stated as one rather than dressed as a design. Measured at 71s warm on a 32-core machine and a full cold build of every workspace twice over otherwise; R1079 named what happens to a gate that expensive in a hook — it gets routed around. So it runs in CI only, which means a commit that darkens a test is caught after the push rather than before it. The owner may want the opposite trade.

THE TWO MACHINES TAKE DIFFERENT BRANCHES. `studio` is checkable here and skipped on a runner (its path dependencies name a sibling checkout no runner has), so its target is in both sides of this gate locally and in neither of them there. Symmetric on each machine, which is why it yields no false finding, and asymmetric between them, which is why the local number and the CI number differ by one test and both are right.

THE TRANSPORT BETWEEN THE LISTER AND THE GATE IS WHITESPACE-SEPARATED WORDS. A suite argument containing a space cannot cross it. It fails loudly rather than silently — the split would hand cargo a word it rejects, and the gate refuses on the build — and no suite command in this repository has one.

The second authority that would close it is a `syn` census of every `#[test]` in every tracked `.rs`, compared against the compiled population by module path, which is the same shape R1078 used when it made a test harness's `--list` the second authority for rustdoc. THE LAW: every Rust file this repository tracks is one cargo compiles.

R1084 gated the level below — every test this repository COMPILES is one some
CI command runs — and both of its sides start from a build. A test in a file
cargo never opens is therefore absent from its population AND from its run set
at once, and two absences that cancel produce no finding. R1084 shipped that
gap named, with today's instance count measured at zero, which is a statement
about today rather than about the gate.

IT WAS MEASURED HERE RATHER THAN ARGUED. With `autotests = false` added to
`crates/mnemosyne-atomic/Cargo.toml`, three test files and the eight tests
inside them leave every build. The new gate names all three files and all eight
tests; `unrun-tests`, pointed at the same tree in the same minute, reports
"every test this repository compiles is run by CI", 2150 of 2150. The
arithmetic closes: 2140 tests before this round, plus this crate's 18, minus
the 8 that left, is exactly 2150. Eight real tests went dark and the gate one
level down did not move.

BOTH SIDES ARE ASKED OF THE MACHINE. TRACKED is `git ls-files '*.rs'`: a file
git does not track is not this repository's, and a CI checkout does not have it
either. COMPILED is, for every workspace the workspace lister says this machine
can build, `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` — once with `--all-features`
and once without — and then the files each compilation READ, taken from rustc's
own dep-info.

DEP-INFO RATHER THAN A MODULE WALK. Following `mod` declarations from each
target root is a MODEL of what rustc does, and it has to re-implement `#[path]`,
`mod.rs` versus `name.rs`, `cfg`, and `include!`. This repository already holds
the file that breaks a walker:
`bench/crates/codegen-prototype/tests/fixtures/salsa_wire_emit.rs` is named by
no `mod` and pulled in by `include!(concat!(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"), …))`, a
path nothing resolves without evaluating macros. rustc records it because rustc
opened it, and there is no second implementation to drift.

TWO FEATURE RESOLVES, because one flag cannot both enable and disable.
`--all-features` is what makes a file behind `#[cfg(feature = "x")] mod x;` part
of the population and what hides a file behind `#[cfg(not(feature = "x"))]`, so
the read set is the union of the two. What survives is stated rather than
implied: a file visible only under some third combination of mutually exclusive
features is in neither, and enumerating combinations is exponential.

THE JOIN IS LOAD-BEARING. Cargo never garbage-collects dep-info, so a unit
removed from the build graph leaves its record behind naming every file it used
to read. Only dep-info that this build's own `compiler-artifact` messages join
to is counted — by output filename, and for a build script by the directory
cargo and rustc share, since cargo reports `build-script-build` where rustc
wrote `build_script_build-<hash>`. Without the join the gate would credit dead
units on a warm machine and not on a cold runner, which is the worst kind of
disagreement: one that depends on who ran it.

AND IT REFUSES RATHER THAN PASSING when it could not look — a probe that did
not compile, an artifact cargo reported whose dep-info the gate could not find,
or a target root cargo NAMES that the same build was not measured to have read.
That last is the self-check that makes the rest trustworthy: cargo states its
targets independently of rustc stating its reads, and a join that quietly
matched nothing disagrees with it instead of returning a large, confident,
empty answer.

probes over 9 workspaces, 11 seconds fully warm, zero declared exceptions. A
drift guard with no occupant today, so its non-vacuity is proved by injection
rather than by a finding.

lister's DIRECTORY and its REASON as two fields. This gate needs the directory
per file (a workspace this machine cannot compile must not make the verdict a
fact about which machine ran it), and R1082's `feature_coverage_smoke` needed it
per manifest and was recovering it by splitting the reason sentence. Two readers
of one line is the shape R1083 turned main red with.

(owner's word, 2026-08-08). `unrun-tests` costs 73 seconds warm on 32 cores and

Every `Round NNN` written in this round's code and manifests was verified against the store with `query --changelog-entry` before it was written — twelve of them, all exit 0.
carry_forward_bullets: A file cargo CAN compile that no CI COMMAND compiles is a different law one level up, and this gate does not hold it: "compiled" here means reachable by `cargo check --all-targets` under two feature resolves, not built by a job. Today's instance count is zero and that was measured — all seven example and bench targets live in `bench/`, which the workspace lister lints with `--all-targets` on every push, and the root workspace has none of either. Closing it means re-issuing every CI cargo command for its dep-info, which costs roughly all of CI a second time inside one job; modelling the commands instead is the thing R1084 refused to do. That is a COST decision rather than a design one, and it is the owner's to make.

Mutually exclusive features stay outside the population. The two resolves cover default and all-features, which is every selection this repository's own commands use; a file visible only under some third combination is in neither, and enumerating combinations is exponential. This is the world, not an omission.

The new job's 90-minute budget is argued from the other jobs, not measured on a runner: `cargo check` skips the codegen and linking `unrun-tests` pays for (27 minutes of its 90), then doubles because a second feature resolve is a second dependency graph, C dependencies included. The first run is what measures it.

A workspace the lister declines is outside this machine's answer, so its files are counted and printed but never reported. On this machine that is nothing; on a hosted runner it is `studio`, whose path dependencies name a sibling checkout no runner has. Each machine is internally symmetric and the two disagree by exactly that workspace.

Round 1086 — an exception nothing excuse.decision_summary:
THE LAW IS UNCHANGED. What changed is that its EXCEPTION is a thing a test can
be aimed at. R1085 shipped `DECLARED` — the table of tracked Rust this
repository deliberately does not compile — as a `const` read inside the
function it steers. Ten injections were swept over that gate and all ten fired,
which reads as coverage. Not one of them could be aimed at the branch under the
table, and not because the branch is subtle: the table is EMPTY, so there was
nothing to point an injection at. An untested policy looked exactly like a
tested one, and the sweep could not say otherwise because a sweep is a list of
mutations and the missing one is invisible in a list.

THE REPAIR IS DEPENDENCY INJECTION AND NOTHING CLEVERER. `conclude` and
`examine` take the table they are to honour; `run` passes `DECLARED`. What an
entry DOES is now a question with an answer, asked through the same function
the gate runs: a fixture holding an uncompiled file has it excused with the
entry and reported without it.

AND THE OTHER DIRECTION, WHICH IS THE ONE A TABLE ONLY EVER GROWS WITHOUT. An
entry stops excusing anything the moment somebody wires its file up or deletes
it, and a dead entry is INVISIBLE in a printed list of live ones — it matches
nothing, so it prints nothing, and this table is reviewed by being printed. So
an entry that excuses nothing is now a REFUSAL (`Refusal::StaleDeclaration`),
naming which of the two happened, because "something compiles it now" and "this
repository no longer tracks a file by that name" are different repairs. Where
staleness STOPS is the asymmetry `in_skipped_workspace` already exists for:
inside a workspace the lister declined, this machine can see the file neither
compiled nor uncompiled, and refusing there would make one table reject on the
runner and pass here — a verdict about which machine ran the gate.

THE THIRD MECHANISM HAD A SENTENCE AND NOW HAS A FIXTURE. R1085 claimed this
gate catches a package no workspace claims; a file no `mod` reaches and a
`tests/` entry point the manifest disowns each had a fixture, and that one had
prose. The shape is `[workspace] members = ["claimed"] exclude = ["disowned"]`
with a `#[test]` inside the excluded package, the control is the same package
as a member, and membership is the only difference between them. The injection
that proves the fixture is the plausible repair somebody would reach for — a
gate that WALKS for `Cargo.toml` instead of asking the lister, which compiles
the excluded package itself and reports the tree clean.

Round 1087 — the backlog knows which pai.decision_summary:
THE BACKLOG SAID WHICH PAIR TO COMPARE NEXT AND COULD NOT SEE WHICH PAIRS WERE
DONE. Round 1040 derived, by perturbation rather than by heuristic, the pairs of
shipped reads that both ANSWER ABOUT a subject, and pinned them as a ranking of
87 — the list the last six declared cross-read contracts were taken from, and
the list that says where the next one goes. Nothing in it recorded that a pair
had a contract. Its top row has had one since Round 1052 and its second since
Round 1048, so the answer to "what is next" was two rows of finished work, and
the session memory that carried that answer between sessions named the top row
as the next job for six sessions after it stopped being one.

MEASURED: 7 of the 87 pairs are judged by a contract in this suite, and the
highest-ranked pair no contract judges is `report-authoring-frontier <->
report-playthrough-manuscript` at 158 shared subjects — the third row, not the
first. That line is printed and ASSERTED, so it moves the day a round declares
a contract over it, and the round after this one reads it off a green run
rather than out of a memory file.

THE DECLARATION LIVES IN THE CONTRACT. A list of judged pairs kept beside the
walk would be a second thing to update, and a second thing to update is exactly
what went stale here. Each contract states its pair in one `const DECLARES` that
the contract itself RUNS ON — the verbs it asks are that const's elements — and
the walk reads that statement out of the source. One place to write it, and it
cannot name a pair the test does not ask.

WHY THE INSTRUMENT IS A PARSER AND NOT A SEARCH FOR THE VERB'S NAME. Every one
of these files names other reads in its header: the arc's history is written
there, in prose, and `frontier_playable_agreement.rs` alone mentions four. A
text match reports a pair as judged because a comment mentioned it. `syn` sees
the `const` item and nothing a comment says — the same reasoning that made this
repository parse its own workflows with a YAML parser in R887 rather than grep
for `fetch-depth`. The injection that reverts it to a text match turns the
control test red, and the control test is a source holding both a comment naming
one pair and a declaration naming another.

THE NET IS IN THE DIRECTION THAT MATTERS, AND ITS FINDING ARM COULD NOT BE
REACHED. A file this repository named `*agreement*` that declares nothing is a
contract the walk cannot see, which is how the marks go stale again — so that is
a check. Pointed at the real tree it can never fire, because every contract in
the tree declares: a calculation with nothing aimed at it, which is the defect
Round 1086 closed one crate over, one round earlier. Same repair: the directory
is an argument, the caller passes `tests/`, and the test passes a tree built to
make the arm fire — with the control being the SAME tree after the declaration
is added, so the net is shown to be about the declaration and not the file name.

USING THE SWEEP FOUND A DEFECT IN THE SWEEP, AND IT IS THE FOURTH ROUND RUNNING
THAT HAS HAPPENED. All six injections landed exactly where they were aimed and
nowhere else; the harness reported all six as MISAIMED. A plan names the
`#[test]` function; a harness reads the name the target prints, which for a test
inside a module is `read_agreement_population::the_walk`. Held against each
other as plain strings they never match, so the strongest verdict this tool has
— "a sweep that comes back 0 is a misaimed injection until something says
otherwise" — was spent on forty minutes of runs in which nothing was misaimed.
A gate that refuses for a reason outside its own law is the same defect as a
gate that does not fire, and it is worse here, because the message it prints
tells the author to distrust the evidence. Fixed in the same session: a name
matches a red at a MODULE BOUNDARY (`a::b::name` answers to `name` and to
`b::name`), never as a substring — `walk` must not answer for `the_walk`, or the
harness credits an injection with a failure it did not cause.

The pair is named once per contract; a file cannot ask one pair and declare another.

`surface/read_agreement_population.rs` — `declared_in` reads that const out of a source with `syn`, and `declared_pairs(tests)` walks the test directory for every one of them. The directory is an argument, not `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR` baked into the body, so the arm that reports an undeclared contract can be reached by a test at all.

Four checks join the walk's existing six: the derived marks match the pin; a test file the walk could not parse is a failure and not a pair nobody judges; every `*agreement*` file declares; every declared pair is inside the ranking (a contract over two reads sharing nothing is stale, or the walk lost the pair). Round 1087 — the backlog knows which pai.publishable_decision_summary:
THE BACKLOG SAID WHICH PAIR TO COMPARE NEXT AND COULD NOT SEE WHICH PAIRS WERE
DONE. Round 1040 derived, by perturbation rather than by heuristic, the pairs of
shipped reads that both ANSWER ABOUT a subject, and pinned them as a ranking of
87 — the list the last six declared cross-read contracts were taken from, and
the list that says where the next one goes. Nothing in it recorded that a pair
had a contract. Its top row has had one since Round 1052 and its second since
Round 1048, so the answer to "what is next" was two rows of finished work, and
the session memory that carried that answer between sessions named the top row
as the next job for six sessions after it stopped being one.

MEASURED: 7 of the 87 pairs are judged by a contract in this suite, and the
highest-ranked pair no contract judges is `report-authoring-frontier <->
report-playthrough-manuscript` at 158 shared subjects — the third row, not the
first. That line is printed and ASSERTED, so it moves the day a round declares
a contract over it, and the round after this one reads it off a green run
rather than out of a memory file.

THE DECLARATION LIVES IN THE CONTRACT. A list of judged pairs kept beside the
walk would be a second thing to update, and a second thing to update is exactly
what went stale here. Each contract states its pair in one `const DECLARES` that
the contract itself RUNS ON — the verbs it asks are that const's elements — and
the walk reads that statement out of the source. One place to write it, and it
cannot name a pair the test does not ask.

WHY THE INSTRUMENT IS A PARSER AND NOT A SEARCH FOR THE VERB'S NAME. Every one
of these files names other reads in its header: the arc's history is written
there, in prose, and `frontier_playable_agreement.rs` alone mentions four. A
text match reports a pair as judged because a comment mentioned it. `syn` sees
the `const` item and nothing a comment says — the same reasoning that made this
repository parse its own workflows with a YAML parser in R887 rather than grep
for `fetch-depth`. The injection that reverts it to a text match turns the
control test red, and the control test is a source holding both a comment naming
one pair and a declaration naming another.

THE NET IS IN THE DIRECTION THAT MATTERS, AND ITS FINDING ARM COULD NOT BE
REACHED. A file this repository named `*agreement*` that declares nothing is a
contract the walk cannot see, which is how the marks go stale again — so that is
a check. Pointed at the real tree it can never fire, because every contract in
the tree declares: a calculation with nothing aimed at it, which is the defect
Round 1086 closed one crate over, one round earlier. Same repair: the directory
is an argument, the caller passes `tests/`, and the test passes a tree built to
make the arm fire — with the control being the SAME tree after the declaration
is added, so the net is shown to be about the declaration and not the file name.

USING THE SWEEP FOUND A DEFECT IN THE SWEEP, AND IT IS THE FOURTH ROUND RUNNING
THAT HAS HAPPENED. All six injections landed exactly where they were aimed and
nowhere else; the harness reported all six as MISAIMED. A plan names the
`#[test]` function; a harness reads the name the target prints, which for a test
inside a module is `read_agreement_population::the_walk`. Held against each
other as plain strings they never match, so the strongest verdict this tool has
— "a sweep that comes back 0 is a misaimed injection until something says
otherwise" — was spent on forty minutes of runs in which nothing was misaimed.
A gate that refuses for a reason outside its own law is the same defect as a
gate that does not fire, and it is worse here, because the message it prints
tells the author to distrust the evidence. Fixed in the same session: a name
matches a red at a MODULE BOUNDARY (`a::b::name` answers to `name` and to
`b::name`), never as a substring — `walk` must not answer for `the_walk`, or the
harness credits an injection with a failure it did not cause.

THE PAIR THE PROGRAM NAMED, DECLARED — AND THE FIRST ROUND OF THIS ARC WHOSE
NEXT JOB WAS READ OFF A GREEN RUN. Round 1087 made the backlog walk print and
assert the highest-ranked pair no contract judges, so that the answer would stop
being carried in a session's memory, where it had named finished work for six
sessions. It said `report-authoring-frontier <-> report-playthrough-manuscript`
at 158 shared subjects. This round declared it, the walk went red on its own
pin, and the line it now prints is `135 report-frame-view <->
report-playable-world` — 8 of 87 judged. The steering came from the suite, not
from a note.

WHY THIS PAIR IS NOT THE TWO CONTRACTS BESIDE IT COMPOSED, which is the first
question a third contract over the same three reads has to answer. Round 1048
pins that the playable world EMBEDS this manuscript verbatim; Round 1052 pins
the frontier against that embedded copy. Under a telling, this pair's scene laws
follow from those two, and restating them would be two copies of one thought —
the R1041 shape this arc has already paid for. Both of those contracts stand on
`report-playable-world`, and that read REFUSES without `--telling`. So the
composition is not available:

- to any store that declares no telling, and 18 of the 44 authored corpora
  declare none. They reach NEITHER existing contract. This pair answers about
  all of them: 28 stores here against the 13 (store, telling) pairs those two
  contracts see;
- to the READING COPY at all, from any store. `--reading-walk` is an argument
  only the manuscript has, and the playable world cannot be asked it.

Both halves are MEASURED, not argued. A test asks `report-playable-world` for an
authored store with no telling and requires the refusal to name the missing
argument; the same test requires both reads of this pair to answer. The count of
corpora that declare no telling is derived here rather than quoted from the file
that skips them. "The other contract cannot reach this" is exactly the claim
that rots when the other contract grows, so it is a red test and not a sentence.

THE LAW NO OTHER PAIR CAN STATE: a scene the frontier calls zero-fact is DROPPED
from the reading walk of every road that travels it. The frontier's
`zero_fact_scenes` is the author's list of scenes with nothing in them yet; the
reading copy is what a reader is walked through; a reader must not be walked
through an empty scene. The prune's own mechanics were pinned one crate down at
Round 1048 — one hand-built store, one road, one scene — and nothing joined it to
the read whose whole subject is which scenes are empty.

THE CONVERSE IS COUNTED, NOT ASSERTED, and the constructed store authors the
reason. `k-join` is dropped from the right road while the frontier's census holds
a fact there: the fact belongs to the left road, so the traveller who never sees
it is not walked through the scene. A law stated both ways would be false, and a
residual left as a number nobody can read is the R1029 failure — so the pair
(road, scene) is named in the assertion itself.

TWO POPULATIONS, ASSERTED SEPARATELY. The authored corpora leave four arms at
zero: no corpus holds a section outside its order, a scene with nothing in it, a
confluence, or a fact no order can place — and across all 28, over 823 scenes,
the reading prune drops NOTHING. That silence is asserted rather than averaged
in, because it is what says the constructed store is carrying those laws. The
constructed store goes through the same import recipe an author would use, and
declares no telling — a constructed store that declared one would be a store the
composition beside this file could have judged.

THE CONFLUENCE EXCEPTION IS PROVED BY THE OTHER READ, TWICE OVER. The frontier
reports density for every registered road; the manuscript's unfiltered dump omits
confluences, because a merge node is not a playthrough (R533). Round 1052 judged
that same difference against the playable world's fork tree. Here it is judged
against the manuscript's OWN `confluence_fragment` marker, asked road by road
with `--world` — a second reading of one fact, from the read that is present in
both pairs, and a re-derivation drifts between them.

WHAT THIS ENTRY DOES NOT CLAIM. The injection sweep that would show each law
going red when the read it is about breaks was WRITTEN and STARTED and did not
finish: the machine rebooted mid-run, taking the sweep's logs and leaving one
injection in the working tree, which was found by `git status` and reverted
before anything else. Nine injections are named in the carry, each aimed at a
read and not at a test. So the laws below are stated on a green suite and are
NOT yet shown to be breakable, which is the weaker half of this arc's own
standard and is said here rather than left to be noticed.

A sweep whose tree is restored only by a live supervisor has one failure mode the supervisor cannot cover, and the check that catches it is reading `git diff` before trusting any suite result that follows.

carry_forward_bullets: THE CI CACHE BUDGET IS MEASURED AND UNREPAIRED, AND THAT IS UNDONE WORK RATHER THAN A LIMIT. This repository's workflows declare EIGHT cache keys and GitHub currently holds THREE; six of the eight cache a whole root `target`. Measured: `unrun-tests` 10.71 GB, `validate` 9.58 GB, `side` 65.91 MB, 21.87 GB active against a documented 10 GB per-repository limit, whose eviction policy deletes by last access until the total fits and which GitHub's own documentation calls cache thrashing. Three consecutive pushes ran `unrun-tests` at 27m, 27m and 28m — never once warm, its cache alone larger than the whole budget — while `uncompiled-sources` beside it swung 14m1s, 14m43s, 1m36s. That oscillation is the thrash, and two thirds of this repository's CI wall-clock is in it.

THE CONSTRAINT WAS ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN, WHICH IS THE PART THAT MATTERS. Round 1067 measured the 10 GB budget and recorded it in `side-workspaces`' own comment as the reason that job deliberately caches nothing. Rounds 1078, 1081, 1084 and 1085 then each added a job with its own full-`target` key, every one carrying a comment explaining that a shared key would make each run evict the other's artifacts. Every one of those comments is right about cargo's feature resolves. Nobody re-added the total. A prose constraint with no program to enforce it is one that four locally-correct rounds contradicted without anything noticing.

THE GATE FOR IT MUST NOT BE THE OBVIOUS ONE, and this is worth carrying because the obvious one is what a later round will reach for. Summing the caches that exist CANNOT FAIL: eviction holds that total under the limit by construction, so a repository asking three times its budget measures exactly what a healthy one measures. The observable eviction cannot hide is ABSENCE — every declared cache is one GitHub still holds. Demand is then reckoned by pricing each absent cache from the largest present cache declaring the SAME PATHS, since a registry-only cache is two orders of magnitude smaller than one holding a `target`. Two further traps are already known: the join must give a cache to the LONGEST matching declared prefix, because this repository's oldest key `Linux-cargo-` is a prefix of every other key in the file and a plain `starts_with` would credit the small job with the huge job's cache and report a third of the real demand; and the repair must keep the existing key prefixes, because renaming them leaves the old caches as orphans for seven days and the gate would fail on those instead.

THE REPAIR NEEDS A MEASUREMENT THIS ROUND DID NOT TAKE: what fraction of a `target` is debuginfo. Six full-`target` caches cannot fit a 10 GB budget however they are shrunk, so the answer needs both levers — smaller artifacts and fewer cached targets — and the allocation is an argument from the job durations above, since jobs run in parallel and the wall-clock is the longest of them. Quoting a ratio instead of measuring it is the thing this repository has been wrong about before.

WHETHER THE CACHE THEN SURVIVES IS ONLY OBSERVABLE IN CI. The size lever can be measured locally and the workflow can be changed locally, but a cache that lives through the next run is a fact about GitHub's eviction queue and nothing on this machine can stand in for it.

Round 1090 — every cache declared is one.decision_summary:
EVERY CACHE THIS REPOSITORY'S CI DECLARES IS ONE IT GETS TO KEEP — the level
above every cache step in the workflow file, and the constraint four rounds broke
without anything noticing. Round 1067 measured GitHub's 10 GB per-repository
cache budget and wrote it into `side-workspaces`' own comment as the reason that
job deliberately caches nothing. Rounds 1078, 1081, 1084 and 1085 then each added
a job with its own whole-`target` key, every one carrying a comment explaining
that a shared key would make each run evict the other's artifacts. Every one of
those comments is right about cargo. Nobody re-added the total, and this round
measured it with the gate it built: 63.07 GB of a 10 GB budget.

WHY THE OBVIOUS GATE IS VACUOUS, which is the whole shape of this one. "Sum the
caches and compare against the limit" CANNOT FAIL. GitHub deletes caches, least
recently used first, precisely until the total is under the limit, so a
repository asking three times its budget measures exactly what a healthy one
measures, and the gate would print a clean number forever while every cache in it
was deleted before its next use. The observable eviction cannot hide is ABSENCE.

So the law is: the DEMAND fits, where an absent cache is priced from the largest
present one holding a SUBSET of its paths. Subset rather than the identical path
list Round 1089 proposed, because no two keys here hold quite the same set and
identity would leave every one of them unpriceable; subset rather than any
overlap, because every key here holds `~/.cargo/registry` and overlap would price
a 65 MB registry cache as a 10 GB build tree and invent demand that is not there.
A subset is a LOWER BOUND WITH A PROOF: this cache holds everything that one
holds and more. Three further refusals ride with it — a key held that no workflow
declares, two jobs disagreeing about what one key holds, and a report that could
price nothing, which is refused rather than passed because a gate that could not
look and a gate that found nothing wrong print the same silence.

THE NEWEST GENERATION UNDER A KEY IS THE ONE JUDGED, not the largest, and that is
the rule this gate would have failed itself on. Every key here ends in a
`hashFiles` of the lockfiles, so a dependency bump changes all of them at once and
leaves the previous generation held until it ages out. Judging the largest would
read a repository at the size it had before it shrank its caches and keep it red
for the seven days that takes — this round's own repair, reported as the failure.
The superseded generations are PRINTED, because they are bytes GitHub really is
holding; they are not counted, because no edit to a workflow can prevent them.

WHAT THE CACHED ARTIFACTS ARE MADE OF, measured rather than assumed, which is the
measurement Round 1089 carried as missing. Of the 44.2 GB in this project's own
`target/debug`, 29.1 GB is DWARF: the 401 test executables cargo left in `deps/`
come to 26.2 GB and 83.2% of those bytes are `.debug_*` sections, and the rlibs,

It was going to be: this commit adds no lockfile, so every key would have kept its hash and every cache would have had to be RESTORED. But the same commit changes the workflow, and the keys now hash the workflow, so all eight are legitimately rebuilt and all eight are EXCUSED — the exception path is what gets exercised, printed with the eight names, and the refusal path waits for the run after. That is the honest reading of what the next run can and cannot show.

AND THE BUDGET IS A PROJECTION AGAIN, which is the shape this round should be most careful about, having just watched one be wrong by a factor of two. About 8.4 GB of 10 is arithmetic over parts that were measured on a runner — `unrun-tests` at 7.83 GB and six registry-only caches between 0.06 and 0.15 — but `validate`'s new registry-only cache has never been saved, and neither has any of them under the new keys. The gate reports the number; nothing here should be believed ahead of it.

IT CATCHES A PREFIX FALLBACK TOO, which is worth writing down because it was not designed for: `actions/cache` saves whenever there was no EXACT key hit, including after `restore-keys` handed the job an older generation. So a partially warm job also creates a cache inside the run and is refused with the fully cold ones. The law is sharper than the sentence that motivated it.

`last_accessed_at` REMAINS UNMEASURED AND UNUSED, deliberately. It is the field that would say whether a restore touched a cache, and every cache this repository has been observed holding had it equal to `created_at` because every one was freshly saved. The day a run restores one, that pair separates and the question is answered by looking — not before.

⛳**NN8 IS THE BIGGER PRIZE AND IS STILL OPEN.** Seven jobs build the same workspace seven times on every push; caching HIDES that duplication rather than removing it, and a 10 GB budget being fought over is the consequence. The long-term answer is one build whose artifacts are handed between jobs, or fewer jobs. What makes it hard is real and worth recording: the seven resolve different features (default, `--all-features`, and the MSRV toolchain), so an artifact handed from one is not an artifact the next can use unchanged. This round and the last one both stopped short of it for effort, and that is a cost judgement rather than a design one.

⛳**NN9 CARRIES: sccache was ruled out without measuring it.** "The Actions cache backend eats the same 10 GB" is an argument, not a measurement, and sccache deduplicates at the compilation-unit level, which is exactly where seven overlapping builds waste the most. It is now cheap to settle, because this repository has a gate that reports what its caches cost.

⛳**NN3 IS NOW THE WHOLE REMAINING WALL-CLOCK QUESTION, and the numbers say it does not fit.** `separate in-repo workspaces` is the floor at 20m48s and keeps nothing; Round 1067 measured its workspaces' build trees at 3.9 GB, and the projected headroom after this repair is about 1.6 GB. So it cannot be cached as things stand — which makes it the first debt whose answer is "the world does not allow it at this size", and the lever that would change that is `debug = 0`, already measured at 4.40 GB of test executables against the roughly 8.7 GB line tables leave. That is a trade against the file and line a panic reports, and it should be made with the gate's number in hand.

⚠**THE MEASUREMENT DISCIPLINE THIS ROUND OWES ITS OWN LEDGER:** Round 1090 predicted `unrun-tests` at ~3.9 GB by scaling an old ratio and was wrong by a factor of two, and it wrote that prediction into a carry as though it were nearly a reading. The ratio it scaled (10.71 / 9.58) was measured BEFORE the debuginfo change, and the change did not act on both jobs equally — `unrun-tests` links test binaries for every workspace under `--all-features`, so it had proportionally more to keep. A ratio measured under one regime is not a ratio under the next.

Carried, unchanged: **AA11** (the binary-by-binary cost census, now nine sessions), **KK8**, **LL8/LL9**, **KK9/KK13/JJ3**, **PP2**, **PP5**, **KK5**, **ZZ6/ZZ7-ZZ10**, **BB1**. Owner decisions carried: **EE1**, **II1**, and where the next arc goes.

Round 1092 — every compilation CI pays f.decision_summary:
EVERY COMPILATION THIS REPOSITORY'S CI PAYS FOR IS ONE JOB'S, and until this
round nothing here could say how many of them were not. Seven jobs in
`mnemosyne-validate.yml` build this workspace, and what has kept them apart is a
sentence — that they resolve different features — written into four separate
comments by four rounds, none of which counted anything. The bill for that
sentence is legible in the gate beside it: of the 8.49 GB Round 1091 left this
repository asking GitHub to hold, `unrun-tests` alone is 7.83 GB, because a build
tree per job is what a job per build tree costs. Round 1090 named the whole
shape and deferred it twice as a cost judgement.

THE POPULATION CANNOT BE ASKED OF CARGO, and that is why this took an
instrument rather than a flag. A job's cost is not one cargo invocation but a
tree of them: three of these gates are programs that shell out to cargo
themselves, and `--message-format=json` reaches the outermost call and nothing
underneath it. `RUSTC_WRAPPER` reaches all of them, because it is an environment
variable and a child process inherits one. So `tools/rustc-log` sits in front of
every `rustc` this CI runs, writes down the invocation, and becomes the compiler.
It has no dependencies, which is a requirement and not a preference: it must
exist before the build it records, and every crate it pulled in would be a
compilation this repository pays for in order to measure what it pays for.

A UNIT IS CARGO'S OWN, not this crate's idea of one. `-C metadata=<hash>` is the
fingerprint cargo computes from the package, its resolved features, the profile
and the compiler's version; it is on every `rustc` cargo drives and on none of
the probes it runs first. Two jobs that emit the same hash are compiling the same
thing, and two that do not are genuinely resolving differently — so the sentence
those four comments carried is now answered by cargo instead of argued here. The
`msrv` job is the control that shows the key can tell: it runs the same words as
`validate` over the same sources on a different compiler, so its units have to
come back disjoint from everything, and if they did not the key would be wrong.

WHAT IT MEASURED, with every job replayed cold in a git worktree of its own on
this machine: 5484 compilations across six jobs, against a floor of 2352 distinct
units. THREE THOUSAND ONE HUNDRED AND THIRTY-TWO OF THEM — 57.1% of everything
this CI compiles — are compilations of something that had already been compiled.
Six of nine jobs, because `msrv` and `cache-budget` have environments only GitHub
resolves and `twice-compiled` is the gate itself, so the real figure is above
this one. Per job: `side-workspaces` 1188, `unrun-tests` 1160, `uncompiled-
sources` 1105, `validate` 954, `item-citations` 567, `server-features` 510. The
heaviest pair is `unrun-tests` + `validate` at 525 units both compile.

AND THE SPLIT IS WHY THE REPAIR R1090 WROTE DOWN IS HALF AN ANSWER. It recorded
NN8's fix as "build once and pass the artifacts between jobs, or merge the jobs".
That reaches 2236 of the 3132. The other 896 are inside single jobs — `validate`
repeats 295 and `side-workspaces` 242 — because those jobs build SEPARATE
workspaces, and cargo gives each workspace its own `target`. One runner, one
cache key, one job, and still two compilations of the same unit. Merging jobs
cannot touch that half, and nothing in the file had ever separated the two.

WHAT IS DUPLICATED IS DEPENDENCIES, NOT THIS REPOSITORY. 482 crates are compiled
more than once, and the head of the list is `build_script_build` at 483 surplus
compilations, then `proc_macro2` 62, `syn` 62, `quote` 59, `unicode_ident` 55,
`serde_core` 48, `memchr` 47. That is the shape a compilation cache is for and
the shape "they resolve different features" is least true of: a build script and
a proc-macro crate are compiled for the host, with no features from the workspace
above them, and they are exactly the units every one of these jobs needs first.

WHAT IT ASSERTS TODAY IS THAT IT REACHED EVERY JOB, and that is the half worth
having first. A job added tomorrow without the recorder in its environment builds
perfectly and contributes an absence, and an absence prints exactly like a job
with nothing to compile — the failure this repository keeps meeting, most
recently in R1085's two gates and R1086's summary line. So the law is read off
the workflow: every job it declares must carry both variables on every step,
must record to a file named after itself, and must leave a non-empty log; every
log must name a job the workflow declares. The one step excused is the step that
BUILDS the recorder, which cannot use what it is building, and that excuse is
derived from the manifest the step names rather than kept as a job id in a list —
so it stays exactly one step wide, with the same empty variable on any other step
refused as its control.

THE LOG PATH IS SPELLED OUT PER JOB, and that is a defect avoided rather than a
style. `${{ github.job }}` is defined by the runner only inside a step: in a job's
`env:` block it evaluates to nothing, so a single workflow-level declaration
would have had all nine jobs appending to one file — and a census of one job
reports no duplication at all, which is a wrong answer wearing the shape of a
clean one. Written by hand, the name can be pasted wrong instead; what makes a
hand-written name safe is that the gate checks it is the job's own, which is the
paste error this repository already has a rule about from R295.

THE DUPLICATION IS REPORTED AND NOT YET REFUSED. There is no honest limit to
assert before the repair exists, and R1090 is the reason that sentence is worth
writing down: it shipped a gate whose limit was a prediction, the prediction was
wrong by a factor of two, and its own gate caught it seventeen seconds into the
first run. The number this round produces is what licenses the repair; the limit
is what will keep it afterwards.
changes_bullets: `tools/rustc-log` (new, its own workspace, NO dependencies) — the `RUSTC_WRAPPER` that records one line per `rustc` and then `exec`s the compiler. Dependency-free because it must exist before the build it records, and because every crate it pulled in would be a compilation this repository pays for in order to measure what it pays for. It REFUSES when `$MNEMOSYNE_RUSTC_LOG` names no file rather than passing quietly through: a job wired without it would build perfectly and hand the census an absence, and an absence reads exactly like a job with nothing to compile.

`tools/twice-compiled` (new, its own workspace) — joins the per-job logs into a census and reports it. A unit is keyed by CARGO'S OWN `-C metadata` fingerprint plus `--emit`, so "these jobs resolve different features" is answered by cargo instead of argued in a comment, and a `cargo check` unit is not confused with the `cargo build` of the same crate. It also reports the surplus PER CRATE, because duplication in a third-party dependency and duplication in this repository's own crates are the same number and different repairs.

`tools/ci-plan` — `run_steps` now returns a `RunStep` carrying the environment of all three levels GitHub allows (workflow, job, step), and `CargoCommand` carries it too. THE ENVIRONMENT IS PART OF THE COMMAND and this repository holds both proofs: `msrv` runs the same words as `validate` and is a different build only because of `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` on its step, and R1090 set `CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_DEBUG` for the whole file. The five call sites were updated in the same change.

`.github/workflows/mnemosyne-validate.yml` — `RUSTC_WRAPPER` at workflow level, a per-job `MNEMOSYNE_RUSTC_LOG` on each of the nine jobs, one `Build the compilation recorder` step per job, an `upload-artifact` per job and a new `twice-compiled` job that waits for all eight others and joins their logs. The log path is spelled out per job rather than derived from `${{ github.job }}`, because the runner defines that expression only inside a step: in an `env:` block it is empty and every job would append to one file.

`--replay` — the same census taken on this machine, by running each job's `run:` steps in a git worktree of its own. A worktree per job rather than one checkout with `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` moved aside, because a job's cost is spread over several `target` directories and redirecting them into one would make cargo share units a runner compiles twice. It refuses a job whose environment only GitHub can resolve (`msrv`, `cache-budget`) instead of replaying it on the wrong toolchain.
verification_bullets: RED FIRST, AGAINST THE LIVE WORKFLOW. `tools/twice-compiled/tests/this_repository.rs` holds the file itself to the law, and before the wiring all three failed — the first naming all eight jobs in sixteen refusals, two per job, one per variable. After the wiring the same three pass. Suites: 18 law tests over pinned records, 3 against the tree, 5 for the recorder, 13 for `ci-plan` (one new, over an environment written at all three levels GitHub allows). fmt and clippy clean in both new workspaces.

THE ONE CLAIM A COMMENT CANNOT MAKE IS TESTED. cargo runs as many compilers at once as the machine has cores, every one appending to one file, and a torn record is a compilation the census would miscount. `every_record_survives_many_compilers_appending_at_once` runs 16 writers x 64 records of 4 KB and checks every record came back whole and none went missing.

THE EXEMPTION HAS A CONTROL. The step that builds the recorder is excused from using it — it cannot use what it is building — and the excuse is derived from the manifest the step names, not from a job id in a list. Its control is the same empty `RUSTC_WRAPPER` on a step that builds anything else, which is refused.

THE RECORDER COMPILES ON THE MSRV. Built with `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=1.88.0` before the `msrv` job was wired to do so, because that job installs only the MSRV toolchain and building the recorder on the dev one would make rustup fetch a second toolchain for a crate with no dependencies.

THE ARTIFACT ACTIONS WERE READ, NOT GUESSED (the R893 discipline). `upload-artifact@v7` and `download-artifact@v8` declare `runs.using: node24` in their own `action.yml`; `download-artifact@v6` still declares node20, so matching the two majors by number would have picked a node20 action while believing otherwise.

A DEFECT THE REAL DATA FOUND AND THE FIXTURE HAD NOT. The first per-crate breakdown printed `272 duplicated` on one line and `269 surplus` on the next, because the breakdown counted per-job DISTINCT units and a job that compiles one unit twice lost that repeat. The test that was meant to pin the identity passed, because its fixture had no repeat in it. `JobLog::units` is now a count per unit rather than a set, the fixture has the repeated row, and the two lines agree by construction.

THE CENSUS ITSELF, run on this machine with every job replayed cold in its own git worktree: 5484 compilations across six jobs, floor 2352, duplicated 3132 = 57.1%, of which 2236 cross-job and 896 inside single jobs. Per job (compiled / distinct / repeated): side-workspaces 1188/946/242, unrun-tests 1160/985/175, uncompiled-sources 1105/924/181, validate 954/659/295, item-citations 567/564/3, server-features 510/510/0. Probes and unkeyed invocations are printed beside them rather than dropped, so the classes this reader cannot key are visible instead of silently absent.

THE MSRV CONTROL IS NOT YET DISCHARGED, and it is named rather than assumed: the local replay refuses to run `msrv`, so the claim that cargo's `-C metadata` separates two compilers has not been observed in this repository. The first CI run of this gate is what tests it — if `msrv` shows any shared units at all, the unit key is wrong.
carry_forward_bullets: THREE THINGS THE RECORDER CANNOT SEE, and all three under-count, which is the safe direction for a finding of the form "this work is done more than once". `rustdoc` does not go through `RUSTC_WRAPPER`, and `item-citations` documents 134 targets. A build script's own `cc` is not `rustc`, and `librocksdb-sys` compiles C in six of these jobs. A unit that was already fresh is never handed to a compiler at all.

`evidence-replay.yml` IS NOT IN THE CENSUS and closing that is not worth a job. Artifacts do not cross workflow runs, so a second workflow needs a second gate — and that workflow has exactly ONE job, which makes its cross-job duplication zero by construction. What it would buy is a guaranteed zero; what it would cost is a whole job.

THE GATE REPORTS THE DUPLICATION AND DOES NOT YET REFUSE IT. There is no honest limit to assert before the repair exists: R1090 shipped a gate whose limit was a prediction, and the prediction was wrong by a factor of two on the first run. When the repair lands, the limit is what keeps it.

THE LOCAL REPLAY CANNOT RUN TWO OF THE NINE JOBS, and it says so rather than running them wrong. `msrv` reads its toolchain from `${{ steps.msrv.outputs.version }}` and `cache-budget` needs `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`; both are resolved by GitHub from things this machine does not have. Replayed on the dev toolchain, `msrv`'s units would collide with every other job's and the report would claim a duplication that does not exist.

THE REPAIR IS NOT IN THIS ROUND AND THE MEASUREMENT IS WHY. 2236 of the 3132 go away if the jobs that share units become one job; the remaining 896 do not, because they are one job compiling one unit twice over its own separate workspaces. A compilation cache (`sccache`, the NN9 carry that was excluded by argument rather than by measurement) is the only thing that reaches both halves — AND THIS GATE CANNOT JUDGE IT: cargo still asks for every one of those units and the recorder still records them, so the census does not move when the cache is hit. The number that would move is time, and that needs a second instrument. Writing "sccache is the answer" today would be R1090's mistake again, one field over.

THE 57.1% IS A COLD FIGURE AND THE CI FIGURE WILL BE LOWER, because a job that restored a warm cache runs `rustc` fewer times. Both are honest and they answer different questions: the cold one is the structural duplication, the CI one is the bill that run actually paid. The gate reports whichever it is given, and the first CI run is what says how far apart they are here.

A WAITER THAT MATCHED ITSELF, found by the owner asking what was still running. Two background loops of the form `until ! pgrep -f "cargo test --workspace"; do sleep; done` never terminated, because the shell running the loop has that string in its own command line — so the chained verification behind them never started while this session believed it was in progress. It is the same shape as the third defect this round repaired in code: the gate's own job wrote its log into the directory it then read, putting the instrument inside its own reading. A process check must exclude the checker, exactly as a census must exclude the job taking it.

Per job (compiled / distinct / repeated): side-workspaces 1188/946/242, unrun-tests 1160/985/175, uncompiled-sources 1105/924/181, validate 954/659/295, item-citations 567/564/3, server-features 510/510/0. Probes and unkeyed invocations are printed beside them rather than dropped, so the classes this reader cannot key are visible instead of silently absent.

THE MSRV CONTROL IS NOT YET DISCHARGED, and it is named rather than assumed: the local replay refuses to run `msrv`, so the claim that cargo's `-C metadata` separates two compilers has not been observed in this repository. The first CI run of this gate is what tests it — if `msrv` shows any shared units at all, the unit key is wrong.
publishable_carry_forward_bullets: THREE THINGS THE RECORDER CANNOT SEE, and all three under-count, which is the safe direction for a finding of the form "this work is done more than once". `rustdoc` does not go through `RUSTC_WRAPPER`, and `item-citations` documents 134 targets. A build script's own `cc` is not `rustc`, and `librocksdb-sys` compiles C in six of these jobs. A unit that was already fresh is never handed to a compiler at all.

`evidence-replay.yml` IS NOT IN THE CENSUS and closing that is not worth a job. Artifacts do not cross workflow runs, so a second workflow needs a second gate — and that workflow has exactly ONE job, which makes its cross-job duplication zero by construction. What it would buy is a guaranteed zero; what it would cost is a whole job.

THE GATE REPORTS THE DUPLICATION AND DOES NOT YET REFUSE IT. There is no honest limit to assert before the repair exists: R1090 shipped a gate whose limit was a prediction, and the prediction was wrong by a factor of two on the first run. When the repair lands, the limit is what keeps it.

THE LOCAL REPLAY CANNOT RUN TWO OF THE NINE JOBS, and it says so rather than running them wrong. `msrv` reads its toolchain from `${{ steps.msrv.outputs.version }}` and `cache-budget` needs `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`; both are resolved by GitHub from things this machine does not have. Replayed on the dev toolchain, `msrv`'s units would collide with every other job's and the report would claim a duplication that does not exist.

THE REPAIR IS NOT IN THIS ROUND AND THE MEASUREMENT IS WHY. 2236 of the 3132 go away if the jobs that share units become one job; the remaining 896 do not, because they are one job compiling one unit twice over its own separate workspaces. A compilation cache (`sccache`, the NN9 carry that was excluded by argument rather than by measurement) is the only thing that reaches both halves — AND THIS GATE CANNOT JUDGE IT: cargo still asks for every one of those units and the recorder still records them, so the census does not move when the cache is hit. The number that would move is time, and that needs a second instrument. Writing "sccache is the answer" today would be R1090's mistake again, one field over.

THE 57.1% IS A COLD FIGURE AND THE CI FIGURE WILL BE LOWER, because a job that restored a warm cache runs `rustc` fewer times. Both are honest and they answer different questions: the cold one is the structural duplication, the CI one is the bill that run actually paid. The gate reports whichever it is given, and the first CI run is what says how far apart they are here.

A WAITER THAT MATCHED ITSELF, found by the owner asking what was still running. Two background loops of the form `until ! pgrep -f "cargo test --workspace"; do sleep; done` never terminated, because the shell running the loop has that string in its own command line — so the chained verification behind them never started while this session believed it was in progress. It is the same shape as the third defect this round repaired in code: the gate's own job wrote its log into the directory it then read, putting the instrument inside its own reading. A process check must exclude the checker, exactly as a census must exclude the job taking it.

Round 1093 — a compilation is not a comp.decision_summary:
A COMPILATION IS NOT A COMPILATION, and until this round nothing here could say
so. Round 1092 built a census of what this repository's CI compiles and found
that half of it is compiled twice — 2718 of 5402 on the first CI run, 3132 of
5484 replayed cold. It ranked that surplus by rows, and the head of the list was
`build_script_build` with 409 surplus compilations, then `proc_macro2` 62 and
`syn` 62. A build script is among the cheapest units cargo drives. One
`mnemosyne-store` test binary is among the dearest. Ranked by rows the repair
goes to the dependencies; ranked by seconds it may not go there at all, and the
report had no way to tell the two orders apart.

TWO CARRIES NAMED THE SAME MISSING THING. QQ2 said the repair must weigh the
1921 cross-job duplicates against the wall-clock that merging spends, because
two jobs beside one another cost the longer of them and one merged job costs
both — and then said, of the gate that had just been built, that it answers
compilation counts and does not answer time. QQ3 said `sccache` cannot be judged
by this census at all: a cache hit does not stop cargo asking for the unit, so
the recorder still records it and the census does not move. What moves is time.
Both carries end at the same sentence, which Round 1092 wrote down as the thing
it could not do: THE NUMBER THAT WOULD MOVE IS TIME, AND THAT NEEDS A SECOND
INSTRUMENT. This round is that instrument, and it is not a second one — it is the
same one, given a clock.

THE WRAPPER STOPS BECOMING THE COMPILER AND WAITS FOR IT. That is the one thing
here that costs something, and it is the whole reason the clock is possible: an
`exec` replaces the wrapper's process, so the only moment left to write a record
is BEFORE the compiler starts, and a record written then can say what was
compiled but never what it cost. What waiting buys is the duration. What it
risks is the exit status — with `exec` cargo saw the compiler's own, because the
wrapper WAS the compiler, and now a process stands between them and has to hand
it over unchanged. Both halves of that are tested: a compilation that exits 7
reaches cargo as 7, and a compiler the kernel kills reaches it as 128 + the
signal rather than as the `unwrap_or(0)` that would turn the loudest failure a
build can have into a pass. Nothing else in this repository would notice that.

TWO CLOCKS PER RECORD, AND THE SECOND IS NOT DECORATION. The duration is read
monotonically, so it cannot move because something stepped the system clock
mid-compilation. The start is read off the wall clock, because its whole purpose
is to be compared against starts recorded by OTHER processes — the dozens of
wrappers cargo has running at once — and a monotonic instant has no meaning
outside the process that read it. Having both is what separates a job's WORK
from its WINDOW: the durations sum to the area under every compiler the job ran,
which is larger than the job, and the window from the earliest start to the
latest exit is the shape that sum was spread over. Their ratio is how many
compilers were alive on average, and that ratio is what says whether removing
work from a job removes minutes from it.

THE WINDOW IS READ OFF THE CLOCKS AND NOT OFF THE ORDER OF THE LINES, which is a
defect avoided rather than a style. A record is appended when a compiler EXITS,
and the long compilation that began a job finishes after the short ones that
began later — so the earliest start routinely arrives last. A reader taking the
first and last lines of the log would read a window shorter than the job's, every
time, and a job that looks busier than it was is a job whose duplication looks
cheaper to remove than it is.

EVERY FIGURE ERRS IN A NAMED DIRECTION, and the directions are chosen so that
this report can never talk somebody into a repair. The same unit takes different
times in different jobs, and the one compilation that survives a merge has to be
priced at one of them: it is priced at the DEAREST observed, which makes the
floor as high as the evidence allows and every reported saving the LEAST the
repair could win. A pair's saving prices the compilation that disappears at the
CHEAPER of the two jobs' figures, for the same reason from the other side. Both
choices are pinned by injections that flip them.

MERGING TWO JOBS CAN ONLY EVER SPEND WALL-CLOCK, and the report now says so in
the same breath as the saving. Today a pair runs side by side and costs the run
the longer of the two windows; merged, it cannot be quicker than that and cannot
be slower than the two end to end. Those two bounds are arithmetic on observed
spans and nothing else.

BETWEEN THEM SITS AN ESTIMATE, AND THE FIRST DRAFT OF IT ASSUMED SOMETHING THE
RECORDS CAN SAY. Scaling a pair's combined window by the work that remains
treats every minute in that window as compiling — and a window holds the minutes
a job spends running the binaries it just built, which do not get shorter because
it compiled less. The two jobs in this repository with the most to share are the
two that spend the longest running what they built, so that assumption was
pointed exactly at the case it is worst for. It was not carried: the records
already say when each compiler ran, so the union of those intervals is the part
of a window with a compiler alive in it and the rest is measured idle. The
estimate scales the first and carries the second across whole. What remains
assumed is only that the merged job compiles at the rate the two of them did,
which a runner with a fixed core count makes very nearly true.

A JOB WHOSE COMPILATIONS TOOK NO TIME AT ALL IS NOW REFUSED. It is the quieter
way this instrument can go silent, and no count can notice it: the compilations
are all there, every total adds up, the percentages print — and only the seconds
are zero, which reads as work that is free. Free work is exactly the finding a
reader of this report is hunting for, so the wrong answer here is the one shaped
like an argument for merging every job in the file. It is what a job running an
OLDER recorder produces, which is a real state on a runner that restored a
cached binary, and it is refused with the same law that refuses a job that left
no record at all — once, never twice, because a job with no compilations has no
seconds either and naming both would send whoever reads it after a clock when
the recorder never ran.

WHAT THIS ROUND DOES NOT HAVE IS THE ANSWER. It has the instrument and the proof
that the instrument can fail; the priced census of this CI arrives with the next
run, which will be a cold one for every job because every cache key in the
workflow hashes the workflow and the workflow changed. That is the run that says
whether the 1921 cross-job duplicates are worth the minutes merging would spend,
and it is the first thing this gate has ever been able to be asked.
changes_bullets: `tools/rustc-log` — the record grew a clock and the wrapper stopped `exec`-ing the compiler. A record is now `started_at` (microseconds since the Unix epoch, a WALL clock because it is compared against starts written by the other wrappers running at the same moment), `micros` (read monotonically, so a stepped system clock cannot move it) and then the compiler and its arguments as before. The wrapper runs the compiler, waits, writes the record — including for a compilation that FAILED, because a build that broke still paid for every `rustc` it ran — and exits with the compiler's own status, `128 + signal` when the kernel killed it rather than a code of its own.

`rustc_log::decode` REFUSES a record whose clock field is not a number instead of reading it as zero. The case is a log left by an older wrapper: its first field is the compiler's path, so it decodes into perfectly plausible arguments with every compilation costing nothing — and free work is the finding a reader of these logs is hunting for, so the tolerant spelling is how a wrong answer arrives wearing the shape of a discovery.

`tools/twice-compiled` — every number in the census now comes in two. `Cost { times, micros }` replaces the per-unit count; `JobLog` carries the whole job's invocation time and its compiling WINDOW (earliest start to latest exit, taken from the clocks rather than from the order of the lines, because a record is appended when a compiler exits and the earliest start routinely arrives last). `Census` gained `paid_micros` / `floor_micros` / `repeated_within_jobs_micros` / `shared_between_jobs_micros`, split the same way and by the same definition-as-remainder as the counts, so the two halves and the whole cannot drift apart by a rounded microsecond.

`JobLog` keeps the INTERVALS rather than folding them into a window, because a window cannot answer what a window is asked for. `busy_micros` is the union of them — the part of the job with at least one compiler alive, which is what compiling less can shorten — and `idle_micros` is the rest, the minutes a job spends running the binaries it just built. Summing the intervals instead of unioning them would report a job busier than the clock allows and leave it with no idle time at all.

`twice_compiled::Merge` states both sides of merging a pair: the compilations it removes and what they cost, priced at the cheaper of the two jobs' figures; and the merged job's window as a RANGE — never quicker than the longer of the two it replaces, which is also exactly what the pair costs the run today, and never slower than the two end to end. Between them the estimate scales only the BUSY part by the work that remains and carries the idle part across whole. Scaling the whole window would have promised a merged job shorter than either of the jobs it replaces, and the two jobs here with the most to share are the two that spend the longest running what they built.

`Census::surplus_by_crate` returns a priced `Cost` per crate and the report ranks by seconds rather than by rows. That ordering is the round's finding: `build_script_build` heads the row ranking with 409 surplus compilations and is among the cheapest units cargo drives, so a report that ranks by rows recommends a repair for the crates that cost the least.

`Refusal::JobRecordedNoTime` — a job that compiled and whose compilations took no time at all is refused. Counts present, totals adding up, seconds zero: the shape a job running an older recorder leaves, and the one no count can notice. A job that recorded nothing at all is still refused once and not twice.

`tools/rustc-log/injection-sweep.json` and `tools/twice-compiled/injection-sweep.json` (new) — eleven injections between them, each removing one mechanism this round added and naming the test that must go red for it. Both are scoped to their own crate's suite, which reads records rather than building anything, so each sweep is seconds.

`.github/workflows/mnemosyne-validate.yml` — the two comment blocks that state what the recorder records and what the gate asserts now say that a record carries what a compilation cost and that a census with no clocks in it is refused. No step changed; every cache key hashes this file, so the next run is a cold one for every job.
verification_bullets: THE INJECTION SWEEPS, both green and both non-vacuous: `tools/rustc-log/injection-sweep.json` 5 of 5 fired, `tools/twice-compiled/injection-sweep.json` 8 of 8, missed 0, target drift 0, and each control run green first (9 passed over 4 targets, 28 passed over 5). Every mechanism this round added is pinned by an injection that removes it and a named test that goes red.

THE INJECTION A LOWER BOUND CANNOT CATCH. `the-duration-is-a-constant` writes 1_000_000 µs instead of measuring, which satisfies every assertion of the form "the compilation took at least this long" — the obvious test for a clock. What catches it is the window: the record's start and end must lie inside the window the test itself observed around the child, and a constant large enough to pass the first assertion overruns the second. The start has its own injection (`the-start-is-not-a-clock`) and fails the same assertion from the other end.

THE EXIT STATUS, both halves, because waiting for the compiler is what put it at risk. `a_compilation_that_failed_is_reported_as_failed_and_still_recorded` runs a child that exits 7 and requires cargo to see 7 AND the record to be written anyway; `a_compiler_the_kernel_killed_is_not_handed_over_as_success` runs one that kills itself with SIGKILL and requires 128 + 9. Injections `the-compilers-exit-code-is-swallowed` and `a-killed-compiler-exits-zero` turn each of them red.

THE WINDOW IS PROVED AGAINST THE CASE THAT MAKES IT NECESSARY: two records where the LATER line has the EARLIER start, which is what a long compilation and a short one look like in a log appended at exit. The window is the earliest start to the latest exit, the span is 900 µs, and the work is 1000 µs — larger than the window, because the two overlapped. `the-window-is-the-first-line-to-the-last` reduces it to 400 µs and goes red.

THE TWO ERROR DIRECTIONS ARE PINNED BY THE INJECTIONS THAT FLIP THEM. `the-surviving-compilation-is-priced-at-the-cheapest` prices the retained compilation at the minimum instead of the maximum and turns the floor red; `a-merge-is-credited-with-the-dearer-of-the-two` credits a merge with the larger of the two prices and turns both the census test and the merge test red. Neither could be caught by a total, because both keep every total adding up.

THE FINDING ITSELF IS A TEST. `the_most_numerous_surplus_and_the_dearest_are_not_the_same_crate` builds two jobs that each compile three `build_script_build` units at 5 µs and one `mnemosyne_store` unit at 900, and asserts that the row ranking heads with the build scripts and the second ranking heads with the store — the two orders naming two different repairs. `the-crate-breakdown-is-counted-and-not-priced` stops accumulating the seconds and turns it red along with the per-crate identity.

THE NEW LAW HAS A CONTROL. `a_job_whose_compilations_took_no_time_at_all_is_refused` takes the census that is otherwise accepted, zeroes one job's seconds, and requires exactly that refusal; the accepted census is the same fixture with its clocks intact, and `a_job_that_recorded_nothing_is_refused_once_and_not_twice` holds the two laws apart.

END TO END ON REAL CARGO, not fixtures: `tools/ci-plan` built twice under the recorder into two separate target directories named for two real jobs, then the census read over both. It reported 12 compilations paid, 6 distinct, 50.0% duplicated by rows and 49.0% by seconds (2.2 s paid, 1.1 s floor), each job compiling within a 0.9 s window at 1.2 compilers at once, a merge removing 6 compilations and 1.1 s and lengthening the window from 0.9 s to an estimated 1.0 s — and refused the seven jobs of the workflow that did not run in the smoke, exiting 1, which is the law working.

THE IDLE TIME IS MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED, which is a carry this round refused to write. `the_part_of_a_window_with_no_compiler_alive_is_measured_and_not_assumed` pins the union of the intervals against their sum — two compilers overlapping and a gap after them make a 600 µs window in which 250 µs is busy, where summing would claim 300 µs of busy and no idle at all. `a_merge_estimate_does_not_shorten_the_time_no_compiler_was_alive` builds the pair this repository actually has, jobs that spend nine tenths of their window running what they built, and requires the estimate to be 1900 µs where scaling the whole window says 1000 — a merged job shorter than either of the two it replaces. Both injections (`a-job-is-busy-for-the-sum-of-its-compilers`, `the-estimate-scales-the-whole-window`) turn them red.

THE GATE THAT RUNS THESE WORKSPACES IN CI: `scripts/check-side-workspaces.sh tools/rustc-log tools/twice-compiled` clean end to end — `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings`, the item-citation gate, the blind-wait gate and both suites, checked 2, skipped 0. Suites are 9 tests for the recorder (4 new) and 28 for the census (25 law, 3 against this repository's own workflow), all green.
carry_forward_bullets: THE PRICED CENSUS OF THIS CI DOES NOT EXIST YET, and only a run can make it. The gate reads logs the jobs wrote while doing work they were doing anyway, so the numbers arrive with the next push and cost nothing; the alternative is a local replay, which takes hours and cannot run `msrv` or `cache-budget` at all because GitHub resolves their environment. The next run is a COLD one for every job — every cache key hashes the workflow and the workflow changed — which is the run that gives the structural figure rather than the warm bill.

WHAT THE SECONDS STILL CANNOT SAY IS A JOB'S DURATION. The window is the first compiler's start to the last one's exit: it excludes the checkout, the toolchain install, the cache restore and the artifact upload, and merging two jobs saves one of each of those, which nothing here counts. GitHub knows those numbers and `cache-budget` already reaches the API with a token, so joining a run's job durations to this census is a describable piece of work rather than a limit — it is deferred as a COST judgement, and this bullet is where that is said out loud rather than dressed as impossibility.

QQ3 IS NOW JUDGEABLE AND STILL NOT JUDGED. `sccache` cannot move this census — a cache hit does not stop cargo asking for the unit, so the recorder records it either way — and what it moves is the seconds, which now exist. What would decide it is a job whose unit count is unchanged and whose compiling seconds fall, which is a comparison between two runs and needs the baseline above first. Writing "sccache is the answer" before that is R1090's mistake one field over, which is the mistake Round 1092 named and did not commit.

THE RECORDER CANNOT SEE FOUR THINGS AND ALL FOUR UNDER-COUNT, which is the safe direction for a finding of the form "this work is done more than once". A unit that was already fresh is never handed to a compiler. `rustdoc` does not go through `RUSTC_WRAPPER`. A build script's own `cc` is not `rustc`, and `librocksdb-sys` compiles C in six of these jobs. And now: a compilation that never finished, because the record is written when the compiler exits — that is where the duration becomes known — so a job killed at its timeout loses whatever was in flight.

THE ESTIMATE KEEPS ONE ASSUMPTION AND IT IS NAMED. The idle part of a window is measured and carried across untouched; the compiling part is scaled by the work removed, which assumes the merged job compiles at the rate the two of them did. A runner with a fixed core count makes that very nearly true, and the two bounds around the estimate hold whether or not it is: a merged job is never quicker than the longer of the pair and never slower than the two end to end.

MERGING CAN ONLY EVER SPEND WALL-CLOCK. Two jobs beside one another cost the run the longer of them; one merged job cannot be quicker than that. So the trade this gate now states is compute against minutes, and there is no arrangement of the numbers in which merging is free. That is a property of the shape and not of this repository's figures, and it is worth having in front of whoever reads the census first.
