publishable_carry_forward_bullets: A PATH CANNOT SAY IT IS NOT CARGO'S. `Origin` demands cargo's whole layout below the pair that names it, and a crate of this repository's own called `registry` holding a `src/<name>-<version>/` would still read as fetched. Nothing in a path distinguishes those two, and the reader is given no repository to check against — `compare` holds censuses of two commits and has neither. The direction is chosen and the rule is the tightest one a path admits.

THIS INSTRUMENT SAYS WHAT WAS COMPILED AND CANNOT SAY WHAT WOULD HAVE BEEN. That 73.9% of compilations are fetched crates is a measurement; that a compile cache would remove them is not, and no census of what ran can be made to answer it. XX2's second half — WHY a runner recompiles dependencies whose sources it restored exactly — still needs the experiment it has been carried with: a dedicated `CARGO_HOME` and a cold fetch, run twice, which is a thing done to a machine rather than read off one.

THE DRIVER IN THE KEY IS A MACHINE-SPECIFIC STRING, so a census taken on a runner and one taken by a local replay now share no unit at all. That is the cost of keeping what the record says instead of parsing a meaning out of it, and it is affordable only because `compare` is for two runs of the same CI. A comparison of a runner against a replay was never available and is now unavailable for a second reason.

THE COUNTS ARE STABLE ACROSS RUNS AND THE SECONDS ARE NOT. The two runs compared here differ by 13 compilations and by 155.6 seconds of compiler time over an unchanged 5531 of them — runner speed, not work. So a delta in seconds is not readable as a change in what CI does, and every finding this arc has drawn has been drawn from the counts. Pricing a repair still needs the seconds, and they carry that noise into it.

Round 1110.decision_summary:
CI WENT RED ON A RACE THIS SUITE HAD CARRIED SINCE THE ROUND THAT WROTE IT, and
the shape it goes red in is the one that teaches people to ignore a gate. Run
31318819564 failed on `separate in-repo workspaces` with
`ExecutableFileBusy` — "Text file busy" — from
`a_suite_that_replaces_the_tool_does_not_end_the_sweep`, the R1108 test that
copies the harness binary and runs the copy. The commit under it touched
`tools/twice-compiled` and the store and nothing else; the same test had been
green on the run before. A gate that fails on a commit it has nothing to do with
is a gate whose next red gets read as noise.

`ETXTBSY` IS NOT A MYSTERY AND IT IS NOT THIS TEST BEING CARELESS. The kernel
refuses to exec a file some process holds open for writing, and after `fs::copy`
returns THIS process does not. Another does: a sibling test thread that forks
between our write and our exec hands its child a copy of the whole descriptor
table, and until that child reaches its own `exec` — which is where `O_CLOEXEC`
finally closes our descriptor — the kernel is right. `RUST_TEST_THREADS` is 4
here and the other tests in this file all spawn processes, so the window is
open constantly and is microseconds wide. That is why it fires on a loaded CI
runner and not on a developer's machine, which is the worst possible place for
a gate's only failure mode to live.

SO THE EXEC RETRIES ON THAT ONE ERROR KIND AND ON NOTHING ELSE. A program that
is genuinely missing, or not executable, fails on the first attempt with its own
message; only `ExecutableFileBusy` is tried again, and the bound is there so a
permanent one ends as a failure rather than a hang. It is a condition and not a
sleep — there is no wait in it at all, which is what `tools/blind-waits` is in
this repository to insist on.

WHAT THIS CANNOT HAVE IS AN INJECTION. Every other contract in this arc is held
non-vacuous by breaking it and requiring a named test to go red; removing this
retry does not make anything red, it makes something red SOMETIMES. A defect
whose signature is intermittency cannot be proved absent by the method this arc
uses, and saying so is the honest half of shipping the repair.
changes_bullets: `tools/injection-harness/tests/harness.rs` — `run_a_freshly_written_program`, which execs a program this process wrote a moment ago and retries only on `ErrorKind::ExecutableFileBusy`. `a_suite_that_replaces_the_tool_does_not_end_the_sweep` is its one caller and the one place in this repository that copies a binary and runs the copy.

The retry is bounded, so a permanent `ETXTBSY` ends as a named failure rather than a hang, and it holds no wait at all — the window it is crossing is another thread's fork-to-exec, which is microseconds.
verification_bullets: THE FAILURE IS QUOTED RATHER THAN CHARACTERISED: run 31318819564, job `separate in-repo workspaces`, `panicked at tests/harness.rs:827: the copied tool runs: Os { code: 26, kind: ExecutableFileBusy, message: "Text file busy" }`, 20 passed and 1 failed. The commit under it, `cd1c8ee`, changed `tools/twice-compiled` and the atomic store and nothing that this test reads.

IT IS INTERMITTENT AND THAT IS ESTABLISHED FROM THE LEDGER RATHER THAN ASSERTED: the same suite ran for the first time in CI on run 31316052015, the commit before, and was green — which is what makes this a race and not a break.

The `injection-harness` suite is 31 green locally on this repair, run with the exact command the workflow uses (`cargo test --manifest-path tools/injection-harness/Cargo.toml --locked --no-fail-fast`).

GATES: `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` clean; `tools/blind-waits` reports no blind or spelled wait site, which is the gate that would have refused a sleep here; `mnemosyne-cli validate-workspace` clean.
carry_forward_bullets: THIS REPAIR CANNOT BE HELD NON-VACUOUS THE WAY EVERY OTHER ONE IN THIS ARC IS. An injection proves a contract by breaking it and requiring a named test to go red; removing this retry makes a test red SOMETIMES, on a loaded machine, in a window microseconds wide. The method this arc runs on cannot speak about intermittency, and the only evidence that the repair holds is that the race it names is the one the kernel reported.

THE WINDOW IS ANOTHER THREAD'S AND NOTHING HERE OWNS IT. The fix crosses the race rather than removing it: any test in this file that spawns a process can still hand a child a descriptor to a file another test just wrote. What removes it is a test harness that does not fork while a sibling holds a writable descriptor, which is not something a test can arrange for itself.

NO OTHER COPY-THEN-EXEC SITE WAS FOUND IN THIS REPOSITORY, and that is a search rather than a guarantee: a future test that writes a program and runs it inherits the same race and nothing will tell it so until CI is red on an unrelated commit.

Round 1111.decision_summary:
THE NUMBER THE ROUND BEFORE THIS PRODUCED READ AS AN INDICTMENT AND IS NOT ONE.
R1109 measured that 73.9% of the compilations this CI pays for are crates cargo
fetched, in a run where every cached job restored `~/.cargo/registry` on an
exact hit — and the sharpest single line of it was `unrun-tests`, the one job
that also caches `target`, restoring 27258 MB exactly and still compiling 461
fetched units. Read as it stood, that is a cache that is not working. It is the
opposite. Of those 461, ZERO went into the tree the cache restored: the root
`target` received 242 compilations and every one of them was this repository's
own code, which is exactly what a working restore of a fresh commit looks like.
The 461 went into `bench/target` (281) and ten `tools/*/target` directories,
none of which appears in any `path:` list in the workflow.

SO THE MISSING AXIS WAS WHERE THE OUTPUT WENT, and it was in the records all
along — `--out-dir` is an argument of every compilation cargo drives, and the
reader was keeping the input path and dropping the output one. A destination is
now read beside the origin and the two travel together, because neither answers
the question alone: the fetched share cannot say whether that work landed in the
tree the cache brought back or in one no cache holds, and those are opposite
findings about the same count.

THE DESTINATION IS NOT PART OF THE UNIT AND MUST NOT BECOME ONE. A job holding
two `target` directories compiles a shared crate into both, and that second
compilation IS the finding — the within-job repetition no merge of jobs can
remove, which this arc has carried as an open debt since R1097. Putting the
destination in the key would split those two into two units and erase it,
reporting a job that pays twice as one that paid once for two different things.
So it is a second axis over the same population, and that the two axes sum to
the same compilations and the same seconds is asserted rather than assumed:
nothing about the way each is folded makes them agree.

WHAT THE COVERAGE READING JOINS is the workflow's `path:` list against the
destinations, with the declared paths made ABSOLUTE against the checkout first.
That is not tidiness: `<root>/bench/target` does not begin with `<root>/target`
however much the two spellings share, and a suffix search would report the
bench workspace's 314 compilations as held by the root cache. The longest
declared path wins, so a job caching two nested trees is not told everything
landed in the shallower.

AND IT REFUSES TO ANSWER FROM THE WRONG MACHINE. An `--out-dir` written on a
runner begins `/home/runner/work/…`, and no path under a different checkout will
ever prefix it — so a reader that answered anyway would report every compilation
in a downloaded census as work no cache could spare. Not one destination under
the root it was given is exactly that, and it is said rather than answered. The
same census read from the machine it was taken on resolves, which is what the
test holds it to.
changes_bullets: `tools/twice-compiled/src/lib.rs` — `Compiled { unit, into }` and `Destination { out_dir, origin }`. `read` now returns both, and `read_log` folds the destination into `JobLog::written` beside the unit table. The destination is a SECOND AXIS and not a finer key, because a job compiling one crate into two `target` directories is the within-job repetition this arc has carried as a debt since R1097, and putting the destination in the key erases it.

`tools/twice-compiled/src/lib.rs` — `JobLog::coverage`, returning `Coverage { held, outside }`: what each declared cache path holds and what none of them reaches, split by whose source it was. The declared paths are made absolute against the checkout before anything is compared, and the longest match wins, so `<root>/bench/target` is never reported as held by `<root>/target`.

`tools/twice-compiled/src/lib.rs` — `Coverage::outside` is keyed by TREE and not summed into one number, because the repair is a `path:` line naming a directory and one total says a cache is not reaching without saying where to point it. `Destination::tree` cuts at the last `target` component, which is cargo's default and this repository's, and returns the destination WHOLE when there is none rather than at a guess.

`tools/twice-compiled/src/lib.rs` — `coverage` returns `None` when not one destination lies under the root it was given: a census taken on another machine, where answering would report every compilation as work no cache could spare.
`tools/twice-compiled/src/lib.rs` — `Refusal::JobWroteWhereNothingSaid`. A compilation naming no `--out-dir` is absent from both halves, which still sum and still print.

`tools/twice-compiled/src/main.rs` — the per-job coverage rows, naming each held path and each tree outside every one of them; and, for a census from elsewhere, the destinations themselves rather than a bare refusal to read them.

`tools/twice-compiled/tests/law.rs`, `tests/entrances.rs` — 7 new tests: both halves summing to the job, the deeper declared path not shadowed by the shorter, a cargo-home path holding no compiler output here, the wrong-machine refusal held against the same census read from the right one, the destination refusal with its accepting sibling, and the two axes agreeing on the origin totals. The runner fixtures now name an `--out-dir`, which the new refusal caught them not doing.

`tools/twice-compiled/injection-sweep.json` — 5 new injections: the wrong-machine check, the longest-match assignment, the tree grouping, the destination refusal, and the report row that carries the finding.
verification_bullets: THE FINDING, read off run 31316052015 with the gate itself: of `unrun-tests`'s 796 compilations, 242 went into the root `target` its cache restored on an exact 27258 MB hit and EVERY ONE OF THOSE 242 was this repository's own code. Its 461 fetched compilations went to `bench/target` (281) and ten `tools/*/target` directories (180) — trees no `path:` list in the workflow names. The 27 GB restore was not failing; it was never asked.

AND IT IS NOT ONE JOB. Summed over the run, ALL 4095 fetched compilations landed in a tree their job's cache does not hold. The two `target` trees any job caches — `unrun-tests`'s root `target` and `tools/unrun-tests/target`, plus `item-citations`' and `uncompiled-sources`' own tool trees — received 0 fetched compilations between them. The registry cache brings dependency SOURCES and every job then compiles them into a directory nothing carries.

BOTH BREAKDOWNS OF ONE POPULATION AGREE, ASSERTED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. The origin totals folded from the unit table and the ones folded from the destinations are held equal in a test, and the two halves of a coverage are held to sum to the job's compilations. Nothing about the way either is built makes them agree.

THE WRONG-MACHINE REFUSAL IS HELD AGAINST THE SAME CENSUS READ FROM THE RIGHT ONE. A destination beginning `/home/runner/work/…` resolves against that root and refuses against another, which is one test with both arms rather than an assertion that something is absent.

THE NEW REFUSAL CAUGHT THIS SUITE'S OWN FIXTURES. `record_a_compilation` named no `--out-dir`, which cargo always passes and which leaves a compilation absent from both halves of the coverage; the runner test went red on the first build and the fixtures now say where they wrote — anchored to the checkout the gate runs in, which is what exercises the join at all.

INJECTION: 41 injections, 41 fired, 0 missed, drift 0, control 97 green over 6 targets. The five new ones break the wrong-machine check, the longest-match assignment, the tree grouping, the destination refusal, and the report row that carries the finding.

AND THE ANCHOR LAW R1108 BUILT CAUGHT A BAD ANCHOR IN THIS ROUND'S OWN SWEEP before it could become a silent no-op: one `from` was written with the wrong indentation and matched 0 times. That is the failure it exists for, on its second real day.

GATES: `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` clean on `tools/twice-compiled`; its suite 97 green; the anchor law over every tracked sweep green; `mnemosyne-cli validate-workspace` clean.
carry_forward_bullets: THE REPAIR THIS MEASURES IS NOT ONE THIS ROUND MAY MAKE ALONE. Declaring `bench/target` and the eleven `tools/*/target` trees in the caches that build them is what these rows argue for, and it is a decision rather than a fix: it changes the workflow, which invalidates every key and costs one cold run of everything, and `tools/cache-budget` holds this repository to 10 GB against an API that already reports 7.83 GB held. Which trees are worth the space is a judgement about what CI is for, and the number that would settle it — what each tree costs restored — is not in any record here.

"NO RESTORE COULD HAVE SPARED THIS" IS NOT "A CACHE WOULD SPARE IT". The reading says a compilation landed where the declared paths do not reach, which is a fact about a run; whether a cache declaring that tree would then find those units fresh depends on fingerprints this instrument never sees. The 4095 is a ceiling and the round after this one would have to measure the floor.

THE TREE IS CUT AT THE LAST COMPONENT CALLED `target`, WHICH IS AN ASSUMPTION. It is cargo's default and this repository sets no `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`; a checkout that did would print whole `--out-dir` values — long rows rather than wrong ones — and nothing here would say why. The coverage halves themselves do not depend on it, only the naming of the rows.

A DOWNLOADED CENSUS CANNOT BE ASKED WHAT ITS CACHE REACHED. The join is against a checkout and the destinations are absolute, so only the machine a census was taken on can read its coverage. The report prints the destinations instead, which is the data the join would have been made of, and this is the second reading (after the driver in the key) that a runner census and a local one no longer share.

`~/.cargo/registry` AND `~/.cargo/git` COVER NOTHING HERE, correctly — a cargo home holds sources, not compiler output — but the reason is that `~` is a shell's and no path this reader builds will ever prefix a destination. A cache path that failed to resolve for any OTHER reason would be silently uncovered the same way, and nothing distinguishes the two.

fetched, in a run where every cached job restored `~/.cargo/registry` on an
exact hit — and the sharpest single line of it was `unrun-tests`, the one job
that also caches `target`, restoring 27258 MB exactly and still compiling 461
fetched units. Read as it stood, that is a cache that is not working. It is the
opposite. Of those 461, ZERO went into the tree the cache restored: the root
`target` received 242 compilations and every one of them was this repository's
own code, which is exactly what a working restore of a fresh commit looks like.
The 461 went into `bench/target` (281) and ten `tools/*/target` directories,
none of which appears in any `path:` list in the workflow.

SO THE MISSING AXIS WAS WHERE THE OUTPUT WENT, and it was in the records all
along — `--out-dir` is an argument of every compilation cargo drives, and the
reader was keeping the input path and dropping the output one. A destination is
now read beside the origin and the two travel together, because neither answers
the question alone: the fetched share cannot say whether that work landed in the
tree the cache brought back or in one no cache holds, and those are opposite
findings about the same count.

two `target` directories compiles a shared crate into both, and that second
compilation IS the finding — the within-job repetition no merge of jobs can
remove, which this arc has carried as an open debt since R1097. Putting the
destination in the key would split those two into two units and erase it,
reporting a job that pays twice as one that paid once for two different things.

the same compilations and the same seconds is asserted rather than assumed:
nothing about the way each is folded makes them agree.

destinations, with the declared paths made ABSOLUTE against the checkout first.

declared path wins, so a job caching two nested trees is not told everything

runner begins `/home/runner/work/…`, and no path under a different checkout will

the root it was given is exactly that, and it is said rather than answered. The
same census read from the machine it was taken on resolves, which is what the

Round 1112.decision_summary:
THIS REPOSITORY COMPILED INTO THIRTEEN BUILD DIRECTORIES AND CACHED THREE OF
THEM. R1111 measured where every compilation of a run was written and found that
all 4095 of its fetched ones landed in a tree no cache of their job holds — and
the run this round reads decomposes that: 1959 into the root `target` in the
five jobs that do not declare it, 1186 into `bench/target`, 707 into eleven
`tools/*/target`, and 243 into temporary directories a test made and deleted.
The three trees that ARE cached received zero fetched compilations between them.

THE OBVIOUS REPAIR IS THE WRONG ONE. Declaring the twelve missing trees in the
caches that build them stores one copy of the same `libserde.rlib` per (job,
tree) pair, and this repository is already holding 7.83 GB against a 10 GB
budget with three trees declared. The duplication being paid for is
CONTENT-IDENTICAL WORK AT DIFFERENT PATHS — a shape a key made of paths cannot
dedupe by construction — so buying more paths buys more copies of one artifact.

SO THE INPUT IS REDUCED BEFORE ANYTHING IS CACHED. `.cargo/config.toml` sets
`build.target-dir`, which cargo resolves against the directory holding that file
rather than against whoever ran the command, so every one of this checkout's
workspaces now compiles into ONE directory — measured here rather than assumed,
by running a tool's build from inside its own workspace and finding the binary at
the repository root. Thirteen trees become one; 3852 of the 4095 collapse into a
single directory per job, and the 243 left are compilations into temporary trees
that no cache could ever have held.

AND IT REMOVES DUPLICATION RATHER THAN STORING IT. The units two workspaces share
are the SAME unit to cargo — `-C metadata` hashes the package, the features, the
profile and the compiler, not the path — so a shared build directory makes the
second compilation not happen at all. The census had already priced that: 891
compilations and 588.4 seconds are repeats a job pays inside itself, over its own
separate workspaces, and R1097 recorded them as work that merging jobs could
never reach. This is what reaches them.

WHAT THE CHANGE COST WAS ITS OWN ASSUMPTIONS, TWICE, AND BOTH WERE CAUGHT BY
TESTS RATHER THAN BY A RUN. The replay builds the recorder in a REPOSITORY OF ITS
OWN, and a fixture carrying no `.cargo/config.toml` puts that binary under the
tool's workspace — so the path is now TOLD to cargo instead of assumed, and the
answer is the same in any tree. And the fixture repository itself now carries the
file, because a fixture that is not shaped like the thing it stands for tests a
shape nothing has.

Round 1113.decision_summary:
THE FIRST FULLY COLD RUN THIS REPOSITORY HAS HAD SINCE THE RECORD EXISTED KILLED
THREE JOBS, and what it killed them on was a state nobody had ever seen.
`actions/cache` has THREE answers and this program knew two: `cache-hit` is
`true` on an exact key match, `false` when a `restore-keys` PREFIX matched — the
state R1099 misread when it deleted a cache that was saving ten minutes — and the
EMPTY STRING when nothing matched at all. Every run since R1101 wired this had
warmed from a prefix, so `false` was the coldest thing that had ever arrived.
R1112 moved every key, and three jobs of the run that followed stopped with
"$MNEMOSYNE_CACHE_HIT is unset or empty, and this program will not guess it".

THE REFUSAL WAS RIGHT AND ITS READING WAS ONE STATE SHORT. What it defended is
real: an absent output read as `false` would report every warm job as the state
this crate exists to distinguish. But the empty string is not an absence — it is
a VALUE the action sets and means, and folding it in with "unset" made a
legitimate answer indistinguishable from a wiring mistake.

SO THE TWO ARE TOLD APART BY THE DISK RATHER THAN BY THE STRING. Nothing matched
means nothing arrived; the measurements are already taken either side of the
restore, so the record itself decides. An empty `cache-hit` with a tree that grew
is the contradiction — two steps reading two different caches — and it is still
refused, loudly and by name. An unset variable is still a step not reading the
action at all, and that is refused too: `required` treats empty as missing, which
is right for every other variable here and wrong for this one.

AND THE RECORD NOW SAYS WHAT THE CACHE COST. The two readings already bracket the
`actions/cache` step, so the interval between them IS the restore's wall-clock —
the record was throwing it away by not writing the clock down. Every number this
arc has produced about caching has been a benefit with no price beside it, which
is exactly how R1099 came to delete a cache on a guess. The gate now prints them
together: what a job started from, what that restore took, and what the job spent
compiling. A cache that takes longer to restore than the compiling it spares is a
cache that made the job slower, and nothing here could previously say so.

Round 1114.decision_summary:
THE QUESTION R1112 PUSHED TO FIND OUT HAS ITS ANSWER AND IT IS NO. Consolidating
thirteen build directories into one made every cache that named a build directory
hold the WHOLE of it, and this repository had three: `unrun-tests` went from 7.83
to 8.90 GB, and `item-citations` and `uncompiled-sources` — which had been
holding their own 0.08 and 0.15 GB tool trees — came to 1.20 and 1.24 GB of very
nearly the same archive. The demand reached 11.87 GB against a 10 GB budget and
GitHub had already begun evicting least-recently-used: `Linux-cargo-replay-` was
absent when the gate looked.

THIS IS THE ARITHMETIC THAT DECIDES THE WHOLE CACHING QUESTION, arriving as a
measurement rather than as an argument. A cache keyed by a PATH stores one copy
per job. This repository's build directory archives to 8.90 GB. GitHub gives a
repository 10. The number of copies the budget affords is ONE — so the five jobs
that compile into a build directory nobody caches cannot each be given one, and
the 1959 fetched compilations R1111 measured landing in those trees cannot be
reached by declaring more `path:` lines. Not because it is inelegant: because
the second copy does not fit.

SO THE TWO JOBS THAT NEVER MEANT TO HOLD IT GIVE IT BACK. Both were caching a
tool workspace's `target` before R1112 folded those into one tree; neither was
asking for the root build directory and both inherited it. They return to their
registry and git, which is what they had, and `unrun-tests` keeps the one copy.

AND THE LAW SAYS `== 1` RATHER THAN "NOT A WORKSPACE'S OWN". R1112 wrote the
file law with a non-vacuity floor of two, because three jobs held a build
directory the day it was written — a number taken from the tree rather than from
what the budget allows, and it refused the repair. The honest floor is the
arithmetic: one build directory, one copy, one job. What remains outside this
law is what a shared entry or a content-addressed cache could do, and both are
decisions rather than repairs.

Five jobs compile into a build directory nothing caches, and R1111 measured 1959 fetched compilations landing there; this round establishes that a per-job cache cannot be what reaches them. What can is a SHARED entry — every job restoring the one key and a single job saving it — or a content-addressed cache, where one stored artifact serves every job. Round 1115.decision_summary:
A GATE THAT RESOLVES FREELY REPAIRS THE EVIDENCE THE NEXT GATE READS, and this
repository had been in that state for an unknown number of rounds without a
single red run. `scripts/check-side-workspaces.sh` runs five checks over each
separate workspace in a fixed order — fmt, clippy, item citations, blind waits,
suite — and only the last said `--locked`. A cargo command allowed to resolve
freely REWRITES a lockfile that disagrees with its manifests instead of failing
on it, so the clippy two steps earlier repaired the file the suite was going to
check. The one `--locked` in that gate was structurally unable to fail.

WHAT IT COST, MEASURED. `studio/Cargo.lock` was stale in the working tree, and
the only way anybody found out was `git status` noise that R1114 nearly swept
into an unrelated commit. Running `cargo metadata --manifest-path
studio/Cargo.toml` here adds `x11rb` to `pinion-shell`'s dependency list —
`pinion/crates/pinion-shell/Cargo.toml` was last written on 2026-08-10, in
another repository, by somebody else.

THAT IS THE SECOND FINDING AND IT REFRAMES THE FIRST. `studio` path-depends on
the sibling `pinion` checkout, so its resolution is a fact about a tree this
repository does not own: it changes when SOMEBODY ELSE commits. Regenerating
that lockfile fixes it until pinion's next manifest change, which was today, so
"run cargo update and commit it" is the repair that re-drifts by construction.
`--locked` there would be worse — a gate that turns red for a commit nobody here
made, which is R1110's defect exactly, and R1110 is one round old.

SO OWNERSHIP IS THE AXIS, AND IT IS ASKED OF THE MANIFESTS. A workspace whose
path dependencies all land inside this checkout is one whose lockfile this
repository can pin; nothing else is. Owned: every resolving command says
`--locked`, and the lockfile is tracked, because that is the file the flag
reads. Foreign: no command says it, and no lockfile is tracked, because every
gate run rewrites one. The lister already computed a NEIGHBOURING predicate —
which workspaces this MACHINE can build — and one function served both; they are
different questions, and `studio` answers them differently on a runner. It is
now two, and the ownership line prints on every machine because `realpath -m`
does not need the tree to exist.

WHICH SUBCOMMANDS RESOLVE IS MEASURED, NOT READ OUT OF THE DOCUMENTATION. A
fixture workspace with one dependency-free package and a lockfile naming a
version its manifest does not, and every subcommand this repository issues run
against a fresh copy of that disagreement twice — once free, to see whether the
file moves, once with `--locked`, to see whether it refuses. Eight subcommands:
`build`, `check`, `clean`, `clippy`, `run`, `test` rewrite it and refuse under
the flag; `fmt` and `sweep` leave it alone and REJECT the flag outright, so a law
demanding `--locked` everywhere is one no correct command could satisfy. The
same fixture pins the cheap check that is not one: `cargo metadata --no-deps
--locked` accepts a stale lockfile, because it never resolves.

THE POPULATION IS THREE WALKS AND EACH HAD TO ARRIVE. Workflows, the workspace
lister's declarations, and tracked shell — the git hooks and `scripts/`, which no
gate's population had ever reached. Reading them turned up a hole in the reader
itself: `parse_script` took the first word of a segment, and four of the hooks'
five cargo invocations are written `if ! cargo …`, so the answer was `if` and
none of them were in anybody's population. The lister's own commands cannot be
read from its text at all — they are assembled at runtime from a `locked` array
— so it now DECLARES all five rather than only its suite, one array expanded
twice, and the gate reads what it prints.

THE WALK FOUND THIRTY. Thirty cargo commands in this repository resolved without
`--locked`: fifteen instrument builds and gate invocations across seven workflow
jobs, four in the lister, four in the hooks, three in `scripts/`. Every one is
fixed here. And the non-vacuity floor is PER SOURCE rather than a total, because
dropping one walk of three takes the count down without taking it to zero, and
fifty compliant workflow commands read exactly like a clean repository.

MY OWN CHANGE THEN TURNED SEVEN TESTS RED AND THEY WERE RIGHT. The hooks run
over ANOTHER tree — their smoke test does exactly that — and `--locked` on a
fixture with no lockfile is a refusal. The answer is R1112's, one round old: a
fixture that does not look like a repository fails for a reason that is about the
fixture. Cargo writes the lockfile now, not the test, because a hand-written one
pins a format version.
changes_bullets: `scripts/check-side-workspaces.sh` splits the ownership question from the checkability one: `outside_dependencies` names every path dependency landing outside this checkout whether or not that tree is here, `missing_siblings` filters those to the absent ones, and a `LOCK <ws> ours|foreign` line prints on every machine because it is answered by `realpath -m` rather than by the disk.

The same script declares every command it runs — `COMMAND <ws> <role> <words>` for fmt, clippy, citations, waits and suite — through one helper that prints the array it then executes, so a flag cannot be in the report and out of the run; `--locked` is on all of them for an owned workspace and on none for a foreign one.

`ci_plan` gains the reading half: `Ownership`, `DeclaredCommand`, `CargoCommand::manifest` (deepest tracked suffix wins, a tail under a shell variable must carry a directory of its own), `resolves_the_lockfile`, `lock_verdict` with its six answers, and `script_files` / `script_cargo_commands` for the git hooks and `scripts/`; `parse_script` now steps over the shell keywords that hid four hook commands from every population.

`crates/mnemosyne-cli/tests/locked_resolution_smoke.rs` walks all three sources over this repository, asserts each contributed, and measures against cargo itself which subcommands rewrite a lockfile they disagree with.

Thirty unlocked resolves fixed across `mnemosyne-validate.yml`, `.githooks/pre-commit`, `.githooks/pre-push`, `scripts/gc`, `scripts/mn`, `scripts/verify.sh` and the lister; `studio/Cargo.lock` untracked and ignored; the hook fixtures generate a lockfile with cargo because a repository has one.

Round 1115.publishable_decision_summary:
A GATE THAT RESOLVES FREELY REPAIRS THE EVIDENCE THE NEXT GATE READS, and this
repository had been in that state for an unknown number of rounds without a
single red run. `scripts/check-side-workspaces.sh` runs five checks over each
separate workspace in a fixed order — fmt, clippy, item citations, blind waits,
suite — and only the last said `--locked`. A cargo command allowed to resolve
freely REWRITES a lockfile that disagrees with its manifests instead of failing
on it, so the clippy two steps earlier repaired the file the suite was going to
check. The one `--locked` in that gate was structurally unable to fail.

WHAT IT COST, MEASURED. `studio/Cargo.lock` was stale in the working tree, and
the only way anybody found out was `git status` noise that R1114 nearly swept
into an unrelated commit. Running `cargo metadata --manifest-path
studio/Cargo.toml` here adds `x11rb` to `pinion-shell`'s dependency list —
`pinion/crates/pinion-shell/Cargo.toml` was last written on 2026-08-10, in
another repository, by somebody else.

THAT IS THE SECOND FINDING AND IT REFRAMES THE FIRST. `studio` path-depends on
the sibling `pinion` checkout, so its resolution is a fact about a tree this
repository does not own: it changes when SOMEBODY ELSE commits. Regenerating
that lockfile fixes it until pinion's next manifest change, which was today, so
"run cargo update and commit it" is the repair that re-drifts by construction.
`--locked` there would be worse — a gate that turns red for a commit nobody here
made, which is R1110's defect exactly, and R1110 is one round old.

SO OWNERSHIP IS THE AXIS, AND IT IS ASKED OF THE MANIFESTS. A workspace whose
path dependencies all land inside this checkout is one whose lockfile this
repository can pin; nothing else is. Owned: every resolving command says
`--locked`, and the lockfile is tracked, because that is the file the flag
reads. Foreign: no command says it, and no lockfile is tracked, because every
gate run rewrites one. The lister already computed a NEIGHBOURING predicate —
which workspaces this MACHINE can build — and one function served both; they are
different questions, and `studio` answers them differently on a runner. It is
now two, and the ownership line prints on every machine because `realpath -m`
does not need the tree to exist.

WHICH SUBCOMMANDS RESOLVE IS MEASURED, NOT READ OUT OF THE DOCUMENTATION. A
fixture workspace with one dependency-free package and a lockfile naming a
version its manifest does not, and every subcommand this repository issues run
against a fresh copy of that disagreement twice — once free, to see whether the
file moves, once with `--locked`, to see whether it refuses. Eight subcommands:
`build`, `check`, `clean`, `clippy`, `run`, `test` rewrite it and refuse under
the flag; `fmt` and `sweep` leave it alone and REJECT the flag outright, so a law
demanding `--locked` everywhere is one no correct command could satisfy. The
same fixture pins the cheap check that is not one: `cargo metadata --no-deps
--locked` accepts a stale lockfile, because it never resolves.

THE POPULATION IS THREE WALKS AND EACH HAD TO ARRIVE. Workflows, the workspace
lister's declarations, and tracked shell — the git hooks and `scripts/`, which no
gate's population had ever reached. Reading them turned up a hole in the reader
itself: `parse_script` took the first word of a segment, and four of the hooks'
five cargo invocations are written `if ! cargo …`, so the answer was `if` and
none of them were in anybody's population. The lister's own commands cannot be
read from its text at all — they are assembled at runtime from a `locked` array
— so it now DECLARES all five rather than only its suite, one array expanded
twice, and the gate reads what it prints.

THE WALK FOUND THIRTY. Thirty cargo commands in this repository resolved without
`--locked`: fifteen instrument builds and gate invocations across seven workflow
jobs, four in the lister, four in the hooks, three in `scripts/`. Every one is
fixed here. And the non-vacuity floor is PER SOURCE rather than a total, because
dropping one walk of three takes the count down without taking it to zero, and
fifty compliant workflow commands read exactly like a clean repository.

MY OWN CHANGE THEN TURNED SEVEN TESTS RED AND THEY WERE RIGHT. The hooks run
over ANOTHER tree — their smoke test does exactly that — and `--locked` on a
fixture with no lockfile is a refusal. The answer is R1112's, one round old: a
fixture that does not look like a repository fails for a reason that is about the
fixture. Cargo writes the lockfile now, not the test, because a hand-written one
pins a format version.

Round 1116.decision_summary:
THE MEASUREMENT DESIGN'S OWN PREMISE WAS WRONG, AND IT WAS WRONG IN THE LEDGER.
R1115 carried forward that GG1b's control run is confounded by construction —
"a workflow edit invalidates every key, so the control is cold in every cache at
once". That sentence was written while editing the very file whose comment
records the opposite measurement, put there by R1100: the exact key missed
because the workflow had moved, `restore-keys` matched the prefix, and GitHub
served the previous generation.

RUN 31337461298 SETTLES IT WITH NUMBERS. That run is R1114's, which edited the
workflow. Five of its seven caching jobs report `no exact hit` and then say what
arrived anyway: 221 MB, 246 MB, 281 MB, 756 MB, and — for `unrun-tests` — 32063
MB. Two jobs started from NOTHING, and those two are the ones R1114's own gate
had just found EVICTED at 11.87 GB against a 10 GB budget. So an edit costs an
exact miss; what makes a cache cold is the PREFIX moving or the entry being
deleted. Those are three different mechanisms and this arc had been treating the
first as if it were the second.

WHY NOTHING COULD HAVE CONTRADICTED THE SENTENCE. The property is declared in
`restore-keys:` and, until this round, read by nothing. `CacheDeclaration`
carried `prefix`, DERIVED from the key, and every gate in this repository joins
on it; GitHub falls back to what is WRITTEN. Two spellings of one identity, one
of them unread — so a workflow where they disagreed would leave every gate
answering about a key nothing ever tries, and each spelling would go on reading
correctly by itself. That is the shape this repository keeps finding, and it had
it in the field its whole caching arc rests on.

`survives_an_edit` IS THAT PROPERTY, NAMED AND GATED. Three ways to lose it, and
this repository has none of them, which is why the fixtures are written rather
than demonstrated by the tree: no `restore-keys` at all; a fallback that still
carries an expression, which moves when the primary key moves; and a fallback
that disagrees with the derived prefix. The third is the quiet one — it restores
something, so every job looks warm.

NOW THE DESIGN, AND THE BLOCKER IS NOT THE ONE R1115 NAMED. `unrun-tests`
declares ONE cache step holding `~/.cargo/registry`, `~/.cargo/git` AND
`target`. That single step is what makes GG1b unanswerable, twice over:

  - THE PRICE CANNOT BE ATTRIBUTED. The 385.7 s is the whole step. The registry
    half is separately known to be overwhelmingly profitable — 756 MB restored
    in 5.4 s against 381.4 s of compiling in `validate`, 281 MB in 1.9 s against
    169.0 s. Charging that 385.7 s to the build directory is the arithmetic
    R1099 got wrong.
  - THE CONTROL CANNOT BE ISOLATED. Removing the build directory from `path:`
    does not produce a cold arm, because a restore extracts the archive AS
    SAVED and the previous generation's archive contains `target`. The only way
    to cold it is to move the prefix — which colds the registry with it.

SO THE DESIGN IS TO SPLIT THE STEP. `unrun-tests` declares two caches on two
prefixes: the cargo home on `Linux-cargo-unrun-`, and the build directory on its
own. Then arm A is the status quo, arm B moves ONLY the build directory's
prefix, and the registry is held equal by construction rather than by hope. The
reading is that job's wall-clock plus, per cache, what it brought and what it
cost — which is why `restored` has to record per CACHE STEP rather than per JOB,
and that is the next round's build.

THE STRONGER DESIGN IS EXCLUDED BY ARITHMETIC ALREADY MEASURED. A paired control
INSIDE one run — the same job twice, once uncached — would remove the cross-run
question entirely, and it cannot be had: it needs a second copy of the build
directory, and R1114 established that at 8.90 GB against a 10 GB budget the
number of copies the budget affords is exactly one. The same arithmetic that
forbade per-job caches forbids the best experiment for judging them. That is why
the design is a two-run A/B and not a paired one.

AND R1105'S LAW WILL REFUSE THIS PAIR AS IT STANDS, correctly, because the two
runs begin differently — which is the whole point of the arm. The licence has to
become per cache: a comparison is legitimate when every cache but the one under
test started from the same state, and the one that differs is NAMED in the
report. Widening it to "differences are fine" would give back exactly what R1105
was built to refuse.

WHAT THIS DESIGN STILL CANNOT SAY, stated rather than discovered later: a census
records what WAS compiled and never what WOULD have been. Two arms give the
counterfactual empirically, for one job on one commit — not a saving that
generalises to the next tree.
changes_bullets: `ci_plan::CacheDeclaration` gains `restore_keys`, read off the step and resolved the same way the derived prefix is; `survives_an_edit` names the three ways a declaration stops being able to serve an earlier generation, and `reading.rs` takes all three arms on fixtures because this repository has none of them.
A repository law asserts every cache here survives an edit to the workflow it is written in — the premise every cross-run comparison in this arc rests on, and a sentence until now.
Three injections: the field goes back to being unread, a fallback that still hashes is accepted, and the two spellings of the identity need not agree.

An edit costs an exact miss, not a cold run.
`cargo test -p ci-plan --locked` 28 green, including the four-arm fixture for `survives_an_edit` and the repository law over the live workflows.
`tools/ci-plan/injection-sweep.json` 23 injections, all fired, missed 0, control 28 green.
The law's reach is asserted beside it: a walk that found no declaration would pass an all-empty loop, so the count and the presence of a fallback on every declaration are checked too.

Splitting one archive into two is expected to leave the total roughly where it is, since the same bytes are stored either way, but `cache-budget` holds this repository to 10 GB and that expectation is not a measurement. The run that splits it is the one that says.

Round 1117.decision_summary:
A RESTORE RECORD IS A CACHE'S AND NOT A JOB'S, and until this round it could only
be a job's. `unrun-tests` declares ONE `actions/cache` step holding
`~/.cargo/registry`, `~/.cargo/git` AND `target`, and the 385.7 seconds R1113
measured is that step's whole interval. The registry half of it is separately
known to be overwhelmingly worth having — 756 MB restored in 5.4 s against 381.4
s of compiling in `validate`, 281 MB in 1.9 s against 169.0 s — so charging the
whole 385.7 s to the build directory is the arithmetic R1099 got wrong when it
deleted a cache that was in fact saving 426 compilations and ten minutes. GG1b
cannot be answered by a price that belongs to two things at once, and the record
had nowhere to put the attribution: one file per job, one interval, whatever the
job happened to cache.

SO THE RECORD NAMES ITS CACHE, AND THE NAME IS THE IDENTITY EVERYTHING ELSE
ALREADY JOINS ON — the resolved key prefix, `Linux-cargo-unrun-`. Absent or
doubled, it is a refusal rather than a default: a job may declare more than one
cache, and a record that did not say which would be matched to whichever the
reader picked, which is precisely the shape where a 32 GB build directory's price
is read off a 756 MB registry's restore.

AND THE FIELD IS READ, WHICH IS THE POINT. R1116 had just found `restore-keys`
declared in the workflow and read by nothing, which is how a property the whole
caching arc rests on went years with nothing able to contradict a sentence about
it. Adding a third spelling of the prefix without comparing it would have been
that defect, newly built: `tools/twice-compiled` now refuses a record naming a
cache its job does not declare, against the prefix `ci_plan` derives from the
key. It is checked only when the record is that job's — a record pasted into
another job's file names the wrong cache as well as the wrong job, and that
event already has a name; two names for one defect send two readers to two
different repairs, which is R1113's ordering discipline.

THE WORKFLOW WRITES THE PREFIX RESOLVED, AND THAT IS MEASURED RATHER THAN
PREFERRED. Writing `--cache '${{ runner.os }}-cargo-unrun-'` put a GitHub
expression inside a `run:` script, and `twice_compiled::unresolvable` refuses to
replay a step carrying one — so all seven cached jobs left the local replay's
census at once, and its own law said so. The literal `Linux-cargo-unrun-` keeps
them replayable, and what makes a hardcoded `Linux-` safe is that nothing trusts
it: it is compared against the derived prefix on every run.

WHAT IS NOT DONE, PRECISELY. `Declared::caches` still MERGES the paths of a job's
caches into one region, and `judge_wiring` still asks for one measuring pair
outside all of them, which is exact today because every job here declares exactly
one cache. Splitting `unrun-tests` into a cargo-home cache and a build-directory
cache on separate prefixes is the change that makes those two laws wrong at the
same moment, so it is one round with them and not this one: a pair per cache
step, and the region model retired. That split is the arm-B design R1116
recorded, and this round is what its record needed first.
changes_bullets: `tools/restored` — `Restored` gains `cache`, the resolved key prefix; `restored before --cache <prefix> <path>…` is the only spelling accepted, an absent or empty name fails in the step that knows rather than one further on, and `Malformed::CacheIsNotSaidOnce` refuses a record that says it twice or not at all.

`tools/twice-compiled` — `Declared::prefixes` carries what each job declares, unmerged, and `Refusal::RestoreRecordNamesACacheTheJobDoesNotDeclare` refuses a record whose cache is not one of them, checked only when the record is that job's so a pasted record keeps its one name.

`.github/workflows/mnemosyne-validate.yml` — all seven cached jobs name the cache they measure, written as the resolved prefix because a `${{ }}` expression in a `run:` script takes the job out of the local replay's census.
verification_bullets: `tools/restored` 44 green over five targets; `tools/twice-compiled` 99 green over six; `cache-budget`, `ci-plan`, `unrun-tests`, `uncompiled-sources`, `item-citations` green.

The repository's own laws found two mistakes of mine while this landed, both real: the workflow's `${{ runner.os }}` took all seven cached jobs out of the replay census (`the_jobs_a_local_replay_cannot_run_are_exactly_these_three` named exactly which), and the new refusal fired a second time on a record pasted into another job's file until it was ordered behind the name that event already had.

Round 1118.decision_summary:
THE CACHE WAS OVERWRITING THE INSTRUMENT THAT WAS ABOUT TO RUN, and R1117's push
is what made it visible. Run 31345340220 turned main red on exactly one job:
`unrun-tests`, with `restored: the record 'restored before' wrote holds a line
this step cannot read: "cache\u{1f}Linux-cargo-unrun-"`. The line was one R1117
had just taught the program to write AND to read, so the program that refused it
was not the program that wrote it.

THE MECHANISM IS IN THE STEP ORDER AND THE LOG SAYS IT PLAINLY. `Build the
instruments` compiles `tools/rustc-log` and `tools/restored` into `target`;
`restored before` runs and writes the record; then `Cache cargo (unrun tests)`
restores 8.90 GB INTO `target`, replacing both binaries with the previous
generation's; then `restored after` runs the old one. Six other jobs ran the same
two steps and passed, and the one that failed is the only job in this file that
caches a build directory — which is what named the mechanism rather than leaving
it to be guessed.

WORSE THAN THE RED RUN, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT MATTERS. No round before this
one had changed the record format, so the substitution had no symptom and has
been happening on every run. `RUSTC_WRAPPER` points at one of those binaries, so
`unrun-tests`' entire compilation census — every number this arc has quoted for
that job, including the 331 compilations and 174.4 seconds GG1b is being decided
on — was measured by whatever recorder the last generation's cache happened to
hold. The instrument was inside the thing it was measuring.

THE REPAIR IS STRUCTURAL AND NOT AN ORDERING TRICK. The instruments build into
`instruments/`, which no cache in this file holds, so a restore cannot reach
them. Rebuilding them after the restore instead would have relied on cargo's
staleness detection over a restored tree, and "warm and stale at once" is exactly
what R1099 got wrong.

RELATIVE, NOT `${{ github.workspace }}/instruments`, AND THAT COST A MEASUREMENT
TO LEARN TWICE. R1117 put a GitHub expression in a `run:` script and took seven
jobs out of the local replay's census; this round put one in an `env:` and took
all nine out, including the jobs with no cache at all. Cargo resolves a relative
`CARGO_TARGET_DIR` against the working directory — measured, by setting it and
finding the binary at `<root>/instruments/release/rustc-log`.

AND THE LAW THAT SHOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT IS A NEW AXIS. `judge_wiring` reads where
the measuring steps SIT relative to the cache step, and by that reading this
workflow was correct: the measurements bracketed the restore exactly as required.
What it could not ask is what the restore OVERWRITES. So a program a job runs
after a restore may not live under a path that cache holds — derived from the
`run:` scripts' first words and the cache's own `path:` list, asked of every job
rather than only of the one that broke, because a cache added tomorrow to a job
whose programs sit under `target/` is the same defect.

THE SWEEP THEN FOUND A DEAD FILTER IN MY OWN LAW. The first version excluded
`~`-rooted cached paths from the held list; removing it turned nothing red,
because a `~` path cannot be a prefix of a checkout-relative program — and it was
the WRONG answer for the one case it would have decided, since a program under a
restored `~/.cargo/...` is replaced exactly as one under `target/` is. The filter
is gone and the case it would have excused is now asserted.

Round 1119.decision_summary:
THE INSTRUMENTS NOW SAY WHICH BUILD OF THEM MEASURED A RUN, and R1118 is why. That
round found `unrun-tests` restoring its own build directory over the two binaries
it had just built, so every census that job produced had been measured by whatever
recorder the previous generation's cache happened to hold. The repair moved the
instruments out of the cache; what it could not do is make the RECORD able to say
so. Nothing in it distinguished one build of the recorder from another, which is
why the substitution ran silently for an unknown number of rounds and surfaced
only when R1117 changed a format.

WHAT IT COST IS MEASURED, AND IT IS NOT SMALL. The first run with the fresh
recorder read `unrun-tests` at 332 compilations / 667.1 s of compiling / 188.8 s
of restore, against 331 / 174.4 s / 385.7 s from the run before. The counts held
— 4706 against 4703 across the workflow, floor 2718 against 2716, duplicated
42.2% either way — and the SECONDS moved by a factor of four. That is the arc's
own reading of GG12 sharpened: counts are stable across runs, seconds are not,
and one reason they are not is that the thing measuring them was not the same
program.

`option_env!("GITHUB_SHA")` AND NOT AN ARGUMENT, which is the whole design. A
value handed in at run time is the ENVIRONMENT's answer, and a substituted binary
reads the current environment and looks right. Baked in when the crate is
compiled, a binary out of a cache answers with the commit it was built from,
which is not this run's. Off a runner there is no commit and the answer is
`local` rather than an invented one — "could not tell" is a different answer from
"they agree", and this repository has paid for that distinction before.

THE MOMENT BELONGS TO `restored after`. It runs between the restore and the
compiling, which is exactly where a substituted binary is already on disk and has
not yet measured anything. It answers for itself from its own constant and it
ASKS the recorder — running the one `RUSTC_WRAPPER` names and reading its stdout.
A path and a version this program derived would be a second reading of the thing
it expected rather than the thing that is there, and the thing that is there is
the whole question. A recorder that cannot be run is a refusal: every compilation
of the job is about to go through it.

AND THE FIELD IS READ, in the same round, which is now the standing rule here.
R1116 found `restore-keys` declared and read by nothing; R1117 added a field and
its reader together; this one does the same. `tools/twice-compiled` refuses two
ways, both answered from the census alone so neither needs an environment: one
job whose two instruments disagree — they are built by one step from one commit,
so a difference is one of them having arrived from elsewhere — and a run whose
jobs were measured by different builds, which is R1118's run exactly, six jobs on
the commit's recorder and one on its cache's, summed into one total.

`none` IS AN ABSENCE THIS WORKFLOW ARRANGES. The instruments' own build sets
`RUSTC_WRAPPER: ""` to tell cargo there is no wrapper, and reading that as a
mismatch would refuse every correct file in this repository. It is asserted as a
non-refusal rather than left to the reader to notice.

WHAT THIS CANNOT SEE, stated rather than discovered later: a run in which EVERY
instrument came from a cache of the same older commit is internally consistent and
this says nothing about it. The guard for that case is R1118's — the programs live
where no cache reaches — and the two laws are the two halves of one question.
changes_bullets: `tools/rustc-log` — `BUILT_FROM` is `option_env!("GITHUB_SHA")` baked in at compile time, and `rustc-log --built-from` prints it. Safe as a first argument because cargo always passes a compiler path there, never a flag.

`tools/restored` — the same constant, and `restored after` writes a `built-from` line for itself and one for the recorder it ASKS by running `RUSTC_WRAPPER`; `Malformed::BuiltFromIsNotSaidOncePerInstrument` refuses a record missing either, saying it twice, or naming an instrument this reader does not know. A recorder that cannot be run is a refusal.

`tools/twice-compiled` — two refusals over the census alone: one job's instruments disagreeing, and the jobs of one run measured by different builds. `none` is asserted to be an absence the workflow arranges rather than a substitution.
verification_bullets: `tools/restored` 46 green over five targets, including a stub recorder whose stdout is what lands in the record and a missing recorder that refuses; `tools/twice-compiled` 103 green over six; `rustc-log`, `cache-budget`, `ci-plan` green.

`tools/restored/injection-sweep.json` 18 injections, all fired, missed 0; `tools/twice-compiled/injection-sweep.json` 51, all fired, missed 0, control 103 green — including deriving the recorder's build instead of asking it, and reading a deliberately absent recorder as a substitution.

The numbers this round is about are quoted from run 31348279253 against run 31337461298: 332/667.1/188.8 against 331/174.4/385.7 for `unrun-tests`, with totals 4706/2718/42.2% against 4703/2716/42.2%.
The anchor law over every tracked sweep green; `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings` and the whole workspace suite clean.

Which build measured any census before this round cannot be established — the records carry no stamp — so the arc's per-job seconds before run 31348279253 are superseded rather than corrected. What is recoverable is that the COUNTS were stable across the recorder change, so every counting finding of R1109 through R1114 stands.

GG1b's ARMS ARE NEXT AND THE SPLIT IS UNCHANGED: retire the region model, a bracketing pair per cache step, split `unrun-tests`' one cache step in two, one commit. The alarm that motivated GG1b — a restore costing more than the compiling it spares — did not survive the fresh recorder, so the arms are now expected to confirm the cache rather than condemn it. declaring two caches they DID disagree: two indices, two prefixes, and one merged

Round 1121.decision_summary:
THE WIRING LAW WAS ABOUT A REGION AND IS NOW ABOUT EACH CACHE. Until this round a
job's two measurements had to sit outside EVERY cache it declared, because a
restore record was a JOB's: what arrived between the two readings was what
arrived under every path any of those caches held, and the sum was the honest
reading of it. R1117 made a record a CACHE's, so the pair that writes one file is
the pair that prices one restore — and the law had not moved with it.

THE RECORD PATH IS WHAT GROUPS A PAIR, and nothing else in the file does. Two
`restored` invocations belong to one measurement exactly when they write the same
`MNEMOSYNE_RESTORED`; a position anybody has to count would be a second reading
of the same fact. So the measuring invocations are grouped by that path, and each
group owes: one `before`, one `after`, and EXACTLY ONE cache step between them.

ONE COUNT REPLACES TWO QUESTIONS. The old law asked, per side, whether the
measurement sat on the correct side of every cache — two arms, two refusals for
one defect. The count of caches a pair encloses answers both: zero is a pair
pricing a restore that does not happen (both readings on one side, the difference
an empty tree, which is the state R1099 misread), and two is one interval charged
to both, which is exactly how a 32 GB build directory's price would be read off a
756 MB registry's restore. A pair in the wrong ORDER encloses zero and is caught
by the same count, so the two questions do not need two names.

AND A JOB OWES ONE PAIR PER CACHE. A second cache with no pair of its own is a
restore whose price nobody wrote down while the census reads as complete. That
refusal is also what a job with a cache and NO measurement now gets — one defect,
one name, where the old law produced two refusals for it.

`RestoreIsMeasuredOnTheWrongSide` IS DELETED, not kept beside its successor.
Nothing constructs it once the count exists, and a refusal nothing can raise is a
line future readers will try to reanimate.

THE SWEEP CAUGHT THREE THINGS BEFORE THE COMMIT, and the third is the one worth
writing down. Two were anchors this change had moved. The third was an oracle
that did not exist: an injection grouping the pairs by JOB rather than by RECORD
left every refusal unchanged — one job, one bucket, the same counts — and came
back empty. Only a job that is RIGHT tells the two readings apart, so the missing
test was the POSITIVE one: two caches, each with its own pair writing its own
record, accepted. That is the shape the workflow is about to take, and without it
this law would have refused the very split it exists to allow.

WHAT IS STILL A JOB'S AND NOT A CACHE'S, named because the next round is where it
moves: `judge_restores` looks up ONE record per job, `cache-budget` keys what a

`unrun-tests`. All three are exact while every job declares one cache — the suite
is green with no assertion relaxed — and all three become wrong at the same
moment, which is why the split goes with them rather than here.

Round 1122.decision_summary:
A RESTORE RECORD IS NOW READ AS ONE CACHE'S EVERYWHERE, AND THE WORKFLOW HAS
TWO. R1117 gave the record a `cache` line and R1121 made the wiring law price one
cache per pair; every reader downstream still filed a record under its JOB, which
was the whole of its identity for exactly as long as a job had one cache. This
round splits `unrun-tests`' single cache step into a cargo home and a build
directory, and moves the three readings that would have become wrong at that
moment.

THE JOIN KEY IS `(job, cache)` AND BOTH HALVES COME OUT OF THE RECORD. The census
now keys records by their FILE NAME — a compilation log IS a job's, so its stem
is the job, but a restore record is one cache's and a job may leave several — and
joins them to declarations by what each record says it is. The file name owes
exactly one thing, that it is its job's; which cache it prices is written inside
it. A record that did NOT decode has only its name, which is why the name is the
key rather than the pair: dropping it would report the loudest defect here under
the quietest name.

TWO RECORDS FOR ONE RESTORE IS AN OVERWRITE AND AN OVERWRITE IS SILENT. A map
would keep whichever was read last and print one price with no sign that another
had been offered, and the two are routinely different numbers — the way this
arises is two measuring pairs writing one file. It is a refusal now, naming BOTH
files, because which one a map happens to keep is the order `read_dir` returned
them in and a refusal whose subject is an accident sends the reader to a file
that looks fine.

THE MEASURED PATHS ARE THE CACHE'S AND NOT THE JOB'S REGION. That comparison read
`cached_paths` — every path any of the job's caches holds — which is the same
list only while the job has one cache. For a job with two it is wrong in both
directions at once: each record measures its own cache's paths and is refused for
it, and a record measuring the whole region prices a restore that never touched
half of it and would have been accepted.

THE ONE MISTAKE NO RECORD CAN REPORT, AND IT IS THE ONE THIS SPLIT CREATES.
`restored before --cache <prefix>` is what the record's `cache` line is written
from, and the check on that line asks only whether the prefix is one the JOB
declares — which every one of a job's own prefixes is. So a `--cache` copied from
the step above it yields a well-formed record, naming a real cache of the right
job, carrying the OTHER restore's interval: a 134-second build directory priced
at a 5-second registry, which is the arithmetic R1099 got wrong, arriving by a
route the round that repaired it left open. The wiring law now reads that
argument off the step and refuses a pair that does not name the cache it
brackets. Asked only once the pair is known to bracket exactly one cache, because
until then "which cache is this the price of" has no answer at all.

THE RECORD PATH IS OWED BY THE STEPS THAT MEASURE, NOT BY EVERY STEP. The
variable sat in a job's `env:`, so every step of a cached job carried it and
asking all of them cost nothing. A job with two caches writes two records, so the
value cannot be the job's — and a law still demanding it of the steps that do the
WORK would refuse exactly the workflow this round exists to allow.

THE BUILD DIRECTORY KEEPS THE OLD KEY, and that asymmetry is a constraint rather
than a preference. A renamed key leaves its archive held and declared by nothing,
which `tools/cache-budget` refuses as an orphan for the seven days it takes to
age out — so a split may rename at most one of its halves without turning main
red, and the half worth keeping warm is the 8.90 GB one. The cargo home takes
`Linux-cargo-unruntests-home-` rather than the obvious `Linux-cargo-unrun-home-`
because the obvious one is a key the build directory's own fallback would
restore.

WHICH IS A LAW NOW, OVER EVERY CACHE THIS REPOSITORY DECLARES, AND IT FOUND ONE
PAIR REAL TODAY. `restore-keys` matches over the whole repository's storage, not
over one job's, and an archive unpacks as it was stored — `path:` is what a cache
SAVES and has no say in what a restore of somebody else's archive lands. Six keys
sit under `Linux-cargo-`; for five that is harmless and is what the mechanism is
for, because they hold exactly the two cargo-home trees `validate` holds. The
sixth is the build directory, so `validate` missing its own key can land 8.90 GB

THE GATE REFUSED THE ONLY REPAIR FOR A DEFECT IT HAD ITSELF FOUND, AND THAT IS
WHY R1122 COULD NOT CLOSE IT. That round measured a real one — `Linux-cargo-`,
this repository's oldest key, is a prefix of every other key in the file, so
`validate` missing its own key falls back onto whatever archive is newest under
it, and one of those is an 8.90 GB build directory. An archive unpacks AS IT WAS
STORED: `path:` says what a cache SAVES and cannot stop a tree landing that
nothing measured, nothing declared and nothing can price. The repair is to give
`validate` a key of its own like every other job has. R1122 wrote that repair
down as blocked by an outward action — deleting the archive the rename would
leave behind — and pinned the finding instead.

THE BLOCK WAS THIS GATE'S OWN LAW, NOT THE WORLD. A held archive that no
declaration matches was a refusal of its own, one per key, on the reasoning that
such a key "keeps its share of the budget". The harm named there is the BUDGET,
and a budget is arithmetic — so the honest place for those bytes is INSIDE it.
Every rename in this repository orphans its own archive for the seven days it
takes to age out, so the categorical form refused a tree for repairing itself,
which is the shape R1110 wrote down and R1115 paid for again: a gate that refuses
for a reason outside its own law is as useless as one that does not fire.

AND THE CATEGORICAL FORM MISSED THE OTHER DIRECTION ENTIRELY. It answered the
harm twice on one side and never on the other: a 0.15 GB archive left by a
rename was refused, and a repository whose declarations fit only because an
8.90 GB orphan was excluded from the sum was not. The bytes are GitHub's and they
are against the same 10 GB whoever declared them; leaving them out of the
comparison was the arithmetic error, and the refusal was standing in for it.

SO THE ORPHANS ARE COUNTED AND STILL PRINTED, KEY BY KEY. Nothing is hidden —
what changed is that the verdict is the sum rather than the presence, and the
report's last line now names both quantities and adds them, because the 10 GB
does not care which half is declared.

WITH THAT, THE RENAME LANDS AND THE PINNED FINDING BECOMES A REFUSAL. A cache
whose `restore-keys` reach another cache's archives, where that archive holds a
path the first never declared, is refused by `tools/cache-budget` — over the
declarations alone, so it holds for a repository that has never run. The subset
test is what keeps it from refusing the mechanism working: five of this file's
keys nested under `Linux-cargo-` and held exactly the two cargo-home trees
`validate` held, and falling back onto one of their generations got it the paths
it asked for.

WHAT THE RENAME COSTS, MEASURED AGAINST LIVE STORAGE RATHER THAN ARGUED: demand
9.60 GB declared plus 0.15 GB declared by nothing = 9.75 GB of 10, and the gate
passes. The 0.15 is the archive under the old key, and it ages out. `validate`
runs cold once for its cargo home, which this file measures elsewhere at 6.1 s of
restore against 394.7 s of compiling.

THE ARM THE LIVE FILE CAN NO LONGER WALK IS ASSERTED AS THE ZERO IT IS. After the
rename NO key in this repository nests under another, so the subset branch — the
one that says a nesting is harmless — has no live example left and is exercised
only over a built population. Saying that count out loud is the difference
between "no case reached it" and "nobody looked", and it is the same discipline
R1107 wrote for `Unheard::AnotherWorkflow`.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM. That an orphan is harmless: it is priced, and a big one
now fails the budget where before it failed a category. And that the fallback law
sees everything: it reads DECLARATIONS, so a key created by hand or by another
branch is not in its population — that key shows up on the other instrument, as
an archive nothing declares, counted.

Round 1124.decision_summary:
THE NUMBER THAT CLOSED AN ARC WAS NEVER PRINTED BY ANYTHING, AND THAT IS WHY THE
QUESTION IT SETTLED CAME BACK FIVE TIMES. R1098 measured that 75.4% of these
jobs' compiling windows had no compiler alive in them at all, and concluded — by
hand, in a ledger entry — that every compile-side repair together was worth at
most 394.5 seconds of critical path. The owner took an arc decision on that
figure: sccache not adopted, attention redirected to the other 75%, the time a
suite spends running what it just built. Nothing has re-derived the number since.

SO IT COULD NOT GO STALE LOUDLY. A figure governing a decision, held in prose,
with no reader — which is the shape R1116 found in `restore-keys` and R1092 found
in four comments that had never counted anything. The consequence here is
measurable and embarrassing: the question the figure settled was re-opened under
five successive names (CC6 → DD4 → FF2 → GG2 → KK12), each time as "a decision
for the owner", because no reader could check whether the premise still held.

THE CEILING IS THE BUSIEST JOB'S OWN COMPILING, AND IT IS AN UPPER BOUND. These
jobs run beside each other, so the run waits on whichever is longest. A repair
that removed EVERY compilation shortens that job by exactly the part of its
window with a compiler alive in it, and shortens the run by at most that — less,
if some other job then becomes the longest. No arrangement of caches, merges or
shared trees can win more, so quoting it prices the whole family at once.

IT IS NOT THE SUM. What every job compiles, added up, is 1282.5 s across this
census and is an area under processes that ran in parallel; the bound is 394.7 s.
Holding the two against each other is the work-seconds-against-wall-clock mistake
R1120 made in a report to the owner, one round ago, and it is a factor of three
here.

MEASURED ON THE LAST GREEN RUN, and the premise holds: window 5201.0 s across the
census, 3918.5 s of it with no compiler alive — 75.3%, against R1098's 75.4% —
and a ceiling of 394.7 s against R1098's 394.5. Two rounds of consolidation and a
profile change moved neither.

WHAT THAT SETTLES. KK12 is not a fork. Its two options — one shared build
directory restored by every job, or a content-addressed cache — are both
compile-side, so both are bounded by the 394.7 s the owner has already ruled is
not worth taking. The ledger item is struck rather than answered, and the round
that answers it would have to first show the ceiling has moved.

WHAT THE LEDGER RECORDED AND WHAT IT DID NOT. It kept the NUMBER and not the
DERIVATION, which is exactly what made rechecking impossible: this round inferred
that 394.5 was a maximum rather than a sum from the fact that today's maximum is
394.7 and today's sum is 1282.5. That inference is now unnecessary for anyone
after this — the report states the quantity, and the tests state what it is not.

Round 1125.decision_summary:
THE REPORT ANNOUNCED AN ABSENCE THAT WAS ENTIRELY ITS OWN, AND THE SUITE AGREED
WITH IT. R1122 keyed the census by the record's FILE, because a job may now write
more than one; the judge and the budget gate were both taken to the new key and
the REPORT was left asking `census.restored.get(job)`. That lookup can never hit,
so every cached job of every run printed `started from: NOT SAID` — the words for
a job that wrote no record at all, said about eight records the census was
holding in its hand.

IT SHIPPED IN THREE COMMITS AND SURVIVED THE FIRST GREEN RUN THAT USED IT. The
gates were right the whole time: `judge_restores` joins per cache and refused
nothing, `cache-budget` printed every job's warmth correctly. Only the census
gate's own report was lying, and it is the surface a person reads.

THE ORACLE IS WHAT LET IT THROUGH, AND IT IS THE PART WORTH WRITING DOWN. The
test that covers this line asserted `stdout().contains("started from")` — a
PHRASE, and one that `started from: NOT SAID` contains too. So the test passed on
the exact output it existed to prevent. An oracle that matches a substring of the
failure is not an oracle; the assertion is now the READING — the warmth in the
words the type itself prints, and the prefix of the cache it belongs to — plus
the mirror, that a record the census holds is never reported as one the job did
not write.

ONE LINE PER CACHE, WHICH IS WHAT THE SPLIT WAS FOR AND WHAT THE REPORT NEVER
SHOWED. A job with two caches has two states and two prices; `unrun-tests` now
prints both, each naming the cache it is the price of. The job's own compiling
appears on both lines unchanged, deliberately: what a job compiles is the job's,
and splitting that between two caches would be an attribution nothing measured.
What the split bought is the PRICE being each cache's own.

AND THE RUN'S NUMBERS WERE RECOVERED RATHER THAN LOST. The records themselves
were correct and are uploaded as artifacts, so the run that printed nothing
readable was re-read with the repaired binary: the eight restores, their warmth,
their prices. A report defect costs the reading of a run only if nobody goes back
for it.
changes_bullets: `tools/twice-compiled` — `Census::restore` looks a record up by the restore it says it is, and the report prints ONE LINE PER CACHE naming the prefix each price belongs to; unreadable records are listed by file, which is the only handle they have.

`tools/twice-compiled/tests/entrances.rs` — the oracle is the reading rather than the phrase: the state in the words the type prints, the cache it belongs to, and the mirror that a held record is never reported as absent. The fixture's prefix is one constant, checked against the step that names it.
`tools/twice-compiled/injection-sweep.json` — two injections, the first of them this round's own defect: the lookup put back to asking by job, and the cache name dropped from the line.
verification_bullets: THE DEFECT IS PROVED BY INJECTION AND NOT BY READING: `tools/twice-compiled` 65 injections, all fired, missed 0, control 113 green — and two of them are new, the first being this round's own defect put back (the lookup asking by job) and the second dropping the cache name from the line. Both turn `a_replayed_job_records_that_it_started_from_nothing` red, which the OLD assertion in that test would have passed.

THE RUN THAT SHIPPED THE DEFECT WAS RE-READ WITH THE REPAIRED BINARY, over its own uploaded artifacts: eight restores, each naming its cache — `Linux-cargo-citations-` 242 MB in 2.4 s, `Linux-cargo-msrv-` 221 MB in 1.9 s, `Linux-cargo-serverfeat-` 281 MB in 2.1 s, `Linux-cargo-side-` 246 MB in 3.2 s, `Linux-cargo-uncompiled-` 419 MB in 4.1 s, and three that brought nothing at all (`Linux-cargo-unruntests-home-`, `Linux-cargo-unrun-`, `Linux-cargo-validate-`).
FULL TREE GREEN: `scripts/verify.sh` exit 0 over fmt, clippy `-D warnings`, the workspace suite and `check-side-workspaces.sh` (12 workspaces, 0 skipped) — 2416 passed, 0 failed.

THE RUN THIS SESSION PUSHED WAS READ TO ITS ANNOTATIONS: 31364512079, nine jobs success, annotations 0. `cache-budget` printed `demand 9.51 GB declared + 0.15 GB declared by nothing = 9.67 GB` and passed — which is R1123 doing exactly what it was built for, since the 0.15 is the archive the rename left behind and the old law would have refused the tree for it.
carry_forward_bullets: 📐GG1b HAS ITS FIRST PAIRED READING, and it was a gift of an eviction rather than a designed arm. Run 31364512079 found NOTHING under `Linux-cargo-unrun-` — 0.7 s, no bytes — and the gate's silence about a restorable generation is the evidence that the 8.90 GB archive had already been evicted before the run began. So `unrun-tests` ran genuinely cold, beside a warm reading from the run before it: 332 compilations / 194.6 s of compiling / 134.2 s of restore, against 1017 / 409.2 s / 0.7 s. The cache spares 685 compilations and about 214 s of compiling for 134 s of restore — a NET of roughly 81 s of that job's window, bought with 8.79 GB of a 10 GB budget.

⚠AND THE CONFOUND IS NAMED: the two runs are different commits, so this is a paired reading and not the controlled arm A/B. What makes it better than R1099's — which read two WARM runs as a cold-against-warm pair and deleted a working cache — is that both states here are MEASURED on the job's own disk rather than inferred from a key. The clean test is still two runs of one commit.

⛳THE OLD ARCHIVE WAS EVICTED BETWEEN TWO RUNS AND NOTHING SAID SO AT THE TIME. `cache-budget` reports what is held now; that a generation DISAPPEARED between this run and the last is visible only by holding two reports side by side, which nothing does. The sum of everything GitHub holds for this repository came to 10.03 GB against the 10 GB limit on the run that lost it.
