Round 1208.decision_summary: R1208 (BUILD — N34 CLOSED: the shape Round 1192 repaired in one crate, asked of the whole repository, and the ten other sites it found). ETXTBSY IS AN OWNERSHIP FAILURE WEARING A SCHEDULING FAILURE'S CLOTHES. `exec` refuses a file some process holds open for writing, and the holder is not the thread that wrote it: a sibling test's `Command::spawn` forks, the child inherits every open descriptor, and until it reaches its own exec the kernel is right that somebody has the file open. Round 1192 met it in `unread-declaration`, whose eleven cases each wrote a shell script and ran it — green alone, in every run, until eleven ran beside ten other crates under `check-side-workspaces.sh` and one died. It repaired that crate by not writing the program, and wrote down what it could not do in four words: NOTHING ASKS THE OTHERS. THE LAW IS ONE SENTENCE: nothing here creates an executable file; the bit belongs to a file cargo built or git tracks, and a fixture needing a program at a particular name reaches it by SYMLINK with what varies per case as DATA the program reads. `tools/written-executable` is a sibling of `unowned-scratch` under the same three-code contract, wired into `pre-commit` (Gate 5g) and `check-side-workspaces.sh`, so every one of the twenty workspaces is asked on every commit. IT HAS TWO ARMS BECAUSE A CHMOD-ONLY RULE IS HALF A LAW, and the missing half was what production code used: `fs::copy` carries the SOURCE's mode, so copying `current_exe()` writes an executable with no chmod in the function at all — which is exactly what `injection-harness` did to take its supervisor. THE MEASUREMENT: 10 findings across 7 workspaces, every one real, and 0 false. Four fixtures wrote a `gh`, one a `cargo`, one an `mn`, one a `grep`, one a recorder, one a suite; the tenth is production. WHAT THE REPAIRS ARE, and they are two shapes rather than one, because the packages differ: in the `tools/*` gate workspaces the stand-in is now a cargo-built binary (`src/bin/gh-stub.rs` and siblings), and in `mnemosyne-cli` — a PRODUCT, where `env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_…")` resolves only within the package and a binary added is a binary that ships — the stand-ins are TRACKED files under `tests/stubs/`, reached by the same symlink. Both are the same rule read literally: the executable is a file this process did not write. `injection-harness` needed neither: its supervisor is now `/proc/self/exe`, the running image rather than a path, which is stronger than the copy it replaced (a copy is of whatever was on disk when it was taken); its fixture suites are DATA run as `sh suite.sh`, which deletes the retry loop that was the wrong repair of this very defect; and the one case that needs a removable program uses `fs::hard_link` — a second name over cargo's inode, since `/tmp` and the build directory are different filesystems on this machine, measured. THE GATE FOUND TWO DEFECTS IN ITSELF BY BEING RUN, both by its own tests and both now laws: the ordinary spelling `set_permissions(p, Permissions::from_mode(0o755))` is two calls on one line and was reported twice, once with a path and once without, so a single site counted as both the strongest evidence grade and a weaker one; and `mode` is not a rare method name — `bench/crates/sled-baseline` calls `sled::Config::default().mode(sled::Mode::HighThroughput)`, over which the first draft REFUSED that whole workspace. The second fact for `mode` is the one Rust already requires: a trait method is callable only where the trait is imported. AND ONE HOP OF COPY-SOURCE RESOLUTION, which is not speculative substrate: `injection-harness` held `fs::copy(binary(), &tool)` while this gate was being written, with `binary()` three lines up returning the cargo path, and the gate read it as an ordinary copy and said nothing — a person found it by reading, which is the thing a gate exists to stop being necessary.

Round 1209.decision_summary: R1209 (BUILD — the build-placement program sent a command that WRITES this tree to a machine that throws its tree away, and answered zero). WHAT THIS REPOSITORY SAW. Round 1208 ran `bx -- cargo fmt --manifest-path …`, got exit 0, and the local tree was not formatted at all: what had been formatted was the build machine's copy, which the next transfer erases. It surfaced two steps later as four unformatted manifests in `check-side-workspaces.sh`, a gate with no idea why. THE SHAPE IS A SILENT NO-OP WEARING A GREEN EXIT CODE, and it is the worst answer a wrapper can give — the command really did run, really did succeed, and really did nothing here. It was the SECOND firing of one defect: the first sent an injection sweep away and its `*.firings.json`, which this repository TRACKS as evidence, was written on pc2 and never came back. THE MECHANISM WAS A HAND-KEPT VOCABULARY. `bx` decides placement by scanning the flattened command for words that mean "this writes" — `git commit`, `git push`, `cargo publish`, the mnemosyne mutate verbs — and anything unrecognised is SENT. Its own comment claimed the opposite ("an unrecognised command is not assumed safe, it is assumed LOCAL"), which is the shape where a reader trusts a safety net that is not there; the program is the specification and the comment now says what the program does. WHAT THE REPAIR IS, in four parts. (1) `cargo fmt` writes UNLESS `--check` — the one flag-sensitive entry, and the safe direction is that an unflagged `cargo fmt` is a write. (2) The vocabulary gains what the tools do whoever runs them: git moving the working tree (`checkout`, `switch`, `restore`, `stash`, `merge`, `rebase`, `cherry-pick`, `apply`, `am`, `reset`, `clean`, `add`, `rm`, `mv`, `worktree`) and cargo rewriting sources, manifests or lockfiles (`fix`, `--fix`, `add`, `remove`, `update`, `generate-lockfile`, `vendor`). (3) A REPOSITORY DECLARES ITS OWN, through a new `writes` key in `.claude/remote-build.toml`, because a machine-global tool cannot know one repository's script names and a repository cannot reach into a machine-global tool — this repository declares `scripts/fmt.sh` and `.sweep.json`. (4) The refusal names WHICH reason, where one sentence used to cover four. WHAT THE FIX FOUND THAT NOBODY HAD REPORTED: run the new gate against the previous binary and nine of thirteen cases go red, and two of them are placements this repository had never noticed — `git checkout` and `cargo update` were both being sent to a throwaway tree. AND THE DISCRIMINATOR IS A SUBSTRING, so it has to be one only the WRITING form carries: the first draft declared `injection-harness` and pulled that crate's read-only SUITE onto a machine 14GB into swap, which is why the declaration says `.sweep.json` instead.

Round 1209.publishable_decision_summary: R1209 (BUILD — the build-placement program sent a command that WRITES this tree to a machine that throws its tree away, and answered zero). WHAT THIS REPOSITORY SAW. Round 1208 ran `bx -- cargo fmt --manifest-path …`, got exit 0, and the local tree was not formatted at all: what had been formatted was the build machine's copy, which the next transfer erases. It surfaced two steps later as four unformatted manifests in `check-side-workspaces.sh`, a gate with no idea why. THE SHAPE IS A SILENT NO-OP WEARING A GREEN EXIT CODE, and it is the worst answer a wrapper can give — the command really did run, really did succeed, and really did nothing here. It was the SECOND firing of one defect: the first sent an injection sweep away and its `*.firings.json`, which this repository TRACKS as evidence, was written on pc2 and never came back. THE MECHANISM WAS A HAND-KEPT VOCABULARY. `bx` decides placement by scanning the flattened command for words that mean "this writes" — `git commit`, `git push`, `cargo publish`, the mnemosyne mutate verbs — and anything unrecognised is SENT. Its own comment claimed the opposite ("an unrecognised command is not assumed safe, it is assumed LOCAL"), which is the shape where a reader trusts a safety net that is not there; the program is the specification and the comment now says what the program does. WHAT THE REPAIR IS, in four parts. (1) `cargo fmt` writes UNLESS `--check` — the one flag-sensitive entry, and the safe direction is that an unflagged `cargo fmt` is a write. (2) The vocabulary gains what the tools do whoever runs them: git moving the working tree (`checkout`, `switch`, `restore`, `stash`, `merge`, `rebase`, `cherry-pick`, `apply`, `am`, `reset`, `clean`, `add`, `rm`, `mv`, `worktree`) and cargo rewriting sources, manifests or lockfiles (`fix`, `--fix`, `add`, `remove`, `update`, `generate-lockfile`, `vendor`). (3) A REPOSITORY DECLARES ITS OWN, through a new `writes` key in `.claude/remote-build.toml`, because a machine-global tool cannot know one repository's script names and a repository cannot reach into a machine-global tool — this repository declares `scripts/fmt.sh` and `.sweep.json`. (4) The refusal names WHICH reason, where one sentence used to cover four. WHAT THE FIX FOUND THAT NOBODY HAD REPORTED: run the new gate against the previous binary and nine of thirteen cases go red, and two of them are placements this repository had never noticed — `git checkout` and `cargo update` were both being sent to a throwaway tree. AND THE DISCRIMINATOR IS A SUBSTRING, so it has to be one only the WRITING form carries: the first draft declared `injection-harness` and pulled that crate's read-only SUITE onto a machine 14GB into swap, which is why the declaration says `.sweep.json` instead.

Round 1210.decision_summary: R1210 (BUILD — N32, as far as a witness exists). The build-machine declaration says what a far side must be given (`needs`, `packages`) and NOTHING ASKED WHETHER THAT LIST IS COMPLETE. The only oracle was to build on a host that lacked something and read the failure, which is how `protoc` stayed unnamed for as long as this repository's fleet was one machine that happened to have it: R1188 widened that fleet by repairing a memory budget, the next placement picked a host without it, and 269 crates compiled before `Could not find protoc`. THE FACT WAS ALREADY IN THIS TREE, IN ANOTHER FILE, TWO WEEKS EARLIER. R888 hit the same missing tool on the hosted runner and repaired it where THAT far side is configured — `.github/workflows/mnemosyne-validate.yml` has installed `protobuf-compiler` since 2026-07-31 — and it said in as many words why nothing here would notice: "the local pre-commit and pre-push hooks cannot see it: they run on a machine that HAS protoc". Two statements about what a machine must be given, in one repository, and no law held them against each other. WHY CI IS THE WITNESS and not something stronger: "everything the far side needs" has no answer without a baseline, since a build machine also needs a shell, a linker and a C compiler, and none of those belong in a per-repository declaration. CI is the one far side this repository specifies COMPLETELY — a stock runner image, plus every departure from it written out as a step — so what CI installs is exactly the set this repository has already discovered a bare machine lacks, and the declaration is where that set is supposed to live. `tools/undeclared-requirement` is that join, and it is asked of the files rather than of a table: no dependency-to-tool map, no list of what protoc belongs to, only two statements compared. GENEROUS DETECTION, STRICT READING is the whole design of its reader. Anything install-shaped is DETECTED, including forms it cannot read; only the apt family is JUDGED; and a detected form it cannot read is a REFUSAL rather than a skip. `env DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y x` refuses because the manager is not the head word, `uses: arduino/setup-protoc` refuses because an action installs without writing a package name anywhere shell can be read, and a flag this reader does not know refuses because guessing which flags take an argument is how a release codename gets reported as a missing tool. A gate that skipped those would answer "nothing installed", and zero findings is what a clean tree looks like. TWO ZEROES ARE TOLD APART, which is the correction the hooks' own fixture forced: a workflow that installs NOTHING is a reading — the witness looked and the runner needed nothing added — while a workflow whose only installs are ones this law cannot read is an absence wearing that reading's clothes, and only the second is a refusal. The population comes from `ci-plan`, the one reader of the workflow files, whose shell splitter was made PUBLIC rather than copied: a second splitter is a second answer about where one command ends, and four gates already stand on the first. What this cannot see is said in the report rather than hidden — a tool the runner image ships and a bare Ubuntu host does not is invisible to this witness, which is exactly `libclang-common-18-dev`: declared, needed, installed by no job, and NAMED in every run as not-a-defect.
changes_bullets: `tools/undeclared-requirement` — every package this repository's CI installs is one `.claude/remote-build.toml` names, joined on the package name and reported per key

three exit codes, and the third is the point: an install-shaped step this law cannot read is a refusal, never a skip — a wrapper in front of the manager, an unknown flag, a name the shell decides, or an action that installs

`ci-plan` gains the two readers this needed and did not have: `shell_commands`, its splitter made public so no second one can drift from it, and `uses_steps`, without which a job that installs through an action reads as installing nothing
`.githooks/pre-commit` Gate 5h, on every commit (measured at 0.05s warm), and a step in the `validate` job — a law whose only reader is a local hook stops existing at the first `--no-verify`
the hooks' fixture repository grows a workflow, the same correction its lockfile and its separate workspace already needed: a tree with none is one the shared population loader refuses

It agrees with a repair a person made two days late and would have said so on the first day

and on the live tree in both directions: `protobuf-compiler` removed from `packages` turns the gate red naming all six install sites, and the file is byte-identical again afterwards with `git diff` empty

one case is the live repository: 6 install steps naming 6 packages, judged clean, with the `rustup` step named as recognised-and-not-read and three declared names printed as installed by no job

three hook cases, one per exit code, and the third asserts the MIRROR — a population it could not read must not print as a package nobody declared. 30 of 30 `git_hooks_smoke` cases green, including every one that predates this round

carry_forward_bullets: THE RUNNER'S BASELINE IS INVISIBLE TO ITS OWN WITNESS. A tool the hosted image ships and a bare Ubuntu host does not is installed by no step, so nothing in this tree can know it is required — `libclang-common-18-dev` is the live instance, and it entered the declaration the only way it could, by a build machine failing a bindgen compile for a missing header. The runner image's contents are not a fact this repository holds, and the oracle for the rest of that set remains what it was: build on a host that lacks it. The gate names those declarations in every run rather than passing over them

AN ACTION THAT DOES NOT SAY IT INSTALLS IS NOT SEEN. The reading of a `uses:` step is its NAME, because an action is somebody else's program and this repository holds none of its bytes; four words make it refuse, and `dtolnay/rust-toolchain` matches one of them only by accident of its own naming. The accepted cost runs the other way too: the day a legitimate `actions/setup-*` step lands, this gate is red until a person decides how what it installs is to be named, which is the loud direction and is meant

PACKAGE NAMES AND BINARY NAMES ARE NOT RELATED HERE. The declaration writes `protoc` under `needs` and `protobuf-compiler` under `packages` because the two answer different questions, and nothing checks that a needed binary is provided by a declared package. `dpkg -S $(command -v protoc)` would answer it, and that is a fact about the machine the gate runs on rather than about this tree — the class of fixture this repository has already paid for twice

MANAGERS OTHER THAN APT ARE RECOGNISED AND NOT JUDGED, and this is a decision rather than a limit: judging `rustup toolchain install` or `pip install` would mean joining another vocabulary's names against a declaration written in apt's, and that table is the thing that goes stale silently. What the report does instead is count them and print the command, so the hole has a number

Round 1211.decision_summary: R1211 (BUILD — N18, the basis that was weaker than the law). `tools/named-environment` says every environment variable a spawned program reads is one the test that spawns it NAMES, and what it actually asked was whether the test SAYS the name anywhere in its sources. R1182 chose that weaker question for a reason it wrote down: R1181 had just moved `cache-budget`'s environment into a list the spawn loops over, so the argument of `.env` is a loop variable, and a gate that refuses the tidiest spelling of the shape it enforces is one people route around. THE COST OF THAT CHOICE IS THAT IT WAS UNIVERSAL. One unreadable shape in one fixture bought a fallback for every target in the repository, and nothing printed which targets were standing on it — the module doc promised both numbers and the report printed only the stronger one, so the distance between them was not visible from a run. MEASURED ACROSS ALL 22 WORKSPACES BEFORE ANY CODE MOVED: mentioned equals set everywhere except two — `cache-budget` (6 read, 0 set, the loop) and `item-citations` (1 read, 0 set) — and the whole tree holds exactly ONE `.env` call this walk cannot resolve. So the fallback was buying almost nothing and hiding one real defect: `item-citations` spawns a program that reads `CARGO`, and its fixture said that name only because it reads the variable ITSELF to find cargo for its own spawns. The machine decided which cargo the gate under test would run, and the law reported the variable as accounted for. THE WALK NOW FOLLOWS A VALUE INTO THE LOOP, which is what N18 said closing it needed: `for (name, value) in environment(..)` resolves through the helper that returns the list, BY POSITION — what makes `name` a variable is that it is the first field of every tuple, and a reading that pooled the fields would credit a value as a name. Lists are read out of `vec![..]` and array literals, through `into_iter`/`iter`/`clone`/`to_vec`, and NOT through a method that reshapes them: `.map(..)` falls to the refusal rather than being read as its receiver. AND THE BASIS IS NOW A FACT ABOUT EACH TARGET rather than about the law. Where every `.env` in a target resolved, the walk has seen everything that target controls, so the law is enforced as it is written; where a site did not resolve, what it sets is unknown and demanding a set would reject a fixture for the walk's blindness — that target alone falls back, and the report names the site and counts the fallbacks. Twenty-one of the twenty-two workspaces are now judged on control. The one that is not is the root, whose `all` target hands its environment to a helper as a parameter (`git_hooks_smoke.rs:234`), and the gate prints that file and line every run instead of leaving it as the difference between two numbers.
changes_bullets: the walk follows a value into a loop: a list a helper returns is resolved by POSITION, so `for (name, value) in environment(..)` names what it sets rather than merely saying it
the basis is per target — control where every `.env` resolved, mention only where one did not — and the report counts the fallbacks and names the site that caused each
an unresolved `.env` / `.env_remove` is a counted, named site instead of a silent nothing, and a finding now says which of the two repairs it needs
`item-citations` decides the `CARGO` its spawned gate reads instead of inheriting it, through one resolver the file's three spawns share
verification_bullets: THE POPULATION WAS MEASURED BEFORE THE DESIGN, over all 22 workspaces: mentioned equalled set in 20 of them, `cache-budget` was 6 read / 0 set and `item-citations` 1 read / 0 set, and the whole tree held exactly one `.env` the walk could not resolve. The universal fallback was buying two cases and hiding one of them

the loop walk was proved on the fixture it was written for rather than on a mock: `cache-budget` went from `SETTING 0` to `SETTING 6` — every name resolved through a helper's `vec![..]`, including the two spelled as constants and one of those from another crate

and it found the defect the fallback had been hiding: `item-citations`'s `gate` target spawns a binary that reads `CARGO` and never set it, so the machine decided which cargo that program ran. Repaired, and the same run then reported "every one of them at an .env / .env_remove call site"
after the repair, all 22 workspaces exit 0 and 21 of them are judged on control; the one fallback is printed with its file and line every run

21 gate cases, 5 of them new and each killing a different arm: the helper-returned list, the value half of a pair NOT read as a name, a reshaping method leaving a named site rather than a dropped one, a name said and never set being a finding where control is readable, and a caller-handed list being the named residue

the whole population, not the changed one: root suite 2002 passed / 0 failed with 57 of 57 targets reporting, `scripts/check-side-workspaces.sh` over 21 workspaces green, root `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, the gate's own clippy, and `scripts/fmt.sh`
carry_forward_bullets: A LIST HANDED IN AS A PARAMETER IS NOT REACHED. `run_hook(.., env: &[(&str, &str)])` loops over what its caller built, and the callers build it by mapping over another list — so what that loop sets is decided outside the function the walk is reading, and following it needs value tracking across call boundaries rather than a syntax walk. It is the one such site in this repository, its target is the one judged on mention, and the gate prints `git_hooks_smoke.rs:234` on every run. A partial resolution would be worse than none: crediting the call sites it CAN read would flip that target onto the strong basis while the walk still had not seen everything, which is how a false defect gets written

MENTION IS STILL THE BASIS WHEREVER A SITE IS UNREADABLE, and that is a fallback rather than a law. Its failure is never a false alarm — a test whose sources never say a name is certainly not deciding it — but its success is weaker than what the module doc claims, and the honest statement is now a number the report prints rather than a sentence in a comment

A `.env` INSIDE A MACRO BODY IS READ ONLY WHERE THE MACRO'S BODY PARSES as a comma-separated expression list. `syn` does not walk macro bodies, and the reader here re-parses what it can; a fixture that builds its spawn inside a macro whose body is not that shape is invisible to both halves. Nothing in this tree does it, which is why it is a record rather than a repair

THE VALUE HALF OF A PAIR IS NEVER CREDITED, and that is deliberate: a fixture that passes an environment variable's NAME as a value — `("PROBE_SETS", "GITHUB_RUN_ID")` — is reported as not setting `GITHUB_RUN_ID`, which is true. If a fixture ever legitimately reads names out of position 1, this law will call it a defect and the repair is to write the list the way the loop binds it

Round 1212.decision_summary: R1212 (DEBT — N31, the number that travels and does not govern). `.cargo/config.toml` sets `jobs = 4`, and that is a fact about ONE machine: the 31 GiB workstation whose swap Round 1076 filled. It travels with the tree to every checkout, and the debt read that as "the build machine is held to four". NOBODY HAD ASKED THE PROGRAM. Measured with cargo's own `NUM_JOBS`, which it hands a build script, three arms each with a fresh build directory so the script actually ran: this tree's config alone gives 4; `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=8` against that same config gives 8; and `-j 2` against that same variable gives 2. And on the build machine, where `bx` exports a per-host width, a full cold workspace build ran at `NUM_JOBS=31`. So the config value governs exactly where nothing else decides — this workstation and a CI runner, neither of which has a scheduler in front of it — and the debt's premise was already false. THE HALF THAT WAS REAL IS THE OTHER ONE: the debt also asked for a compile-side peak, which nothing had ever measured. That full cold build (233 crates, 46.07s at 1874% CPU, zero swapping) peaked at 777,424 kB — 0.74 GiB for the heaviest single process, which is what `/usr/bin/time -v` reports and therefore what one rustc costs. Beside the run side's 0.70 GiB per test task and 1.53 GiB for the whole suite, `peak_gb_per_task = 2` is a valid bound for BOTH sides. AND THAT NUMBER WAS ALREADY BOUNDING BOTH, which the declaration denied in writing: its comment said the value is the run side's and that `jobs = 4` bounds compiling separately, while the program derives ONE number from it and exports it as `RUST_TEST_THREADS` AND `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS` (measured on the far side with `printenv`: both 31). A declaration disagreeing with the program that enforces it is the shape this repository keeps paying for, and here it was benign only by luck — the compile peak happens to fit under a bound measured on the other side. So the repair is the SENTENCE, not the value, and both files now carry the measurement instead of the claim. THE THIRD ARM IS WHY THERE IS A NEW LAW. A flag beats the environment, so a `--jobs` or a `--test-threads` written into any command this repository issues would take the width away from every scheduler at once — the build machine's per-host number, a runner's four, a future host's whatever — and it would do it silently, because a build eight times narrower than it could be looks exactly like a slow build. `crates/mnemosyne-cli/tests/build_width.rs` asks that of the whole population: 231 cargo commands from nine sources, assembled once in `ci-plan` rather than twice, since `locked_resolution_smoke` reads the same set and two assemblies are two answers.

Round 1213.decision_summary: R1213 (BUILD — N3, the three arcs nobody had walked and the invention nobody had re-asked). R1176 carried two blind-extraction stores across R697 by rewriting their pre-R697 `allowed` pair list into the store-native map, and it wrote down what that left open in two sentences. The first: today's witnesses are two arms of ONE experiment declaring the SAME one-step arc, so "a multi-step arc, a cycle, or a rule whose FROM token is already a registered entity would each take a path this round did not walk". The second: the carriage INVENTS at exactly three points — an adjacency predicate, a state entity per FROM token, and one edge fact per step — and "nothing DERIVES that these are the minimal additions; the write path taught the constraint by rejecting twice, and what makes this shape minimal is measurement, not proof". BOTH SENTENCES DESCRIBE WORK RATHER THAN A LIMIT OF THE WORLD, which is the carry test this repository applies before accepting one, and both are done here. THE THREE ARCS ARE NOW WALKED, against corpora built for the purpose because no author in this tree writes one. A multi-step arc registers every state a step LEAVES and none it only ENTERS — `c` in `a->b, b->c` stays a token, because a typed subject must be an entity and a token object must not be one, and registering it would be an invention the pair list does not imply. A cycle carries both directions as two edge facts with distinct ids and registers each state once however many steps leave it. A FROM token the corpus already registers is not invented a second time, and — the arm that matters most — a rule whose every FROM token the author already declared adds NO entity kind at all, because a kind with no member is a row the recipe added for nobody. THE INVENTION IS NOW RE-ASKED BY REMOVAL, which is the only form of minimality a measurement can carry: each of the three invented rows is dropped in turn from a manifest that imports, and the import must refuse — measured, all three refuse — while the untouched carriage must import, which is the half that says no FOURTH row is needed. What it cannot say is that no other design would also work; that is not a question a run can answer, and the entry says so rather than letting three green cases read as a proof.
changes_bullets: three cases for the three arcs no corpus in this tree declares: a multi-step arc, a cycle, and a rule whose FROM token the author already registered
one case that removes each invented row in turn and requires the import to refuse, with the untouched manifest importing as the control
the kind a removal names is read off the row the carriage wrote rather than spelled a second time
verification_bullets: the removals are the round's injection and all three fire: without the adjacency predicate, without the state entity, and without the entity kind that state belongs to, the import REFUSES; with all three it imports, which is what says a fourth row is not needed
`drop_row` refuses a removal that removed nothing, so a case aimed at a row the carriage never added fails rather than passing on an unchanged manifest

the three arcs are asserted by their whole output, not by a count: the multi-step arm pins entities [a, b], the predicate's token list [a, b, c], and three fact ids in order; the cycle pins two edge ids that differ; the already-registered arm pins state_entities [b] and then an arm where nothing at all is invented and no kind is declared

The cases pin the WHOLE output per arm, so a corpus needing more fails loud, which is the guard rather than a proof of generality

Round 1214.decision_summary: R1214 (BUILD — the work-list is actionable, asked of the real backlog). `report-authoring-frontier` calls itself "every coverage gap an unattended loop pulls its next work from" (R589), and two laws hold its answer against the reads beside it: R1042 pins that it carries exactly the roads `report-payoff-coverage` calls non-empty, and the playable-agreement law pins what it counts per scene. BOTH ASK WHETHER THE LIST IS CONSISTENT AND NEITHER ASKS WHETHER IT IS ACTIONABLE — which is the loop's inner step and the one an unattended run lives or dies on, because an item nobody can close is a loop spinning on it forever and from outside that looks exactly like a loop that is working. R442's smoke shows a setup dangling until `--pays-off` lands, on a store built for the purpose: three facts, one road. Nothing had asked whether the REAL items behave that way — the ones a blind extractor left in a 95-section corpus, on a road that forks four ways, where the setup's coordinate and the payoff's have to agree for the credit to land. THE ANSWER IS YES, AND IT IS NOW A LAW OVER THE WHOLE POPULATION. For every authored store that loads, the frontier is read and each dangling setup is closed by the payoff its own item implies — seated at the setup's OWN frame, branch and coordinate, because that is what the frontier's answer gives a loop to work from — and the frontier is re-asked after each call: the item must leave every road it was on, every OTHER item must stay exactly where it was, and when the last one is paid the store's list must be empty. Measured: 43 stores asked, 16 owed work across 38 roads, and 73 calls cleared all of it. Round 1216.decision_summary: R1216 (BUILD — the second axis closed, and the size of every axis said out loud). R1214 proved one of the frontier's six axes actionable and wrote down what that left: "ONE AXIS OF SIX ... the other five each need their own implied call, and nothing derives that call from the report". This round counts the axes before closing another, because an axis no corpus reaches is a claim with no evidence behind it and an axis holding hundreds of items is where a loop's time actually goes. MEASURED ACROSS THE AUTHORED POPULATION, 43 stores that load: zero-fact scenes 31 (in 3 stores), dangling setups 73, unplaced 0, unordered 0, map gaps 0. So the entire backlog this repository's records hold is 104 items on TWO axes, and three of the six are empty here — which is why the closability law can only reach two of them, and says so rather than implying the others were checked. THE SECOND AXIS IS NOW CLOSED THE SAME WAY THE FIRST WAS. A zero-fact scene is a registered section no fact anchors — the empty room a loop is meant to write into — and the call it implies is `add-fact` at that coordinate. All 31 fill, one call each, with the frame taken from the store's own registry (a corpus that registers none could not be authored into by any call, which would be a fact about that corpus rather than about this axis; none is). Three things are required of each fill beyond the scene leaving the list: the two placement axes hold still, and — the part that matters for an unattended run — THE PAYOFF AXIS DOES NOT GROW. A work-list that refills itself as it is cleared is a loop that never ends, and nothing until now asserted that closing one axis does not open another. ITS CONTROL IS THE COORDINATE, not the write: a fact seated at a scene that already has one must leave the empty-scene list exactly as it was, which is what separates "the call filled that room" from "any write clears the list". THE PLACEMENT AXIS IS THE ONE TO NOTICE FOR LATER: this repository's CLI has no verb that writes the canon order — every `--order` is a read, and the help says the order is "a DECLARED partial order, never inferred" — so an item on that axis is closable only by editing a manifest the store does not own. It is empty in every corpus here, so this round could not put that to a measurement; the carry names it rather than the law claiming it.

Round 1217.decision_summary: R1217 (BUILD — the telling axis's fourth state: NEEDED, decided by the store's own apparatus). R1215 left two carries; this closes the first with a store-side answer and reframes the second with a measurement. THE FIRST CARRY was whether "no telling" is WORK. R1215 declined to count it, on the ground that the answer is what each corpus was FOR and this repository does not record that. It records something narrower that decides the same thing: WHAT THE STORE CARRIES. Two reads take `--telling` as a REQUIRED argument — the playable-world projection (the seam a pinion runtime consumes) and the quest graph beneath it — and both read apparatus that is visible WITHOUT any telling: world-lines beyond `main`, and quests as the R676 `quest_ids` kernel derives them. For a store carrying either, the seam is not empty, IT CANNOT BE OPENED — and the work-list that exists so an unattended loop can pull its next item answered `0 gap(s)`. So the report carries `telling_needed`: `carried` names the apparatus with its size, `gap` is true when it is carried and the store declares no telling, and it counts in `total_gaps` because ONE `add-disclosure-plan` closes it. A store carrying NEITHER is a flat record and this axis claims nothing about it — whether such a store wants a telling is an authorial question the store cannot answer, and guessing would put R1215's residue back as a false positive on every record in the tree. The map is deliberately not apparatus either: `transition_map` reads it with no telling at all, so a map is not evidence of this need. MEASURED OVER THE POPULATION BY THE LAW, not quoted from a session: of the 43 corpora that load, 22 need a telling they do not have, 17 carry nothing that wants one, and 4 carry apparatus and declare one. The 22 include every one of the richest records this repository holds — seven world-lines, six, four, three — so the stores a runtime would most want are exactly the ones the seam refused. One `add-disclosure-plan` each satisfied all 22, and `report-playable-world`, which refused all 22 before, answered for all 22 after. Round 1218.decision_summary: R1218 (BUILD — the frontier says WHAT TO CALL, and the roster that says it cannot drift from the report). `report-authoring-frontier` calls itself the read "an unattended loop pulls its next work from" and, until this round, published WHAT is outstanding and never WHAT TO CALL about it. Rounds 1214, 1216 and 1217 each closed one axis by hand and each wrote the same carry: the loop reads an axis NAME and learns the verb from a person. A sentence three rounds keep writing is undone work, not a limit (the R1005 carry test), and it was the last row in the ledger's "can be done autonomously right now" column. So `frontier_axes()` lands in `mnemosyne-ops`, BESIDE the report it describes, and `describe-frontier-axes` publishes it on the CLI and on MCP (the loop reads the frontier through MCP, so a roster it cannot reach there is half a repair). FOUR STATES, and none of them is decoration. `closes` = the verb plus the argument that makes it a closure, AND this repository has run that call over its own authored corpora — three of them (`dangling_setups` → `add-fact --pays-off`, `zero_fact_scenes` → `add-fact --canon-from`, `telling_needed` → `add-disclosure-plan`), which are exactly the axes R1214, R1216 and R1217 closed. `believed` = the call this substrate believes closes it, with WHY nothing here has run it — four, and publishing them under the same word as the proven three would let the weaker wear the stronger's evidence (the R1216 discipline). `no_verb` = nothing in this API closes it, and there is exactly ONE: `unordered_scenes`. That one matters more than the rest of the roster: the canon order is a DECLARED partial order this API never infers and no verb here writes the order manifest, yet the axis COUNTS toward `total_gaps` — so a loop that treats every gap as closable spins on it forever, and from outside that is indistinguishable from working. The debt ledger had been carrying that as prose (N88); it is now a machine-readable state with a law behind it. `not_work` = a census, an echo of the argument, or a derived view, never counted. THE ROSTER CANNOT DRIFT, which is the whole engineering content: it is held against the keys the tool ACTUALLY EMITS, asked at the process boundary rather than read off a type — two calls, one with a telling and one without, because the telling-scoped axes are skipped entirely in the first, and their union is every field. 15 fields, 15 rows. AND THE PROVEN CLAIM IS UNDER TEST: the three closure laws in `frontier_closure` now take their verb FROM the roster, so renaming a verb there fails the law that runs it, and the `closes` set is pinned at those three — a fourth may appear only beside a law that proves it. The MCP description of this same report had drifted for four fields across many rounds (R1217 found it), which is exactly the failure mode a hand-maintained table beside a growing struct always has, and the reason this one is checked rather than trusted.

Round 1219.decision_summary: R1219 (BUILD — two of the roster's `believed` calls become RUN, and the third is told why it cannot be). R1218 published, per frontier field, the call that closes it, and had to mark four of them `believed` — a call this substrate believes closes an item and which nothing here has ever run. Three of those four are TELLING-SCOPED, and the reason no law had reached them was structural rather than deep: every population walk in this repository pulls work WITHOUT a telling, so those axes came back `null` and no witness was ever asked. MEASURED FIRST, which is what decided the round's scope: across the 11 authored stores that declare a telling — unresolved quests 1, never-planned disclosures 20, disclosures seated before truth 0. Two axes have witnesses; the third has none and now says so in the roster instead of carrying a reason that was about the population walk. THE QUEST AXIS, and its one witness is the interesting half. The item is `q-main` in the migrated dnd-quest record, reason `completion_gives_nothing` (R1037): three `completed_by` facts name the quest and none pays off an `Expected` setup, so the store says both "this quest is completed by X" and "nothing gives it", and its state reads `unknown` on every road forever. A giving setup is DERIVED, never declared — R619's single rule is "an `Expected` fact the quest's OWN completion pays off" — so the closing call is one that makes a completion pay off an Expected fact, and the frontier's own payoff axis names the candidates. The law AUTHORS that completion rather than amending an existing one, and the reason is a hazard worth recording: `amend-fact` is a REPLACE, not a patch. The first hand-probe of it (`amend-fact --fact f-305 --pays-off …`) was refused with "frame mandatory", which is the loud case; the quiet one is a caller who restates most fields and silently drops the typed leg or the entities list. THE DISCLOSURE AXIS closes with one `set-disclosure`, and the law uses `--mode state` deliberately: `withhold` and any `first_at` pin require the fact to carry a typed claim, so a law reaching for the withhold default would fail on untyped facts for a reason that is about the MODE and not about the axis. Which mode is right is the authorial half, and the roster now says that in place of pretending otherwise. WHAT THE PROOF IS TIED TO: both laws assert that `describe-frontier-axes` publishes the verb they are about to call, and both were RED before the roster was flipped — the R1218 tie works in the direction that matters, refusing to certify a call the contract has not published. The pinned proven set moves 3 → 5 in the same commit, which is the only way that pin is allowed to move.

MEASURED FIRST, which is what decided the round's scope: across the 11 authored stores that declare a telling — unresolved quests 1, never-planned disclosures 20, disclosures seated before truth 0. Two axes have witnesses; the third has none and now says so in the roster instead of carrying a reason that was about the population walk. THE QUEST AXIS, and its one witness is the interesting half. The item is `q-main` in the migrated dnd-quest record, reason `completion_gives_nothing` (R1037): three `completed_by` facts name the quest and none pays off an `Expected` setup, so the store says both "this quest is completed by X" and "nothing gives it", and its state reads `unknown` on every road forever. A giving setup is DERIVED, never declared — R619's single rule is "an `Expected` fact the quest's OWN completion pays off" — so the closing call is one that makes a completion pay off an Expected fact, and the frontier's own payoff axis names the candidates. The law AUTHORS that completion rather than amending an existing one, and the reason is a hazard worth recording: `amend-fact` is a REPLACE, not a patch. The first hand-probe of it (`amend-fact --fact f-305 --pays-off …`) was refused with "frame mandatory", which is the loud case; the quiet one is a caller who restates most fields and silently drops the typed leg or the entities list. THE DISCLOSURE AXIS closes with one `set-disclosure`, and the law uses `--mode state` deliberately: `withhold` and any `first_at` pin require the fact to carry a typed claim, so a law reaching for the withhold default would fail on untyped facts for a reason that is about the MODE and not about the axis. Which mode is right is the authorial half, and the roster now says that in place of pretending otherwise. WHAT THE PROOF IS TIED TO: both laws assert that `describe-frontier-axes` publishes the verb they are about to call, and both were RED before the roster was flipped — the R1218 tie works in the direction that matters, refusing to certify a call the contract has not published. The pinned proven set moves 3 → 5 in the same commit, which is the only way that pin is allowed to move.

Round 1220.decision_summary: R1220 (BUILD — the work-list DRAINS, and it does not drain monotonically). Five laws now each close one axis of `report-authoring-frontier` and stop. None of them asks the question an unattended run actually lives on: if a loop keeps pulling the next item and making the call `describe-frontier-axes` names, does it FINISH, and does it stop where the contract says it must? Those are two distinct failures — a list that never empties is a run that spins forever and looks from outside exactly like a run that is working, and a list that empties past what this API can close would mean the roster is lying about `no_verb`. So this drains one, with the loop given nothing but the report and the roster: it reads the frontier, picks the first item on an axis the roster marks `closes`, asserts the roster names the verb it is about to call, makes that call, and re-reads. The witness is CHOSEN MECHANICALLY and printed — the cheapest store that both needs a telling and holds other work, priced by its own report (the refill is one decision per fact, and the scene census names the facts), because a drain over the whole population would be the same claim at fifty times the wall clock. THE TRAJECTORY IS THE FINDING: `[2, 25, 25, 24, 23, … 1, 0]` over 27 calls on `phase1-concurrency-probe/v1/run/author`. The list does not fall monotonically, and both irregularities are real. The gauge goes 2 → 25 on ONE call: declaring the telling is what makes the telling-scoped axes answerable at all, and the first thing they answer is that every fact in the store is undecided. R1216 named the shape to fear — "a work-list that refills itself is a loop that never ends" — and this is the one axis in the report that genuinely refills. Then 25 → 25, a FLAT step: paying off a dangling setup closes one item and opens exactly one, because the payoff fact it authors is itself a fact nobody has decided a disclosure for. What makes the loop terminate anyway is that the refill is ONE LEVEL DEEP: deciding a fact opens nothing, so the list is bounded by the fact count and each call after the telling is net -1 or 0. That is a property of the substrate no per-axis law can see and no prose could safely assert — R1216 could only check that ITS axis did not refill, and the axis that does was not built yet. THE FLOOR is asserted to be exactly the axes nothing here can close (unordered scenes + seats before truth + map gaps), and in this population that sum is 0, which is a fact about the corpora rather than about the formula: no authored corpus in this tree holds any of the three. The constructed case beside it (R1218's) is what shows the unclosable axis being counted at all, so the two halves are kept apart rather than mixed. The five per-axis laws and the drain now make their calls through ONE builder each, so the drain proves something about the calls this repository publishes rather than about some sequence that happens to empty a list.

Round 1221.decision_summary:
R1221 (BUILD — the description law was one tool wide, and the wall it named was not there). R1217 held ONE MCP tool's description to the fields its report emits, and wrote down why it stopped: "the mapping from a tool to the type it returns is a hand-written pair, which is why this is one pair and not a table pretending to be a rule". That is true of the TYPE and false of the ANSWER. This repository already declares one VALID CALL per tool — `probed!` for the required-argument sweep, `exercised!` for the optional-argument differentials — makes it, and asserts it succeeded. So the pair is not written anywhere: it is OBTAINED, which is the same move R1218 made when it held the frontier roster against the keys the tool actually emits rather than against the type. The cost R1217 priced was the cost of the wrong instrument.

THE FIRST RUN WENT RED ON 72 OF 76, and the reds fall in two classes that need different answers. SIXTY-ONE of them were the same field: every writing tool answers with the envelope `finish_mutate` builds, `{receipt: {primitive, target_kind, target_id, sidecar_path, written_bytes}}`, and NOT ONE description said so. An agent calling `add_section` got back the bytes written and the sidecar they were written to, and nothing had told it there would be an answer at all. Writing that sentence sixty-three times by hand is the copy this repository keeps paying for, so it is STAMPED the way `agent_facing_tools` already stamps the path-resolution rule onto arguments — "the author cannot forget because there is nothing to remember" — and the sentence is GENERATED from the envelope's own serialized keys, so a field added to the receipt tomorrow appears in every description at once. The tools that answer with it are a declared list, and the list is held by execution IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: a writing tool missing from it answers with a `receipt` its description does not name and the field law goes red, which is exactly how `import_facts` was found missing; and a tool wrongly on it is stamped with a sentence about an answer it never gives, which a second law catches by asking whether the declared envelope is in what the tool actually said. The inventory tools' envelope was two `json!` literals spelled inline, and the two branches had already disagreed about their own shape — the failing-scan branch omitted `cascade_decay_hits` entirely — so it is now one `Default`-carrying type that both branches and the stamp read.

THE OTHER ELEVEN WERE THE DRIFT R1217 PREDICTED. `report_quest_graph` named NONE of its five fields, `report_entity` none of its four, `query_changelog_entry` none of its nine.

THEN THE DENOMINATOR, which is what makes "no longer one tool wide" worth something or nothing: 78 OF 105 ROUTED TOOLS. Twenty-seven were held by no law at all, and a tool nothing calls is indistinguishable from a tool whose description is right. Eighteen already had a declared call in `exercised!`, so the law was seated there too — one line, no second table of calls. The remaining NINE take no argument at all, which is why neither macro could reach them and why nothing in this repository had ever called them; they are the cheapest calls on the surface, an empty workspace and no arguments, and they now emit their own tests and their own accounting row from one declaration. The coverage is 105 OF 105, and it is ASSERTED rather than printed, because a seat that stopped holding anything would otherwise shrink it in silence.

THE SECOND SWEEP FOUND TWENTY-ONE MORE, which is the measurement that says the first eleven were not the tail. `validate_continuity` omitted FOURTEEN fields — every honesty surface it carries, the ones that say what the scan could not ask rather than what it found — and `describe_schema` twelve, the whole contract an agent reads before authoring. Thirty-one descriptions were repaired against answers actually observed, never against types read by eye.

THREE OF THE REPAIRS ARE DEFECTS RATHER THAN OMISSIONS, and they share one shape: a field whose absence makes a green answer mean the opposite of what it reads as. `validate_disclosure_leak.vocabulary_shared` is the sharpest — `targeted > 0` with `vocabulary_shared == 0` means the re-extraction used foreign ids, so `leaks: []` is VACUOUS rather than clean, and the description invited an agent to read the empty list as a pass. `report_entity_kind_migration.entities_examined` is the same shape (an empty list over zero entities examined says nothing), and so is `report_timeline_gaps.interval_rules`.

THE INSTRUMENT'S OWN DEFECT IS RECORDED because a green test is where it was caught: the first accounting printed "106 of 105 routed tools", having summed three seats that overlap where one tool is held twice. A set, not a sum.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO, as a decision rather than an omission: the law holds the TOP LEVEL of an answer. `rmcp` carries a real `output_schema` on every tool and this server declares none on any — that is the destination, and reaching it means converting every handler from a hand-built `CallToolResult` to a typed return so the wire actually carries structured content. Declaring the schema without the wire would advertise a contract the server does not honour, which is worse than the prose it replaces.
changes_bullets: a tool's description is held to the fields the answer it actually gave carries, over all 105 routed tools — the pair is obtained from a call this repository already makes, never written down
the write envelope is stamped from its own serialized keys onto the 63 tools that answer with it, and the declaration is held by execution in both directions
31 descriptions repaired against observed answers, and the nine no-argument tools nothing here had ever called now emit a call, a test and their accounting row from one declaration
verification_bullets: THE LAW WAS WRITTEN BEFORE THE DESCRIPTIONS WERE FIXED AND WENT RED 72 OF 76 ON ITS FIRST RUN, then 21 more once the other two seats were wired. That red is the evidence it is not vacuous, and it is why the law exists rather than a second hand-written list — three of the fields it named had gone undescribed for many rounds

SIX INJECTIONS OVER FIVE MECHANISMS, each red naming exactly the thing removed and the tree restored byte-identical after both rounds. (1) a field name struck from `report_quest_graph` — red naming `unresolved_quests`. (2) a writing tool struck from the envelope declaration — red naming `receipt`, the under-declaration direction. (3) a READ added to the envelope declaration — red saying the stamp claims an answer the tool never gives, the over-declaration direction the field law is blind to. (4) a field struck from `report_timeline_gaps`, held only by the `exercised!` seat — red there. (5) a field struck from `describe_schema`, held only by the no-argument seat — red there. (6) one tool's no-argument declaration removed — the accounting red with "104 of 105 ... [report_binding_migration]"

THE COVERAGE IS ASSERTED, NOT PRINTED: 105 of 105 routed tools are held to an answer, and the assertion is what makes a seat that stops holding anything fail rather than shrink quietly. A name accounted for that the router does not expose fails too, so the seats cannot be padded by a misspelling
THE FIRST ACCOUNTING WAS WRONG AND A GREEN TEST SAID SO — "106 of 105", from summing three overlapping seats. Fixed to a set union; the arithmetic is now impossible to get that way

Round 1221.publishable_decision_summary:
R1221 (BUILD — the description law was one tool wide, and the wall it named was not there). R1217 held ONE MCP tool's description to the fields its report emits, and wrote down why it stopped: "the mapping from a tool to the type it returns is a hand-written pair, which is why this is one pair and not a table pretending to be a rule". That is true of the TYPE and false of the ANSWER. This repository already declares one VALID CALL per tool — `probed!` for the required-argument sweep, `exercised!` for the optional-argument differentials — makes it, and asserts it succeeded. So the pair is not written anywhere: it is OBTAINED, which is the same move R1218 made when it held the frontier roster against the keys the tool actually emits rather than against the type. The cost R1217 priced was the cost of the wrong instrument.

THE FIRST RUN WENT RED ON 72 OF 76, and the reds fall in two classes that need different answers. SIXTY-ONE of them were the same field: every writing tool answers with the envelope `finish_mutate` builds, `{receipt: {primitive, target_kind, target_id, sidecar_path, written_bytes}}`, and NOT ONE description said so. An agent calling `add_section` got back the bytes written and the sidecar they were written to, and nothing had told it there would be an answer at all. Writing that sentence sixty-three times by hand is the copy this repository keeps paying for, so it is STAMPED the way `agent_facing_tools` already stamps the path-resolution rule onto arguments — "the author cannot forget because there is nothing to remember" — and the sentence is GENERATED from the envelope's own serialized keys, so a field added to the receipt tomorrow appears in every description at once. The tools that answer with it are a declared list, and the list is held by execution IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: a writing tool missing from it answers with a `receipt` its description does not name and the field law goes red, which is exactly how `import_facts` was found missing; and a tool wrongly on it is stamped with a sentence about an answer it never gives, which a second law catches by asking whether the declared envelope is in what the tool actually said. The inventory tools' envelope was two `json!` literals spelled inline, and the two branches had already disagreed about their own shape — the failing-scan branch omitted `cascade_decay_hits` entirely — so it is now one `Default`-carrying type that both branches and the stamp read.

THE OTHER ELEVEN WERE THE DRIFT R1217 PREDICTED. `report_quest_graph` named NONE of its five fields, `report_entity` none of its four, `query_changelog_entry` none of its nine.

THEN THE DENOMINATOR, which is what makes "no longer one tool wide" worth something or nothing: 78 OF 105 ROUTED TOOLS. Twenty-seven were held by no law at all, and a tool nothing calls is indistinguishable from a tool whose description is right. Eighteen already had a declared call in `exercised!`, so the law was seated there too — one line, no second table of calls. The remaining NINE take no argument at all, which is why neither macro could reach them and why nothing in this repository had ever called them; they are the cheapest calls on the surface, an empty workspace and no arguments, and they now emit their own tests and their own accounting row from one declaration. The coverage is 105 OF 105, and it is ASSERTED rather than printed, because a seat that stopped holding anything would otherwise shrink it in silence.

THE SECOND SWEEP FOUND TWENTY-ONE MORE, which is the measurement that says the first eleven were not the tail. `validate_continuity` omitted FOURTEEN fields — every honesty surface it carries, the ones that say what the scan could not ask rather than what it found — and `describe_schema` twelve, the whole contract an agent reads before authoring. Thirty-one descriptions were repaired against answers actually observed, never against types read by eye.

THREE OF THE REPAIRS ARE DEFECTS RATHER THAN OMISSIONS, and they share one shape: a field whose absence makes a green answer mean the opposite of what it reads as. `validate_disclosure_leak.vocabulary_shared` is the sharpest — `targeted > 0` with `vocabulary_shared == 0` means the re-extraction used foreign ids, so `leaks: []` is VACUOUS rather than clean, and the description invited an agent to read the empty list as a pass. `report_entity_kind_migration.entities_examined` is the same shape (an empty list over zero entities examined says nothing), and so is `report_timeline_gaps.interval_rules`.

THE INSTRUMENT'S OWN DEFECT IS RECORDED because a green test is where it was caught: the first accounting printed "106 of 105 routed tools", having summed three seats that overlap where one tool is held twice. A set, not a sum.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO, as a decision rather than an omission: the law holds the TOP LEVEL of an answer. `rmcp` carries a real `output_schema` on every tool and this server declares none on any — that is the destination, and reaching it means converting every handler from a hand-built `CallToolResult` to a typed return so the wire actually carries structured content. Declaring the schema without the wire would advertise a contract the server does not honour, which is worse than the prose it replaces.

Round 1222.decision_summary:
R1222 (BUILD — the output-schema arc, step one: the write envelope stops being described and starts being DECLARED). R1221 generalised a law that holds a tool's DESCRIPTION to the fields its answer carries, and named what that law is a substitute for: `rmcp` carries a real `output_schema` on every tool and this server declared none on any, so prose was the whole contract. It also named why it stopped — declaring a schema the wire does not honour tells an agent something false, and honouring it means changing what every handler returns. This round does the first group properly rather than the whole surface badly.

THE MECHANISM, MEASURED BEFORE ANYTHING WAS WRITTEN. The `#[tool]` macro reads the handler's return type SYNTACTICALLY: `Json<T>` or `Result<Json<T>, E>` makes it derive the tool's output schema from `T`, and `Json<T>` converts to `CallToolResult::structured(..)`, which fills `structuredContent` on the wire beside the text. An alias over that `Result` — far tidier at sixty-five call sites — is a path the macro cannot see through, so the schema would silently be `None` again; the type is therefore spelled out at every one, and the reason is written where a later round will read it.

THE ERROR HALF IS A DECISION, NOT A DETAIL, and it is the one thing that could have been quietly lost. rmcp turns `Err(E)` into a transport-level JSON-RPC error when `E` converts to one, and into a tool RESULT carrying `is_error: true` when `E` converts to a result. This server has always refused the second way — a typo'd telling is the tool saying "no, and here is why", which a model reads and acts on, not a protocol fault it never sees. `rmcp::ErrorData` in the error slot would have been shorter and would have moved every refusal out of the model's sight, so a `Refused` type exists to keep the old behaviour exactly.

WHAT WAS CONVERTED, and why this group first: SIXTY-FIVE of the 105 routed tools share TWO answer types. Sixty-two answer `ops::MutateOutcome` through the one `finish_mutate` wire and three answer the inventory cascade envelope, so two `JsonSchema` derives buy schemas for 62% of the surface. `mnemosyne-ops` gains the optional `schemars` feature the Round 690 shape established for core and atomic — off by default, enabled solely by `mnemosyne-mcp`.

THE CONVERSION IS INCREMENTAL BY CONSTRUCTION, which is what keeps the arc from being one enormous round. Every seat in the test file that calls a handler now normalises through rmcp's OWN `IntoCallToolResult` — the trait the router itself uses — so a converted handler and an unconverted one are read by the same line and the remaining groups can land without the tests tracking which group a tool is in. The `expect` on that conversion is load-bearing rather than decorative: a handler whose error half became a PROTOCOL error would panic there, which is exactly the regression `Refused` exists to prevent.

TWO LAWS, AND THEY FAIL DIFFERENTLY FROM THE PROSE ONE. The first holds a DECLARED schema to the answer actually obtained: every property the schema declares is one the answer may carry, every `required` property is one it does carry, and the answer names nothing the schema omits. Types are not re-checked — `schemars` derives them from the type the handler literally returns, so a mismatch is a compile error and re-reading it here would be a second reading of a fact the compiler already holds. The second holds the WIRE to the declaration: a tool that publishes a schema must answer with `structuredContent`, because a schema with prose behind it is the half-step this arc refused, and it is invisible from the text half.

THE ARC'S PROGRESS IS A PINNED NUMBER, not a claim. 65 of 105 tools publish an output schema, asserted. A group that lands raises it; a tool that quietly LOSES its schema lowers it and fails — and that is the regression that matters, because the surface would go on answering and only a consumer validating against the schema would ever find out.

WHAT CHANGED ON THE WIRE, stated rather than left for someone to notice: the converted tools' TEXT half is now compact JSON rather than pretty-printed, because `CallToolResult::structured` writes the value and the structured half is the contract now. Nothing in the suite depended on the whitespace.

a refusal stays a tool result an agent reads, not a protocol error it never sees — the one thing the conversion could have silently lost
two laws: a declared schema is one the answer satisfies, and a published schema is one the wire carries; the converted count is pinned

(1) `#[schemars(skip)]` on a serialized field — seven tests red with "`add_inventory_entry` answered with [cascade_decay_hits], which its declared output schema does not describe". (2) `#[serde(skip_serializing)]` on a schema-required field — the other direction, "output schema REQUIRES [cascade_decay_hits], and the answer does not carry them". (3) an `output_schema` declared on a tool that still answers with prose — "publishes an output schema and answered with NO structured content", which is precisely the half-step this arc exists to refuse, and the pinned count went red beside it at 66

THE CONVERSION WAS COMPILER-DRIVEN, NOT PATTERN-MATCHED: the two `finish_mutate` wires were retyped first and `cargo check` then named all 65 handlers and every test call site by file and line. No regex touched this file
THE COUNT IS ASSERTED AT 65 OF 105, so the next group cannot land without moving it and a tool cannot lose its schema quietly
the description law (R1221) and the accounting that keeps it at 105 of 105 are unchanged and still green, so the prose half did not regress while the machine half was added
mnemosyne-mcp 245 tests green; root workspace suite + clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings + the separate in-repo workspaces, run through scripts/verify.sh
carry_forward_bullets: FORTY TOOLS REMAIN, and they are the harder half rather than more of the same. The 65 done here share two answer types; the 40 left are 37 distinct report types spread across `mnemosyne-ops`, `mnemosyne-validate` and `mnemosyne-query`, each needing its own `JsonSchema` derive behind the same optional feature, plus 3 tools that answer PROSE (`validate_workspace`, `validate_projection`, `list_sections`) and have no structured shape at all. That last group is a decision, not a conversion: either a shape is invented for them or they are the tools this surface honestly cannot type, and inventing one to make a number reach 105 would be the drift this repository keeps deleting

THE ERROR PATH STILL CARRIES NO SCHEMA. A refusal is `is_error: true` with text, and MCP has no output schema for that half, so what an agent gets when a call fails is prose exactly as before. Typing refusals is a separate question about whether a model reads a structured error better than a sentence, and this repository has no measurement either way

THE PROSE CHECK IS NOW REDUNDANT FOR THE CONVERTED 65 and is kept anyway, deliberately: the schema says what the shape IS and the description says what the fields MEAN, and R1221 measured that three of the fields it repaired were ones whose absence made a green answer read as its opposite. A schema cannot carry that

NOTHING HERE PROVES A CLIENT VALIDATES THE SCHEMA. What is proven is that the server's own answers satisfy what it publishes. Whether an agent's behaviour improves because the contract is machine-readable is the same prose-band question R1221 left open, and the unattended-loop experiment is where it gets asked

Round 1223.decision_summary:
R1223 (BUILD — the output-schema arc, step two: every read whose answer is a REPORT now declares it, and the two that cannot say why). Round 1222 typed the write envelope — 65 tools sharing two answer types — and left 40 reads whose types live across four crates. This converts 32 of them and records, as a fact about the tools rather than a shortfall, why the rest do not.

THE FEATURE SHAPE IS ROUND 690'S, EXTENDED TWICE MORE. `mnemosyne-validate` and `mnemosyne-query` gain the same optional `schemars` feature core and atomic have carried since Round 690 and ops gained in Round 1222: off by default, pulled only by `mnemosyne-mcp`, forwarding to its own dependencies. Nothing outside the MCP binary compiles a line of schema code.

THE DERIVE IS BLANKET WITHIN THE REPORT MODULES, and that is a decision. A hand-picked list of "types an MCP answer can reach" would be a list nobody maintains — a nested type added tomorrow would need finding. Deriving on every serializable type in the report modules makes the property statable instead: THESE MODULES' TYPES ARE SCHEMA-PUBLISHABLE. The compiler then walked the closure for us: eight more types in core and atomic (`Entity`, `Predicate`, `DisclosureReveal`, `DisclosureSurface`, `EpubLocator`, `Binding`, `PopulationCensus`, `MutationReason`) and the two import verdicts, each named by a build error rather than found by reading.

`ops` NOW RE-EXPORTS WHAT ITS READS RETURN, which is a wart this round exposed rather than created. Those functions have always returned the validator's and the query crate's types, and nothing could NAME them without reaching past `ops` into a crate it exists to wrap — the same reach Round 1009 re-exported `ViolationSource` to avoid. It stayed latent while every caller wrote `match … { Ok(r) => serialize(&r) }` and never spelled a type, and stopped being latent the moment a caller had to DECLARE one. A boundary crate owns the vocabulary of what it answers with.

TWO TOOLS COULD NOT BE TYPED, AND MCP IS WHY. The specification requires a tool's `output_schema` to have root type `object`, and rmcp refuses to publish anything else — which is right, and which turned two shapes in this surface into findings:

- `query_section` answers an ENUM: one shape for the bare section, a different one when a neighborhood is asked for. A schema saying "one of two shapes" tells an agent to branch on what it sent. The fix is to make the answer ONE shape with the neighborhood optional, which changes the wire for the bare case — a decision, not a conversion, and it is left as one.
- `query_term` and `list_inventory` answered a bare JSON ARRAY. That one IS a conversion and was done: each answer is now an object with a named field. Wrapping is an improvement rather than a tax — a named field is where a count or a truncation flag can go, which is exactly what Round 1221 found missing on reads whose empty list read as a clean answer.

THE COUNT IS 97 OF 105. What is left is three tools that answer PROSE (`validate_workspace`, `validate_projection`, `list_sections`), `query_section` above, and `describe_frontier_axes`, `redact_term`, `emit_publishable_override_ledger_draft`, `describe_schema`. Each is a shape question rather than a typing one.

THE OBSERVER HAD TO MOVE WITH THE WIRE, and noticing that was the round's sharpest correction. `Json<T>` writes its text half COMPACT; the differential cases name needles like `"at_placed": false`, pretty-printed. Fifteen of them went red at once — and every one of those failures was a change in the OBSERVER dressed as a change in the tool. The oracle now reads `structuredContent` and pretty-prints it, so what a needle follows is the value the schema describes rather than a rendering choice made inside rmcp. Rewriting fifteen needles would have passed the suite and left the differentials watching the wrong half of the answer.
changes_bullets: 97 of 105 routed tools publish an output schema derived from the type they return; validate and query gain the Round 690 optional schemars feature
ops re-exports the report types its reads return, so a caller can name what it answers with without reaching past the boundary crate

Round 1224.decision_summary:
R1224 (BUILD — the output-schema arc, step three: the tool that answered three shapes answers one, and a law now says so). Round 1223 met `query_section` as a refusal rather than a conversion: rmcp would not publish an output schema for it because `QuerySectionPayload` is an enum, and MCP requires a schema rooted at an `object`. That refusal was correct and it was a finding — a schema saying "one of three shapes" tells an agent to branch on what it sent.

WHAT THE SHAPES ACTUALLY WERE, measured rather than assumed, and there were THREE rather than the two the carry named. Asked for nothing, the tool answered the section's fields FLAT. Asked for a neighborhood, it answered `{section, related, changelog}`. Asked for both, it answered `{section, outbound_refs, inbound_refs, related_changelog_entries}` — the same information as the second under different field names. That last pair is a SECOND SPELLING of one thing, and nothing could see it while the answer had no declared shape: no test compared the two, because no test could say what either was supposed to be.

AND THE TWO ARGUMENTS WERE NOT INDEPENDENT, which is the defect underneath the defect. `include_related` and `include_changelog` read as two switches, and the mode mapping resolved `(true,false)` and `(false,true)` to the SAME mode — so a caller asking only for the changelog was handed the cross-ref neighborhood too, and vice versa. Nothing declared that coupling and no consumer could want it; it survived because with three shapes there was nowhere to notice it. One shape leaves the coupling no reason to exist, and it is gone: each flag now decides exactly its own field.

THE ANSWER IS ONE STRUCT WITH THREE KEYS ALWAYS PRESENT — `section`, `related`, `changelog` — with `null` meaning "you did not ask". Optional-and-absent would also satisfy the schema, and it is the ordinary JSON idiom, but it is not what this fix is FOR: the guarantee worth having is that an agent never has to discover which shape it got. The wire changes for the bare case (the section's fields now nest under `section`), which is the cost, stated.

A LAW NOW ASSERTS IT, and writing it found that NEITHER EXISTING LAW WOULD HAVE. The schema law asks that every key carried is declared and every REQUIRED key is carried — an optional key that vanishes when unasked satisfies both. The description law asks that a carried key is named — an absent key is not carried. So the tool could have gone back to three shapes with the suite fully green, which is exactly the regression this round exists to prevent. The new law calls the tool with all four flag combinations and asserts the KEY SET is identical, with a non-vacuity check on each arm that asked for something — four calls all answering nothing would otherwise agree for the wrong reason. Injecting `skip_serializing_if` on one field turns it red naming both key sets.

THE COUNT IS 98 OF 105. What remains is three tools that answer PROSE and four that assemble their shape at the wire; each is a shape question rather than a typing one, and none is blocked by anything the world does not allow.
