Round 770 — the emitter, compiled by the.decision_summary:
R770 (BUILD, new crate + engine, no store change) — the emitter, and the round where the arc's claim gets compiled instead of asserted. `mnemosyne-engine-build::emit_playable_projection(root, telling, overrides)` runs the whole fail-loud projection at BUILD time and returns Rust source defining `pub fn playable_projection() -> PlayableProjection`. The consumer's `build.rs` writes it to `OUT_DIR`, the crate `include!`s it, and startup does no store read, no parse, and no validation — `from_parts` (R769) takes no `Result`.

A DEFECT IN R769 THAT ONLY THIS ROUND COULD SEE, and the reason it could not be seen earlier is worth more than the fix. `ProjectionParts` carried `Fork` and `Door` directly, and both are `#[non_exhaustive]`: a downstream crate cannot write a literal for either. So the parts type — whose entire purpose is to be constructed by GENERATED CODE IN ANOTHER CRATE — was not constructible from another crate. R769's equivalence test passed because it lives INSIDE mnemosyne-engine, where `non_exhaustive` does not apply. An in-crate test is structurally blind to downstream constructibility. The fix is `ForkPart` / `DoorPart`, the same mirror move `LinePart` / `CastPart` already made; the guard against regression is that this crate is downstream, so its test constructing a `ProjectionParts` by hand stops compiling the moment the parts type readmits a non-constructible member. This is the third time in the arc that round N+1 found what round N's tests could not reach (R767's fan-out found by R768, R769's constructibility found here), and each time the blindness was structural rather than careless.

THE GENERATOR IS COMPILED BY ITS OWN CRATE, EVERY BUILD. A round whose thesis is compile-time verification would be absurd if the one artifact nobody compiled were the generator's output. So this crate's `build.rs` renders a fixture through `render` and writes it to `OUT_DIR`, and a `#[cfg(test)] mod baked { include!(...) }` compiles it INTO the crate. If `render` emits invalid Rust, or names a kernel type that changed shape, the failure lands here — in this workspace, on the same build — rather than in a consumer's repository. `src/render.rs` is `include!`d by the build script rather than imported, because a build script cannot depend on its own crate and a second copy of the generator would be free to drift from the one CI compiles. The fixture exercises every emitted form: all three door kinds, an anchored rung, both locator kinds, `Option` in Some and None, a count, and strings carrying an embedded quote, a newline, a backslash and non-ASCII prose. `render`'s claim that `{:?}` on a `&str` is exactly Rust's literal escaping is therefore checked by rustc, not asserted in a comment.

WHAT THE BUILD SCRIPT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT CONTAIN. The consumer's script is a delegation and nothing else — the store read, the `rerun-if-changed` declarations and the rendering all live here. That constraint is the whole reason R768 moved the interactive layer into the store: a build script that DERIVED anything would put the derivation back in the consumer's repository, which is the artifact class the engine census drives to zero. The documented example is the entire body of the consumer's `main`, and it is compiled as a doctest rather than shown as prose, so the API it demonstrates cannot rot.

`rerun-if-changed` is declared for the workspace config, the atomic sidecar and the canon order — listed conservatively, so a path that does not exist yet is still declared and CREATING it triggers a rebuild rather than being silently ignored. Together with `to_parts`'s sorted-order determinism (R769), an unchanged store yields a byte-identical file and a no-op rebuild churns nothing downstream.

VERIFICATION: 2 tests plus a doctest, and the compile is itself the largest gate. The generated-source test asserts the values SURVIVED the round trip through Rust source — telling, walk, divergent ending, the nasty string in both a line and a title, `Option` in both states, the disclosure mode, cast, forks, and all three door kinds — so a generator emitting syntactically valid but WRONG code still fails. The constructibility test builds a `ProjectionParts` by hand from this downstream crate, which is the check R769 structurally could not make. 1197 workspace tests green via scripts/verify.sh (+3 on R769's 1194), clippy -D warnings clean, fmt clean, validate-workspace T1 orphan = 0 and T3 reject = 0, validate-code-refs 0. The one clippy finding (`needless_doctest_main`) was resolved by unwrapping the example rather than by an allow, keeping the doctest compiled.

NEXT is R771, the small closing round: narrow `from_report` out of the public API so `ProjectionParts` is the single ingestion door rather than one of two — which is what finally makes the module doc's claim that invention is a compile error TRUE (R764 found it false) — and correct the `quest.rs` sentence that justifies runtime store reads by the staleness of a baked snapshot. After that the mnemosyne half of this arc is done and the consumer's half is a consumer session: author its ladder map, import it, then delete its anchors file, its derive half, its hand-built interactive layer, and its runtime store read.

Round 771 — the ingestion door closes an.decision_summary:
R771 (BUILD, engine + render, no store change) — the ingestion door closes, and the crate's headline promise becomes true. `mnemosyne-engine`'s module doc has said since R643 that invention is unrepresentable: a downstream crate can READ a `Line` but never fabricate one, "a compile error here, not a test to remember". R764 found that claim was true of the RENDER side and false of the INGEST side — `PlayableProjection::from_report` was public and every type inside a `PlayableWorldReport` is a pub-field struct with no `non_exhaustive`, so a consumer could hand the kernel a fabricated world and receive real `Line`s minted from it. The guard sat one layer above the hole. This round takes `from_report` off the public API, leaving `ProjectionParts` as the single ingestion door.

WHAT THAT DOES AND DOES NOT BUY, stated carefully because the temptation is to overclaim a win. It does not make forgery impossible: `ProjectionParts` is plain data BY NECESSITY, since generated code cannot construct a `#[non_exhaustive]` type, so an author who edits their own build script still forges their own game — which the threat model always allowed and R764 recorded as weak point 1. What it buys is that there is now ONE door instead of two, and the remaining one is filled by a build from the store rather than written by hand. The render-side guarantee — a renderer holds a `Line` and cannot mint a sentence — is untouched and was never the thing in doubt.

THE NARROWING IS PROVEN BY A PAIR OF DOCTESTS, not by one. A lone `compile_fail` passes when its snippet fails for ANY reason, so a typo'd path would "prove" the guard while proving nothing — the classic way this kind of test lies. So the positive half (`from_parts` resolves) must COMPILE and the negative half repeats the same path spelling before adding `from_report`. A wrong path now breaks the suite instead of faking a pass.

GATED, NOT MERELY NARROWED. Taking `from_report` off the public API left it with no caller outside tests, and the dead-code lint said so immediately. Rather than silence that with an allow, the function is marked `#[cfg(test)]`, which is what it now is: a test helper that builds a projection from a report with no passages. The alternative — deleting it and inlining `HashMap::new()` at some thirty in-crate call sites — is churn for no gain, and the name carries meaning the inline would lose.

THE ONE EXTERNAL CALLER WAS REHOMED, and usefully. `mnemosyne-render`'s test fixture built a `PlayableWorldReport` by hand and called `from_report`; it now builds a `ProjectionParts` and calls `from_parts`. That is not just a port: it makes render a SECOND downstream crate exercising the ingestion door, so if parts ever readmit a type a foreign crate cannot construct (the R769 defect R770 fixed), two crates stop compiling instead of one. The fixture also got smaller — a report is a manuscript shape that the projection immediately indexes away, while parts are what the projection actually holds.

ALSO CORRECTED: `quest.rs` said the kernel reads the quest graph "at runtime" so that "the compile-time snapshot a consumer would otherwise bake in cannot drift from the store". R764 decided to reverse that reasoning rather than quietly contradict it, and this is where the sentence gets rewritten: the anti-drift property comes from DERIVING FROM THE STORE, not from the timing. A projection baked under `cargo:rerun-if-changed` and never committed cannot go stale either, and it carries a check a runtime read cannot — change a kernel type and the generated source stops compiling. The honest residual is stated where the claim is: a pre-built binary is pinned to the store revision it was built from, the same trade a consumer already makes pinning this workspace by git rev. The quest axis has no baked path yet; nothing there argues against one now.

Round 772 — the bake watched a file the.decision_summary:
R772 (BUILD, ops + engine + engine-build, no store change) — a defect found in R770 while reading the consumer's second lift request, fixed before its actual ask is built on top of it. R770's emitter printed `cargo:rerun-if-changed` for three HAND-WRITTEN paths: `mnemosyne.toml`, `docs/.atomic/workspace.atomic.json`, `canon-order.json`. The first real consumer declares `[atomic] sidecar_path = ".atomic/tide.atomic.json"`. So the bake watched a store that does not exist in that workspace and never watched the one it read: rebuild the store, and the baked projection stays whatever it was, silently.

THE CLAIM THAT WAS FALSE. This crate's module doc carries a section titled "Why the artifact cannot go stale", and its argument is exactly the rerun declaration. The argument held for a workspace that happens to use every default and failed for the only consumer the crate was written for. A declared input that is not the file the loader OPENS is worse than making no claim: an undeclared dependency is visibly absent, while a wrong one reads as watched. Two of the three paths were wrong the same way — `canon-order.json` is `[continuity] canon_order_path`, configurable — and the third assumed `mnemosyne.toml` at the root, though `discover_config` also accepts `.mnemosyne/config.toml` and walks upward.

THE FIX IS STRUCTURAL, NOT A SECOND CORRECT LIST. `mnemosyne_ops::projection_inputs` resolves the config through `discover_config` and the sidecar through `resolve_sidecar` — the same two resolutions `playable_world_report` and `quest_graph_report` use to open those files — and returns the resolved config path, the declared canon-order file, and the sidecar. `mnemosyne_engine::projection_inputs` reads it through so a consumer talks to its kernel rather than past it into `ops` (the `store_entity_kinds` precedent), and `emit_playable_projection` calls that. `mnemosyne-engine-build` now holds no path knowledge at all. Writing a second, correct list would have fixed today's bug and left the same drift open for tomorrow's.

THE ORACLE IS THE RESOLVER, NOT A HAND-WRITTEN EXPECTATION. The test asserts the declared sidecar EQUALS what `resolve_sidecar` returns for that workspace, because a hand-written expected list is a copy of exactly the class of bug being killed and would have been just as wrong in R770. Non-vacuity was proven by injection rather than argued: putting `default_sidecar_path` back made the test fail with "the sidecar the loader opens (/tmp/.../.atomic/tide.atomic.json) is not declared", which is the consumer's real configuration.

WHAT WAS KEPT AND WHAT WAS DROPPED. R770's conservative-listing property — a path that does not exist is still declared, so creating it rebuilds — was right and is kept: a workspace with no config declares its would-be `mnemosyne.toml`, since creating one moves the sidecar. What is dropped is guessing the contents. The list stays exactly what the two projections open; `[continuity] rules_path` is not declared because neither reads it, and declaring an unread file buys spurious rebuilds. Inputs are now declared BEFORE the projection runs, so the dependency registers even when the projection then fails.

R772 (BUILD, ops + engine + engine-build, no store change) — a defect found in R770 while reading the consumer's second lift request, fixed before its actual ask is built on top of it. R770's emitter printed `cargo:rerun-if-changed` for three HAND-WRITTEN paths: `mnemosyne.toml`, `docs/.atomic/workspace.atomic.json`, `canon-order.json`. The first real consumer declares `[atomic] sidecar_path = ".atomic/tide.atomic.json"`. So the bake watched a store that does not exist in that workspace and never watched the one it read: rebuild the store, and the baked projection stays whatever it was, silently.

THE CLAIM THAT WAS FALSE. This crate's module doc carries a section titled "Why the artifact cannot go stale", and its argument is exactly the rerun declaration. The argument held for a workspace that happens to use every default and failed for the only consumer the crate was written for. A declared input that is not the file the loader OPENS is worse than making no claim: an undeclared dependency is visibly absent, while a wrong one reads as watched. Two of the three paths were wrong the same way — `canon-order.json` is `[continuity] canon_order_path`, configurable — and the third assumed `mnemosyne.toml` at the root, though `discover_config` also accepts `.mnemosyne/config.toml` and walks upward.

THE FIX IS STRUCTURAL, NOT A SECOND CORRECT LIST. `mnemosyne_ops::projection_inputs` resolves the config through `discover_config` and the sidecar through `resolve_sidecar` — the same two resolutions `playable_world_report` and `quest_graph_report` use to open those files — and returns the resolved config path, the declared canon-order file, and the sidecar. `mnemosyne_engine::projection_inputs` reads it through so a consumer talks to its kernel rather than past it into `ops` (the `store_entity_kinds` precedent), and `emit_playable_projection` calls that. `mnemosyne-engine-build` now holds no path knowledge at all. Writing a second, correct list would have fixed today's bug and left the same drift open for tomorrow's.

THE ORACLE IS THE RESOLVER, NOT A HAND-WRITTEN EXPECTATION. The test asserts the declared sidecar EQUALS what `resolve_sidecar` returns for that workspace, because a hand-written expected list is a copy of exactly the class of bug being killed and would have been just as wrong in R770. Non-vacuity was proven by injection rather than argued: putting `default_sidecar_path` back made the test fail with "the sidecar the loader opens (/tmp/.../.atomic/tide.atomic.json) is not declared", which is the consumer's real configuration.

WHAT WAS KEPT AND WHAT WAS DROPPED. R770's conservative-listing property — a path that does not exist is still declared, so creating it rebuilds — was right and is kept: a workspace with no config declares its would-be `mnemosyne.toml`, since creating one moves the sidecar. What is dropped is guessing the contents. The list stays exactly what the two projections open; `[continuity] rules_path` is not declared because neither reads it, and declaring an unread file buys spurious rebuilds. Round 773 — the quest seam, and the same.decision_summary:
R773 (BUILD, engine, no store change) — the JOURNAL axis gets the seam the narrative axis got in R769, because the consumer's second lift request asks for the emitter that sits on top of it and there is nothing under it yet. `QuestProjection` had no plain-data shape, and it could not have one by accident: `QuestView`, `QuestWorldView` and `QuestCompletionView` are `#[non_exhaustive]`, so generated code in another crate cannot construct one. That is the same wall `LinePart` and `CastPart` were built for, and the answer is the same — `QuestProjectionParts` with `QuestPart` / `QuestWorldPart` / `QuestCompletionPart`, `to_parts` to emit, and a `from_parts` that takes no `Result` because the quest-graph read and the precondition join already ran.

THE SAME DOOR WAS OPEN HERE, AND CLOSED THE SAME WAY. `quest.rs` opens by saying every quest is store-derived and the kernel invents none, "so a consumer's quest list cannot drift from the store". `QuestProjection::from_report` was public and takes a `QuestGraphReport`, which is a pub-field struct — so a downstream crate could hand the kernel quests the store never declared and get `QuestView`s back, and the module's opening promise was false in exactly the way R764 found the crate's headline promise false on the narrative axis. R771 fixed the one; this fixes the twin. It is worth naming that the twin existed at all: R771's entry closed "the mnemosyne half of this arc is DONE", and it was, for the axis being worked. The identical hole one module over went unlooked-at because nothing was pulling on it yet.

PROVEN BY A PAIR, NOT BY A LONE compile_fail. The negative doctest is preceded by a positive one using the same path spelling, so a typo cannot fake the guard — R771's argument, reused because it is right and because a second axis is exactly where an argument gets copied badly.

WHAT DOES NOT MOVE TO THE BUILD. The completability gate stays where it is. R764 said quest preconditions are game rules over player state and stay at runtime, and the consumer's own request agreed with that sentence while asking for something else: the DERIVATION of the projection, not the EVALUATION of its rules. So `QuestProjectionParts` carries no gate result, and the equivalence test insists a baked projection can still ANSWER the gate — it builds a two-road world where one road digs the precondition in time and the other never does, asserts the verdict has length one, and only then asserts live and baked agree. Two empty vectors comparing equal would have proven nothing.

`to_parts` SORTS NOTHING, and that is documented rather than left to be rediscovered as a bug. The playable seam sorts because the projection holds `HashMap`s; this one holds a `Vec` the graph derived from a `BTreeSet` and a `BTreeMap` per world, with preconditions sorted and deduped at ingestion. Determinism is inherited, and saying so is cheaper than a future round wondering whether the omission was an oversight.

Round 774 — the quest emitter, and the s.decision_summary:
R774 (BUILD, engine-build, no store change) — the consumer's second lift request, answered. `emit_quest_projection` is the sibling of `emit_playable_projection`: it projects the quest graph at build time and returns Rust source defining `quest_projection() -> QuestProjection`. With both emitters in hand, a consumer that bakes both never opens the store at startup, which is the whole of the owner's directive rather than the half the first emitter bought — the consumer measured that half exactly: 3.5 billion instructions removed from `Narrative::load` and a nearly identical 3.5 billion still standing next to it in `Knots::load`.

THE REQUEST DID NOT ARGUE WITH R764 AND NEITHER DOES THIS. R764 wrote that quest preconditions are game rules over player state and stay at runtime. The request quoted that sentence back and said it is asking for something else: the DERIVATION of the projection, not the EVALUATION of its rules. That distinction is exactly right and it is the shape built here. `QuestProjectionParts` carries no gate result, and a baked projection still answers `completability` against a playable projection whenever it is asked, because the gate is a question, not a field.

ONE THING THE EMITTER DELIBERATELY CANNOT DO. `QuestProjection::from_workspace` takes an order override; this takes none and passes `None`. An `--order` override is CWD-relative CLI semantics with no meaning in a build script, and worse, it would read a canon order this crate did not declare to cargo — the exact divergence between the file declared and the file opened that R772 closed two rounds ago. The right fix for a footgun found once is to leave no way to hold it, not to write a warning next to it.

THE RENDERER IS ONE TEXT, NOT TWO. `render_quest` shares the quoter, the vec helper and the `Option` helper with `render`, so the claim that `{:?}` on a `&str` is exactly Rust literal escaping is proven once for both axes and cannot be fixed on one and missed on the other. The quest fixture is compiled by this crate's own `build.rs` on the same terms as the playable one — all three `QuestState` variants, a completion with an actor and one without, a quest spanning two roads, and the nasty string in an objective, because a quest objective is authored prose and quotes as freely as a line does.

THE DOWNSTREAM CHECK IS REPEATED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. Every `QuestView` type is `#[non_exhaustive]`, so a struct literal for one fails to compile outside `mnemosyne-engine` — and R773's round-trip test lives INSIDE that crate and structurally cannot see it. That is precisely how the R769 defect survived until R770 caught it from here. So this crate, which is downstream, builds a `QuestProjectionParts` by literal; if the parts type ever readmits a member no foreign crate can construct, this stops compiling.

VERIFIED AGAINST THE LIVE STORE, NOT ONLY FIXTURES. The emitter was run on the consumer's real workspace: 45,060 bytes of source out, compiled, and the baked projection compared EQUAL to the live one across all 22 real quests — all seven knots present, seven quests carrying `opened_by` preconditions. The same run confirmed R772 end to end, resolving the consumer's own `mnemosyne.toml`, `canon-order.json` and `.atomic/tide.atomic.json`, where R770's declaration had named a store that does not exist in that workspace.

Round 775 — one body was the cost, not o.decision_summary:
R775 (BUILD, engine-build, no store change) — the consumer filed a measurement it explicitly declined to turn into a request: the baked playable source is 2.6MB in 18 lines, 98% of it a single nested `from_parts` expression, and it did not ask for a change because it had not measured any alternative's compile time. That is the right discipline and it left the question with the party holding the emitter. So it was measured here.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENT SAYS. The cost is FUNCTION BODY SIZE. Not line length, not total volume, not nesting as such. A controlled pair settles it: the same element literals, the same types, byte counts within 0.4%, differing only in whether they sit in one function or a hundred — 5,000 elements took 29.1s and 1.21GB of rustc in one body and 5.5s and 0.57GB in a hundred. And it is superlinear, so it worsens as a store grows: the same one-body encoding at 2,500 elements took 9.0s, meaning 2x the input cost 3.2x the time.

SO THE EMITTER SPLITS BODIES AND KEEPS THE TYPES. Every list it writes, at every depth, becomes chunk functions of at most 50 literals; the top-level function holds one call per chunk — the structure, never the prose. On the consumer's real store that is 34.5s and 1.13GB before, 6.3s and 0.55GB after, with the longest line falling from 2,623,420 bytes to 26,816 across 520 chunk functions. The file grew 1.6%, paid once for a 5.3x compile win. The regenerated source was compiled and compared EQUAL to the live projection — 66 sections, 799 lines — because a faster bake that is a different bake is not a win.

THE PROPOSED REMEDY WAS NOT NEEDED, AND SAYING SO IS THE POINT. The consumer sketched a flat `&'static [(&str, &str)]` table plus an index, reasoning that it would parse near-linearly. It would — and it would give up the type checking that is the entire reason the bake is Rust source and not JSON (R764 rejected `Deserialize` precisely because a serialized snapshot cannot carry a shape contract). The measurement shows that trade was never necessary: the same win is available without touching the typing. A hypothesis can be right about the SYMPTOM and wrong about the remedy, and the way to tell is to measure rather than to reason from the sketch.

ONE FINDING THAT ONLY THE NEW ENCODING COULD PRODUCE. Generated FUNCTIONS have signatures, and a signature is a lint surface the old single expression never had — `clippy::type_complexity` rejects the expanded four-level `by_world` element type, in the generated file, in a consumer's build, under the `-D warnings` a consumer is entitled to run. Found by this workspace's own fixture compile, which is the reason that fixture is compiled by `build.rs` at all, and fixed at the cause with the kernel's existing `SectionLines` alias rather than an allow. A generator whose output does not survive its consumer's lints has not finished generating.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED. 50 is the chunk the measurement used, not a tuned optimum; no sweep was run, and the finding is that a BOUND must exist, not that this is the best one. The generated file's RUNTIME cost is untouched and unmeasured here — it still allocates a `String` per quoted value at startup — and interning would be a separate round with its own numbers.

Round 776 — a world it cannot see is not.decision_summary:
R776 (BUILD/DEBT, mnemosyne-engine, no store change) — the owner asked whether the default engine had a problem. A review of the crate found two, both of the same shape: a FAIL-LOUD GATE THAT ANSWERS A QUESTION IT CANNOT SEE WITH THE WORD FOR SAFE. This round fixes the playable one; the quest one is the next round.

WHAT WAS WRONG. `PlayableProjection::gate(world)` opens by taking `self.walk(world)`, which returns an empty slice for a world the projection does not carry. The loop that produces every finding then never runs, and the function returns an empty vec — which the same doc comment defines as "the interactive layer is play-clean". So a typo'd, stale, or foreign world name did not fail; it PASSED. This was measured before it was fixed rather than argued from the code: on one projection, `gate("main")` returned its real EmptySpot finding and `gate("mian")` returned nothing.

WHY IT SURVIVED, WHICH IS THE MORE USEFUL HALF. The kernel held the authoritative world set privately and exposed no way to ask for it. `by_world`, `walks` and `forks` are all private and there was no enumerator anywhere in the public API, so a consumer wanting to gate every road had to bring its own list. The first consumer did exactly that: it rebuilt the list by walking the fork graph from `main` through `walk` and `forks_at`. That is a DIFFERENT definition — "fork-reachable from the trunk" instead of "carried by this projection" — and a registered world-line that no fork edge points at would simply never have been gated, with nothing anywhere able to say so. This is the mistake R766 refused to make on the prose axis, where the slicer exposes `in_prose_order()` precisely so an ordered caller never re-implements the search and drifts from it. The world set had no such door, so the caller re-implemented it. On today's store the two definitions happen to coincide at seven worlds, which is worth saying plainly: the defect is structural rather than currently-manifesting, and the reason it is worth paying now is that nothing would report it if they diverged.

THE FIX IS TWO THINGS, AND THEY BELONG TOGETHER. `worlds()` returns the projection's own world list, sorted, so the question can be asked. `GateViolation::UnknownWorld` is what `gate` returns, alone, when it is asked about a world it does not carry — alone because with no walk the remaining checks would each spend themselves on emptiness and hand back the clean verdict, which is the bug wearing a longer form.

THE PREDICATE IS THE WORLD MAP, NOT THE WALK'S LENGTH, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE CARE OF THIS ROUND. `walks` holds an entry for every world in the report, so a REGISTERED world whose walk is empty is known with nothing on it, while an unknown name has no entry at all. Those are different facts and they deserve different answers: the first is a clean verdict honestly earned, the second is a question the gate cannot answer. Spelled the lazy way — `walk(world).is_empty()` — they collapse into one answer that is wrong for both, turning every empty-but-real world into a fabricated violation while the actual defect stays half-fixed. A test pins both directions on one projection so the distinction cannot be optimised away later.

WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY LEFT ALONE. The read accessors — `lines`, `walk`, `cast_at`, `scene`, `live_doors_at` — still answer empty for an unknown world, and their docs already say so. The line drawn here is not "emptiness is bad": an accessor that says "nothing here" has answered, while a GATE that says "clean" has issued a verdict about something it never examined. Only the verdict was changed.

ONE SMALL THING FOUND WHILE FIXING IT. The baked-equivalence test — the one that proves a projection survives `to_parts`/`from_parts` — iterated a hand-written `["main", "dark"]`. That is the same hand-list mistake in miniature, inside the test whose job is to prove the artifact, where a world added to the fixture would silently stop being checked. It now derives the list from `worlds()`.
changes_bullets: `PlayableProjection::gate` answered an unknown world with an empty vec, which its own doc comment defines as play-clean — measured before the fix on one projection: `gate("main")` returned its real EmptySpot finding and `gate("mian")` returned nothing at all

New `GateViolation::UnknownWorld`, returned alone and nothing else: with no walk there is nothing the remaining checks could examine, so continuing would spend each of them on emptiness and hand back the clean verdict

New `PlayableProjection::worlds()` — the authoritative world set, sorted; it existed only privately, so the first consumer rebuilt the list by walking the fork graph from `main` through `walk` + `forks_at`, which is the different definition "fork-reachable from the trunk" rather than "carried by this projection"

The membership test is the world MAP, not `walk(world).is_empty()`: a registered world whose walk is empty is KNOWN and honestly clean, an unknown name is a question the gate cannot answer, and the lazy spelling collapses both into one answer that is wrong for both

Read accessors deliberately keep answering empty for an unknown world (`lines`, `walk`, `cast_at`, `scene`, `live_doors_at`): an accessor that says "nothing here" is an answer, a gate that says "clean" is a verdict, and the line drawn is the verdict rather than the emptiness
The baked-equivalence test's own hand-written `["main", "dark"]` now derives from `worlds()` — the same hand-list mistake in miniature, sitting inside the test that proves the bake

Non-vacuity proven by RUNNING the assertion against the unfixed code first: a throwaway probe asserted `gate("mian").is_empty()` and PASSED on the pre-fix engine, so the permanent test that now demands UnknownWorld fails without the fix
Non-vacuity in the other direction, in the same test and against the same projection: `gate("main")` still returns its real EmptySpot finding, so the new early return is not swallowing the walk

Round 778 — the pair nothing was checkin.decision_summary:
R778 (BUILD/DEBT, mnemosyne-engine, no store change) — the sibling of R776, and the second half of the review the owner asked for. The playable gate answered an unknown world with the word for clean; the quest gate did the same thing one axis over, and for a reason R776's fix did not reach.

WHAT WAS WRONG. `QuestProjection::completability(&PlayableProjection)` takes the deadline for each road as the earliest completion scene's position on that road's walk. A world the playable projection does not carry has an empty walk, so no position is found, so there is no deadline, so the road was `continue`d — silently. Every precondition on that road went unchecked and the gate returned no finding about it, which is indistinguishable from having checked it and found nothing. Measured before it was fixed rather than argued from the code: one quest layer declaring a road called `braid`, paired with a playable projection that knows only `main`, returned an empty vec; paired with one that walks `braid`, the same layer returned the real precondition violation.

THE DEEPER PROBLEM IS THAT NOTHING JOINED THE PAIR. These are two independently built projections. Each carries the `telling` it was resolved under; neither ever looked at the other's. Each constructor takes `telling` as its own argument, and a build-time bake makes that TWO separate emitter invocations (R774), so producing a mismatched pair required no mistake more exotic than typing a different string twice. The first consumer already hands the two DIFFERENT overrides — precondition predicates to the quest side, defaults to the playable side — so the pairing was loose in practice before it was loose in theory.

WHAT IT DOES NOW. A pair cut for different tellings is `TellingMismatch`, returned ALONE: every finding underneath would be a statement about the wrong world, and a list of those reads as work done. A quest road the playable projection does not carry is `WorldNotWalked` naming the quest that lost its check, rather than a skipped iteration.

THE STRICTNESS WAS SET BY MEASUREMENT, NOT BY TASTE. Before writing a check that can fail a real store, both world sets were read off the first consumer's store: `report-playable-world` and `report-quest-graph` under `reader` return the same seven names, and both report nine registered branches, the difference being the three `weave-*` confluences that neither projection carries as a world. So the new violation cannot fire there, and its non-vacuity comes from injection in a test instead — which is the right source, because a check that fires on a correct store is a check that will be deleted.

ONE THING CORRECTED RATHER THAN FIXED, SAID PLAINLY. A comment here claimed that because a withheld fact emits no line, "offered" is exactly "diggable under this telling". That is false whenever a consumer declares `journal_predicates`: the projection routes typed journal facts OUT of the line stream, so a precondition fact that is itself a typed leg is offered by the store and invisible to this gate, which would report it unreachable when it is not. The direction is a false alarm rather than a silent pass, and no consumer pairs a journal-routing playable projection with this gate today, so the behaviour is left alone and the sentence is not. "Offered" here means "disclosed as prose". Making the gate see the store's offer rather than the consumer's prose stream needs an accessor that does not exist and a decision about what offered should mean, which is a round, not a clause.

WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT ADDED. A quest whose completion beats all sit off its world's walk still yields no deadline and is still not gated. That is a different defect — a store inconsistency rather than a mispaired projection — and the first consumer's store demonstrably carries quests that are Done on a road with no completion beat at all, a neighbourhood this round did not characterise. Turning it red without measuring it is how a gate earns its reputation for being wrong.

Round 779 — a shared rule one caller cou.decision_summary:
R779 (BUILD/DEBT, mnemosyne-engine + mnemosyne-render, no store change) — the third and last confirmed finding of the review that produced R776 and R778, and the one whose fix makes a sentence already written in this crate true.

WHAT WAS WRONG. `PlayableProjection::scene` bundled a spot as a `SceneView` and filled its `doors` from the UNFILTERED `doors_at`, while `live_doors_at` filtered the same doors through the disclose-freshness rule. Two public read paths to one datum, under two different invariants. R762/R763 built that rule precisely so the tide field-report dead-door class could not recur, and recorded that its strength was being a SHARED RULE rather than a gate — one definition every disclose-door calls, so the half-enforced-invariant class is structurally impossible. It was not shared. It was available, and the accessor a renderer reaches for first declined it.

The doc on `live_doors_at` said, in as many words, that the dead-door class "cannot recur through the kernel's own doors". That was false while `scene` existed in its old shape, and it was false in the most expensive way a doc comment can be: it described the guarantee a reader would rely on instead of writing their own check.

WHAT IT DOES NOW. `scene` takes `known` and builds its doors through `live_doors_at`. There is one path. A reader with no session state passes an empty set, which filters nothing — freshness is a set difference — but states "this reader holds nothing" rather than leaving the question unasked. The engine's own text renderer does exactly that in `render_playthrough`, where it is not a workaround but the truth: a playthrough rendering lays out the whole declared walk at once, so there is no reader partway through it holding anything.

WHY A SIGNATURE CHANGE RATHER THAN A DOC FIX. The two-path shape was the defect, so a doc that described it accurately would have preserved it. The old call is exactly recoverable — `scene(w, s, &HashSet::new())` — so nothing is lost but the ability to skip the rule by accident, and the cost falls entirely inside this workspace: the first consumer never called `scene`, building its own doors and calling `fresh_disclosure` itself, which is why this was latent rather than live.

THE TEST IS THE POINT, NOT THE EDIT. The assertion is that `scene(...).doors` EQUALS `live_doors_at(...)` at every `known` the surrounding test already establishes — nothing known, one fact known, both known. A future short-cut back to the unfiltered set now fails in this crate rather than in a consumer's chrome. Non-vacuity was proven by injection rather than by reading: putting `doors_at` back makes the assertion fail on the both-known case, which was run.

Round 780 — the axis the emitter's own g.decision_summary:
R780 (BUILD/DEBT, mnemosyne-engine-build, no store change) — the first consumer's third field report returned a measurement of Round 775 on a store larger than any fixture here, and reported an axis that round had also fixed without knowing it: before it, the baked artifact compiled at cargo's DEFAULT dev profile aborted at run time with `fatal runtime error: stack overflow`. This round builds the gate that was missing.

WHAT WAS NOT MEASURED. When the whole store is one function body holding one nested expression, every temporary in it is live until the expression ends and each gets its own slot, so the frame grows with the store until it exceeds the thread's stack. Round 775 removed that shape and measured the win in COMPILE time. Nothing here would have noticed the runtime half either way: this crate's fixtures are two lines long, and the Round 775 regression test weighs the emitted TEXT, never a running artifact. A property whose only evidence is that a different property held is not gated — it is inferred, and it stops being true silently.

WHAT IS ASSERTED, AND WHY NONE OF IT IS A THRESHOLD. A byte figure is fitted to today's store and turns a gate into an argument about the constant. The claim is a RATIO — the artifact must cost the same stack at four times the size — the Round 775 scaling assertion moved from the emitted text to the running artifact. A ratio has its own failure mode: "did not grow" is also what a broken measurement says. So the same test measures a CONTROL, the identical parts emitted with the bound removed, and requires it to GROW. One test rather than two, because that arm licenses the others: split apart, the flat arms could report green while the instrument sat broken in another test's red.

THAT IS ROUNDS 776 THROUGH 779 IN CONSTRUCTIVE FORM. Those rounds removed three gates that returned the word for SAFE about input they could not examine. The way not to write a fourth is not to check more carefully; it is to make the gate demonstrate, on every run, that it can see. `render_bounded` exists for exactly that — the bound is a value rather than a constant read so the control can be EMITTED, and without it non-vacuity could only have been a comment claiming someone checked once.

MEASURED, AND ONE PREDICTION CORRECTED. Playable 32 KiB at both sizes, quest 28 KiB at both, control 96 KiB then 344 KiB. Injecting the bound removal back into the emitter put both shipped artifacts on the control's curve and turned every assertion red, which was run and then reverted. The correction: optimization does NOT fold the growth away, as this round first assumed and wrote down. At opt-level 3 the control still wants 44 KiB then 160 KiB — the same 3.6x — while the shipped artifact sits at 4 KiB flat. So the consumer's `[profile.dev] opt-level = 1` never made the pre-Round-775 artifact safe. It halved a cost that grows with the store, which only doubles the size at which the abort arrives. The crash was scheduled, not avoided, and this gate is profile-independent as a result.

New `tests/projection_stack.rs` + `src/bin/projection_stack_probe.rs`: the probe builds one baked artifact on a thread of an exact size and lets the EXIT STATUS carry the answer, because an overflow aborts rather than returning a `Result` and a test hosting the attempt in its own process would die with it instead of reporting on it; the parent bisects over probe runs for the smallest stack each artifact builds within

No threshold is asserted. A byte figure is fitted to today's store and turns a gate into an argument about the constant, so the claim is a RATIO — the artifact must cost the same stack at four times the size — which is the Round 775 scaling assertion moved from the emitted text to the running artifact

So the same test measures a CONTROL, the identical parts emitted with the bound removed, and REQUIRES it to grow. One test rather than two, because that arm licenses the others — split apart, the flat arms could report green while the instrument sat broken in another test's red

`render_bounded` (crate-private) makes the bound a value rather than a constant read, which is the seam the control needs; without a way to EMIT the pre-Round-775 shape, non-vacuity could only ever be a comment claiming someone checked once. `NonZeroUsize` because `slice::chunks(0)` panics

The quest axis is repeated rather than inferred from the playable one: `render_quest` is free to stop calling the shared chunker while `render` still calls it, and assuming across that seam is how the Round 769 defect survived to Round 770

The probe is located through `CARGO_BIN_EXE_`, so the binary measured is this package's at this profile, guaranteed current; searching `target/` for it would reintroduce the stale-artifact failure `scripts/verify.sh` exists to prevent

MEASURED at cargo's default dev profile: the playable artifact needs 32 KiB at 200 lines and 32 KiB at 800, the quest artifact 28 KiB at 200 quests and 28 KiB at 800, and the unbounded control 96 KiB then 344 KiB — 3.6x for 4x the store against a shipped artifact that did not move a single page

Non-vacuity proven by INJECTION and actually run: setting the emitter's bound to `usize::MAX` put both shipped artifacts on the control's curve (playable 92 KiB to 332 KiB, quest 76 KiB to 272 KiB) and turned every assertion red, the quest arm firing independently of the playable one; the injection was then reverted and the suite re-run green

The bisection is measured TWICE per fixture and required to agree, because a bisection that does not repeat is not a measurement and a gate built on one fails intermittently — which is how a gate gets called flaky and then gets ignored

A PREDICTION MADE WHILE BUILDING THIS WAS WRONG AND THE MEASUREMENT CORRECTED IT: optimization does not fold the growth away. At opt-level 3 the control still wants 44 KiB then 160 KiB, the same 3.6x, while the shipped artifact sits at 4 KiB flat. So the consumer's `[profile.dev] opt-level = 1` never made the pre-Round-775 artifact safe — it roughly halved the requirement, which on a cost that grows with the store only doubles the size at which the abort arrives. The crash was scheduled, not avoided, and this gate is profile-independent as a result

The probe distinguishes "the OS refused a thread this small" (exit 2) from "did not build", because scoring a platform floor as a failed build would fabricate a measurement; and a result at or below that floor is documented as "at most this much", since every assertion is an upper bound or a ratio between figures well above it

Rounds 769, 771, 774, 775, 776 and 779 verified present via query_changelog_entry before being cited; the code-citation gate itself rejected this round's `Round 780` citation until this entry existed, which is the rule working
carry_forward_bullets: The 200/800 sizes and the 4 KiB bisection grain are the measured setup, not a swept optimum; nothing was tuned, and any pair where the second is a multiple of the first would carry the same claim

This gate weighs STACK, not allocation. The same field report raises a separate axis it explicitly did not file as a request: the baked artifact builds 34,825 allocations and 2.78 MB at every startup, over 43% of the process's instructions in malloc/free, copying string data that already sits in the binary's `.rodata`. Nothing here touches that, and the shape it asks for — projection types that can borrow `&'static` rather than own `String` — needs its own round with its own numbers, including the compile cost of `Cow` that neither side has measured

A known obstacle for that round, not yet costed: `PlayableProjection` holds six `HashMap`s, and there is no `static HashMap`. Borrowing the strings would remove the ~29,658 `to_string` allocations, but reaching genuine zero-allocation startup needs a separate decision about the map representation (sorted `&'static` slices with binary search, or a once-built lazy map)

The code-citation gate scans `crates/*/src/`, so `crates/*/build.rs` is production code carrying UNSCANNED `Round NNN` citations — found here when the gate rejected the probe's citation while never looking at the build script that emits its fixtures. Measured: 7 distinct rounds cited across all build scripts, of which exactly 2 do not resolve (`Round 91` and `Round 96`, both pre-252 legacy annotations in `mnemosyne-server/build.rs`). Extending the configured path is small but not mechanical, because it needs the orphan-ledger allow-list decision for the pre-252 class

Extending the same gate to `tests/` was CHECKED AND REJECTED rather than deferred: test files legitimately hold fake round numbers as fixture DATA (`crates/mnemosyne-atomic/tests/atomic_store_view_parity.rs` inserts a `Round 999` entry; `validate_code_refs_smoke.rs` feeds the gate invented numbers on purpose), and a regex cannot tell a citation from a fixture. 104 distinct round numbers live outside `src/`, of which 38 do not resolve — almost all pre-252 or deliberate fixtures. The `src/` boundary is a real one, not an oversight

Round 782 — the compile-cost worry was b.decision_summary:
R782 (MEASUREMENT, mnemosyne-engine-build, no store change, no shipped type changed) — the first consumer asked for projection types that can borrow instead of own, and named the thing it had not measured: what borrowing costs to compile. Round 775's whole lesson is that the emitted shape gets measured before it gets chosen, so this round measures it and changes nothing.

THE CONTROLLED TRIO. The same data, at 200 lines and 800, held three ways: owned as shipped; borrowed, with every string pointing at .rodata and the Vec-of-chunks assembly deliberately kept; and static_slice, chunk statics under a static of slices over them, which keeps Round 775's bound while materializing nothing. Literal content, field count and order, chunk bound and sizes are held equal, so the only thing that varies is how the data is held. Allocations are counted in-test through a thread-local counting allocator, with the owned arm serving as the control that must grow or nothing else in the file can be read.

THE FIRST SURPRISE. Borrowing removes 99.5% of the allocation CALLS — 4,020 to 20 at 800 lines — and only 38% of the BYTES, 501,600 to 312,800. The strings were never the memory. The element is, and it is still copied into a Vec. The consumer's report was about call traffic, 43% of instructions in malloc and free, so the middle arm answers exactly what was asked; the 2.78 MB it also reported would largely survive it. Only the third arm is zero, at both sizes, which is a count and needs no threshold to read.

THE SECOND SURPRISE, AND IT IS THE ROUND. Borrowing does not cost compile time. It saves it — 0.60s to 0.11s of rustc user time at 800 lines, 5.5x, and the static arm 8.6x on a quarter of the marginal peak memory. The worry was backwards, and in hindsight plainly so: a literal followed by .to_string() is a method call per literal for rustc to resolve, typecheck and codegen, while a literal is a literal. Round 775 was fought over rustc's per-body cost, so the shape that removes the allocations being the same shape that reduces the compile cost is worth stating rather than leaving to be rediscovered.

WHAT IS NOT DECIDED. What the shipped types become is the next round. The trio is synthetic and holds a Vec of lines rather than a whole projection, so the residual it prices is the Vec spine — the five HashMaps the real projection builds are not in it, and a map has no static equivalent.

New `tests/projection_alloc.rs` counts allocations through a thread-local counting global allocator. Thread-local because the harness runs tests in parallel and a process-wide counter would charge one test for another's work; `Cell` with a `const` initializer because a thread-local that allocated on first touch would be counted by the allocator it is installed in

The `owned` arm is the CONTROL as well as the subject: it must charge more at four times the store or the counter is not seeing the work, and every other assertion in the file is licensed by that one having moved

`STACK_SMALL` / `STACK_BIG` are now `SMALL` / `BIG`, shared by both gates. The stack gate and the allocation gate make the same shape of claim about the same emitter, and two pairs of sizes would be two places for "four times the store" to drift apart

WHAT IS LEFT OPEN AND WHY IT IS NOT DECIDED HERE. Nothing still reports that studio has stopped compiling. Closing that means some gate compiling studio on a schedule it does not control, which trades directly against the separation that keeps pinion out of the core build. Round 785 — the handle they did not ask.decision_summary:
R785 (DESIGN, code 0, no store change) — the first consumer's field report asked for projection types that can hold `&'static` instead of owning `String`, and their reply named the constraint that actually decides the shape: not whether the FIELD is a `Cow`, but what LIFETIME the accessor returns. With `fn text(&self) -> &str` they keep copying regardless of the field, because the accessor borrows `&self` and their struct holds the projection, so borrowing would be self-referential.

THE REFRAME. The larger half of their win needs no type change at all. `pub fn text(&self) -> &str` desugars to `fn text<'s>(&'s self) -> &'s str`, so a `&'static` projection already yields `&'static str` from today's unmodified accessors. What blocks them is not the signature; it is that the baked entry point hands back a value they must own. This was compile-checked against the current engine rather than reasoned about: a probe feeding five accessors from a `&'static PlayableProjection` into functions accepting only `&'static str` and `&'static [String]` builds clean.

THE LADDER. Step 1: the baked emitter returns `&'static PlayableProjection` from a `OnceLock`. No kernel change, `from_workspace` untouched, and the consumer's second copy of 4,612 lines stops being forced. Step 2: `Cow<'static, str>` fields — Owned from the workspace, Borrowed from the emitted literal — which is the arm Round 782 measured at 99.5% fewer allocation calls and 5.5x cheaper to compile, with `Cow` kept an implementation detail so scalar accessors still return `&str`.

STEP 3 IS REJECTED. Chunk statics under a static of slices reach zero allocations and 8.6x compile, and are the only rung that cannot be one type: const construction admits no map, vector or string, and this projection holds five maps and a set, so the runtime constructor could not produce one. That means two projection types and a trait over them, permanently, in every consumer — a standing API tax for a residual measured in bytes that no consumer has been shown to need. Their own reply says what has value to them is building nothing at startup, not faster lookup, and steps 1 and 2 deliver that for everything they hold.

SEQUENCING. Step 1 alone first: the only rung needing no type change, the larger share of the win, and validatable against the consumer before any kernel type moves.

changes_bullets: BUILD. Round 778 left this open in its own carry: `QuestProjection::completability` read the playable projection's PROSE stream to decide whether a completion-precondition fact was OFFERED in time, and a consumer's `journal_predicates` policy removes facts from that stream. So a precondition that is itself a typed journal leg is offered by the store and invisible to the gate, and came back as a FALSE `PreconditionUnreachable`

THE DECISION, which is what the carry was really waiting on: "offered" is the STORE's offer, not the consumer's prose. A fact is offered where the audience MEETS it — where it has a locator under this telling — and the journal policy decides only which STREAM carries it. The kernel now draws that split in one sentence: `lines` is what the audience is SHOWN, `offers` is what the audience can KNOW

Withholding still narrows it, which is the narrowing that was always intended rather than a side effect of reading the prose stream: a withheld fact emits no locator, so `offers` is false for it at every spot

WHY A SEPARATE FAMILY RATHER THAN REUSING THE LINE PAIR: prose is the OPPOSITE shape. Round 782 weighed 4,612 strings of a few dozen characters; this is 56 strings of a few thousand. Reusing that pair would have measured the same shape twice and called the second one prose
verification_bullets: MEASURED, allocations at 56 spots then 224, in-test with the thread-local counting allocator: owned 171 then 680 allocations and 363,752 then 1,476,732 bytes; borrowed 3 then 8 allocations and 7,488 then 44,352 bytes

THE FIRST RESULT IS THAT ROUND 782's CONCLUSION DOES NOT CARRY. That round found borrowing removed 99.5% of the allocation calls and only 38% of the BYTES, and stated why: the strings were never the memory, the elements were. On prose the strings ARE the memory — borrowing cuts the bytes by 97.0%. Had this been assumed rather than measured, the design would have inherited a 38% figure that is wrong by a factor of two and a half on this axis

THE SECOND RESULT CONTRADICTS WHAT BOTH SIDES EXPECTED TO BE THE PROBLEM. The consumer's request warns that prose in one function body would repeat the very-long-expression trouble of Round 771, and it is right that the line is enormous: the longest emitted line is 319,510 bytes, twelve times the worst line in their current baked projection. It costs nothing. Compiling the whole 1.43 MB artifact is 0.05s of rustc user time against an empty-fixture baseline of 0.02s, with 30 MB of marginal peak RSS

THE COMPARISON THAT MAKES THAT READABLE, and the reason it is a finding rather than a small number: the line fixture at 4,612 items emits 1.34 MB and costs 2.47s. The prose fixture at 224 items emits 1.43 MB and costs 0.05s. Nearly the same bytes, roughly fifty times the compile cost, and what differs is the item count. Stated as a direction rather than an isolated variable, since the two families also differ in fields per item — but byte volume is plainly not the axis rustc charges for

SO THE ROUND 775 BOUND ALREADY HOLDS HERE AND THE EXISTING GATE ALREADY PASSES. `CHUNK` bounds ITEMS per body at 50, so a body holds at most 50 spots however many the store has, and the longest line is 319,510 bytes at 56 spots against 319,560 at 224 — flat. The Round 775 regression test asserts a RATIO rather than a byte threshold, which is exactly why a bake whose constant is twenty times larger than the projection's still satisfies it

The instrument is checked before it is read, the Round 780 discipline carried into this test: the owned arm must charge more at four times the prose, and must charge at least three allocations per spot, or the borrowed figures below it are vacuous. Both are asserted in the same test rather than in a comment

Compile figures are the median of three runs each, all six compilations exit 0 with zero rustc errors, checked by reading the real exit status rather than a filtered tail — the Round 782 lesson, which had already caught one silent failure earlier in this session

carry_forward_bullets: THE DESIGN IS NOT MADE HERE, and these numbers move where it has to look. Compile cost is not the constraint anyone expected it to be, and the borrowed arm wins by more on prose than on lines, so what remains to decide is the FORGERY GUARD: how a build-time emitter produces a `Passage` without `from_excerpt` becoming public. The projection seam answered the same question with a pub-field `LinePart` and a public `from_parts`, which is a weaker guard than the one `Passage` carries today — whether that trade is acceptable for prose is the design round's first question, not a detail of it

It is a third arm. The kernel's type must hold both a run-time-derived projection and a baked one, so it is Cow<'static, str>, which is neither String nor &'static str, and this round weighed it. On allocation CALLS the design was exactly right and that is the half the consumer asked about: 80.0% of the win for a plain Vec of Cow and 100.0% for a borrowable list, landing not near the fully borrowed arm but ON it. On COMPILE it was wrong: 1.07x and 2.3x, never 5.5x. Varying one thing at a time also separates a cause Round 782 could not, because its single step changed the strings and the per-line vec! together: four .to_string()s per line are worth 0.46s to 0.43s and the one vec! beside them is worth 0.43s to 0.20s, so what rustc charges for is the per-line constructor call. And the one decision Round 785 deferred is settled without needing the call sites at all: both list holdings deref to the same slice and yield the same iterator, so the accessor choice is orthogonal to the field, and the field goes to the borrowable list on cost.

Round 785 sequenced step 2 of the static-projection ladder and wrote that it "is exactly the arm Round 782 measured at -99.5% allocation calls and 5.5x cheaper compile". It is not that arm. `from_workspace` derives at run time and must OWN, so one type carrying both a live and a baked projection is `Cow<'static, str>` - 24 bytes, neither `String` nor `&'static str`'s 16 - and Round 792 is the round that established what this crate gets wrong when a design reasons about an arm nobody weighed

TWO ARMS ADDED to the existing controlled trio, `cow` and `cow_list`, differing from each other in ONE field: whether the entity list is a `Vec<Cow<'static, str>>` or a `Cow<'static, [Cow<'static, str>]>`. That field is also the one decision Round 785 deliberately deferred to the build round. Both are emitted by one function taking the list fragment as a closure, so "everything else is equal" is true by construction rather than by review

ON ALLOCATION CALLS THE DESIGN WAS EXACTLY RIGHT, and it is the half that matters: it predicted 80% of the win for the plain `Vec` and 99% for the borrowable list; measured, 80.0% and 100.0%. `cow_list` does not land near the fully borrowed arm, it lands ON it, 20 allocations against 20, because `Cow::Borrowed` costs nothing to hold and the residual in both is the same chunk spine

ON COMPILE IT WAS WRONG, and the arms separate a cause Round 782 could not. That round moved from owned to borrowed in one step, changing the strings AND the per-line `vec![..]` together, and attributed the 5.5x to `.to_string()`. Varying one at a time: dropping four `.to_string()`s per line moves rustc from 0.46s to 0.43s, and dropping the one `vec!` beside them moves 0.43s to 0.20s. rustc charges for the per-line CONSTRUCTOR CALL; `.to_string()` was the most visible instance, not the expensive one. The reachable arm is 1.07x and the borrowable-list arm 2.3x, never 5.5x

ON BYTES BUILT it is worse than the trio implies, for a structural reason rather than a measurement one: `Cow<'static, str>` is 24 bytes where `&'static str` is 16, so the element the `Vec` copies is larger. Borrowing everything cuts 38% of the bytes; the arm the kernel can reach cuts 12%. Step 2 takes the whole call win and under a third of the byte win - and calls are the axis the first consumer reported (43% of instructions in malloc and free), bytes the axis they did not

THE DEFERRED LIST DECISION IS SETTLED, AND NOT ON ERGONOMICS. Round 785 framed it as a choice between `&[Cow<'static, str>]` (leaks the mechanism) and `impl Iterator<Item = &str>` (hides it). Both holdings expose the SAME surface - each derefs to `&[Cow<'static, str>]` and each yields the iterator form through the same `iter().map(AsRef::as_ref)`, compile-verified rather than argued - so the accessor choice is one decision about the accessor, orthogonal to the field. The field is then free to be picked on cost, and on cost it is not close: the borrowable list buys the last 20% of the calls, 2.1x of compile time and 11 MB of rustc memory, for a type nobody outside the kernel can see. Take `Cow<'static, [Cow<'static, str>]>`

THE EMITTED SOURCE GROWS WHILE COMPILING FASTER - 232,520 bytes owned against 313,354 for `cow_list`, at 2.3x the speed - because `::std::borrow::Cow::Borrowed(..)` is longer text than `.to_string()` and rustc is not charging for text. Round 789's per-item-not-per-byte finding, reappearing on a different axis

TWO DOC CORRECTIONS IN THE SAME ROUND, because a round that refutes a sentence and leaves it standing is worse than one that never looked. The trio's own module doc keeps Round 782's 5.5x, which is right, and now says plainly that the sentence explaining it is not. `str_literal`, introduced by Round 793 on that attribution, keeps its two real reasons - a different TYPE, and one allocation per field removed - and drops the compile-time promise it cannot keep

TWO ARMS ADDED to the existing controlled trio, `cow` and `cow_list`, differing from each other in ONE field: whether the entity list is a `Vec<Cow<'static, str>>` or a `Cow<'static, [Cow<'static, str>]>`. That field is also the one decision Round 785 deliberately deferred to the build round. Both are emitted by one function taking the list fragment as a closure, so "everything else is equal" is true by construction rather than by review

ON ALLOCATION CALLS THE DESIGN WAS EXACTLY RIGHT, and it is the half that matters: it predicted 80% of the win for the plain `Vec` and 99% for the borrowable list; measured, 80.0% and 100.0%. `cow_list` does not land near the fully borrowed arm, it lands ON it, 20 allocations against 20, because `Cow::Borrowed` costs nothing to hold and the residual in both is the same chunk spine

ON COMPILE IT WAS WRONG, and the arms separate a cause Round 782 could not. That round moved from owned to borrowed in one step, changing the strings AND the per-line `vec![..]` together, and attributed the 5.5x to `.to_string()`. Varying one at a time: dropping four `.to_string()`s per line moves rustc from 0.46s to 0.43s, and dropping the one `vec!` beside them moves 0.43s to 0.20s. rustc charges for the per-line CONSTRUCTOR CALL; `.to_string()` was the most visible instance, not the expensive one. The reachable arm is 1.07x and the borrowable-list arm 2.3x, never 5.5x

ON BYTES BUILT it is worse than the trio implies, for a structural reason rather than a measurement one: `Cow<'static, str>` is 24 bytes where `&'static str` is 16, so the element the `Vec` copies is larger. Borrowing everything cuts 38% of the bytes; the arm the kernel can reach cuts 12%. Step 2 takes the whole call win and under a third of the byte win - and calls are the axis the first consumer reported (43% of instructions in malloc and free), bytes the axis they did not

THE DEFERRED LIST DECISION IS SETTLED, AND NOT ON ERGONOMICS. Round 785 framed it as a choice between `&[Cow<'static, str>]` (leaks the mechanism) and `impl Iterator<Item = &str>` (hides it). Both holdings expose the SAME surface - each derefs to `&[Cow<'static, str>]` and each yields the iterator form through the same `iter().map(AsRef::as_ref)`, compile-verified rather than argued - so the accessor choice is one decision about the accessor, orthogonal to the field. The field is then free to be picked on cost, and on cost it is not close: the borrowable list buys the last 20% of the calls, 2.1x of compile time and 11 MB of rustc memory, for a type nobody outside the kernel can see. Take `Cow<'static, [Cow<'static, str>]>`

THE EMITTED SOURCE GROWS WHILE COMPILING FASTER - 232,520 bytes owned against 313,354 for `cow_list`, at 2.3x the speed - because `::std::borrow::Cow::Borrowed(..)` is longer text than `.to_string()` and rustc is not charging for text. Round 789's per-item-not-per-byte finding, reappearing on a different axis

TWO DOC CORRECTIONS IN THE SAME ROUND, because a round that refutes a sentence and leaves it standing is worse than one that never looked. The trio's own module doc keeps Round 782's 5.5x, which is right, and now says plainly that the sentence explaining it is not. `str_literal`, introduced by Round 793 on that attribution, keeps its two real reasons - a different TYPE, and one allocation per field removed - and drops the compile-time promise it cannot keep

Round 795 — a baked line points at the b.decision_summary: R795 (BUILD, step 2 of the Round 785 ladder) — `Line` and `LinePart` hold `Cow<'static, str>` for every string and `Cow<'static, [Cow<'static, str>]>` for the entity list, so a baked line points at the literals in the binary while `from_disclosed` keeps owning what it derives at run time. The shipped emitter on the 800-line fixture now writes 4,000 `Cow::Borrowed` and five `.to_string()`, and the artifact it produces builds in 32 allocations against the 4,020 Round 794 measured for the same 800 lines owned. The list is a `Cow` and not a `Vec` because that is the difference between 80% and 100% of the win, and it costs nothing at the API. The accessor Round 785 left open is an iterator of `&str`: with the call sites finally in hand there is exactly one outside this crate, so what decided it was not ergonomics but the design's own commitment that `Cow` stays an implementation detail — a slice of `Cow` would publish the representation in the signature of the most-read accessor on the most-read type. Scope is the line axis on purpose; the other part types are the same change again and are the next round, not a carry buried in this one.
changes_bullets: BUILD, step 2 of the Round 785 ladder, on the axis Round 794 priced. `Line` and `LinePart` now hold `Cow<'static, str>` for every string and `Cow<'static, [Cow<'static, str>]>` for the entity list. A BAKED line points at the literals in the binary; `Line::from_disclosed` keeps owning, because it derives its strings from a store read at run time. One type with two ownership modes rather than two types - the Round 785 decision, reached again here for the same reason it was reached for prose in Round 793

THE LIST IS A `Cow` AND NOT A `Vec<Cow<..>>`, which is the decision Round 785 deferred to this round and Round 794 settled: a `Vec` spine costs one allocation per line whatever the strings do, so stopping there is 80% of the win rather than 100%. The emitter writes the slice INLINE and relies on rvalue static promotion, verified by compilation together with its discriminating half rather than assumed, because a named `static` per line would add an item per line and Round 789 measured that rustc charges per item

THE ACCESSOR IS AN ITERATOR, `entities(&self) -> impl ExactSizeIterator<Item = &str>`, and this is the one form Round 785 left open on the grounds that it needs the call sites. With them in hand there is exactly ONE caller outside this crate, so ergonomics did not decide it - the design's own commitment did. `Cow` is meant to stay an implementation detail, and `&[Cow<'static, str>]` would publish it in the signature of the most-read accessor on the most-read type. SCOPE IS THE LINE AXIS AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. `CastPart`, `ForkPart`, `DoorPart`, `Rung`, `ChoiceEntityRef` and the quest parts still own. `Line` is the shape Round 794 measured, and it is where the count is: the first consumer holds 4,612 lines against tens of everything else, so the line axis is the overwhelming majority of the per-startup allocations the whole ladder exists to remove. Extending the same holding to the rest is mechanical and is the next round, not a carry hidden in this one

A SECOND EMITTER PRIMITIVE PAIR, `cow` and `inline_cow_strings`, beside the `string` / `inline_strings` the other axes still use. Separate functions rather than a flag for the reason Round 793 gave when it added `str_literal`: the two produce different TYPES, and a boolean deciding a type at a call site reads correct while being wrong

INTERNAL READS GO THROUGH THE ACCESSORS. `gate.rs` and `projection.rs` read `line.fact_id()` and `line.entities()` where they read the fields directly before. One reader per datum, and it is why the field-type change touched two call sites in those files instead of every use

Round 796 — the sweep was pointed at the.decision_summary: R796 (MEASUREMENT + BUILD) — Round 795 carried that the remaining part types were a mechanical sweep. Emitting the first consumer's real store says otherwise: of the 1,329 owned strings the artifact still writes, the part types are 182 and the projection's own map keys and scalar lists are 1,147. The boundary that matters is not engine-local versus shared but HIDDEN versus PUBLISHED — every design in this ladder promised `Cow` stays an implementation detail, and that is only available where the representation is already private behind accessors. `Line`, `CastMember` and `PlayableProjection`'s own fields qualify; `Fork`, `Door` and `ChoiceEntityRef` publish their fields, and `Door` is an enum consumers match on. The measurement makes respecting that nearly free: the published-field types are 24 strings, 1.8%, so the rule covers 98.2% and changes no public signature. `CastMember` and `CastPart` move on exactly `Line`'s terms; the three published types stay owned as a decision with a reopen condition; and the 1,147 in the projection's own keys and lists are named as the next round rather than half-started at the end of a session.

THE ATTRIBUTION, parsed out of the emitted source by the element type each chunk function declares rather than reasoned from field counts: bare `String` chunks (walks, objects, journal offer ids) 465; the SECTION KEYS in `by_world` 462; `CastPart` 158; titles 132; cast section keys 66; `ForkPart` 24; the three world keys 21; the telling 1; and `LinePart` ZERO, which is Round 795 already banked

`Door`, `ChoiceEntityRef` and `Rung` emit NOTHING on this store under default overrides, because they come from a consumer-loaded overrides file rather than from the store. A sweep costed by counting types in the source would have put them in the same bucket as the rest

THE BOUNDARY IS NOT ENGINE-LOCAL VERSUS SHARED, IT IS HIDDEN VERSUS PUBLISHED. Every design in this ladder has committed that `Cow` stays an implementation detail. That is only available where the representation is already hidden: `Line` and `CastMember` keep crate-private fields behind accessors, and `PlayableProjection` keeps its maps and lists private behind `walk`, `spine`, `title` and the rest. `Fork`, `Door` and `ChoiceEntityRef` have PUBLIC fields, and `Door` is an enum consumers pattern-match on, so moving them writes `Cow` into the signature every consumer reads and every match arm they wrote

AND THE MEASUREMENT SAYS THAT COSTS ALMOST NOTHING TO RESPECT: the published-field types are 24 of 1,329, which is 1.8%. The rule "move where the representation is already hidden" covers 98.2% of what is left and changes no public signature. `Fork`, `Door` and `ChoiceEntityRef` stay owned, and that is a decision with a reopen condition, not an omission

`CastMember` and `CastPart` move, on exactly the terms `Line` did: `Cow<'static, str>` fields, accessors still returning `&str`, `from_presence` still owning because it reads the store at run time, and the emitter writing `cow` where it wrote `string`. Round 799 — a separator is interior or i.decision_summary: R799 (FIX, MNEMO-GAP-002) — the `§<id>` extractor swallowed a separating slash into the preceding id, so `§1/§3` parsed as `1/` and `3` and the gate reported SectionMissing — the hallucination class — against a comment citing two real sections. The reporter's recommended repair was to close the id charset to numerics, which was declined: slash slugs are a documented, tested id shape and this very store holds `code-citation-defense/bidirectional-binding`, so that repair would have traded one false hallucination verdict for another. The rule landed instead is the one the grammar already applied to `.`: a separator belongs to the id only when it is INTERIOR, flanked by id characters on both sides. A slug never starts or ends with its separator and a slash between two cites never has one on the far side, so the cases separate without a delimiter list to maintain. `§1/x` stays one id, which is the honest limit — with an id char on both sides the slash is interior, and no token can tell a two-segment slug from a pair whose second cite lost its sigil.

Round 802 — the shape picks the slice, n.decision_summary: R802 (BUILD) — `is_document_number_token` required a leading ASCII digit, so `pinion R1345 §5` read `R1345` as a name and dispatched to the bare axis where the prose ends with the number rather than the registered prefix; `R` plus digits is this ecosystem's document-name shape the way `#9` is Unicode's, and it was two of the reporting workspace's residual violations. The token now admits an optional leading ASCII-alphabetic run before the digits. That widening alone would have BROKEN a working case: the two modes were mutually exclusive on token shape, so a bare prefix carrying digits (`ISO9001 §3`) worked only because it did not look like a number and would have stopped the moment the shape admitted it. So the shape now selects WHICH SLICE a prefix must end, not which axis is allowed — numeric is tried where the shape permits and bare answers otherwise, which also fixes a latent case where a registered multi-word bare prefix ending in a number could never resolve. The axis invariant is untouched: neither path skips without a verbatim-registered prefix, so this false-negative surface did not grow for free, per Round 801.
changes_bullets: BUILD, the second gap from the same downstream field report. `is_document_number_token` required the token before the sigil to START with an ASCII digit, so `pinion R1345 §5` read `R1345` as a name and dispatched to the bare axis, where the prose ends with `R1345` rather than with the registered prefix `pinion`. `R` plus digits is the standard document-name shape across this ecosystem, the way `#9` is Unicode's and `802.11ax` is IEEE's. Two of the reporter's residual violations were this

THE TOKEN NOW ADMITS AN OPTIONAL LEADING ASCII-ALPHABETIC RUN before the digits, over the same all-alphanumeric-or-dot body. `Color` and `Standard` still fail because a run with no digit after it is a name; `WAI-ARIA` still fails on the hyphen; a non-ASCII prefix word like `설계` still fails at the first character

AND THAT WIDENING ALONE WOULD HAVE BROKEN A WORKING CASE, which is the half worth recording. The two modes were MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE on token shape: a document-number-shaped last token committed to the numeric axis and returned false there rather than trying bare. So a bare prefix that carries digits — `ISO9001 §3` — worked only because the token did not look like a number, and would have stopped working the moment the shape widened to admit it

SO THE SHAPE NOW SELECTS WHICH SLICE A PREFIX MUST END, NOT WHICH AXIS IS ALLOWED. Numeric is tried where the shape permits, and bare answers otherwise. This also fixes a latent case nobody had met: a registered multi-word bare prefix ending in a number (`설계 1.2`) could never resolve, because its own last token dispatched it away from the list it was registered in

THE AXIS INVARIANT IS UNTOUCHED, which is what makes the widening admissible under the Round 801 rule that a false-negative surface must not grow for free. Neither path skips a citation without a verbatim-registered prefix; the fall-through consults a second registered list rather than inventing a match, so the widening is bounded by an explicit act of the workspace

Round 806.decision_summary: R806 (DESIGN, code 0 — answer to tide lift request 4, 'a claim outlives its evidence'). They asked for an evidence fingerprint on the fact, auto-stamped at authoring time, so that when the evidence prose moves the fact drops to un-reviewed. REPRODUCED the hole on current main first: prose moved through the legitimate mutate API leaves validate-continuity, validate-content-drift and validate-workspace all green while the claim asserts words the excerpt no longer holds — scan_content_drift (R404/R756) only asks whether an excerpt hashes to its OWN sha, and a legitimate re-import moves text and sha together. The same probe found a SECOND hole they did not report: a fact's declared verbatim quote is accepted with no relation at all to its evidence section's excerpt, so R758's no-invented-prose guarantee stops at the Section boundary and never reaches the fact layer (tide does not see it because their own gate re-derives the check consumer-side — the re-implementation their request argues against). KILLED the requested shape by reading their tracked build script: it wipes the sidecar and replays every primitive, its 1,000 add-fact calls start at line 727, and import-content-excerpts runs at 5712 — after all of them. So an auto-stamped pin is empty for all 1,105 facts (no excerpt exists at add-fact time) AND the rebuild would re-affirm every fact against today's prose, making the cheapest command in their repo a total pin refresh — the exact thing their own section 4 forbids, and the R796 defect class R797 already paid for. DECIDED the inversion: unlike quote_sha256 and R439's target_claim_sha256, whose referents are in the store at write time, an evidence pin points at prose the author READ — an unobservable act — so a computed value asserts a review that never happened. The datum is an AUTHORED affirmation the machine adjudicates, never manufactures; their own prose-ratchet.json already embodies this by living OUTSIDE the store. SHAPE: NarrativeFact.evidence becomes Vec<EvidenceRef { section, reviewed_excerpt_sha256 }> at schema v44, migrated with an EMPTY affirmation (stamping live would assert 1,105 reviews that did not happen — the R402 call); ONE adjudicator, the continuity scan beside ConflictEdgeStale, and no write-time check (it could not run under their build order, so it would be a second path with different reachability). Truth table decides every cell: unpinned is a printed count, never silently clean, and always measured even when not failing (R801).
