Round 807.decision_summary: R807 (BUILD — Stage A of the R806 design, answering tide lift request 4). A claim can no longer outlive its evidence silently. NarrativeFact.evidence moves from Vec<String> to Vec<EvidenceRef { section, reviewed_excerpt_sha256 }> at schema v44, migrated with an EMPTY affirmation because seeding the live hash would assert reviews that never happened. The affirmation is AUTHORED, never computed — the deliberate inversion of the R439 conflict-pin rule directly above it: a conflict pin points at another fact's claim, which is in the store at write time, while an evidence affirmation points at prose a human READ, which the store cannot observe, and which under the requesting consumer's build shape (facts created thousands of lines before excerpts land, whole store rebuilt each run) an auto-stamp would leave empty forever and refresh with the cheapest command in their repo. import_evidence_reviews is the ONE primitive that writes the field (every fact-creating path writes EvidenceRef::unreviewed), adjudicating fail-before-save that the fact exists, cites that section, that the section HOLDS prose, and that the affirmed sha is the excerpt's live one; a section carrying no excerpt is a REJECT and never a skip, because a skip is what makes a check silently vacuous — the R796/R797 defect class. The continuity scan carries the same relation on the FINAL store beside ConflictEdgeStale, so it is order-independent where the write path cannot be: EvidenceStale and EvidenceReviewUnanchored are structural violations with actionable repairs, and evidence_unreviewed is a printed count rather than a violation (an absent affirmation certifies nothing, but silence would read as 'every claim is affirmed', which is exactly what a store that never affirmed one looks like). Sections holding no prose stay off both axes — that is every spec section. The CLI surface is import-evidence-reviews --reviews, not an inline section@sha: section ids here are free-form and already contain separators, so a by-convention delimiter would rebuild the id-swallowing bug R799/R800 just closed. Three injections each broke exactly one new test and zero existing ones. SSOT = this entry; scratch = claudedocs/prose-provenance-design.md sec 12.

It adjudicates fail-before-save on four counts: the fact exists, the fact actually cites that section, the section HOLDS a content_excerpt, and the affirmed sha equals the excerpt's live one. An evidence ref whose section carries no excerpt is excluded from both axes: that is every spec section, and counting them would drown the signal

Round 808.decision_summary: R808 (FIX + DEBT — answering the consumer's R807 field report). A PARENTHETICAL GLOSS was breaking a citation chain, so the cites after it fell to the bare axis and came back as hallucination-class SectionMissing at reject severity, blocking the commit. Their remaining two GAP-002 violations were this one line, and it reproduced here on the release binary before it was believed. The fix applies the R380 rule to the gap with its balanced groups removed: strip balanced ASCII parens, and what remains must still be a non-empty run of chain separators, so a gloss chains while a word OUTSIDE the gloss still breaks. That is the chain-side of the R802 correction. Two conservatisms, both because widening this predicate is a false-negative surface that stops the cite behind it from being checked at all: an unbalanced paren breaks rather than swallowing the line, and only ASCII parens are recognized because the fullwidth and bracket forms measure ZERO in both corpora, so adding them by symmetry would be the move R801 refused for the dash. This round also pays three corrections that report forced. First, R806's noise model was structurally wrong, not merely imprecise: one section's excerpt can cover many authored passages, so a rewritten passage flags a median of 64 facts and a max of 137, eighteen of twenty-six passages living inside another section's excerpt, which puts the finer-granularity re-open condition EARLIER than R806 estimated. Second, R806 advised the consumer they could retire their own passage-scoped ratchet after backfilling, and they cannot: it is five to eleven times finer than this axis, and two of their six drifted items are Entity.description prose that this axis cannot reach at all, so it is a complementary layer. Third, R806's evidence sentence cited line numbers in their build script that have since been refactored away; the load order the argument rests on is unchanged and the conclusion stands, but a structural argument was anchored to volatile coordinates in another repository's live file when it only needed the ordering property. Their measurement also stood R798's attribution up at one allocation apart, and their open question about total bytes is left OPEN here rather than guessed: the obvious hypothesis was tested and refuted by measurement. SSOT = this entry.

Round 809.decision_summary: R809 (FIX — the second half of the consumer's R807 report). A circled digit is a document NUMBER, and a document number may follow a name registered on EITHER axis. The reported shape was a bare-registered document carrying an instance number, which before this round reached neither axis: the numeric one declined because the name is not in its registry, and the bare one saw prose ending in the number rather than in the name. Probing that showed the larger half, which the report did not contain — the same failure holds for an ASCII number after a bare-registered name, so it was never about the glyph. This is the R802 correction one level apart: R802 closed the case where the prefix ITSELF ends in a number-shaped token and so could not reach its own registry, and this closes a prefix FOLLOWED by a separate number token; in both, what a shape selects is where the prefix's slice ENDS, never which axis is allowed. Admitting the circled-digit block is derivable rather than symmetric — every member is one character class with one reading, with no second-versus-third distinction to draw — which is what separates it from the dash R801 refused; parenthesized and fullwidth digit families stay out, being different classes with zero measured instances. The widening remains bounded by an explicit workspace act, the slice must still end with a verbatim-registered prefix, and that guard is tested at both the predicate and citation level. Measurement also splits the report's attribution: of the three lines they assigned to us, two name a registered document and are closed here, and the third names a document their config never declared — the same shape as the missing declaration they self-reported for their upstream sibling one section earlier. SSOT = this entry.
changes_bullets: is_document_number_token now accepts a circled-digit run as a document number. Unlike the chain-separator set, whose members had to be enumerated one measured instance at a time because nothing about a slash or a period says which one joins, the circled-digit block is DERIVABLE: every member is one character class with one reading and there is no second-versus-third distinction to draw, so taking the contiguous block is not the add-by-symmetry move R801 refused for the dash. Parenthesized and fullwidth digit families are NOT admitted — different classes, and neither corpus holds one

The slice before a document number is now matched against BOTH prefix registries instead of the numeric one alone. Which registry a document NAME is declared in says how that document is usually written, not whether it may ever carry an instance number

That second half is the larger finding and it was not in the report: a bare-registered name followed by ANY document number reached NEITHER axis. The numeric axis declined because the name is not in its registry; the bare axis saw prose ending in the number rather than in the name. Verified by probe, so it holds for ASCII numbers too and is not specific to the glyph form the report happened to hit

R802 is NOT superseded and was not wrong: it closed the case where the PREFIX ITSELF ends in a number-shaped token and therefore could not reach its own registry. This closes a prefix FOLLOWED by a separate number token. Both are the same correction one level apart — what a shape selects is where the prefix's slice ENDS, never which axis is allowed

The report attributed all three circled-number lines to us; measurement splits them TWO ours and ONE theirs. The two naming a registered document are closed here; the third names a document their config never declared, which is the same shape as the missing declaration they self-reported for their upstream sibling one section earlier

The widening stays bounded by an explicit act of the workspace: the slice must still end with a VERBATIM-registered prefix, so an enumeration marker in running prose never reaches the skip. Their own evidence is stronger than the guard needs — measured across their corpus, enumeration markers are never followed by a section sigil at all
verification_bullets: Reproduced before believing, on the release binary and with their prefix registry copied verbatim: their glossed-free circled-number line returned section_missing at reject severity, while the SAME name without the number was clean, so only the number token ever distinguished them

Both classes pinned: four circled digits that are document numbers, five tokens that are not (a different circled family, a fullwidth digit, two mixed tokens, empty), and at the citation level a registered-bare name with a number, the same name without one, an ASCII number after a bare name, an UNREGISTERED name with a number, and an enumeration marker in running prose

The guard is the load-bearing assertion: an unregistered name carrying a circled number must still be reported, or the widening would be unbounded. It is tested at both the predicate and the citation level

Round 813.decision_summary: R813 (DESIGN, code 0 — the finer coordinate for the R807 evidence axis). R806 named ladder rungs as the re-open condition for section granularity; measuring it on the consumer's real store gives 5 of 66 sections laddered, 19 rungs, and 29 of 1,105 facts named by any rung — 2.6%. That is the WRONG AXIS, not merely an unmet one: a rung exists where there is an interactive hold and an evidence ref exists where a claim is backed, so no amount of authoring makes the first cover the second. R806 reasoned from a sub-section coordinate existing somewhere to that coordinate carrying this pin; the vocabulary transfers and the population does not. The same measurement corrects a second overstatement from this session — R811's fact-quote membership covers ZERO facts there, because none carry a quote, so it is a real guarantee for any consumer that stores quotes and NOT something that closed a hole they were living with. A third finding was probed: a rung anchor whose prefix does not occur in the section's own excerpt imports clean and no gate mentions it, because import_ladders checks the anchor's shape and never resolves it, the resolver living in the engine. DESIGN: the finer coordinate is AUTHORED, the R806 inversion one level down — the store cannot know which region of a 15,516-character excerpt a claim was judged against, for the same reason it cannot know whether a human read it. The fork is how the region is addressed: pasting region text is rejected because it re-creates the very duplication the consumer complained of in their own ratchet; two boundary prefixes per affirmation is rejected on cost at the measured shape, since closing the worst section would mean authoring 137 region pairs; a named passage division per section, referenced by affirmations, is the recommendation because boundaries are declared once and it is the shape the consumer already authors. Its cost — a second segmentation beside the ladder — is answered by making the ladder reference the division, named as a separate round. The next BUILD is the missing resolver, a defect present today; the division itself waits on the consumer's promised measurement rather than on this round's arithmetic. That condition is not merely unmet, it is the WRONG AXIS. A rung exists where there is an interactive hold (a carrier entity, a needs/reveals gate); an evidence ref exists where a claim is backed. Round 817.decision_summary: R817 (BUILD — the scan verdict Round 815 left owed). Round 815 made the store RESOLVE a ladder rung's prefix against its section's excerpt at import, and a resolution is only true of the text it was resolved against: re-importing that excerpt moves the prose under every rung on it while the rungs stay exactly as authored, so the guarantee expired the moment the prose did. That is the same way an evidence affirmation goes stale, and the Round 440 boundary doctrine gives it the same answer — what a write path enforces, the scan re-reads on the FINAL store. scan_continuity now re-resolves every rung through mnemosyne_core::resolve_prefix, which gains a third caller rather than a second copy. The load-bearing decision is that the misses are kept APART: Absent, Ambiguous with its count, ForeignSource with both document names, and NotAPrefix for a shape only an out-of-band edit can produce. Flattening them into one stranded verdict would be Round 815's own error one level up, since naming one when it is another lies about what has to be repaired, and verdict.rs carries a distinct repair sentence for each. A section whose excerpt is gone from under a ladder gets ONE verdict for the section rather than one per rung, because the missing thing is the same prose every rung addresses. A CFI rung is named but never counted as resolved: skipping it would leave that rung on no axis, counting it would inflate the denominator with rungs nothing resolved. ladder_rungs_resolved is printed every run on the Round 807/811 rule that an axis quietly covering nothing reads exactly like an axis that passes — and this workspace prints 0, holding no ladders at all, which is precisely the case that rule exists for. Four injections under --no-fail-fast, each breaking only the new test. SSOT = this entry.
changes_bullets: scan_continuity re-resolves every ladder rung against the prose its section CURRENTLY holds, calling mnemosyne_core::resolve_prefix — the same rule Round 815 gave one home. Three callers now: the store's write path, the engine's slicer, this scan, so a rung the gate calls landed is a rung the slicer can place

LadderRungStranded carries a RungMiss saying WHICH way the coordinate fails to land: Absent, Ambiguous with the occurrence count, ForeignSource with both document names, NotAPrefix with the locator. Four states rather than one "stranded", because each names a different missing thing and therefore a different repair — move the rung, lengthen the prefix, point at this document, or re-author a coordinate a resolver can use at all

LadderUnanchored is a SECTION-level verdict: when the excerpt is gone from under a ladder, every rung addresses the same absent prose, so naming each rung separately would report one missing thing N times

A CFI or blank locator is NAMED but never counted as resolved. The write path rejects that shape, so it reaches the store only out-of-band; skipping it silently would leave that rung on no axis at all, and counting it as resolved would inflate the denominator with rungs nothing resolved

ContinuityReport gains ladder_rungs_resolved, mirrored in the ops view and printed by validate-continuity beside the evidence and quote counts, on the Round 807/811 rule that an axis quietly covering nothing reads exactly like an axis that passes. This workspace prints 0 — it holds no ladders, which is precisely the case the rule exists for

verdict.rs maps both variants into the actionable shape with a repair sentence PER miss, so the generate-gate-repair loop gets the specific action rather than "the rung is stranded". The exhaustive match is what forced this to be written at all
verification_bullets: The new test asserts the ACCEPT first and the resolved count with it, because a check that stranded every rung would satisfy every rejection assertion after it and a store holding no ladder would satisfy them by having nothing to strand. It then walks all five verdicts on ONE store: a re-import that removes the rung's line (Absent, with the sibling rung still landing — a partial strand, never collapsed to "the ladder is broken"), a re-import whose prose holds the prefix twice (Ambiguous 2), a re-import from another document (ForeignSource on both rungs), an out-of-band CFI anchor (NotAPrefix, and the count drops to 1), and an out-of-band excerpt deletion (LadderUnanchored once, with zero rung verdicts)

The load-bearing case goes through the REAL primitive: import_content_excerpts is what moves the prose, it knows nothing about ladders, and no write path can see the strand it causes — which is the whole reason this scan exists

Four injections under --no-fail-fast, each breaking ONLY the new test and no existing one: the scan block made unreachable, a ladder on a section with no prose skipped instead of named, ForeignSource reported as plain Absent, and an unusable locator dropped silently

End to end on the built binary over a throwaway store: excerpt imported, ladder imported, gate clean with "ladder rungs: 1 coordinate(s) resolved"; then the excerpt re-imported WITHOUT the rung's line — the import succeeds, and the gate reports {"kind":"ladder_rung_stranded","section":"ch-1","prefix":"Seward counted","miss":"Absent"} with exit 1

1257 workspace tests green (R816 1256, +1) with --no-fail-fast and the baseline confirmed at zero under the same flag, clippy -D warnings and fmt clean, validate-workspace exit 0 with T1=0 and T3 reject=0, validate-code-refs violations total=0

A METHODOLOGY DEFECT in this round's own injection loop: reverting an injection with git checkout discarded the round's own UNCOMMITTED implementation, because Round 816 ran that loop against a clean tree and the habit carried into a round that was building. The implementation was re-applied and re-verified identical (1257 green), and the remaining injections were reverted from a saved pristine copy instead
carry_forward_bullets: Revert an injection from a SAVED COPY, never with git checkout, whenever the round is also building: git checkout reverts to HEAD, which for uncommitted work is the round itself. The rule belongs beside the --no-fail-fast one Round 816 established, since both are defects of the same loop

Declared rung ORDER is still unchecked, and that half of Round 765's reasoning stands: order is a property of the anchor SET against the document, which is what the slicer computes when it places them. The scan now knows every anchor resolves, which is the precondition an order check would need

The reply to the consumer is still unwritten: how Round 815 answered Round 765's deferral, the fail-fast methodology defect and its re-measurement in Round 816, and this round's own revert defect. Two self-reports now, not one

Round 818.decision_summary: R818 (DESIGN/communication — the reply Round 815 left owed, now covering three rounds). A reply to the first playable consumer covering Round 815 (the rung coordinate check they were told we had deferred), Round 816 (the re-measurement of every injection claim in the arc) and Round 817 (the scan half). Its center is not the build: it is TWO self-reports of our own verification being wrong — cargo test halting at the first failing binary, which made every 'no existing test broke' claim in Rounds 806 through 814 weaker than written, and a git checkout revert that destroyed Round 817's own uncommitted implementation mid-injection. Both are stated as defects rather than softened, because a consumer calibrating trust in our gates needs to know how our numbers were produced. The load-bearing honest half concerns Round 817's value TO THEM: their build wipes the sidecar and replays with the excerpt import ordered before the ladder import, so the write path already re-resolves all 19 of their rungs every run and the round fixes nothing they have today — what changes is that the guarantee attaches to the store rather than to their script's step order, and a convention drifts silently where an invariant does not. Every claim about their side was read from their tree first: the pin at 75eddce, the 66/56/5/19 ladder surface, the commit that removed their clock copy, and the wrapper that consumes section_at. One drafting error was caught by that discipline — a truncated grep nearly produced the claim that they had not adopted Round 812, which their narrative.rs contradicts. The pin situation is stated plainly rather than generously: Round 815 is pullable, Rounds 816 and 817 are local and await a push word. SSOT = this entry; the document is claudedocs/send-r815-r817-reply.md.

Round 819.decision_summary: R819 (DESIGN — the axis Round 803 named and left undesigned). No axis checks fact or entity citations in code: the citation gate covers sections, rounds and inventory, while the north-star consumer cites FACTS. The design is two-tiered because the measurement forced it. A MARKED citation, written behind a configured prefix the way rounds and Round 810 external ledgers already are, is enforceable at reject with structurally zero false positives. An UNMARKED shape match cannot be, and the reason is not discipline but information: of the ten shape-matching tokens in the consumer 43 source files that are not store keys, EIGHT are ids invented on purpose to test rejection, and a deliberately invented id is indistinguishable by shape from a hallucinated one. The ninth is sharper still — a token that is the shared PREFIX of four real ids, used as a guard that no id leaks to the screen, which no shape rule can avoid because the prefix of a real id is itself id-shaped. The verdict stops at "this id is not in the store" and never guesses the intended name, the same restraint Round 803 used when it answered a residual with a question instead of a build. The tenth token is why this matters: engine/src/irony.rs cites f-jiun-thinks-natural in the doc comment carrying that module entire rationale, and no such fact exists among their 1,105 — drawing zero violations today. Round 820.decision_summary: R820 (BUILD — tier B of the Round 819 design, the axis Round 803 named). scan_id_citations reads every id-shaped token in the configured trees and names the ones that carry a namespace DERIVED from the store own key space yet match no key. It is advisory by construction rather than by configuration: it returns a report and never a violation, so no severity knob can turn it into a gate. The round also corrects its own design: Round 819 argued for the advisory ceiling from ten shape-matches, but it counted them over FULL TEXT while the gate inherits comment_only, and the two surfaces are different places — ids invented to test rejection live in CODE (fixtures, string constants) and citations live in prose COMMENTS. On the real corpus the ten collapse to one and that one is real, so the measured precision is far better than the design argued; the ceiling stands anyway, because one corpus is not proof and a prefix guard can sit in a comment too. A namespace needs two ids, since one id does not establish one. Token boundaries are hand-rolled because the rule needs lookaround the regex crate lacks, and the scan boundary is inherited from walk_paths rather than invented, which is what keeps a baked projection thousands of emitted ids off an axis about what an author wrote. A store deriving no namespace prints "axis not applicable" with its counts instead of a clean line — this workspace, holding zero facts, is exactly that store. Round 821.decision_summary:
R821 (BUILD — the scan half of the ladder ORDER rule, the standing Round 440 obligation Round 817 named and Round 815 carried before it). A ladder's nth declared hold must be the nth passage of the prose it addresses. The engine's projection has enforced that since Round 767, and the scan did not: Round 817 asks each rung's coordinate a question about ITSELF (does this prefix resolve, uniquely, in this document) and order is a property of the SET, so a ladder whose every rung resolves while its holds run against the prose passed the scan silently. Worse than silently — it passed while PRINTING "N coordinate(s) resolved", which reads as a sound ladder. That is the misleading-green class this project keeps naming (Round 796, Round 811, Round 813), reached here not by an empty axis but by a half-covered one.

THE RULE NOW HAS ONE HOME. Round 766 deliberately kept order out of the generic slicer — an anchor set may arrive from a map, and a slicer has no business demanding a caller's iteration order match a document — and said an ordered caller "judges its declared order against that". While the projection was the only ordered caller, that judgement was written inline there. A second copy in the scan would have made one invariant answer to two homes, the half-enforced class CLAUDE.md names, so the judgement moved to mnemosyne_core::declared_order_break: the same move Round 815 made for resolve_prefix, one level up. Each caller supplies the offsets its OWN single resolve pass already produced — the projection through the new PrefixSlices::declared_offsets (captured before the existing sort, so no second search), the scan by keeping the offset it was discarding from PrefixResolution::Unique. The injection proves the sharing rather than asserting it: neutralising the core function fails the Round 767 projection test that has been shipped for fifty rounds, which it could not do if a hand-rolled copy were still there.

THE ANSWER NAMES THE HOLD TO MOVE. The break is the first index at which the declared sequence differs from the same coordinates in document order — the hold sitting where a later one belongs — not the hold that follows it. Behaviour preserved exactly: the shipped projection test pins index 0 for a two-hold swap, and a monotonicity-break reading would have said index 1 and sent the author to the hold that is already in the right place.

ONE DELIBERATE ASYMMETRY, and it is not drift. The projection dedups anchors (Round 768: the kernel prices a rung per revealed fact, so one authored hold arrives there as several rungs sharing an anchor) and the scan does not, because import_ladders rejects two rungs at one anchor outright (Round 765) — in the store a hold IS a rung. Copying the dedup here would have imported a rule from a representation this side does not have. A duplicated anchor reaching the store out-of-band produces EQUAL offsets, which run in any order, so the axis does not turn it into a false accusation; naming it is a different rule and is carried, not silently absorbed.

A STRANDED RUNG IS NOT ALSO ACCUSED OF BEING OUT OF ORDER. A missing hold has no position, so a sequence verdict over the holds that happen to remain would be about a ladder nobody declared, and it would send the author to reorder when the repair is the coordinate that no longer lands.

SELF-REPORT — the fourth injection was VACUOUS and was fixed rather than counted, the Round 816 rule catching this round the way it caught Round 820. Removing the stranded-rung guard broke nothing, because the fixture stranded two of three rungs and left ONE surviving hold, and one hold runs in any order. A fixture that cannot tell the guard from its absence reports a passing check while testing nothing. The stranded case was rebuilt so the SURVIVING holds are themselves out of order — which also had to be reached the way a consumer reaches it, by re-importing the excerpt under an already-valid ladder, since Round 815 made the write path resolve every rung at import and an absent prefix cannot be declared directly any more.

SSOT = this entry. No design doc: the design is the Round 440 boundary doctrine applied to a rule that already existed.
changes_bullets: mnemosyne_core::declared_order_break is THE ladder-order rule — the first index at which a declared sequence of prefix coordinates differs from those coordinates in document order, or None when the declaration runs the way the prose does. It lives beside resolve_prefix for the same reason (Round 815): two callers, and the store side cannot depend on the engine

scan_continuity judges each ladder's declared order, not only each rung's coordinate — new violation LadderRungsOutOfProseOrder { section, prefix, declared_at }, naming the hold that is out of place and its position among the declared holds

The engine's projection stops hand-rolling the comparison and calls the shared function; PrefixSlices::declared_offsets exposes the offsets in the order `new` received them, captured BEFORE the existing sort so the rule is shared without a second search (the Round 766 in_prose_order discipline, one level up)
Order is judged only when every rung landed: a missing hold has no position, so a sequence verdict would be about the holds that happen to remain and would name one fault twice

The scan does NOT dedup anchors while the projection does, and the comment says why: import_ladders rejects two rungs at one anchor (Round 765), so a hold is a rung on this side, and copying the projection's Round 768 dedup would import a rule from a representation the store does not have

R821 (BUILD — the scan half of the ladder ORDER rule, the standing Round 440 obligation Round 817 named and Round 815 carried before it). A ladder's nth declared hold must be the nth passage of the prose it addresses. The engine's projection has enforced that since Round 767, and the scan did not: Round 817 asks each rung's coordinate a question about ITSELF (does this prefix resolve, uniquely, in this document) and order is a property of the SET, so a ladder whose every rung resolves while its holds run against the prose passed the scan silently. Worse than silently — it passed while PRINTING "N coordinate(s) resolved", which reads as a sound ladder. That is the misleading-green class this project keeps naming (Round 796, Round 811, Round 813), reached here not by an empty axis but by a half-covered one.

THE RULE NOW HAS ONE HOME. Round 766 deliberately kept order out of the generic slicer — an anchor set may arrive from a map, and a slicer has no business demanding a caller's iteration order match a document — and said an ordered caller "judges its declared order against that". Round 822.decision_summary:
R822 (BUILD — the last Round 765 write-path ladder rule to reach the scan). import_ladders rejects two rungs of one ladder declaring the SAME anchor, because an ambiguous hold resolves to one slice and swallows the other; the scan never re-read that rule, so an out-of-band edit could leave a ladder whose gate silently never opens for one of its holds — the exact failure Round 765 said a store is for. Round 817 covered resolution, foreign source and non-prefix shape, Round 821 covered order, and this closes the set.

THE SCAN IS THE ONLY PLACE THIS CAN BE SEEN, and that is a structural fact rather than a division of labour. Round 768 expands each store rung into one ENGINE rung per revealed fact, so a single hold opening two facts and two holds illegally sharing an anchor arrive at the projection as the identical rung sequence — verified by reading the expansion, not assumed. The projection dedups both and cannot distinguish them; worse, it must not try, since the rung-per-fact case is legitimate there. A hold is a rung on the STORE side and nowhere else, so the store side is the only side that can ask the question. This is the mirror of Round 821's asymmetry, arriving at the same seam from the other direction: there the scan had to refuse the projection's dedup, here it turns out the projection could never have owned the rule at all.

N COPIES ARE ONE FAULT. The count is taken over the whole declaration and reported once per repeated coordinate, in declared order, carrying its occurrence count — the Round 817 reason RungMiss::Ambiguous carries one, since two and eleven are different repairs. A per-extra-rung report would say "two problems" about a single coordinate an author fixes once. Two different coordinates each repeated are both named, because a report that names one and stops hides half the repair. Comparison is on the whole ContentAnchor (source plus locator), the same key the write path's duplicate guard uses, so the same prefix into a different document is not a duplicate on either side.

A DUPLICATE DOES NOT SUPPRESS THE ORDER VERDICT, unlike a stranded rung, and the line between them is drawn precisely rather than by analogy: a stranded coordinate has NO position, so any sequence verdict would be about the holds that happen to remain, while a duplicated one has the SAME position twice, so the declaration is still fully positioned and an inversion elsewhere is still a real question. Equal offsets run in any order, so the duplicate cannot become a false accusation on the order axis while a genuine break beside it is still named. The test pins exactly that combination, and the injection that makes a duplicate suppress order fails it.

Round 823.decision_summary:
R823 (BUILD/DEBT — the tool that gates every commit stops being a shared, stale, or unreproducible slot). Three defects, all found by MEASURING rather than by reading, and the third is the root the other two grew from.

FIRST, ~/.cargo/bin/mnemosyne-cli is a slot every checkout on the machine shares, and this repo was the one overwriting it. The dev loop ran cargo install --path --force after schema bumps so hand-run commands would use the current tool; each of those replaced whatever a consumer had installed. That is not hypothetical and it was ours: the first playable consumer's README records the collision on 2026-07-29 (their pinned 75eddce5 replaced mid-session by 11d703bf-dirty), and their gate harness resolves the tool by PATH with NO pin assertion, so their gates measured with a tool that did not build their store. Their build script asserts the pin and fails loud; the test harness does not. Half a rule.

SECOND, both git hooks preferred target/release/mnemosyne-cli if it merely EXISTED, with no freshness check, and fell back to the PATH entry. Two ways to gate a commit with the wrong tool, written out twice byte-identically. They now share ONE resolver, scripts/mn, which asks cargo whether the build is current instead of guessing — staleness is cargo's question and a second answer here would be free to drift from it.

THIRD AND CAUSAL: the build script that stamps the git rev into the binary reran on EVERY build. `cargo:rerun-if-changed` resolves against the PACKAGE root, so the bare `.git/HEAD` and `.git/index` it emitted named crates/mnemosyne-cli/.git/HEAD — files that do not exist — and cargo reads a missing rerun path as CHANGED. Because the script emits rustc-env, the crate then recompiled every time: 46s of release rebuild with nothing changed, measured warm, against 0.126s once fixed. The same bug sat in mnemosyne-mcp's build script, which is a copy of this one; both have carried it since Round 286. THIS is why the hooks preferred a possibly stale artifact and why the dev loop reached for cargo install: keeping the tool current looked expensive, and it was, for a reason nobody had measured.

DEBUG, NOT RELEASE, and measured rather than assumed. A hook runs immediately after `git add`, so the index has just moved and the stamp must be recomputed; from there release costs ~50s and debug ~4s, and debug shares artifacts with the clippy run the hook already does. Release wins only on execution (0.19s vs 1.0s on this store), which does not repay the build. The old "prefer release, it is much faster than cargo run" comment was reasoning from a cost that was itself the defect.

WHAT THE FIX DOES NOT COVER, recorded because the defect was hiding it: an edit that is never staged moves neither HEAD nor index, so a local binary can keep a stamp that fails to say -dirty. It matters only for a locally built binary, and those no longer reach anyone — scripts/mn keeps them in target/, and the pinned path builds from cargo's own pristine checkout of the revision, where the tree cannot be dirty (evidence: the installed mnemosyne-mcp, installed by rev, stamps 25d30d16 with no -dirty).

The consumer-facing half is documented rather than built: SCHEMA_GUIDE's Round 381 CI recipe is safe because a runner is fresh and has one consumer, and it now carries the local-machine half — resolve the binary FROM the pin into a per-rev root so several pins coexist, and assert the rev wherever the tool is USED, not only where the store is built.

Now emitted from `git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir`, which is also correct inside a worktree. Fixed in BOTH mnemosyne-cli and mnemosyne-mcp, which have carried the same copy since Round 286

Round 824.decision_summary:
R824 (DEBT — one home for the build stamp, paying the carry Round 823 named and declined on cost). Every Mnemosyne binary embeds `git describe` as BUILD_GIT_HASH so a consumer can say WHICH tool they are holding; the store is built by that tool, and a different tool is a different store. That rule was written TWICE — mnemosyne-cli's build script and mnemosyne-mcp's, the second described in its own comment as "mirrors the mnemosyne-cli build.rs (same format, same fallbacks)".

THE COPIES ARE THE EVIDENCE, not the argument. Both carried the SAME defect from Round 286 to Round 823: package-relative `cargo:rerun-if-changed` paths naming a `.git` that lives at the workspace root, so each named a file that does not exist and cargo read the miss as a change. Five hundred rounds of two files nobody diffed against each other. The usual case against duplication is that copies drift; this pair never drifted and still cost twice, because a copy is also a second thing to get wrong and a second place to have to notice.

The rule now lives in mnemosyne-build-stamp, a build-dependency crate whose whole surface is `emit()`, and both build scripts are four lines that call it. The doc comment carries what Round 823 measured (why the paths must be absolute, why a worktree resolves correctly) and what the stamp CANNOT see (an unstaged edit moves neither HEAD nor index, so a local build can fail to say `-dirty` — contained because local builds stay in target/ behind scripts/mn and the pinned path builds from cargo's own pristine checkout).

`run_git` collapses four failure shapes into one answer: a missing git, a non-zero exit, non-UTF-8 output and empty output all mean this build cannot know and must not guess. That was already the behaviour; it now reads as a decision instead of a chain of adapters.

The new crate needed no gate configuration. Round 783 replaced the hand list of scanned trees with a derived `crates/*/src/` + `crates/*/build.rs` pattern precisely so a new crate is gated the day it exists, and the coverage count moved 212 to 213 sources and 92 to 93 scanned on its own.

Round 825.decision_summary:
R825 (DESIGN — the tool pin: a workspace declares which Mnemosyne revision may act on it, and the tool enforces it). Cargo pins a consumer's LIBRARY dependencies through Cargo.lock and pins nothing about a BINARY they invoke by name. Every Mnemosyne consumer therefore runs its gates with whatever tool happens to be resolvable, and the two live ones show both failure shapes: the first playable consumer declares MN_PIN in its build script and asserts it there, but its gate harness resolves by PATH with no assertion, so its gates measured with a tool that did not build its store; the spec consumer names an absolute path to a shared binary in its host config, where there is no revision to declare at all and three workspaces share one file. The pin is a convention today, and a convention is not a gate.

WHY schema_version DOES NOT ALREADY COVER THIS, which is the objection to answer first. The store carries schema_version with a monotone guard, so DATA-FORMAT skew is caught. Behaviour skew is not: Round 821 and Round 822 changed no schema and changed what validate-continuity reports. A consumer pinned only by schema sees no difference at all while its gate verdicts move underneath it. The two guards are complementary — one protects the shape of what is written, the other protects the judgement that produced it.

THE DECLARATION GOES IN mnemosyne.toml, as `[tool] pin`. It is the file the consumer owns and versions alongside the store, it is already what the MCP server's `--workspace` points at, and that last part matters most: the host config that launches an MCP server is not ours to change, so a pin that lives in the workspace reaches a surface we otherwise cannot. The same declaration then serves every entry point uniformly, which means the first consumer's gate-harness gap closes structurally — they would not need to add an assertion to their test harness, because the tool itself refuses.

WHERE IT IS ENFORCED, and this is the decision the round turned on. Three shapes were weighed. (1) Each binary checks at its entry point: minimal rebuild fan-out, but it covers only the entry and a forgotten call passes SILENTLY. (2) mnemosyne-config carries its own build stamp so the check needs no caller cooperation: impossible to forget, but it puts a git-volatile input at the bottom of the dependency graph, so every commit rebuilds everything that depends on config — which is nearly the whole workspace. (3) discover_config performs the check against a stamp each binary registers once through a process-global OnceLock. This covers all eighteen config-load sites, keeps the stamp in the two leaf binaries where its fan-out is minimal, and — the property that decided it — FAILS CLOSED when the registration is forgotten: an unregistered process meeting a pinned workspace cannot verify itself, so it refuses. A mistake surfaces as a loud stop rather than a silent pass. Shape 3.

THE COMPARISON RULE. The stamp is `git describe --always --dirty --abbrev=8`, so it is at least eight hex characters and may be longer, with an optional `-dirty` suffix; a declared pin is written by hand at whatever length its author found convenient (the first consumer writes eight, a Cargo.toml rev is forty). So: a `-dirty` stamp satisfies NO pin, because a dirty build corresponds to no revision and that is precisely what a pinned consumer must be told; an `unknown` stamp (built without git) satisfies no pin either, since it cannot be verified rather than being verified as wrong; otherwise the shorter of the two must be a prefix of the longer, and a declared pin shorter than seven characters is a config error, git's own abbreviation floor.

OPT-IN, and it has to be: a workspace with no `[tool] pin` behaves exactly as today, or every existing consumer breaks the moment they upgrade. The escape hatch is MNEMOSYNE_PIN_SKIP=1, mirroring the first consumer's own MN_PIN_SKIP, and it WARNS on stderr every time it is used — a silent skip is how a skip becomes permanent. Mnemosyne's own workspace will not carry a pin: the tool here IS the repository, so pinning it would be circular.

REFUSAL, NOT DEGRADED SERVICE. The tool exits non-zero and names the workspace, the declared pin, its own stamp, and the remedy. For the MCP server this means it does not start, which is less legible in-session than an error per tool call — the alternative was considered and rejected: a server that starts successfully while being unusable reports health it does not have, and carries a permanently-broken state through more code. A gate that cannot answer must not answer.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO, stated so the next round does not assume it. It converts silent skew into loud refusal; it does not PROVISION the right binary. Provisioning stays the consumer's, through the per-rev `--root` recipe documented in SCHEMA_GUIDE at Round 823. A tool that downloaded and executed another version of itself would be a supply-chain hazard, and is refused on purpose rather than deferred.

Round 826.decision_summary:
R826 (BUILD — the tool pin, built to the Round 825 design, plus the Round 823 defect this feature exposed in its own foundation). A workspace declares `[tool] pin = "<rev>"` and every Mnemosyne binary refuses to open it while carrying a different revision. Cargo pins a consumer's library dependencies and pins nothing about a binary they invoke by name; this is the declaration that closes that, and it lives in mnemosyne.toml because that file is the consumer's own and because an MCP server's host config is not ours to script while `--workspace` already points here.

ENFORCED AT CONFIG LOAD, so all eighteen call sites that reach a config are covered by construction rather than by each one remembering to ask. The identity comes from a process-global registered once in each main, which is fail-closed by design: a process that never says what it is cannot verify itself against a pin and is REFUSED, not waved through. Forgetting the registration is therefore a loud stop, not a silent pass — the property that chose this shape over checking in each binary's entry point.

THE FEATURE FOUND A HOLE IN ITS OWN FOUNDATION, and this is the round's real finding. Round 823 fixed the stamp's rerun rule and picked the wrong files to watch: `.git/HEAD` and `.git/index`. On a branch, HEAD is a SYMREF whose bytes are the branch NAME — a commit does not rewrite it, it rewrites `refs/heads/<branch>`. So a commit left the binary stamped with the PREVIOUS revision, and on a clean tree with no `-dirty` suffix to betray it: a build claiming to be a revision it is not, which is precisely the lie this round's pin exists to prevent, sitting inside the mechanism the pin reads. Caught because the new binary-level test compared two binaries' stamps and found them disagreeing. The watch set is now HEAD (checkout, detach), the branch's own ref (commit), packed-refs (where that ref lives when packed), and index (staging flips `-dirty`) — each resolved through `git rev-parse --git-path`, which is also correct inside a linked worktree, where HEAD and index are per-worktree while refs are shared. Emitted only when the file exists, because a missing rerun path is what cargo reads as changed and is how Round 823's 46s-per-build defect worked.

THE REFUSAL NAMES WHAT IT MUST. The message carries the workspace, the declared pin, this build's own stamp, WHY it does not satisfy (four separate refusal variants, because a dirty build, an unidentifiable one, a git-less one and a genuinely different revision are four different repairs — the Round 817 rule that naming one failure when it is another lies about what to fix), and the install command for the right revision. It names the BINARY THAT IS REFUSING rather than a hardcoded one: both binaries reach this single message, and telling someone whose MCP server just failed to start to install `mnemosyne-cli` sends them to the wrong tool. The test asserts that, and caught it.

The MCP server refuses by not starting. A server that came up while unusable would report health it does not have; a gate that cannot answer must not answer.

TWO OF THIS PROJECT'S OWN GATES CAUGHT THIS ROUND MID-BUILD, both correctly: `docs_match_reality_smoke` failed because `[tool]` existed in the type and in neither schema guide, and the full-suite run failed because the new test read the MCP binary out of `target/`, which `scripts/verify.sh --fresh` had cleaned. The second fix is the more interesting one — the test now runs both binaries through `cargo run` rather than a path, which makes staleness AND absence impossible for the same reason `scripts/mn` asks cargo instead of comparing mtimes: freshness is cargo's question and a second answer to it is free to be wrong. An earlier attempt at a hand-rolled staleness guard was deleted rather than kept.

Round 827.decision_summary:
R827 (DEBT — three defects in Round 826, found by asking whether it was actually built the long-term-correct way rather than by anything failing). The pin shipped working and was wrong in three places, and the third one shipped a broken binary.

FIRST, THE STAMP WAS A DESCRIPTION, NOT A REVISION. `git describe --always --dirty --abbrev=8` returns the nearest reachable TAG and only falls back to a hash when there is none. This repository has no tags, so the defect was invisible; tagging it and reading the output back turned the stamp into the bare tag name. The day anyone tags a release, every stamp becomes something like `v1.0-3-gabc12345`, the pin comparison stops matching for consumers holding exactly the right build, and the first playable consumer's own sed — which extracts `([0-9a-f]{7,})` — extracts nothing and halts their store build. It also made the value disagree with its own watch set: `describe` depends on tags, which nothing watches, while `rev-parse` depends on HEAD, the refs and the index, which are precisely what Round 826 does watch. The stamp is now `git rev-parse --short=8 HEAD` plus a separate `git diff --quiet HEAD` for the dirty suffix, so it is a function of exactly the inputs cargo has been told to invalidate it on.

SECOND, THE BINARY LIST WAS A HAND LIST — the anti-pattern Round 783 named and inverted, reproduced one round later. `PINNED_BINARIES` restated the tree and drifted from it immediately. The set is now DERIVED from `cargo metadata`, minus an explicit `NOT_WORKSPACE_BINARIES` with a reason per entry, and a declared exclusion that matches no binary is reported STALE — the Round 783 shape exactly, where a binary merely absent is loud and only a written-down name is quiet. The per-binary invocation stays written down, because each has its own command line, but an unknown name PANICS rather than being skipped.

THIRD, AND THIS IS WHAT THE HAND LIST COST: `mnemosyne-render` takes a workspace as its first argument, was never in the list, and never registered its identity — so it refused EVERY pinned workspace, including one pinned to its own revision. Fail-closed did its job (the failure was loud and safe rather than silently wrong, which is the property that chose the enforcement shape), and it was still a shipped binary that could not do its work. It registers now, and the derived set covers it.

THE TEST WAS ALSO NOT TESTING WHAT IT CLAIMED, and an injection is what said so. Removing the registration from `mnemosyne-render` reported ZERO failures: the test asserted only that each binary REFUSES, and a binary that never registers refuses too. Refusal was satisfied equally by the correct case and the broken one, which is exactly how the broken one shipped. The refusal REASON separates them — an identified build says which revision it is, an unregistered one says it cannot tell — and the test now asserts that, so removing the registration from either binary fails it. This is the Round 816 rule paying out again: an injection reporting nothing is a suspect injection, and here it was the test that was wrong rather than the injection.

`revision` also gained `revision_in(dir)`, a seam that lets the tag case be tested against a scratch repository instead of against whichever repository happens to be the current directory. The regression test builds a repo, commits, tags it, and asserts the stamp is still hex.

SELF-REPORT: one injection was reverted with `git checkout` rather than from a saved copy, which is the rule Round 817 established after losing a round's implementation that way. Nothing was lost here only because that file's change was already committed in Round 826 — the rule held by luck, not by discipline.

`revision_in(dir)` is the testable seam behind `revision()`, so the tag case can be exercised against a scratch repository rather than only against the current directory

Round 828.decision_summary:
R828 (DOCS — the tool pin cannot be adopted by any consumer holding it, and nothing said so). Round 826 shipped `[tool] pin` and Round 827 hardened it, and neither noticed that a workspace declaring the section is unreadable to every binary built before the section existed. `WorkspaceConfig` denies unknown fields — deliberately, so a typo'd key fails loud instead of being silently ignored — so an older binary stops at TOML parse with `TOML parse error … [tool]` and says nothing about revisions.

REFUSING IS CORRECT AND THE MESSAGE IS NOT. Round 829.decision_summary:
R829 (BUILD — scripts/gc, reclaiming target/ without guessing which artifacts matter). The workspace target directory had reached 32G. The obvious reach is `cargo sweep --time <days>`, and it is wrong on this tree twice over: measured here, ZERO files carried an mtime older than seven days, so the window would have reclaimed nothing at all — and more importantly an age window is a guess about which files matter wearing a policy's clothes. It keeps stale artifacts that happen to be recent and deletes live ones that happen not to be, while reading as safe.

TWO MODES, because there are two jobs and one answer would be wrong for one of them.

The DEFAULT is `--installed`: keep every artifact any currently installed toolchain made, which removes the debris of toolchains since uninstalled and nothing else. Its rebuild cost is ZERO — verified rather than claimed, `scripts/mn` answering in 0.081s immediately after. Its yield is a function of toolchain churn, and on this machine, with all six installed toolchains still present, it currently reclaims NOTHING. That is the correct answer rather than a failure, and it is written down so the next reader does not mistake a quiet run for a broken one.

`--deep` is the stamp/build/sweep protocol: stamp, build the workspace, then delete everything that build did not touch. What survives is not "recent" but "used" — the same discipline as `scripts/mn` asking cargo whether a binary is current instead of comparing mtimes, since freshness is the build system's question and a second answer to it is free to be wrong.

I RAN THE AGGRESSIVE MODE FIRST AND DESTROYED A MEASUREMENT DOING IT. The deep sweep executed before the cheap mode was even considered, so by the time `--installed` was measured there was nothing left for it to find. Its real yield on a 32G tree is now unknown and cannot be recovered without letting the tree grow again. The order was mine and it was the wrong way round: measure the cheap thing before the expensive one destroys its subject.

AND THE HEADLINE NUMBER I FIRST REPORTED WAS A VACUOUS ONE. The deep sweep took target from 32G to 990M, and I reported that. It does not survive the next `cargo test --workspace`, which rebuilds every test binary and returns the tree to 11G. The durable reclaim is 32G to 11G — about 21G — and 990M was a state measured in a moment that does not last. That is this session's own recurring lesson landing on its author: a number is not a result until you know whether it holds.

The gc holds the SAME lock `scripts/verify.sh` takes, across the whole operation. Not politeness: in deep mode a cargo run starting after the stamp leaves its artifacts unmarked and loses them, and in either mode a build running during the sweep can have files deleted from under it. Round 743 is this repository's own evidence that overlapping cargo on one target corrupts the fingerprint cache and runs a stale binary.

Release artifacts are not kept by `--deep`, deliberately: since Round 823 nothing in this flow produces or reads them, because the `cargo install --path` step that once did was removed and `scripts/mn` is debug. `--release` keeps them at the price of a release build inside the gc, and is rejected with an explanation when passed to the default mode, where it would mean nothing.

Round 830.decision_summary:
R830 (MEASUREMENT, code 0 beyond a pointer comment — why target/ is large, and why the two obvious ways to shrink it are both refused). Round 829 built the gc and left the real question open: 9.8G is the steady state after a full workspace test build, and reclaiming it repeatedly is a treadmill. The structural answer would be to produce less. Two candidates were measured. Both failed, and the second failed in a way worth writing down.

FIRST CANDIDATE, DEBUG INFO — FALSIFIED BY MEASUREMENT. `[profile.release]` already carries `debug = "line-tables-only"` while `[profile.dev]` was never configured, so dev ran on the default full debug info; the hypothesis was that this explained a ~10G build. Setting dev to `line-tables-only` and rebuilding from clean produced 9.8G against a 9.8G baseline, and the individual test binaries came out BYTE-IDENTICAL — 223.5 MB and 222.9 MB before and after, the same two files. The 223 MB is code: each test binary statically links RocksDB and tonic and the whole server. The profile change was REVERTED rather than kept, because a setting that does nothing, carrying a comment claiming it does something, is a false claim planted for the next reader.

SECOND CANDIDATE, TEST CONSOLIDATION — FORBIDDEN, AND THE CODE SAID SO BEFORE I RECOMMENDED IT. Rust compiles every `tests/*.rs` to its own binary, so mnemosyne-server's 22 files become 22 statically linked binaries at ~223 MB each: 4.9G, half the tree. Merging them into one `mod`-based binary would save about 4.67G. It cannot be done. Two separate mechanisms forbid it, both documented in the files themselves:

  - FOUR files install a GLOBAL tracing subscriber, and `registry().try_init()` is one-shot per process. `grpc_otlp_config_smoke.rs` says so in a comment explaining why two assertions were combined into one test: a second install panics.
  - `handler_span_hierarchy_smoke.rs` carries a header recording that it was split into its own binary DELIBERATELY, after running in the same binary as `grpc_tracestate_smoke.rs` interleaved the callsite Interest cache and the sharded-slab span Pool, so the `gate.evaluate` and `audit.append` child spans went to the global dispatcher instead of the test-local one. The split places a process boundary between the two state spaces. (The header attributes this to a round predating this ledger, so it is cited here by file and mechanism rather than by number.)

THE DECISIVE PROPERTY IS THAT THE FAILURE IT FIXED WAS INTERMITTENT. A merge could be attempted and the suite could come back green without that meaning the race is gone — the same green-is-not-proof shape this session has hit four times already, arriving here as an argument against an experiment rather than as a defect found after one. Consolidation is therefore not testable by running the tests, which is what moves it from risky to refused.

SO THE FLOOR IS REAL: of the 9.8G steady state, about 4.9G is isolation-mandated test binaries and about 2.6G is the librocksdb-sys C++ build (1.7G of build output plus an 853 MB rlib). Roughly 7.5G is structural. The management answer is to CYCLE the tree, not shrink it: `scripts/gc --deep` when it hurts, accepting that the next full build restores it. `--maxsize` is rejected on the arithmetic — a cap below 9.8G deletes what the next build immediately needs, and a cap above it never fires.

SELF-REPORT, TWO. I recommended consolidation BEFORE reading the files I was proposing to merge; both refusals were sitting in their headers. That is the same class the first playable consumer reported to us the same day — that a scan which opens a file and does not read it counts the file anyway, and opening is not reading. And an earlier count in this round briefly showed twenty files with zero tests, which was my grep failing to match `#[tokio::test(flavor = …)]` rather than a finding; it was caught before it was reported as one, but it was one command away from being written down as fact.

Truly reducing this means redesigning the tracing test strategy — removing the global-subscriber dependency and resolving the dispatcher race — and it needs a reproduction harness for an intermittent failure before it can be attempted, not a suite run. Not recommended now, and named rather than left implicit.

Round 832.decision_summary:
R832 (BUILD — one declaration is now enough: a pinned workspace makes the tool become the pinned tool). Round 826 shipped the pin as detection only and said so plainly: silent skew became a loud refusal, and procurement stayed the reader's problem. Round 831 then measured what that leaves standing — a consumer with two acquisition paths at two revisions, where the repair is a wrapper script per repo and an edit to a host config this project does not own. This round removes both by making the refusal a fallback rather than the answer: when the pinned build is ALREADY INSTALLED, the binary hands over to it.

USING AN INSTALLED REVISION IS NOT PROCURING ONE, and that boundary is the whole design rather than a caveat on it. The switch resolves a path on disk and execs it — no network, no compile. Downloading and running another version of oneself remains refused, so an absent build still falls through to the refusal carrying the install line. Round 826 refused procurement and was right to; it did not distinguish the half that costs nothing.

EXEC, NOT SPAWN, AND THAT IS LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN A DETAIL. Replacing the process image preserves stdio pipes, working directory and exit code, which is what lets an MCP server hand over mid-launch without its client noticing — a spawned child would need every one of those relayed, and the server's stdout is a protocol stream that cannot carry a note. The announcement therefore goes to stderr, because a tool quietly becoming a different tool is the one surprise this must not be.

IT COSTS NO NEW ENFORCEMENT POINT. Round 825 chose `load_config` because forgetting the identity fails closed, and that same choke point is where the switch goes: every binary and every path that opens a workspace already passes through it, so the CLI, the MCP server and the renderer all gain this without being told about it individually.

THE PATH IS ONE DEFINITION, not two. `pinned_root` is what the switch looks in AND what the refusal prints, and it honours the `MN_ROOT` knob SCHEMA_GUIDE's shell recipe already documents instead of inventing a second one. Two spellings would drift, and the drift reads as the tool searching where its own advice never pointed — the failure class Rounds 815 and 824 keep closing.

AN UNIDENTIFIED BUILD IS REFUSED, NEVER SWITCHED AWAY FROM. The other three refusals mean "this is not the pinned revision", which another binary fixes; `Unidentified` means this build never declared what it is, which is a defect no installed binary repairs and which a hand-off would hide inside a second process. Round 826 chose fail-closed for exactly that case and it stays chosen.

THE SWITCH HAPPENS AT MOST ONCE. After an exec the replacement runs with the same argv and cwd, so it finds the same config and the same pin: a second mismatch can only mean the build installed under that pin is not the revision the path names. That is a broken install and is reported as one.

`pinned_root` / `pinned_binary` are the single definition of where a pin resolves, used by both the lookup and the refusal's install line, with `MN_ROOT` as the documented override rather than a new knob
`switch_can_repair` states which refusals a hand-off can fix, and `PIN_EXEC_ENV` records that one already happened so a mis-installed root reports itself instead of exec'ing in a circle

SCHEMA_GUIDE and the MCP schema-guide resource now say that one declaration suffices — no per-repo wrapper, no host-config edit — and draw the use-versus-procure line where the old text drew a blanket "does not provision"
`tool_pin_refusal_smoke.rs` is renamed `tool_pin_smoke.rs`, since refusal is now one of two answers it covers

Round 833.decision_summary:
R833 (BUILD — the ladder's four registry refs reach the scan boundary, and the completeness guard that should have said so watches one depth). The ref-emitting-field class has been closed one member at a time: predicate endpoints (Round 742), branch fork/converge edges (Round 743), disclosure override refs (Round 506). Each re-checks at the scan boundary what a write path already refuses, because a raw-JSON edit reaches what no primitive can. Round 765 then added ladders — a carrier entity, and per rung a needs list, a reveals list and an object — validated by `import_ladders` and scanned by nothing. This adds `ladder_ref_violations` and wires it into the aggregate.

THE INTERESTING PART IS WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT, and it is a defect in a guard rather than an omission in a list. `every_side_table_detector_is_wired_into_the_aggregate` exists precisely to stop this: an exhaustive destructure of `AtomicStore` stops compiling when a field is added, forcing whoever adds it to classify it as detector-guarded or not. It classified `sections` as content, which was TRUE when written. `AtomicSection::ladder` is nested inside that field, so no top-level field was ever added, the destructure never stopped compiling, and the guard reported complete about a depth it does not watch — for sixty-eight rounds. The comment now says so rather than leaving the next reader to infer the same false comfort. Detection at one depth is not detection; it is a scoped verdict that reads as a total one.

THE R506 COMMENT WAS ALSO FALSIFIED AND IS DELETED RATHER THAN MOVED. It called disclosure overrides "the LAST member of the ref-emitting-field class" — a claim about the future that Round 765 refuted a class-member later. The replacement does not re-make it for ladders.

SCOPE IS DRAWN AGAINST THE OTHER LADDER SCAN, not assumed. Round 834.decision_summary:
R834 (DESIGN — the completeness guard watches one depth, and the fix is not the obvious one). Round 833 closed the ladder's scan-boundary gap and found that the guard meant to prevent exactly that had reported complete for sixty-eight rounds: `every_side_table_detector_is_wired_into_the_aggregate` forces classification of TOP-LEVEL `AtomicStore` fields, and `AtomicSection::ladder` is nested inside one, so nothing ever stopped compiling. This round measures the space that guard does not watch and chooses how to close it.

THE MEASUREMENT THAT DECIDES IT IS NOT THE SIZE OF THE GAP BUT ITS UNDECIDABILITY. Walking the type graph from `AtomicStore` reaches 52 structs and enums, of which the guard watches one. Those types carry 91 String-typed fields — and WHICH of them are registry refs is not written in any type. `SectionLadder.carrier` and `AtomicSection.intent` are both `Option<String>`, one an entity ref and one prose; `LadderRung.needs` and `AtomicSection.rationale_bullets` are both `Vec<String>`, one a list of fact ids and one a list of sentences. So no mechanical type walk can decide, and "just recurse" — the obvious fix, and the one this round expected to recommend — is dead on the measurement rather than on argument.

COVERAGE IS ALSO NOT SINGLE-SOURCE, discovered by nearly writing a second live defect into the design. `set_section_decision_status` accepts a `superseding` id it never checks against the store, which reads as an unguarded ref. Measured instead of argued: the write path does accept `§ghost-does-not-exist`, and `validate-workspace` then exits 1 with `atomic orphan new (sections=1)`, because `project.rs` projects `superseded_by` as a cross-ref and the orphan scan resolves it. It is covered — by a DIFFERENT path than the detectors. `project.rs` projects `superseded_by`, `resolved_by` and `impact_scope` and does not project ladders, which is why Round 833 was a real gap and this is not. A guard that knows only about `*_violations` detectors would therefore demand a redundant detector for a field already guarded, so the classification has to record WHICH PATH covers a field, not merely whether it is a ref.

THE FAILURE MODE UNDER STUDY REPRODUCED ITSELF INSIDE THE ROUND. The first field count came from a hand-written list of 26 types and reported 68 pairs. Derived from the source instead, it is 52 types and 91 pairs — the hand list missed ten types and 23 pairs, a quarter, including `TypedClaim`, `EvidenceRef`, `BranchFork` and `SectionSkeleton`. A hand list restated the tree and drifted from it, in the round about hand lists drifting. The design therefore cannot contain one.

CHOSEN: a source tripwire that DERIVES the (type, String-field) pairs from the type graph and requires every pair to appear in a classification table naming its coverage path — detector, projection, or not-a-ref-because. Rejected: a recursive forced destructure at every type, which repeats the mechanism at all depths but records no reason, so a nested `carrier: _` can be silently wrong exactly as `sections: _` was — it moves the blind spot rather than closing it. Deferred: newtyping the ref ids, which would make the walk decidable and is the structurally right answer, but touches every ref field and its callers to close one defect; and an attribute plus proc macro, which is the strict improvement on the chosen design and should be priced after the table has caught something.

WHAT THE CHOSEN DESIGN DOES NOT DO, stated because a completeness guard that oversells is worse than none: it catches an UNCLASSIFIED field, not a MISCLASSIFIED one. A field recorded as not-a-ref that later becomes one by convention is still silent. The difference from today is that a line already exists for someone to change; Round 833's defect had no such line anywhere.

SSOT = this entry; the working notes are claudedocs/nested-ref-completeness-design.md (gitignored).
changes_bullets: The design for a source-derived completeness tripwire over nested ref-emitting fields, with the four measurements that chose it and the three alternatives priced and rejected or deferred

The build steps it hands to the next round: derive the pairs from the type graph with a non-vacuity floor, classify all 91 by coverage path, assert both directions so a vanished field is stale rather than silent, and inject a nested field to reproduce Round 833's blind spot
A warning written into the design from this round's own error: the derivation must read `mnemosyne-core`'s sources too, since half the reachable types live there
verification_bullets: THE TYPE GRAPH IS DERIVED, NOT LISTED: 52 reachable structs and enums at depths 1-4, 91 String-typed fields. The first attempt read only the two `lib.rs` files, found 24 types, and reported the rest as external primitives — a silent undercount corrected by walking every source in both crates

THE UNDECIDABILITY IS SHOWN BY EXHIBIT, not asserted: `Option<String>` holds an entity ref in `SectionLadder.carrier` and prose in `AtomicSection.intent`; `Vec<String>` holds fact ids in `LadderRung.needs` and sentences in `AtomicSection.rationale_bullets`

THE SECOND COVERAGE PATH WAS MEASURED ON THE SHIPPED BINARY rather than reasoned from `project.rs`: a section superseded by `§ghost-does-not-exist` is accepted by the write path and then rejected by `validate-workspace` with `atomic orphan new (sections=1)`, exit 1. Without that run this design would have recorded a live defect that does not exist
THE HAND-LIST DRIFT IS MEASURED, not recalled: 26 hand-listed types / 68 pairs versus 52 derived types / 91 pairs, naming the ten types missed
No production code changed this round, so the test count stands at Round 833's 1274. The probe workspace built for the `superseded_by` measurement was removed
carry_forward_bullets: The chosen design catches unclassified fields, never misclassified ones. That residual is inherent to detection here and is why the newtype option is deferred rather than dismissed — it is the only candidate that makes the distinction structural

The 91-entry table is a real one-time cost and is itself a thing that can rot into folklore. Its defence is that it is asserted against a DERIVED set in both directions, so an entry for a field that no longer exists fails as stale (the Round 783 rule); nothing defends the accuracy of a reason once written

Nothing yet enforces that a new ref field lands in one of the two coverage paths rather than neither. The tripwire will make the choice visible at the moment the field is added, which is the whole point, but the choice remains a human one
The build is a separate round. This round deliberately stops at the design because the table's 91 entries are mechanical work whose correctness depends on the derivation being right first

Round 835.decision_summary:
R835 (BUILD — the baseline gate ignored the root every other path in the tool honours, and it was blocking a live consumer). A field report from the external spec consumer answered the Round 831 notice: they closed the write hazard by aligning DOWN to their CI revision rather than up, because remedy #1 as written — bump the pin first — turns their CI red immediately, independent of any store write. All five of their enrolled workspaces are rejected by `validate-workspace` with `configured scan paths resolve to nothing`, on paths the SAME BINARY resolves correctly in `validate-code-refs` one command over. They named the line. They were right.

`validate_workspace(workspace_root)` takes an ANCHOR — a discovery start, the directory a command was invoked from — and the Round 783 scan-coverage precheck passed that anchor straight to `scan_coverage`. Scan paths are declared relative to `[workspace] root`, which the load already resolved into `loaded.workspace_root`. The rule is not implicit: `cascade::workspace_root_from`'s own doc comment states that every workspace-relative path resolves against the declared root and never the anchor, and names `root = "../../.."` as the case it exists for — which is character-for-character the consumer's config. One call site disobeyed a rule the codebase writes down.

THE DEFECT IS INVISIBLE TO DOGFOOD BY CONSTRUCTION, which is why it survived. This repo's config declares no `[workspace] root`, so anchor and code root are the same directory and the two spellings cannot disagree. The playable consumer's config declares none either. Only a ledger that lives BELOW the code it documents can see it — the shape every external adopter has and no internal test had. The regression fixture is therefore a nested ledger; a fixture where the two agree would pass with the bug in place.

THE MESSAGE WAS THE SECOND HALF OF THE DEFECT, and the consumer generalised Round 831's own observation back at us: `resolve to nothing under <dir>` names no revision and no provenance, so read cold it accuses the reader's `paths` and the obvious repair is to start editing correct entries. They found the cause only by running a second subcommand and seeing it disagree. The failure now states which root it resolved against and where that root came from — `[workspace] root = "..."` in a named file, or the config's own directory when unset. Measured consequence: with the provenance clause in place, the injected original bug is self-contradicting on its face — it says nothing resolves under the toml directory while stating the root is the repo — so the diagnosis that cost three commands now costs one.

THE GUARD IS THE COMPARISON THEY HAD TO MAKE BY HAND. Beside the fixture test, a second test asserts the baseline gate and the citation gate cover the SAME files for one configured path set under a declared root. That is exactly how the consumer diagnosed this, and encoding it means a future divergence in root handling fails here rather than in someone else's CI.

THE FIX IS NECESSARY AND NOT SUFFICIENT, verified rather than assumed. Re-running the fixed binary read-only over all five of their workspaces moves the scan from `nothing` to 1028 Rust sources considered — and they still exit 1, now for a DIFFERENT and legitimate reason: 79 scanned, 949 unscanned across `backends/rust`, `tests/forge` and `sce-build/{tests,examples}`. Round 783's premise — every Rust source is scanned or declared out — was written for a pure-Rust repo and lands differently on a C++ project with Rust sub-trees. Copying their workspace and adding four exclusion globs takes it to exit 0 with 0 unscanned, so the remaining blocker is four lines on their side rather than another round here; that was measured on a copy, not predicted.

`LoadedConfig::root_provenance` states the resolved root AND its origin, so a scan-coverage failure names whether the declared root was honoured or the config's own directory was used. One definition, so two callers cannot describe the same provenance differently

A regression fixture with a NESTED ledger (`[workspace] root = "../.."`), the only shape in which the defect exists, asserting the gate passes and — for non-vacuity — that it actually saw the source file

All five of their enrolled workspaces are rejected by `validate-workspace` with `configured scan paths resolve to nothing`, on paths the SAME BINARY resolves correctly in `validate-code-refs` one command over. They named the line. They were right.

`validate_workspace(workspace_root)` takes an ANCHOR — a discovery start, the directory a command was invoked from — and the Round 783 scan-coverage precheck passed that anchor straight to `scan_coverage`. Scan paths are declared relative to `[workspace] root`, which the load already resolved into `loaded.workspace_root`. The rule is not implicit: `cascade::workspace_root_from`'s own doc comment states that every workspace-relative path resolves against the declared root and never the anchor, and names `root = "../../.."` as the case it exists for — which is character-for-character the consumer's config. THE DEFECT IS INVISIBLE TO DOGFOOD BY CONSTRUCTION, which is why it survived. This repo's config declares no `[workspace] root`, so anchor and code root are the same directory and the two spellings cannot disagree. The playable consumer's config declares none either. Only a ledger that lives BELOW the code it documents can see it — the shape every external adopter has and no internal test had. The regression fixture is therefore a nested ledger; a fixture where the two agree would pass with the bug in place.

THE MESSAGE WAS THE SECOND HALF OF THE DEFECT, and the consumer generalised Round 831's own observation back at us: `resolve to nothing under <dir>` names no revision and no provenance, so read cold it accuses the reader's `paths` and the obvious repair is to start editing correct entries. They found the cause only by running a second subcommand and seeing it disagree. The failure now states which root it resolved against and where that root came from — `[workspace] root = "..."` in a named file, or the config's own directory when unset. Measured consequence: with the provenance clause in place, the injected original bug is self-contradicting on its face — it says nothing resolves under the toml directory while stating the root is the repo — so the diagnosis that cost three commands now costs one.

THE GUARD IS THE COMPARISON THEY HAD TO MAKE BY HAND. Beside the fixture test, a second test asserts the baseline gate and the citation gate cover the SAME files for one configured path set under a declared root. THE FIX IS NECESSARY AND NOT SUFFICIENT, verified rather than assumed.
