Round 836.decision_summary:
R836 (BUILD — a branch that rejoins is not a divergence, and its own record never said so). Lift request 5 from the playable consumer, and the strongest kind: they arrived having already been wrong. Their authoring-floor gate counted forks as divergences, reported `1` mid-story divergence GREEN and with a witness, and the true answer was `0` — every fork it counted rejoined a confluence. `report-fork-tree` carried only the INCOMING half of a merge, so "does this branch come back" required scanning every other branch's `converges` looking for yourself as a parent. That inversion is one line and produces a plausible number when omitted.

THE ASYMMETRY IS STRUCTURAL, WHICH IS WHY IT IS THE KERNEL'S TO CLOSE. A fork is stored on the child and a merge on the confluence — both on the receiving side — so a world-line's own record states where it came FROM and never where it goes. Fork and confluence are both upstream vocabulary (Rounds 438 and 532), so "a branch that rejoins" is a relation between two of our concepts rather than anything about their story. This is the accepted class: not a schema field for derivable data (the refused GAP-005) but a derivation moved into the read, the same call Rounds 617/618 made for `structural_facts` and `branch_owned_density`.

A BOOLEAN WOULD HAVE BEEN WRONG, and they offered one. Their request says `rejoins: true` would suffice with the coordinate merely nice for drawing. Measured on their store against their own 54-scene axis, the fork-to-rejoin spans are 0, 0 and 1 — small today, and already not all zero. Their axis is how much of a playthrough differs, so a branch forking at scene 10 and rejoining at 40 differs for thirty scenes and IS a divergence by their own definition, which a boolean would silently exclude. The coordinate ships because it is what keeps the predicate honest as spans grow, not because a graph screen wants it.

THE INVERSION PRESERVES `at_placed` EXACTLY, which is what makes it safe rather than merely convenient. A converge edge's flag resolves the merge point against the merge PARENT's composed order — and inverted, that parent IS the rejoining branch. So the flag arrives meaning "this coordinate is a node of MY order", which is precisely what measuring a span on one's own axis requires. It is read from the same resolution the converge side reports rather than recomputed, because two spellings of one question drift.

NOT `ForkTreeEdge`. That type's field is `parent`, and a confluence a branch flows into is the opposite direction; reusing it would name one relation with another's word.

I LOOKED FOR A WAY THEIR PREDICATE COULD BE WRONG IN THE OTHER DIRECTION and failed to find one: a "rejoin" into a single-parent confluence would be a rename rather than a reconvergence, but `build_branch_converges` already rejects that — "a confluence merges >= 2 parent world-lines; converges_from names only 1 (a 1-parent merge is just a fork)". The refutation strengthens the request rather than weakening it.

The trunk never appears: `main` is a merge parent in their store and is not a registered branch, so it is never a row of this report. That silence is structural, and is pinned by a test anyway — a consumer inverting by hand DOES surface main and has to remember to drop it, which is exactly the class of thing they asked be nailed down.

SSOT = this entry; the request is the consumer's MNEMOSYNE-LIFT-REQUEST-5 document.
changes_bullets: `ForkTreeRejoin { into, at, at_placed }` and `ForkTreeBranch.rejoins` — the outgoing half of every merge, derived by inverting `converges` across the registry in one pre-pass before the projection walk. Schema untouched; nothing new is stored
The CLI prints one line per rejoin beside the existing converge lines, and the MCP tool description now distinguishes the incoming half from the outgoing one
An unplaced rejoin does NOT push to `unplaced_fork_points` a second time: it is the same edge the converge side already counted, and one declaration gap must not list a branch twice
The engine's fork-tree test fixture states `rejoins: Vec::new()` with the reason — a fixture describes one branch in isolation, and a rejoin is an edge another branch declares
verification_bullets: THE CONSUMER'S OWN TABLE WAS VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY BEFORE ANY CODE WAS WRITTEN, on a read-only copy of their store: 6 forks, 3 rejoining (`braid-letter`, `braid-firstcall`, `braid-ledger`), 3 permanent (all endings). Their correction was right and their original `1` was wrong

THE SHIPPED VERB NOW PRODUCES THAT TABLE: run against the same copy it prints every rejoin, and their axis computed from the JSON alone gives 6 forks / 3 rejoining / 3 true divergences / 0 before the 27-scene midpoint — the number they had to hand-roll an inversion to reach

THREE INJECTIONS, EACH CHANGING BEHAVIOUR: never attaching the derived rejoins; collapsing the rejoin coordinate to a constant (the boolean-equivalent, which fails the span assertion); and leaking `main` in as a world-line row

FIVE ASSERTIONS COVER THE FOUR CASES THEY ASKED BE PINNED plus the span: a rejoining branch names where, a permanent one carries nothing, a CONFLUENCE can itself rejoin (their chained `weave-letter -> weave-firstcall -> weave-ledger` shape) without reading as unplaced or cyclic, the trunk is never a row, and two rejoins at different depths stay distinguishable

carry_forward_bullets: THE SYMMETRIC GAP IS STILL OPEN AND WAS NOT ASKED FOR: a fork is stored on the child, so "what forks off ME" needs the same inversion in the other direction. A graph screen wants both, the consumer requested only one, and the same pre-pass would produce it. Left out deliberately rather than folded in, and worth raising with them rather than guessing

Their stopgap can now be deleted, but only they can do that, and their gate's number does not change — it was already corrected by hand in their own commit

Round 837.decision_summary:
R837 (BUILD — Round 834's design, and filling the table found more than the table was for). Round 833 closed a scan-boundary gap and found the guard that should have prevented it reporting complete for sixty-eight rounds: `every_side_table_detector_is_wired_into_the_aggregate` forces classification of TOP-LEVEL `AtomicStore` fields, and `AtomicSection::ladder` carried four registry refs NESTED inside one. Round 834 measured the unwatched space, killed the obvious fix on the measurement, and chose a source tripwire over a table. This builds it: every place a `String` can live under the store, at any depth, must appear in a classification naming the gate that covers it.

THE DESIGN SAID TWO COVERAGE PATHS. THERE ARE FIVE. Round 834 had found that coverage is not single-source — detectors plus the projection-to-orphan-scan route that guards `superseded_by` — and treated that as the refinement. Filling ninety-four entries found three more: `scan_continuity` guards `pays_off`, `conflicts_with` and `supersedes_in_frame`, each with its own violation variant, and it lives behind a DIFFERENT command than the baseline gate; the publishable mirror fields are guarded by the publishable/audit divergence check rather than any ref scan; and seven places are guarded by the write path with no re-check found at all. A three-variant classification would have forced most of these into a wrong answer, which is the argument for filling a table rather than describing one.

THOSE SEVEN ARE THE ROUND 833 CLASS, INVENTORIED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER. `TypedObject::Fact.id` and `Token.token` are excluded from the registry facets on purpose — the fact ref has staging semantics and resolves in phase 2 against store-union-staged, the token against the predicate's declared vocabulary — and neither is re-checked at any boundary. `ScenePresence.entity`, `SectionSkeleton.parent_section`, `ConfirmationClaim.section_id` (both variants) and `InventoryEntry.section_ref` are refs for which no scan was found. They are recorded as `WritePathOnly` with that wording exactly: a statement about a reading, not a proof. The table's value turns out to be less "it will catch the next one" than "it made me look at all ninety-four".

I WAS WRONG TWICE WHILE FILLING IT, both times by reading instead of measuring, and both times the check saved a false entry. `pays_off` looked unguarded until the continuity violation variant turned up; `publishable_impact_refs` looked unguarded until its divergence check did. That is the third and fourth time this session that a claim derived from reading source did not survive being checked, and it is why the seven remaining unknowns are labelled as unconfirmed rather than as gaps.

THE PARSER REPRODUCED THIS FILE'S OWN FAILURE MODE INSIDE THE FILE. The first version handled struct fields and tuple variants and silently dropped inline enum struct-variants, so `TypedObject::Entity.id` — an entity ref — was missing from the derivation. A completeness guard with a blind spot is precisely what Round 833 was about, so it was fixed rather than noted, and the fix found five more places, four of them refs.

NON-VACUITY IS ENFORCED, because an empty derivation is a subset of any table and would pass while checking nothing. Floors of 80 places and 20 types sit below the measured 94 and far above zero. `include_str!` rather than a runtime read, so a moved source file is a compile error — Round 834's first measurement read two `lib.rs` files, saw a third of the graph, and reported the rest as external primitives.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO, unchanged from the design: it catches an UNCLASSIFIED place, never a MISCLASSIFIED one. A field recorded as not-a-ref that becomes one by convention is still silent. The difference from Round 833 is that a line now exists for someone to change.

SSOT = this entry; the design is Round 834 and claudedocs/nested-ref-completeness-design.md (gitignored).

The parser covers struct fields, tuple variants AND inline enum struct-variants, keyed `Variant.field`, because enums carry refs (`TypedObject::Entity { id }`)
A 94-entry classification naming the covering gate per place: 28 Detector, 4 Projection, 3 Continuity, 5 Divergence, 47 NotARef with a reason, and 7 WritePathOnly
`Coverage` documents each path including what `WritePathOnly` means and does not claim, and a second test asserts the table has no duplicate key and no reasonless NotARef
verification_bullets: FOUR INJECTIONS, EACH CHANGING BEHAVIOUR. The first is the round's point: adding a nested `Option<String>` to `LadderRung` — Round 833's shape exactly, at the depth that stayed silent for sixty-eight rounds — now fails naming the field. Removing a table entry fails as unclassified; adding an entry for a non-existent place fails as stale; restricting the parser to one type collapses the derivation to zero and the non-vacuity floor catches it
THE TABLE WAS BOOTSTRAPPED FROM THE DERIVER, not hand-listed: the test prints the exact lines to paste, and Round 834's hand list had already been shown to drift by a quarter against the same tree
TWO WRONG CLASSIFICATIONS WERE CAUGHT BEFORE LANDING by checking rather than reading — `pays_off` (continuity) and `publishable_impact_refs` (divergence) both looked unguarded and are not
THE PARSER'S OWN BLIND SPOT WAS FOUND AND FIXED mid-build: inline enum struct-variants were dropped, which hid `TypedObject::Entity.id`; the fix added five places, four of them refs

carry_forward_bullets: THE SEVEN `WritePathOnly` PLACES ARE THE NEXT WORK, and each needs confirming by measurement before it is called a gap: `TypedObject::Fact.id`, `TypedObject::Token.token`, `ScenePresence.entity`, `SectionSkeleton.parent_section`, `ConfirmationClaim.section_id` (two variants) and `InventoryEntry.section_ref`. An out-of-band edit to any of them is, by this reading, invisible to every gate

Round 838.decision_summary:
R838 (DESIGN — the ref ids become types, because the cheaper answer was chosen under a frame the owner had already overturned). Round 834 deferred newtyping the ref ids as "structurally the right answer but it touches every ref field and its callers to close one defect", and picked a source tripwire plus a hand classification instead. That parenthetical is a COST argument, and Round 824 established the standing instruction that cost is not the deciding factor. Asked directly whether the built answer was the most long-term-correct one, it is not. This designs the migration to types.

WHAT THE TABLE CANNOT DO, from its own entry: it catches an UNCLASSIFIED place and never a MISCLASSIFIED one, its parser is a line-based reading of Rust rather than a parse, and it is ninety-four lines of artifact maintained beside the types it describes. A type says the same thing in the one place that cannot drift from the value. It also buys something the table can never see: a detector that checks a ref against the WRONG registry is a compile error, where today nothing would notice.

ROUND 837 WAS NOT WASTE AND IS THE PRECONDITION. Round 834 said the table would become the work list for exactly this, and it did — but more than that, filling it is what found the five coverage paths, the seven places with no re-check, and the fact that continuity checks live behind a different command. Starting the migration without that map would have meant touching forty-three ref fields blind.

"SCHEMA 0" IS MEASURED, NOT ASSERTED, on a scratch crate outside the repo. A `#[serde(transparent)]` newtype over String is byte-identical to a bare String in FIELD position and in MAP-KEY position, deserializes as a key, keeps `contains_key("literal")` working through `Borrow<str>`, sorts identically to String, and emits the same JSON Schema in field position with or without `#[schemars(transparent)]`. The map-key result is the one that matters: the registries keyed by id are where a type turns "which registry is this a key of" into something the compiler holds. The ordering result is the one that would have been expensive to miss — a different Ord moves BTreeMap iteration and every deterministic-order claim in the codebase with it.

THE MEASUREMENT ALSO CAUGHT ME COMPARING THE WRONG THING. The first schema comparison included the schema `title`, which differs by fixture name, and reported the newtype as changing the schema. Comparing the `properties` subtree — the part a consumer reads — shows it identical. That is the third time this session a conclusion from a quick reading did not survive being checked properly.

THE COST IS 763 CALL SITES across nine registries, and it is stated rather than softened: sections 225, narrative_facts 152, branches 109, entities 104, frames 72, entity_kinds 52, predicates 38, units 6, parameters 5.

`Borrow<str>` IS ADOPTED, DECIDED BY MEASUREMENT: of 132 `contains_key` calls, 53 pass a literal, and without `Borrow` every one becomes a constructor call that adds noise without adding safety. What this concedes must be said plainly — the safety a newtype buys is in ASSIGNMENT and FIELD position, not in lookup. `fact.frame = entity_id` becomes a compile error; `entities.contains_key(frame.as_str())` does not. Closing lookup too is a typed accessor per registry, not the removal of `Borrow`, and it is follow-on work.

ORDER: smallest first, one or two registries per round, each round compiling and green — `UnitId` + `ParameterId` (11 sites) proves the recipe end-to-end including a map-key change, then ascending to `SectionId` (225) last. Every round verifies store JSON byte-identity against real stores, moves its rows in the Round 837 table, and injects a cross-registry assignment that must fail to compile — the class the table can never catch.

WHAT THIS DELIBERATELY DOES NOT BUY, so the next round does not overclaim: lookup safety (above); WHICH gate covers a field, which stays a hand classification of the five paths; and the seven `WritePathOnly` places, where a type makes it obvious where a check belongs without writing one. And going further than newtypes is WORSE, not better: enforcing registry membership at construction would make a corrupted store fail at LOAD, when `validate-workspace`'s whole job is to enumerate violations rather than die on the first, and would make the phase-2 forward ref structurally impossible.

Round 839.decision_summary:
R839 (BUILD — the first two registry ids become types, and the recipe is proven on eleven call sites before it is applied to two hundred). Round 838 designed the migration from `String` ids to nine typed ones and ordered it smallest-first so the recipe is established where a mistake is cheap. This is `UnitId` and `ParameterId`: the two smallest registries, five and six call sites, carrying every shape the larger ones will hit — a struct field, an enum struct-variant field, two map keys, a nested map key, and a generic helper written against `BTreeMap<String, T>`.

THE PROOF IS THE INJECTION THE OLD GUARD COULD NEVER RUN. Round 837's table catches an unclassified field; it cannot catch a check that resolves a ref against the WRONG registry, because to a `String` every registry looks alike. Two injections now fail to COMPILE: assigning a `ParameterId` into `EdgeCost.unit`, and — the one that matters — `store.units.contains_key(&gate.parameter)`, a detector looking a parameter up in the units registry. Neither was visible to anything before today.

THE CONCEDED LIMIT WAS INJECTED TOO, rather than only written down. `store.units.contains_key(gate.parameter.as_str())` still compiles, exactly as Round 838 said it would: `Borrow<str>` is kept because 53 of 132 `contains_key` calls pass a literal, and the safety a newtype buys is in assignment and field position rather than in lookup. Measuring the limit matters as much as measuring the win — a design note claiming a hole exists is worth less than a run showing it.

ONE MACRO, NOT TWO TYPES. The trait set — `Borrow<str>`, `AsRef<str>`, `Display`, `From<String>`, `From<&str>`, `PartialEq<str>`, `as_str`, `into_inner`, plus the derives and `#[serde(transparent)]` — is declared once and instantiated per id, so nine ids cannot drift into nine slightly different types. Each later round adds one line.

THE BOUNDARY IS EXPLICIT AND ONE-DIRECTIONAL. Wire and CLI DTOs stay `String` and become ids where a value enters the store's vocabulary (`TypedObject::from_exclusive_args`); report rows and the baked engine projection turn ids back into text at the output edge. Both directions are commented at the conversion, because a conversion without a reason reads as an accident.

MEASURED ON REAL DATA, AND THE FIRST ATTEMPT AT THAT WAS VACUOUS. Our own store holds ZERO units, parameters, deltas and edge costs, so round-tripping it proved nothing about any of them — an empty axis reporting clean, the failure this project keeps naming. The playable consumer's store holds 2 units, 2 parameters, 4 delta maps and 28 edge costs; a copy loaded through the new types, written back through a real mutate, and compared field-by-field is identical to the original.

ROUND 837'S TRIPWIRE FIRED, WHICH IS THE DESIGN WORKING. Three rows went stale the moment their fields stopped being `String`. Deleting them would have traded one blind spot for another — the type answers "is this a ref" and never "which gate checks it" — so the derivation was widened to include ref-TYPED places, and the rows stay with their coverage intact. That is Round 838's stated endgame applied one round early, and the `REF_ID_TYPES` list it keys off grows by one line per migration.

Round 840.decision_summary:
R840 (BUILD — an exclusion is a claim, and nothing checked it; plus the two message defects and the pin-floor correction the field report raised). The external spec consumer adopted Round 835 in order, reported all five workspaces green, and sent back four observations. One of them indicts advice this project gave: our reply told them to silence the remaining scan-coverage failure with four exclusion globs, they checked the trees BY HAND before declaring them, and found 55 hand-authored citations those exclusions would have silently un-gated. The advice produced exit 0 and would have cost real coverage. Nothing in the tool could tell the difference.

`scan_exclusions` ASSERTS "no citation this ledger gates lives here" and nothing verified the assertion. This adds the verification, and it is the vacuity Round 783 already refuses seen one level up: that round made a configured-but-EMPTY scan set loud, and this makes a scan set emptied BY DECLARATION loud.

THE AXIS IS "ONLY", NOT "ANY", and that distinction is the whole design. The same consumer's other exclusions are honest and must stay silent: their codegen output cites the same section ids as the templates that generate it, the templates stay scanned, so excluding the output re-checks one string twice. A detector firing on any citation inside an excluded tree would reject that and teach people to stop declaring exclusions at all. So a citation also present in a scanned file loses nothing, and a citation present only in excluded trees is gone — set difference.

THE FIRST VERSION WAS WRONG AND THE CONSUMER'S OWN STORE SHOWED IT. Run against their WIRE ledger it reported fifteen swallowed citations on a CORRECTLY configured workspace: `§10.2`-shaped SCXML citations that the SCXML ledger gates and the wire ledger never could. Their report said "no citation of this namespace lives here" and I had dropped the namespace. Round 841.decision_summary:
R841 (BUILD — `PredicateId`, the third registry id, and the first one whose ref reaches every layer). Migration 2 of 8 in the Round 838 arc. Predicates are the rule a typed claim keys off, so a typo'd predicate silently escapes its rule — the reason Round 681 added the facet in the first place, and the reason this id is worth typing before the larger registries.

THE RECIPE FROM ROUND 839 HELD AND THE SURFACE DID NOT. Units and parameters touched one crate and its fixtures; a predicate ref reaches mnemosyne-core (the claim), mnemosyne-atomic (the registry, the write path, the facet resolver), mnemosyne-validate (continuity rules, edge-cost and edge-guard checks, the typing-proposal path, disclosure), mnemosyne-engine (journal routing, quest filtering, the baked projection) and mnemosyne-cli (argument parsing). Every one of those is a boundary or an interior, and the migration is exactly the work of deciding which.

TWO INJECTIONS, BOTH COMPILE ERRORS, both the class Round 837's table cannot see: a predicate looked up in the units registry, and a `UnitId` assigned into `TypedClaim.predicate`. The second one is the sharper of the two — it is the mistake a tired author actually makes, and before today the compiler had no opinion about it.

THE MACRO GREW ONE IMPL, NOT NINE. `PartialEq<String>` joins the shared trait set because a configured continuity rule holds an owned `String` and comparing it should not need a conversion at the comparison site. Declared once in `ref_id!`, so the three ids that exist and the six that follow cannot diverge on it — which is the whole reason the macro exists.

THE INTERIOR/BOUNDARY LINE GOT ITS FIRST HARD CASE. `TypingCandidatesReport.predicates` is a report field, and Round 839's rule says report rows stay `String`. It is now keyed by `PredicateId` anyway, because it is not a ROW — it is the registry copied verbatim, and the JSON is identical either way. A row that a human reads becomes text; a registry that a machine indexes keeps its key type. Violation payloads (`EdgeCostNotAnEdge.found`, `SuccessionGap.predicate`) went the other way and convert at the edge.

MEASURED ON REAL DATA, and our own store still cannot do it: we hold zero predicates and zero typed facts. The consumer's store holds 14 predicates across 121 typed facts; a copy loaded through the new types, written back through a real mutate, and compared field-by-field is identical. That dependency was named as a carry in Round 839 and is now load-bearing twice.

SELF-REPORT: two injections had to be re-applied. The first mechanical pass rewrote the very line an injection targeted, so the string no longer matched and the injection silently did not apply — the guard that caught it was asserting the match count rather than trusting the replace. A `count == 1` assertion is what separates "the injection proved something" from "the injection was never there".

Round 842.decision_summary:
R842 (BUILD — `EntityKindId`, the first id that four fields across three registries were already sharing without saying so). Migration 3 of 8. `Entity::kind`, `EntityKind::parents`, `Predicate::subject_kind` and `Predicate::object_entity_kind` all hold entity-kind vocabulary, and until today nothing in any of their types said they were the same vocabulary. That is the shape the recipe had not met: the previous two rounds each typed ONE field plus a map key.

THE ROUND'S REAL WORK WAS TWO HELPERS, NOT THE FIELDS. `entity_kind()` returned `Option<&str>` and `is_kind_or_subkind()` took `&str`, so the obvious migration — convert with `.as_str()` at each call — would have typed the fields and then thrown the type away one line later, at the exact place the reachability question is asked. Both are now typed end to end, which is what makes the injections below fail rather than compile.

TWO INJECTIONS, BOTH COMPILE ERRORS: an entity's KIND looked up in the ENTITIES registry (the two maps this file touches most, one line apart), and a `PredicateId` assigned into `Predicate::subject_kind`. The second is the one this round exists for — `Predicate` carries both a predicate id and two entity-kind ids, and before today they were the same type.

THE MACRO GREW `is_empty`, AND THE REASON MATTERS. `Entity::kind` spells "unset" as the empty string and skips it on the wire with `skip_serializing_if = "String::is_empty"`. Without an `is_empty` on the id the attribute breaks, and the path of least resistance would have been to leave that ONE field a `String` — reopening exactly the hole this migration closes, in the field with 167 live values. One method in the shared macro instead.

SELF-REPORT: I DAMAGED UNRELATED CODE WITH AN OVER-BROAD REGEX. A pattern meant to retype `Some("x"), "y"` in two test calls also rewrote five `assert_eq!` message arguments elsewhere in the file, which surfaced as `format argument must be a string literal`. Recovered by diffing against HEAD and restoring each line, then finishing the work with per-line edits driven by the compiler's own error positions. The project rule about regex risking file damage exists for this; I ran the risk and paid it. The remaining passes asked `cargo` for the exact lines and touched only those.

MEASURED ON REAL DATA WITH ONE AXIS ADMITTEDLY EMPTY. The consumer's store has 8 entity kinds and 167 entities, and ALL 167 carry a kind — that leg round-trips through the new types and compares identical. But `EntityKind::parents` holds ZERO entries in every store that exists, so the inheritance leg is covered by injection and unit tests only. Saying "real-data verified" without that sentence would be the empty-axis claim this project keeps catching.

Round 845.decision_summary:
R845 (BUILD — `BranchId`, and the algebra that turned out to be the round). Migration 6 of 8. Four places hold a branch id, which sounded like the small half — and then the world-line ALGEBRA turned out to be where a branch id actually lives.

THE FIELDS WERE FOUR; THE FUNCTIONS WERE THIRTY. `world_membership` and its memo, `forward_confluences`, `is_confluence`, `is_known_world`, `succession_branch_inherits`, `road_lineage`, `road_of`, `lineage_of`, `world_order_composition`, `visibility`, `WorldCtx`, and eight `CanonOrder` accessors all take or return a world-line, and every one of them would have kept compiling with `&str`. That is the Round 843 rule at full scale: `PartialEq<&str>` means the compiler cannot list this work, so it was found by reading the graph of who takes a world.

`query_worlds` HAD TO STOP BORROWING. It returned `Vec<&str>` because `MAIN_BRANCH` is a `&str` const — there is no registry entry to borrow an id from, main being known by construction and never registered. So it now returns owned ids, and the one function that knows main belongs in the world list is the one that constructs it.

TWO INJECTIONS, BOTH COMPILE ERRORS: a world resolved against the FRAMES registry, and a `FrameId` handed to `lineage_of`. Both live in `frame_view(store, order, frame, branch, ...)`, where a frame and a branch sit adjacent in the argument list and were the same type three rounds ago.

SELF-REPORT — A VACUOUS PARITY CHECK, CAUGHT. The first write-differential reported "byte-identical" while both binaries had REJECTED the command (wrong flag names) and written nothing: two untouched copies compare equal. The check that caught it was asserting the branch count actually rose. A parity test that cannot tell "both did the same thing" from "neither did anything" is the empty-axis claim in a new costume.

DIFFERENTIAL ACROSS EVERY WORLD-LINE THE CONSUMER DECLARES: 9 branches, 6 forks, 3 confluences, 662 of 1106 facts off `main`. The pinned `5481f72e` binary and this build agree byte for byte on 15 runs and ~9.7 MB, including a separate manuscript per branch — which is what actually exercises the fork/merge lattice rather than just loading it.

Round 848.decision_summary:
R848 (DESIGN — lookup safety: the measurement Round 838 made is stale, and it decided the other way). Round 838 kept `Borrow<str>` on the ref ids and wrote the reason down honestly: 132 `contains_key` calls, 53 of them string literals, so removing the impl "converts every one into a constructor call that adds noise without adding safety". That was measured BEFORE the migration. Nine ids later it is worth re-measuring rather than inheriting.

WHAT THE REMOVAL ACTUALLY BREAKS, measured by deleting the impl and reading the compiler: 250 errors in the two crates the build reaches, 175 of them in test fixtures and 75 in source; downstream crates unmeasured because atomic fails first. What it does NOT break is the class Round 838 may have been picturing — the String-keyed report and count maps looked up with `id.as_str()` resolve through std's `String: Borrow<str>`, not ours, and are untouched. So the cost is narrower than the old measurement implies and lands almost entirely on fixture literals.

WHY THE ALTERNATIVE IS WORSE, also measured: privatising the registry maps behind typed accessors touches 489 field uses, 221 of which are test `insert` calls. Fixtures construct stores by inserting directly, so privatisation needs an `insert` accessor — and an `insert` accessor restores exactly the hole privatisation was meant to close. Bigger change, weaker guarantee.

WHAT THE REMOVAL BUYS, precisely: `entities.contains_key(unit.as_str())` — the example `ids.rs` has carried as a known hole since Round 838 — stops compiling, everywhere, including in tests. That is the wrong-REGISTRY class. It is not the wrong-VALUE class, and this entry does not claim it is.

A FIND WHILE MEASURING: two import paths (`import_ladders`, `import_epub_excerpts`) look a raw DTO `String` up in the sections registry and never construct a `SectionId` at all. Their existence checks run on untyped text today. The removal forces those conversions into view, which is the boundary discipline the whole arc has been applying everywhere else.

Round 849.decision_summary:
R849 (BUILD — the lookup hole is closed, and the doc that described it is gone). Round 838 wrote the concession into `ids.rs` itself: "the consequence is honest: `entities.contains_key(unit.as_str())` still compiles". Round 848 re-measured and found the trade had inverted. This round deletes `Borrow<str>` from the shared macro, and that sentence no longer describes the code.

ONE IMPL, TWO EFFECTS, AND THEY WERE THE SAME EFFECT. `Borrow<str>` is what let a fixture write `contains_key("gt")` and what let production write `contains_key(unit.as_str())` against the entities map. There was never a version of the impl that granted the first without the second — which is why the honest fix was removal and not a lint.

`stage_registry_entry` WAS THE LAST GENERIC WAY IN. Its bound was `K: Ord + Borrow<str> + From<String>` and its body did `map.get(id: &str)`, so one helper could probe every registry with any string. It now takes `&K`, and the bound that made the hole generic is gone with it.

THE TWO IMPORT PATHS ROUND 848 FOUND ARE FIXED PROPERLY, not incidentally. `import_content_excerpts`, `import_ladders` and `import_epub_excerpts` looked a wire-DTO `String` up in the sections registry and never constructed a `SectionId`. The removal forced a conversion; the conversion is placed at a named boundary with its reason, rather than inlined at the lookup where the next reader would not see it.

A TRAIT REMOVAL SHOULD CHANGE NO BEHAVIOUR, so that is the thing to check rather than assume: eight reports across the consumer store and ours, byte-identical against the pinned `5481f72e` binary, exit codes included.

WHAT IS LEFT, stated because it is the only piece of this axis still open: `fact_ref_resolves(store, facet, value: &str)` survived by constructing the id per arm. One function, every facet, one untyped string. Round 848 predicted exactly that and it happened exactly that way.

Round 850.decision_summary:
R850 (BUILD — the pair was the last generic mismatch, and it is now a type). Round 849 closed the lookup hole and named exactly one thing it could not close: `fact_ref_resolves(store, facet, value: &str)` survived the removal of `Borrow<str>` by constructing the id inside each arm, so `(FactRefFacet::Frame, some_section_id)` still type-checked. That prediction was correct and this round acts on it.

THE FIX IS THE OBVIOUS ONE AND IT KEEPS WHAT ROUND 688 BOUGHT. Splitting the resolver per facet would have made the mismatch unrepresentable and destroyed the single-home property the function exists for — the write path and the detector share it precisely so they cannot disagree about what "resolves" means. Carrying the typed id in the variant gets both: one enumeration, one resolver, and a slot that cannot be handed the wrong registry's id.

TWO INJECTIONS, BOTH COMPILE ERRORS, and the first is verbatim the case Round 849 wrote down as still open: the enumerator giving the FRAME slot a section id.

SELF-REPORT — I RAN A VACUOUS DIFFERENTIAL AND NO ASSERTION CAUGHT IT. The corrupted-store check compared `validate-workspace` output from both binaries: 542 bytes, identical, exit 1 — and meaningless, because the R783 scan-coverage precheck refuses that copy before the detector runs. Both binaries were agreeing about a refusal, not about the corruption. Reading the payload is what caught it; the comparison alone would have passed. Re-run through `validate-continuity`, both binaries name the same fact and the same phantom frame. Third vacuous check this session, and the first of a shape the Round 845 count-assertion cannot see.

Round 852.decision_summary:
R852 (DEBT — Round 851 introduced this generator's first hash map, and the crate's oldest promise is that an unchanged store emits a byte-identical file). Found by re-reading Round 851 rather than by anything failing, which is the only way this one could have been found: it does not fail.

WHAT THE HAZARD IS. `LinePool` holds a `Vec` for the emission order and a `HashMap` for the lookup, and that separation is what keeps the artifact stable. `HashMap` iteration is SEEDED PER PROCESS. A later round that emits the pool from the map — the obvious simplification, since the map already holds every distinct line — produces an artifact that is completely correct and whose bytes differ on every build. Measured with exactly that change in place: three renders of one unchanged consumer store in three processes gave three different sha256s, and eleven of twelve tests stayed green, including the real-store differential against the previous generator.

WHY IT LANDS ON THE CONSUMER'S FRESHEST FIX. Their lift request 6 closed with a defect they claimed as their own: `build-store.sh` rewrites the sidecar, cargo watches mtime, and an unchanged store rebuilt anyway. They shipped the fix the same day by hashing the file's CONTENT. A generator that emitted different bytes for the same store would defeat that fix in a way that reads as their bug — the store is unchanged, the hash differs, so the hash must be wrong.

THE GATE ASSERTS THE SEPARATION FROM OUTSIDE. Three world-lines whose distinct ids are neither sorted nor reverse-sorted in first-seen order, and the emitted pool must match the walk. That refuses a `BTreeMap` reached for as readily as a `HashMap`: what is gated is that the order comes from `rendered`, not that it happens to be reproducible.

THE HONEST SHAPE OF THIS ROUND. Nothing was broken and nothing is fixed. What changed is that the invariant Round 851 depended on is now enforced instead of merely observed, and the doc on the field says which of the two structures owns the order. This is the class of defect the tests cannot find, so the tests had to be told about it.

The fixture defeats a `BTreeMap` reached for as well as a `HashMap`: any emission order that is not `LinePool::rendered`'s fails, not merely the seeded one

Round 853.decision_summary:
R853 (DESIGN — the owner asked whether Round 851 chose the correct method with cost ignored, and two of the three answers are self-corrections). The question is the one that produced Round 838, and it earns the same kind of answer: the decision was right, one stated reason was wrong, and one deferral was a cost judgment wearing a scope judgment's clothes.

CORRECTION ONE — THE POOL KEY IS RIGHT AND ITS STATED REASON IS NOT. Round 851 refused the consumer's fact-id key because "`mode` is a per-telling disclosure and nothing forbids one world stating what another hints". A `MapLocator` resolves `mode` and `object` per (telling, fact); a projection carries exactly one telling; a world decides only WHICH facts it sees, never how they surface. So a fact cannot carry two payloads, the 882-of-882 measurement is a consequence rather than luck, and the fact-id key WOULD have been correct against today's upstream. The decision survives on a reason Round 851 did not give: the rendered-text key is LOCALLY exact, while the fact-id key would make this generator depend on a property of a type in another crate that nothing at this boundary can check and one added field would break silently. Both keys pool to the same 882, so the general one is free.

CORRECTION TWO — THE DEFERRAL WAS A COST JUDGMENT. Round 851's carry said the runtime cross product is "NOT closed" and that closing it "changes `lines()` from a slice to a sequence and is a consumer API break". Three things are wrong with that sentence. It makes the consumer's request scope the arbiter of what is correct. It calls a materialised read model an unclosed defect, when materialising answers is what a read model is for. And the alternative it names does not even work: positions inside the projection shrink each entry roughly fiftyfold and leave the cross product exactly where it was.

WHAT THE REAL ALTERNATIVE IS, AND THAT IT COSTS NO API. The store's Round 438 shared history means a fork child INHERITS its ancestor's facts up to the fork point, so a child's pre-fork spots are derived rather than authored. A projection can therefore store a spot only where it DIFFERS from what its fork parent answers, and `lines(world, section)` walks up the chain to the owner — returning that world's `&[Line]`, so the API break named as the blocker does not exist. Measured exact: 0 disagreements over 6,607 pre-fork comparisons across three stores, against 84 to 26,484 spots that do differ after the fork. It would store 1,238 lines against 4,654 on the consumer's real store.

AND WHY IT IS NOT BUILT. The cost lands on the read path of a running game: lookup depth 20, mean 7.29, on a twenty-deep chain against one hash lookup today. The consumer's design is a FAN rather than a chain, and at 500 siblings only 21% of spots inherit — the delta shares along the chain and cannot see sibling identity, which is what a fan repeats. Round 854.decision_summary:
R854 (BUILD — the exclusion-integrity axis answered a whole-tree question from a Rust-only file set, and was therefore wrong in BOTH directions). Reported from the field by the external spec consumer, who migrated their codegen templates to the sigil citation form and watched Round 840 name seven Appendix-D sections as reachable only from an excluded tree. Every one of those seven IS cited in a scanned path and IS bound there. The report was false as stated, and it cost them real coverage: with no truthful prose form available for an Appendix D subsection, and 15506 generated citations as the alternative, they dropped the citation from the templates to get the gate green.

THE MECHANISM IS ONE FILTER. `scan_coverage` filtered all three of its sets to `.rs`, and `swallowed_citations` consumes two of them. The citation gate itself walks the configured paths with no extension filter at all — it reads C++ headers, Jinja templates, whatever a consumer enrols. So the detector's "still seen" side was a Rust-only view of a language-agnostic gate, and the doc comment stated the overclaim in as many words: cited nowhere the gate reads. Their control isolates it exactly: two Appendix-D sections stayed quiet under the identical setup, and the only thing separating those two from the seven is that they are additionally cited in a scanned RUST tree.

BOTH DIRECTIONS, FROM THE SAME FILTER, AND THE SECOND IS WORSE. False positive: cited in scanned C++ and in an excluded copy, reported as lost when the gate still reads it. False negative: cited ONLY in an excluded non-Rust file, which is precisely the coverage loss this axis exists to catch, and the axis could not see the file at all. A swallowed citation then reads as clean. The consumer reported the direction that shouted at them; the silent direction was ours to find.

A THIRD SYMPTOM, unreported and also live: `stale_exclusions` called an exclusion stale whenever it matched nothing in Rust, and a stale exclusion is a reject. A C++ consumer excluding a C++ tree was told to delete the declaration that was doing the work.

THE RUST-ONLY AXIS STAYS, AND IS NOW SAID OUT LOUD. Round 783 asks whether every Rust source is scanned or declared, and a language-agnostic version of that question would demand a declaration for every markdown and manifest file in the tree. So the counts stay Rust and the file SETS go language-agnostic, both derived from one walk so the two views cannot disagree about a file. The Round 840 question and the Round 783 question are different questions over the same tree, and only one of them is about Rust.

OUR OWN FIXTURES COULD NOT HAVE FOUND THIS, and one of them was already asserting the property while proving nothing. Every scan path in this repo held Rust only, so the filter was invisible by construction — and the Round 835 test that compares what the baseline gate covers against what the citation gate walks passed for exactly that reason: the two numbers were equal because there was no non-Rust file to disagree about. The fixture is now mixed-language, and that assertion is load-bearing for the first time.

THE CONSUMER'S PIN DECISION IS RIGHT AND ITS STATED RISK IS NOT. They are holding at the Round 840 revision because none of their three items had landed, which was true. But they cited a store-migration risk, and there is none in that range: `CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` is 44 at both ends and no migration was added, so the bump they were weighing is migration-free. The gain was zero; the risk was zero too.

SSOT = this entry; their report is claudedocs/mnemosyne-field-report-r840-rust-only-scope.md in the consumer's tree.

Round 855.decision_summary:
R855 (BUILD — the symbol axis says which files it cannot reach, and reaches `.c` now). The second half of the field report Round 854 answered. The consumer's item was small and their diagnosis of the class was not: `lang_for_file` had no `.c` arm, so enrolling their C runtime — 226 files, 139 hand-authored citations — would have given the `.h` files symbol-level binding and the `.c` files beside them file-level, silently, under `severity_binding = reject`. They named the shape too: adding the arm is the small fix, and making an unreachable file LOUD is the one that closes the class.

THE OMISSION WAS VISIBLE IN THE SAME FILE. `comment_syntax_for`, one screen from `lang_for_file`, has always known `.c` — so the comment axis read those files while the symbol axis did not know what language they were. That is an omitted arm, not a considered scope, and the same disagreement covered case: one function lowercased the extension and the other did not, so a `.H` header was read by one and skipped by the other. The extension list is now a TABLE, the language set is DERIVED from it, and both functions agree about case.

Round 856.decision_summary:
R856 (BUILD — the third site of the class, and a sweep that found the fourth). Round 854 closed the exclusion axis and Round 855 the symbol axis; both were reported from the field. This closes the one our own reading found: the fact and entity citation axis walked the configured paths and then filtered to `.rs`, and unlike the other two its doc comment did not even admit the filter — it said the scan boundary is "inherited, not invented", which was true of the directory rule it was describing and false of the file rule sitting three lines below it.

THE CLAIM IT PUBLISHES IS A COVERAGE CLAIM. `facts_cited` of `facts_total`, over `files_scanned`, reads as "these facts are cited somewhere in the code". Under a Rust-only universe that number is understated for any consumer whose citations live elsewhere, silently, and the axis prints it every run.

MEASURED ON THE STORE THIS AXIS WAS BUILT FOR, and the finding is not a hypothetical: the first playable consumer keeps its scenario files as `.scxml`, and those files carry HAND-AUTHORED fact citations in prose — `f-bell-counts`, `f-knots-are-sins`, `f-unconfessed-stays-bound`, `f-tide-slips`. The axis was blank in exactly the files where that author writes fact citations by hand. Files scanned 53 to 70, citing files 14 to 20, fact sites 37 to 49, distinct facts cited 23 to 28. Shape matches that name nothing in the store: 1 before, 1 after — ZERO new noise from the seventeen non-Rust files, so the widening bought coverage without buying a false-positive list.

NOISE STAYS BOUNDED BY WHAT WAS ALREADY THERE, not by an extension list: the namespace prefixes are DERIVED from the store's own key space and need two ids to exist at all, and the axis is advisory, so a shape match in data costs a printed line and never a red gate. That is the Round 819 design doing its job — this round did not weaken it, it stopped narrowing the universe underneath it.

THEN THE SWEEP, because fixing the third instance of a class and stopping is what the consumer's own field report warned about. Every extension-dependent branch in the citation source, read: the `is_rust` in `scan_coverage` is the documented Round 783 axis, the two `lang_for_file` sites are the symbol axis Round 855 made loud, and the last one was `comment_syntax_for`. `comment_only = true` reads comments only where a comment syntax is KNOWN and the whole text everywhere else, so the knob means two different things depending on the extension and nothing said which files got which. It is load-bearing in both directions — it is why the consumer's prose fact citations are read at all, and it is also why a citation-shaped token in a data file counts as a citation under a reject-level severity.

REPORTED, NOT CHANGED. Making unknown syntax scan nothing would have dropped the very prose citations this round just measured as real coverage. So `validate-code-refs` now prints, every run, how many scanned files have no known comment syntax and under which extensions — 12 of 70 on the consumer's tree, and all nine of its `.scxml` scenario files are in that count.

Round 857.decision_summary:
R857 (BUILD — the quest layer is consumable, and finding that out took being the consumer). The owner's cadence choice was the pinion side of the R568/R569 quest graph: is the fact→quest projection something a narrative runtime can actually wire against. So this round ran it the way that runtime would — against the first playable consumer's real store, asking the questions a quest layer asks — rather than reading the code and pronouncing.

THE FIRST COMMAND LIED, AND IT LIED WITH NUMBERS. `report-quest-graph --telling player` on that store printed 22 quests over 7 worlds with a per-world state column for each, `unresolved_quests: []`, and no complaint of any kind. Underneath, the manuscript walk had visited ZERO scenes in all 7 worlds. Run against the store's declared canon order the same command reports 117 done where the silent run reported 65, and 12 giver locators where it reported none. Every figure was wrong and every figure looked authoritative.

THE CAUSE IS AN OPTIONAL INPUT WITH A DEGENERATE DEFAULT. `resolve_canon_order_file` composes an EMPTY order when there is neither a `--order` flag nor a `[continuity].canon_order_path`, and a world-scoped read over an empty order is empty in every world. `playthrough_manuscript` already refuses a typo'd world — its own comment says a typo "must not read as an empty manuscript" — and a typo'd telling. This was the third and largest source of exactly that emptiness, and it was the unguarded one.

★THE FIRST FIX WAS WRONG AND THIS REPO'S OWN TESTS SAID SO. I put the refusal inside `playthrough_manuscript` and `payoff_coverage`, which broke `authoring_frontier` — the R596 surface whose PURPOSE is to name every scene that is not yet ordered, ratified by a test called `no_declared_order_is_not_an_incomplete_order`. An undeclared order is a defect for one question and the SUBJECT of another, and the guard belongs to the question, not to the math. So the rule sits in `world_scoped_inputs`, the shared preamble of the four report wrappers that serve a per-world question, and the frontier keeps calling the permissive projections directly.

WHAT THE CONSUMER ACTUALLY GETS, measured with the order declared: 22 quests, all giving-bound, 10 carrying prerequisites, `unresolved_quests` empty; 12 giver locators = 3 quests across 4 world-lines. That 3-of-22 is CORRECT and it names the authoring act a runtime depends on: exactly 3 of the 22 giving facts are disclosed in the `player` telling, the other 19 default to withhold, and R643 derives the locator seat from the fact's own canon coordinate — so putting a quest on the map is "disclose its giving fact in this telling", NOT "author a surface". No new substrate is needed for the quest layer; the pull R562 registered is satisfied.

AND ONE HONEST HOLE IN THE STATE AXIS: across 22 quests × 7 worlds, the real store yields 117 done and 37 unknown and ZERO open. Four world-lines complete every quest; the three ending-lines complete some. That is faithful — these are finished manuscripts, not save-states — but it means the `open` verdict, the one a quest LOG would render, has no real-data instance anywhere. A consumer building an active-quest panel has nothing to test against yet.

Round 858.decision_summary:
R858 (DEBT, code 0 — Round 840's positive control was four false positives, and the audit trail says otherwise until this entry). The external spec consumer adopted R854 and R855, bumped its pin to `5bbf4d17`, and opened its report by withdrawing the evidence it had given us a round earlier. That withdrawal invalidates a claim in OUR ledger, so this entry states the correction in prose — the ledger is append-only and R840's own text cannot be edited.

WHAT R840 CLAIMS. Its decision summary says the fixed detector "takes it to zero on their fixed config and to exactly four — `wire-W1`, `W3`, `W4`, `W5` — on the pre-fix config", and its verification bullet reports that same four as measured on the consumer's own wire ledger. It was presented as the positive control: a detector only ever seen returning 0 proves nothing, so we forced it non-zero before trusting the 0.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE. Those four sections are cited in SCANNED C++ all along, so nothing was ever swallowed and the correct answer for that config is 0. VERIFIED HERE, not taken on report: `§wire-W1` is cited in 3 files under the wire ledger's scanned C++ trees, `W3` in 5, `W4` in 7, `W5` in 3 — the consumer's own counts, reproduced by grep against their tree read-only. Under the Rust-only universe R854 removed, those citations were invisible, so excluding the only Rust tree made all four read as excluded-only. The control fired BECAUSE of the defect it was meant to rule out.

★AND THE HAND CHECK WAS NOT A SECOND OPINION. R840 leaned on the four matching what the consumer "found by hand", and treated the agreement as corroboration. It was not: their hand analysis looked at the same Rust-only surface the tool did, so the two measurements shared one blind spot and agreed for one reason. A hand check and a tool that share a blind spot are ONE measurement, not two — and this project has now been fooled by that shape twice, since R854's vacuous R835 test also agreed with the property it was asserting.

THE REPLACEMENT CONTROL, REPRODUCED INDEPENDENTLY. Move the consumer's C++ `parsing` trees from `paths` into `scan_exclusions` and two sections become C++-excluded-only. Our binary on a copy of their tree reports exactly that: `wire-W2` at `sce/include/parsing/Diagnostic.h:66` over 7 files, and `wire-W4.5` at `IXMLDocument.h:45` over 17 files. At the pre-R854 revision the same config is SILENT. That is the false-negative direction R854 named — the one they had not reported and we had to find by reading — reproduced on real data, in the direction that stays quiet.

THE RULE, THEIRS, AND WORTH KEEPING VERBATIM: forcing a detector to return non-zero is not enough — ask WHAT MAKES IT non-zero, because if that mechanism is the broken one, the control is validating the defect.

FIELD ADOPTION, RECORDED. 20 of 20 validate commands green at `5bbf4d17` with the pin ENFORCED, so R855's new startup refusal of a resolver key that maps no extension is the no-op we predicted for a `cpp`+`rust` config. Gate-file counts match ours where their trees have not moved (mesh 57, scxml 430, wire 288); synth and bytesguard read 1684 against our 946 because they regenerated their Kotlin trees between the two runs, which the symbol-axis line shows as `kt` citing files 2 → 96 and out-of-reach 282 → 376. Their mesh ledger, the one whose still-seen side read ZERO files before R854, is the one they name as the silent bite.

AND THE NUMBER R855 ASKED FOR. They enrolled the C11 runtime — 14 files, 26 prose citations migrated, 20 bound, six at symbol level. The scxml symbol axis went from `cpp=323 (144 citing)` to `cpp=336 (156 citing)`: thirteen files and twelve citing files newly reach a resolver, on real sources, with `symbol_mismatch = 0` across all five ledgers. The `.c` arm works in the field.

★"LOUD, NOT REJECT" WAS VALIDATED BY THE CASE IT WAS CHOSEN FOR. Their `backends/c/runtime/CMakeLists.txt` cites two sections in build comments; both are gated for existence and bound file-level, and no symbol axis can reach a CMake comment. They kept the citations and let the line name the gap. As a reject, R855 would have forced them to choose between deleting a true citation and shipping red — which is exactly the trade the advisory-not-gate decision existed to avoid, now confirmed by a consumer rather than argued by us.

Round 859.decision_summary:
R859 (DEBT — every report verb died at exit 101 when its reader stopped early, and Round 857 recorded that as a carry rather than paying it). The debt was found by being the consumer: `report-quest-graph … | head -3` exits 101 with `failed printing to stdout: Broken pipe (os error 32)`, and in R857 I first read that 101 as a defect in the report I was measuring. Every consumer pipes a long report into `head` or a pager, so this was on every report verb, not on one.

THE CAUSE IS IN THE RUNTIME, NOT IN THE REPORTS. Rust installs `SIG_IGN` for `SIGPIPE` before `main`, so a write to a closed pipe returns `EPIPE` instead of terminating the process, and `println!` unwraps that error. Nothing in this codebase asked for that; it is the default every Rust binary starts with, and it is wrong for a CLI whose whole job is printing.

ONE SITE, NOT A PRINT HELPER. `main`'s first statement restores the default disposition, so the process ends by signal 13 the way `cat` and `grep` do. The alternative — an `EPIPE`-aware print wrapper — would have to be adopted by every one of the hundreds of `println!` calls here and in the ops/query crates, and the next one added would reopen the hole. A disposition covers writes that do not exist yet; a helper covers the ones someone remembered.

THE UNSTABLE ROUTE WAS TRIED FIRST AND IS NOT AVAILABLE: `#[unix_sigpipe = "sig_dfl"]` does not compile on stable 1.94 under either spelling. So the fix is one `libc::signal` call, and `libc` becomes a unix-gated dependency of the CLI — no new vendored crate (0.2.186 was already in `Cargo.lock` through the dev-dependency chain), one declared edge.

WHY ONLY THIS BINARY. `mnemosyne-mcp` speaks a stdio protocol and `mnemosyne-server` speaks HTTP; terminating mid-write there truncates a frame a peer is parsing. A CLI report is the case where dying like `cat` IS correct — the reader asked to stop. Neither of the other binaries is touched.

SAFETY IS A POSITION, NOT A HOPE. The call is sound at exactly that point: `main`'s first statement, before any output, in a binary that spawns no thread. The disposition then governs every pipe the process writes, which is only its own stdout and stderr — it opens no socket (verified: zero matches for any socket or async runtime type in the CLI), and its one child, `git log` read through `Command::output`, is never written to. All three facts were checked rather than assumed, because a process-wide signal change is only as narrow as the process is.

★AND THE FIX NARROWS THE PIPE CASE ONLY, WHICH IS THE HALF THAT COULD HAVE GONE WRONG. Making write failures silent would be a worse defect than the panic: a report that gets truncated by a full disk must say so. Measured against `/dev/full`, which fails every write with `ENOSPC`: the panic and the 101 both stay. That control is now a permanent test, compile-gated to Linux rather than skipped at run time — a runtime skip would read as a pass on a platform where the control never ran.

Round 859.publishable_decision_summary:
R859 (DEBT — every report verb died at exit 101 when its reader stopped early, and Round 857 recorded that as a carry rather than paying it). The debt was found by being the consumer: `report-quest-graph … | head -3` exits 101 with `failed printing to stdout: Broken pipe (os error 32)`, and in R857 I first read that 101 as a defect in the report I was measuring. Every consumer pipes a long report into `head` or a pager, so this was on every report verb, not on one.

THE CAUSE IS IN THE RUNTIME, NOT IN THE REPORTS. Rust installs `SIG_IGN` for `SIGPIPE` before `main`, so a write to a closed pipe returns `EPIPE` instead of terminating the process, and `println!` unwraps that error. Nothing in this codebase asked for that; it is the default every Rust binary starts with, and it is wrong for a CLI whose whole job is printing.

ONE SITE, NOT A PRINT HELPER. `main`'s first statement restores the default disposition, so the process ends by signal 13 the way `cat` and `grep` do. The alternative — an `EPIPE`-aware print wrapper — would have to be adopted by every one of the hundreds of `println!` calls here and in the ops/query crates, and the next one added would reopen the hole. A disposition covers writes that do not exist yet; a helper covers the ones someone remembered.

THE UNSTABLE ROUTE WAS TRIED FIRST AND IS NOT AVAILABLE: `#[unix_sigpipe = "sig_dfl"]` does not compile on stable 1.94 under either spelling. So the fix is one `libc::signal` call, and `libc` becomes a unix-gated dependency of the CLI — no new vendored crate (0.2.186 was already in `Cargo.lock` through the dev-dependency chain), one declared edge.

WHY ONLY THIS BINARY. `mnemosyne-mcp` speaks a stdio protocol and `mnemosyne-server` speaks HTTP; terminating mid-write there truncates a frame a peer is parsing. A CLI report is the case where dying like `cat` IS correct — the reader asked to stop. Neither of the other binaries is touched.

SAFETY IS A POSITION, NOT A HOPE. The call is sound at exactly that point: `main`'s first statement, before any output, in a binary that spawns no thread. The disposition then governs every pipe the process writes, which is only its own stdout and stderr — it opens no socket (verified: zero matches for any socket or async runtime type in the CLI), and its one child, `git log` read through `Command::output`, is never written to. All three facts were checked rather than assumed, because a process-wide signal change is only as narrow as the process is.

Making write failures silent would be a worse defect than the panic: a report that gets truncated by a full disk must say so. Measured against `/dev/full`, which fails every write with `ENOSPC`: the panic and the 101 both stay. Their ledgers ARE quiet, but for the opposite reason to the one I gave: not "no tokens" but tokens present, resolving, and already bound. That changes the risk description — the exposure is not dormant, it is active and handled, and the next fixture carrying a NON-resolving token fails immediately rather than someday. No axis ever saw them. The count named the wrong files and inflated the exposure, and it did so in the line whose whole purpose is to say which files the gate reads whole. The split is now MEASURED — the same `read_to_string` question the gate asks, asked of the same file — rather than inferred from an extension, and the unreadable ones get their own advisory because a configured path full of build output is a real finding about the config.

The fix here excludes a binary artifact by the UTF-8 property it inherently lacks, not by a directory name on a skip list — and this codebase's every hand list has drifted (R777, R783). Adding `build/` to the walk's skip names was considered and REFUSED: `build` is a legitimate source directory name, and a false negative there hides real citations, which is worse than the noise it removes.

Round 861.decision_summary:
R861 (DEBT — a delegation instruction read by the delegate has a floor, and three of the four things standing on that floor were wrong). Filed by the first playable consumer, whose commits and pushes were all blocked after they adopted `[tool] pin`: a concurrent session put an older binary back on PATH sixty-five minutes later, and every command that reads a config then told them their config was wrong.

WHAT WAS ALREADY OURS, so the round does not re-decide it. Round 828 documented the parse trap, including the circularity that a pin naming a pre-`[tool]` revision names the one binary that cannot read it, and measured it on two real consumer binaries — one of them the very build in this report. Round 840 corrected the floor to "the newest key in your file". Neither is superseded here.

WHAT IS NEW IS THAT THE FLOOR IS A STANDING PROPERTY, NOT AN ADOPTION STEP. Round 828's remedy is an ordering — upgrade, install, confirm `--version`, then declare — and this consumer followed it. The older binary arrived after the ordering was finished, which no ordering discipline reaches. So the guidance now says to resolve the tool by something that names one revision, because a name on PATH is whatever was installed last.

THE ESCAPE HATCH WAS DOCUMENTED AS UNCONDITIONAL AND HAS A FLOOR OF ITS OWN. `MNEMOSYNE_PIN_SKIP` is read inside `enforce_tool_pin`, which runs only after `parse_config` has returned, so a build that cannot parse the file never reaches the waiver. Measured on the reported binary: the waived run and the unwaived run produce the identical parse error. An escape hatch below the floor it exists to escape is not one, and the guide said otherwise.

THE DIAGNOSTIC THEY ASKED FOR CANNOT EXIST IN THE FORM THEY ASKED FOR IT. Their recommendation was a special message for when the unknown top-level key is `tool`; that message could only ever ship inside a build that already knows `tool`, and such a build never emits "unknown field `tool`". It would be dead the day it landed. The live form is the general one, and this round builds that: any unknown key now carries this build's own revision and the rule that a config is readable only by a Mnemosyne at or after the revision that introduced its newest key. It cannot help the binary in the report — a build too old to know a key is also too old to carry the sentence explaining it — so it is written for the key that does not exist yet.

THE REPORT'S ONE FACTUAL ERROR, AND THE REAL DEFECT UNDERNEATH IT. They wrote that nothing checks whether the build at `$MN_ROOT/<pin>/bin` is the revision that path names. Round 832's loop guard does check, and it was measured doing so: with a current build installed at a mis-named path, the refusal names the broken install and gives the reinstall line. But the check is performed BY THE REPLACEMENT, and the class of replacement that most needs checking is the one least able to check. With a pre-`[tool]` build at that same path the only message is `mnemosyne.toml parse failed` — the same misdirection this whole report is about, emitted from inside the mechanism meant to prevent it. So the check moves BEFORE the hand-off: the switch asks the installed build which revision it is, and refuses when the answer is a different revision or is missing.

ASKING FIRST NEEDED A QUESTION EVERY BUILD ANSWERS, AND ONE BINARY DID NOT. `--version` is that question — Round 286 called it a universal surface — and it is also the ONLY command that survives on a build too old to parse the workspace config, which is measured here rather than assumed. `mnemosyne-render` never had one. That cost nothing while a binary's revision was something only a human read; it stopped costing nothing the moment another binary began asking. The test derives the binary set from cargo, so the next binary owes an answer the day it exists.

ROUND 840 FIXED A DOUBLED SUBJECT AND CREATED ONE. It gave `PinRefusal::Different` a subject of its own so the refusal would stop repeating the pin; the sibling caller in `switch_to_pinned` supplies a subject too, so every switchable refusal has since printed `note: this build this build is ...`. Found by reading the note during this round's own measurements, and reported by nobody.

WHAT IS NOT BUILT, AND WHY. Their recommendation (B) — a permanently ignored namespace so a future launcher directive cannot poison parsing — is REFUSED as stated: it converts a loud refusal into a silent unenforced run, which is precisely the outcome Rounds 825 and 826 chose fail-closed to avoid, and a top-level catch-all would also destroy the typo detection Round 828 names as deliberate. Their recommendation (A) — a separate launcher whose contract is frozen — is the only one of the three that reaches the reported incident, and it is a design question rather than an edit. It is Round 862.

Round 861.publishable_decision_summary:
R861 (DEBT — a delegation instruction read by the delegate has a floor, and three of the four things standing on that floor were wrong). Filed by the first playable consumer, whose commits and pushes were all blocked after they adopted `[tool] pin`: a concurrent session put an older binary back on PATH sixty-five minutes later, and every command that reads a config then told them their config was wrong.

WHAT WAS ALREADY OURS, so the round does not re-decide it. Round 828 documented the parse trap, including the circularity that a pin naming a pre-`[tool]` revision names the one binary that cannot read it, and measured it on two real consumer binaries — one of them the very build in this report. Round 840 corrected the floor to "the newest key in your file". Neither is superseded here.

WHAT IS NEW IS THAT THE FLOOR IS A STANDING PROPERTY, NOT AN ADOPTION STEP. Round 828's remedy is an ordering — upgrade, install, confirm `--version`, then declare — and this consumer followed it. The older binary arrived after the ordering was finished, which no ordering discipline reaches. So the guidance now says to resolve the tool by something that names one revision, because a name on PATH is whatever was installed last.

THE ESCAPE HATCH WAS DOCUMENTED AS UNCONDITIONAL AND HAS A FLOOR OF ITS OWN. `MNEMOSYNE_PIN_SKIP` is read inside `enforce_tool_pin`, which runs only after `parse_config` has returned, so a build that cannot parse the file never reaches the waiver. Measured on the reported binary: the waived run and the unwaived run produce the identical parse error. An escape hatch below the floor it exists to escape is not one, and the guide said otherwise.

THE DIAGNOSTIC THEY ASKED FOR CANNOT EXIST IN THE FORM THEY ASKED FOR IT. Their recommendation was a special message for when the unknown top-level key is `tool`; that message could only ever ship inside a build that already knows `tool`, and such a build never emits "unknown field `tool`". It would be dead the day it landed. The live form is the general one, and this round builds that: any unknown key now carries this build's own revision and the rule that a config is readable only by a Mnemosyne at or after the revision that introduced its newest key. It cannot help the binary in the report — a build too old to know a key is also too old to carry the sentence explaining it — so it is written for the key that does not exist yet.

THE REPORT'S ONE FACTUAL ERROR, AND THE REAL DEFECT UNDERNEATH IT. They wrote that nothing checks whether the build at `$MN_ROOT/<pin>/bin` is the revision that path names. Round 832's loop guard does check, and it was measured doing so: with a current build installed at a mis-named path, the refusal names the broken install and gives the reinstall line. But the check is performed BY THE REPLACEMENT, and the class of replacement that most needs checking is the one least able to check. With a pre-`[tool]` build at that same path the only message is `mnemosyne.toml parse failed` — the same misdirection this whole report is about, emitted from inside the mechanism meant to prevent it. So the check moves BEFORE the hand-off: the switch asks the installed build which revision it is, and refuses when the answer is a different revision or is missing.

ASKING FIRST NEEDED A QUESTION EVERY BUILD ANSWERS, AND ONE BINARY DID NOT. `--version` is that question — Round 286 called it a universal surface — and it is also the ONLY command that survives on a build too old to parse the workspace config, which is measured here rather than assumed. `mnemosyne-render` never had one. That cost nothing while a binary's revision was something only a human read; it stopped costing nothing the moment another binary began asking. The test derives the binary set from cargo, so the next binary owes an answer the day it exists.

ROUND 840 FIXED A DOUBLED SUBJECT AND CREATED ONE. It gave `PinRefusal::Different` a subject of its own so the refusal would stop repeating the pin; the sibling caller in `switch_to_pinned` supplies a subject too, so every switchable refusal has since printed `note: this build this build is ...`. Found by reading the note during this round's own measurements, and reported by nobody.

WHAT IS NOT BUILT, AND WHY. Their recommendation (B) — a permanently ignored namespace so a future launcher directive cannot poison parsing — is REFUSED as stated: it converts a loud refusal into a silent unenforced run, which is precisely the outcome Rounds 825 and 826 chose fail-closed to avoid, and a top-level catch-all would also destroy the typo detection Round 828 names as deliberate. Their recommendation (A) — a separate launcher whose contract is frozen — is the only one of the three that reaches the reported incident, and it is a design question rather than an edit. It is Round 862.

Round 862.decision_summary:
R862 (DESIGN — the floor moves because delegation is read AFTER validation, not because the launcher and the tool are one binary). Round 861 answered the consumer's report and left their recommendation (A) standing: split the launcher into a separate artifact whose contract is frozen, as rustup is to rustc. This round answers it. (A) is the right diagnosis of a symptom and the wrong cut — what has to be separated is the ORDER, not the artifact.

THE MECHANISM, stated precisely because Round 840 recorded the consequence as though it were inherent. `load_config` reads the file, hands it to `parse_config`, which deserialises the whole document into `WorkspaceConfig` under `deny_unknown_fields`, and only then calls `enforce_tool_pin`. A key the binary does not know therefore kills the load BEFORE the pin is ever looked at. "The floor is the newest key in your file" is a description of that sequence, not a property of pinning. Reverse the two and the floor stops moving: a binary that reads `tool.pin` out of a GENERIC TOML table before validating anything delegates correctly no matter how many keys it has never heard of.

IT BUYS WHAT (A) BUYS, and it is the same thing rather than a lesser version of it. A shim's floor is the shim's first release; a loose pin read's floor is the revision that introduces it. Both are frozen from that point, and neither can help a binary that predates them — nothing can. The two designs have equal reach for the class that matters.

IT DOES NOT COST WHAT (A) COSTS. A second shipped artifact is a second thing to acquire, and acquisition is the problem the pin exists to solve: a shim is also a binary invoked by name. Worse, its freeze is a promise maintained by hand, and every hand-maintained list in this codebase has drifted (Rounds 777 and 783). The loose read's freeze is a TEST instead — a fixture carrying both a pin and a key no build knows must still delegate, so a round that couples the pin read back to the schema turns it red. A promise nobody can break quietly beats a promise.

THE FIELD SHAPES WERE MEASURED rather than assumed, and they narrow (A) further. Three ways of resolving the tool exist right now. This repo's own hooks call `scripts/mn`, which builds from the working tree and execs `target/debug` — no name, no floor, and a shim would do nothing for it. This machine's MCP host config names an absolute per-revision path three revisions behind HEAD, which is this very class live in our own setup, kept harmless only by our not having added a config key since. The consumer who filed the report resolves by a bare name on PATH — the shape that broke — and their announced replacement is a submodule build, which is strictly stronger than a shim and needs nothing from us. Their tree is clean at the pre-replacement HEAD, so that migration has not landed; the population a shim would serve is one consumer who is leaving it.

WHAT THE REORDER DOES NOT DO, so it is not oversold. It cannot help a binary older than itself. It helps only a workspace that DECLARES a pin and has the pinned build installed — with no pin there is nothing to delegate to, and dying at the parse error remains the correct answer. And this workspace declares no pin by Round 825's circularity rule, so the win cannot be dogfooded here; the evidence would have to come from a consumer store copy, as Rounds 854 through 856 got theirs.

THE SHAPE, written out so the build round is not a second design. `delegate_if_pinned(content, path)` runs before `parse_config`: parse `content` as `toml::Table`, read `tool.pin` as a string, and on anything unexpected — a syntax error, no `[tool]`, a non-string pin — return WITHOUT COMPLAINT, so the strict parse reports it once and in its own words. When a pin is found it goes through the existing `check_tool_pin` and `switch_to_pinned`, untouched. The early path therefore never produces a refusal the late path would not: it delegates or it declines, and `enforce_tool_pin` stays exactly where it is as the fail-closed refusal for an unregistered process and for an absent pinned build. One real behaviour change, stated rather than discovered later: Round 861's broken-install error can now fire before the strict parse, which is the same message sooner.

RECOMMENDATION (B) STAYS REFUSED and this round does not soften it. A permanently ignored namespace converts a loud refusal into a silent unenforced run, which is the outcome Rounds 825 and 826 chose fail-closed to avoid.

WHAT REMAINS A COST JUDGEMENT, named as one so it can be overruled. (A) is not refused on correctness: a frozen shim would work. It is not recommended because it is dominated by a change an order of magnitude smaller, and because a second artifact is permanent surface. That second half is a cost argument and the owner may decide it differently.

Round 863.decision_summary:
R863 (BUILD — the pin is read before the document is validated, and the floor stops moving). Round 862 designed this and nothing about the design changed on contact with the code.

THE MECHANISM IS ONE REORDERING. `load_config` calls `delegate_if_pinned` before `parse_config`: the file is read as a generic `toml::Table`, `tool.pin` is taken out of it, and the hand-off goes through the existing `check_tool_pin` and `switch_to_pinned`. A key the running binary has never heard of therefore no longer stops the hand-off, so the floor becomes this revision and then stays there — the same reach Round 862 measured a separate frozen launcher would buy, without a second artifact for anyone to acquire.

IT DELEGATES OR IT DECLINES, NEVER REFUSES, and that is what keeps it from being a second enforcement path rather than a reordering of the one. A syntax error, an absent `[tool]`, a non-string pin, a pin that does not name one revision, the waiver being set: every one returns `Ok`, so the strict parse reports it once and in its own words. `enforce_tool_pin` is still the single refusal and its messages are untouched.
