Round 864.decision_summary:
R864 (BUILD — the read set holds build output that no axis can name, and the only thing removing it has been a three-word hand list. Asked for by the external spec consumer; the evidence that they are right came from our own tree.)

★THE ASK, AND WHY ITS SHAPE IS RIGHT. They asked for one advisory: name the files in the read set that the repository's VCS already declares built. Their argument is Round 860's own, one level up — a binary is excluded by the UTF-8 property it inherently lacks, and ignore status is likewise declared by the tree under audit rather than by a list in our source, so it cannot drift the way a skip name would. They were explicit that they were NOT asking us to skip 'build/', which Round 860 refused for exactly the reason they cite.

★THE HALF OF MY R860 REPLY THAT WAS WRONG. I argued to them that every hand list in this codebase has drifted, and did not say that we run one: 'is_skipped_dir' holds dot-prefixed, 'target' and 'node_modules'. SCHEMA_GUIDE stated it; my reply did not, and 'adding build/ to the walk's skip names was considered and refused' reads as though no such list exists. It exists, it is load bearing, and it has already drifted — it knows the two ecosystems this repo is written in and no others. A consumer's '__pycache__' walks straight in, and a generated Go tree has no conventional directory name for any list to hold at all.

★THE MEASUREMENT THAT SETTLES IT IS OURS, NOT THEIRS. Remove 'target' and 'node_modules' from the list and our own read set goes from 100 to 2786 files, of which the VCS calls 2686 build output — and 75 of those are '.rs'. A generated Rust source has a known comment syntax, so the Round 856 line cannot name it, and it is valid UTF-8, so the Round 860 line cannot either. That is precisely the class their 126 generated '.go' files fell into, reproduced in a different language inside our own tree. Two axes, both correct, both structurally blind to the same thing.

THE PREDICATE IS UNTRACKED AND IGNORED, NOT IGNORE-MATCHING. 'git check-ignore' answers whether a rule matches a path, which is also true of a file its author committed with 'git add -f' — deliberately versioned, the opposite of build output. Their tree has zero such files, so both predicates agree there today; that is a measurement and not a property (the Round 862 rule), so the predicate is chosen to be right rather than to match. The fixture carries an 'add -f' file for the same reason.

THREE STATES, NOT TWO. 'N ignored', '0 ignored' and 'not determined' are distinct values in the type, because a workspace with no build output and a workspace no VCS can answer for are different facts, and a report that printed nothing for both would be the Round 856 silence again. Asking git is a process the Round 377 commit scan already runs from this same binary, and it degrades the same way rather than aborting.

ADVISORY, NOT REJECT, and intersected with the walk's own read set so it cannot disagree with 'is_skipped_dir' about a file. It stays quiet on every workspace whose paths hold no build output, including ours.

R866 (BUILD — the set the swallowed verdict is READ OUT OF is the one nobody was asking the VCS about. Round 864 carried it, Round 865 priced it, this round covers it.)

★WHY THE EXCLUDED SET IS NOT MERELY "NOT SCANNED". An exclusion declares that no citation this ledger gates lives in a tree, and Round 840 checks that claim by reading the excluded files and asking whether any section is cited ONLY there. So the excluded set IS read, and its answer inherits every property of the file set it was computed from. Round 864 gave the read set a line saying how much of it exists only where someone has built; the excluded set had none, and it is the larger set on every consumer ledger measured.

★THE PRICE, MEASURED BEFORE IT WAS BUILT AND AGAIN AFTER. On the external spec consumer's five ledgers: 149 of 1920 (synth), 149 of 1920 (bytesguard), 25 of 2949 (scxml), 9583 of 13462 (wire), 9591 of 13685 (mesh). Round 865 counted those independently from outside the tool, and the real binary now prints the same numbers. Their `mesh` ledger computes `0 swallowed` from a set of which 70% exists only on a developer's disk. It is 0 on all five today — a measured result and not a property, the Round 862 rule, which is exactly what the line now says out loud.

THE FUNCTION TAKES THE SET, NOT THE CONFIG. `vcs_ignored_in_read_set(root, paths)` became `vcs_ignored_among(root, files)`, in place with both callers updated, because both already hold the set and a second derivation here could disagree with the walk it reports on (the Round 777 rule). The git query's SCOPE is derived from that same set rather than handed in beside it: a scope passed separately could name a tree the set does not live under, and the query would then answer about the wrong files while looking right. Widening is safe — the intersection removes whatever the scope swept in — so parent directories are collapsed and used.

★THE WIRING IS TESTED APART FROM THE AXIS, BECAUSE THIS WORKSPACE CANNOT CATCH IT. Our excluded set holds no build output, so passing the read set by mistake still prints zero and every test still passes. The fixture therefore makes the two sets differ in SIZE as well as content, and injecting `scanned_files` for `excluded_files` turns exactly that test red. This is the Round 864 lesson applied at authoring time rather than after a consumer found it: a workspace that is quiet cannot test the thing that would make it loud.

ONE FIELD RENAMED AND ONE HELPER ADDED. `Measured::scanned` is now `considered` — with a second caller it is the size of whatever set was handed in, and "scanned" was one caller's word. `summarize_extensions` prints the largest extensions and COUNTS the remainder as `+n more`, shared by both axes: the consumer's `mesh` excluded set names sixty extensions, and a line listing all of them is a line nobody reads, while one that truncates silently is worse.

WHAT WAS NOT BUILT: any change to the swallowed verdict itself. Excluding build output from that axis would silently un-gate a citation living only in generated source, which is the class Round 840 exists to catch. The instability is now NAMED, not removed, and nothing rejects.

Round 867.decision_summary:
R867 (DESIGN — a file speaks some document's numbering, and no axis ever asked whose). The consumer report adopted in Round 861 was REVISED after that reply was written, and the revision added a second, independent defect: Round 840's exclusion-integrity axis rejects `§N.M` citations that live only inside a vendored tree, when that tree is ANOTHER PROJECT'S DOCUMENT and its numbers are not this store's sections at all. The requested remedy was an attribute on the exclusion, `scan_exclusions = [{ path = "vendor/", numbering = "foreign" }]`. The defect is adopted. The shape is refused, because it is not where the defect lives.

THE DEFECT IS NOT IN THE EXCLUSION AXIS, and that is measured rather than argued. A second consumer on this machine declares no exclusions at all and carries `"W3C SCXML"` among seven hand-registered `external_section_prefixes_bare` entries — the same misattribution, suppressed one token at a time on the SCANNED side. The reporter carries fifteen such entries. The exclusion is where this class becomes a REJECT, not where it originates. Attaching the declaration there couples two independent questions — what the gate reads, and whose numbering a file speaks — and leaves the scanned-side instance to a second mechanism, which is the fix-the-instance-three-times failure Round 856 named.

A SECOND LIVE CASE, worse than the reporter's. `watching-zenoh`, measured with this HEAD, read only: five citations swallowed, every one out of `vendor/sce`, and the ids are SINGLE DIGITS — `1`, `9`, `13`, `14`, `16` — because that store numbers its sections that way. The collision surface is therefore any `§N` in 8727 excluded files, and one of those ids appears in 227 of them. That workspace declares no pin, and it is green today only because the binary on this machine's PATH is `25d30d16`, which predates Round 840. It goes red on the next upgrade, for citations it does not own.

THE MISSING DATUM IS PER-FILE NUMBERING PROVENANCE. `external_section_prefixes` and its bare sibling key on the CITING PROSE, so they can only ever reach a citation whose author named the document. Inside SCE's own documents the numbering is implicit, and the residue proves it: `per §6.2` at `SCE_MESH.md:1483` and `§3.7 / §6.4` at `ARCHITECTURE.md:404` carry nothing to match. Nothing in the token distinguishes them from this store's own sections; only WHERE THE FILE LIVES does.

THE REPORTER'S "the axis has no knob" IS HALF TRUE, and the reply must say so rather than accept it. Two of their four — `W3C SCXML §5.10` at `SCE_MESH.md:1194` and `W3C SCXML §5.5` at `docs/SCE_INTEGRATION_FIXTURE_LAYOUT.md:19` — cite the W3C standard, not SCE's numbering, and the token immediately before the section mark is `SCXML`. The sibling consumer above already registers exactly that prefix for exactly that shape. Their residue is two, not four, and the two that remain are the ones no prefix can reach.

FIVE READERS OF `§N.M`, THREE DIFFERENT PREDICATES. `scan`, `propose_implementations` and `citation_index` honour both the prefix registries and `section_namespace` (Round 376). `swallowed_citations` honours the prefixes and NOT the namespace. `scan_section_decay` (Round 266, printed by the Round 268 decay surface) honours NEITHER. Stated as LATENT rather than live, per Round 862's rule against writing a measured result as a structural property: both divergences measure zero on every tree on this machine, because the decay axis needs a superseded section — this store has one, with zero citations, and the reporter has none — and no local workspace sets `section_namespace`. The repair costs the same whether it has fired yet or not, and a half-enforced predicate is how Round 305's paste-error class arrives.

THE SHAPE, written out so the build round is not a second design. ONE resolver answers "does this `§N.M` token, in THIS file, cite this store", and all five readers call it. Its inputs are the existing token prefix registries, the existing namespace segment, and the new file-level numbering origin. The parity test is the substrate Round 305 established for multi-write-path fields, turned on a read predicate: the same discriminating input driven through all five readers, asserting they answer alike.

THE ORIGIN IS DERIVED, NOT DECLARED, for the case that has consumers. `git ls-files --stage` names submodule gitlinks with mode `160000`, and a file under one of those paths lives in ANOTHER REPOSITORY — which, since a store is per-workspace, is as close to definitional as this model gets. Verified by RUNNING it rather than asserting it, after two rounds of doing the opposite (Rounds 860 and 865): one gitlink in the reporter's tree, `vendor/sce`; four in `watching-zenoh`; ZERO here; and a non-git directory fails loudly instead of answering zero, so "no foreign subtree" and "no VCS to ask" stay distinct — the three-state typing Round 864 built for exactly that confusion.

THE DERIVATION LOOSENS THE GATE, SO IT MUST BE LOUD. Every other axis in this family tightens; this one makes citations disappear, and a wrong "foreign" verdict silently un-gates real ones, which is Round 840's own class inverted. So every run prints which subtrees were derived foreign and how many tokens were skipped because of them. A consumer whose monorepo shares numbering across a submodule reads that line and can then ask for an override; nothing is pre-built for a case with no instance.

SEVERITY STAYS REJECT, and the reporter's implied third option is refused. Once attribution is correct, a swallowed citation IS real coverage loss, which is the whole reason Round 840 exists. Lowering severity would trade a precise gate for a quiet one, and the imprecision was never in the severity.

NOT DOGFOODABLE ON THE DERIVATION HALF, said plainly. This workspace has zero submodules and zero vendored trees, so that half can only be exercised by a fixture here; its field evidence comes from the two consumer trees, both read only. The resolver and the parity test ARE dogfooded, because all five readers are ours.

Round 868.decision_summary:
R868 (BUILD — the Round 867 design landed: one attribution resolver, and a file's numbering origin asked of the tree's own VCS). Five production readers of `§N.M` now call one predicate; a subtree the parent's index marks as a submodule is read as another repository's numbering; and because this is the only axis in the family that LOOSENS, both commands print what it removed on every run. The Round 840 reject is unchanged.

THE PAYOFF WAS MEASURED IN BOTH CONSUMER TREES, read only, with the binary this round built. The reporting consumer went from `4 citation(s) swallowed`, rc=1, to rc=0, and its line now reads `1 foreign subtree(s) … 5969 §-token(s) in 5904 of 7197 file(s) are NOT read as this store's {"vendor/sce": 5969}` — 5904 of its 5912 excluded files were another repository. The second consumer, which was red for five single-digit ids and green only because this machine's PATH binary predates Round 840, also went to rc=0: `4 foreign subtree(s) … 11041 §-token(s) in 8591 of 10493 file(s)`, of which THREE of the four vendored repositories contribute zero. That zero matters as much as the count: the axis is not blanket-silencing vendored trees, it is silencing the one that writes section numbers.

WHAT THAT NUMBER DOES NOT CLAIM, corrected after the first run printed it. The first wording was "removed N citation(s)", which reads as coverage lost; most of those 5969 name nothing in that store and would have been hallucination-class violations, not coverage. It now says "§-token(s) … are NOT read as this store's", and the field doc says explicitly that the number is the SIZE OF WHAT WENT QUIET rather than a count of lost coverage. An over-broad derivation is exactly what a comfortable-looking small number would hide.

OUR OWN GATE CAUGHT THIS ROUND'S PROSE, which is the round's subject happening to the round. Writing the report's own examples into doc comments produced three `section_missing` rejects in `code_refs.rs` — a bare `§6.7` and a bare `§6.2` naming nothing in this store: another document's numbering, in our source, in the change that fixes that class. The mechanism is worth recording because it is not obvious: the extractor's backtick suppression is per LINE, so a code span that wraps across two comment lines does not protect the token inside it. R869 (DOCS — the replies, and the consumer who never filed one). Round 868 closed the second defect a consumer reported; this round writes what goes back, and the writing surfaced two things the build round had not: a measurement confound in the evidence, and a second consumer who is affected and never asked.

THREE ARTIFACTS, and one of them is unsolicited. The reporting consumer gets a single reply covering BOTH defects (`send-pinion-reply-r861-r868-the-floor-the-order-and-the-numbering.md`). The consumer who was silently affected gets a notice (`send-watching-zenoh-notice-r868-the-vendored-numbering.md`) — they filed nothing, they were green only because this machine's PATH binary predates Round 840, and their exposure is LARGER than the reporter's. And the external spec consumer's newest reply gets a postscript, because Round 867 and Round 868 changed the predicate of the Round 840 axis they use and its pin pointer went stale mid-day.

THE SUPERSEDED DRAFT WAS DELETED RATHER THAN BANNERED. The reply written at 16:42 answered a version of the report that no longer exists and asserted, in its own section 5, that the consumer had not reported the delegation-note stutter — which their revision does report. Two candidate files in one directory is the hazard the owner actually faces at routing time, so the new reply opens by correcting that claim and the old file is gone. Everything it said is folded in: the reproduction table with its control, the Round 828 scope argument, the section 7 correction, the dead-code finding about recommendation (C)1, the refusal of (B), and (A) being dominated rather than wrong.

A CONFOUND FOUND WHILE WRITING, AND REMOVED. The before/after numbers Round 868 recorded for the second consumer came from two runs an hour apart, and their store moved between them — `entries 1471 → 1473`, `T1 ledger 13 → 14`, a session of theirs running in between. Comparing two REVISIONS across two TREE STATES mis-attributes the delta, which is exactly the discipline the reporting consumer asked for in their own section 11. So the Round 858 revision was built in a throwaway worktree and both binaries were re-run against ONE tree state: `0c82ad73` gives 5 swallowed rc=1 and 4 swallowed rc=1, `d3c60fc7` gives 0 and rc=0, on the same two trees. The vendored submodule revision was identical across both measurements. The conclusion did not change; the evidence for it did.

WHAT THE SECOND CONSUMER IS TOLD, and what they are not. Their five swallowed ids are single digits — `1`, `9`, `13`, `14`, `16` — so any section-shaped token in 8727 excluded files is a collision candidate and one of those ids appears in 227 of them. Their green was a stale-tool artifact and the next `cargo install` on this machine would have taken their commits down, which is precisely what happened to the reporting consumer 65 minutes after a correct adoption. The one real action is to pin, in the order the tool requires: install, check `--version`, then declare. They are also told that nothing in their config is wrong — stale exclusions 0, no overlap advisory, coverage axis clean — because a notice that arrives without that sentence reads as an accusation.

THE ASK THAT GOES BOTH WAYS. Every reply carries the same request about the new line: the number beside `numbering origin` is the SIZE OF WHAT WENT QUIET, not lost coverage, and 5969 and 11041 tokens are too many for us to have read. If a consumer's OWN citation is sitting inside a vendored tree by mistake, it is now quietly outside the gate — and the line is what lets them ask. We did not look, we said we did not look, and we said who can.

THE INJECTION SELF-REPORT IS IN THE REPLIES, not only in the ledger. Two of Round 868's six injections were mis-aimed on the first attempt: one edited an arm the fixture never takes and turned nothing red, which would have been recorded as a control that passed; the other did something different from what its description said. The external spec consumer has twice caught an unverified claim of ours, so their copy leads with this rather than burying it. The non-surgical third is named too, with the reason its second test goes red.

AND THE ROUND'S OWN PROSE IS IN THERE AS WELL: writing the report's examples into scanned doc comments produced three hallucination-class rejects in our own source during Round 868 — the class being fixed, committed by the fix. Both consumer replies carry it, because the mechanism (backtick suppression is per LINE) applies to their trees too.

Round 870.decision_summary:
R870 (DEBT — the three-state vocabulary was retyped in five places and had drifted in three; the definition a consumer had to read did not exist). The external spec consumer classified 173 sections across four ledgers that had never been classified at all, took `impl_missing` from 244 to 163 with `misclassified_coverage` 0 on all five, and sent three reports with no asks. All three are real, and two are worse than they could see from outside.

THEIR SECTION 1 IS A DOCUMENTATION DEFECT WITH A DEEPER CAUSE. `OutOfScopeHere` read "Part of the standard but not implemented by THIS consumer", and they read "the standard" as an EXTERNAL standard — a reading available to them precisely because another of their ledgers IS an external mirror. Under it, a deferred Phase-2 feature had no value: `informational` means inherently non-implementable, so 19 sections across two ledgers stayed `Normative` and produced `impl_missing` warnings no binding could ever clear. They caught it only because four independent agents classified one ledger each without seeing the written principle and disagreed with it in the same place.

The cause is not only the phrase. `coverage_expectation` and `out_of_scope_here` appear NOWHERE in `docs/SCHEMA_GUIDE.md` — the human-facing guide has no entry for this axis at all. So the only definitions a consumer can read are the enum's doc comment, the MCP tool description, and the CLI usage line, and TWO of those three carried the ambiguous phrase. The wording is now "the document this ledger mirrors", with their own Phase-2 example written into both the variant doc and a new `Coverage classification` section in the guide, which also records the two readings that cost them time and the fact that nothing checks a tag against the prose.

THEIR SECTION 3 IS ONE INSTANCE OF A CLASS. They reported that the missing-argument message offers `informative` — the two-state tag Round 422 removed with no alias — while the value message one line later correctly names three. That is the fix-the-instance trap Round 856 named, so the class was swept: FIVE surfaces spelled this closed set out by hand and THREE had drifted. Beyond their report: the CLI note reading "informative exempts the section from the coverage axiom" was MISFILED onto `add-confirmation-event`, so a consumer reading help for the confirmation verb was told about coverage classification in retired vocabulary; the MCP validation message also said "normative or informative"; and the enum's own TYPE-LEVEL doc still described the two-state model, naming an `Informative` variant that does not exist, as did the MCP args doc.

The MCP message is a message defect only, said precisely because the temptation is to call it worse: that path routes through `from_tag`, which accepts all three, so `out_of_scope_here` was always settable there. Only the refusal text was stale.

THE REPAIR IS DERIVATION, not nine corrected strings. `CoverageExpectation::ALL` and `::vocabulary()` (and the same on `VerificationExpectation`, which had not drifted and is the sibling that would drift next) render the closed set through one `join_or`, and every runtime message interpolates it. A usage line is a `&'static str` and cannot; it is CHECKED instead — a derived test parses every `--expectation` alternation in the command table back through `from_tag` and requires it to resolve to exactly one enum and cover that enum completely, so a retired tag fails to parse and a new variant nobody documented leaves the set short. That test carries a count assertion, because a later refactor renaming the flag would otherwise turn it into a pass over zero usage lines.

THEIR SECTION 2 STANDS, AND THE ADJACENT AXIS WAS CHECKED BEFORE SAYING SO. Two sections resisted every value: one whose entire deliverable was DELETING a file, one an interim gate that landed and was removed by the final commit. Both were implemented here, deliberately, and left nothing to bind. The non-obvious candidate they did not raise is `decision_status`, where `Removed` and `Open` ARE exempt from the coverage axiom — but `Removed` means withdrawn, in its own doc's words, and `Superseded` means one decision replaced by another, while these decisions were CARRIED OUT and their artifacts are deliberately gone. So no existing state names the shape, exactly as they judged. Not building a fourth state on two instances, which is also their position; the guide now says "landed then deliberately removed" is not what `informational` means, which is the part that misleads.

THEIR SECTION 4 NEEDS NOTHING. `misclassified_coverage` was 0 throughout, including while their draft held two wrong classifications — the Round 423 blind spot documented as documented, confirmed from outside. The guide now states it in those terms: the contradiction that is structural is caught, the one that is semantic is not, and at scale the check is independent classifiers disagreeing.

FOUR INJECTIONS, EACH EXACTLY ONE TEST RED — and the fourth was malformed on the first attempt, producing a compile error and therefore zero discriminating power, which is the THIRD consecutive round in which an injection needed re-aiming before it measured anything. Recorded because a mis-aimed injection that is not noticed reads in the log exactly like a control that passed.

THE GATE BLOCKED THIS COMMIT ONCE, for `Round 870` cited in code before this entry existed — seven `Missing` violations, the citation-hygiene rule enforcing its own order.

NOT DOGFOODED. This store has five sections and no classification pressure at all; every number in this round is theirs. Their pin is `3e2cb146` (Round 866), so they do not yet have Round 867 or Round 868 either.

Round 872.decision_summary:
R872 (DOCS — the notices landed, a consumer repaired us better than our own advice, and the routing queue this session kept quoting was wrong by a factor of three). Code 0. This entry exists because the whole round-trip lives nowhere else: two consumers adopted, one of them found something the notice had not said, and the follow-up advice this side gave first would have broken them.

THE UNSOLICITED NOTICE WAS ADOPTED IN FOUR HOURS. The consumer who never filed anything — green only because this machine's PATH binary predated Round 840 — declared `[tool] pin` at the current revision and moved the constant their CI installs from in the same commit. Their ledger cites Round 868 and Round 871 by number.

AND THEY FOUND WHAT THE NOTICE DID NOT SAY. Declaring the pin without moving `MNEMOSYNE_REV` would have red-ed every hosted job and killed the agent-session MCP server, because their CI installs from that constant and then validates with it, and the pre-`[tool]` build dies at TOML parse on the key. Our notice gave the install-verify-declare ORDER and never mentioned a second install site. They derived it, measured three revisions on an isolated copy to prove it, and disclosed the mechanism in their own ledger.

THE PATH BINARY MOVED WHILE THE NOTICE SAT UNROUTED, which is the argument the notice was making, happening to it. At 19:56 the machine-global binary was `25d30d16` (Round 807, pre-Round 840) and their workspace was green because the check did not exist; at 21:29 it was `be4c1647` (Round 869) and their workspace was green because the check existed and had been fixed. Same tree, same command, opposite reasons, nothing changed on their side. It also skipped the red window — Round 840 through Round 867, a range whose one measured point (`0c82ad73`) refuses their tree with five swallowed citations. That is field evidence, on our own machine, for the STANDING-PROPERTY framing Round 861 gave the consumer report: adoption order cannot reach a binary installed later.

★THE FOLLOW-UP ADVICE THIS SIDE GAVE FIRST WOULD HAVE BROKEN THEM. The gap was real — their pin had no per-revision root to delegate to, because their installer writes only to the shared cargo slot — and the repair looked like one line: swap `--force` for `--root`. Reading their hooks first showed that swap removes the binary from `PATH`, and their pre-commit, their pre-push and their own pin-verifier all resolve through `command -v`, with the two hooks hard-failing on absence. The follow-up said ADD, never swap, and said why.

THEY THEN REPAIRED IT BETTER THAN THE ADVICE. Instead of a second `cargo install --root`, they COPY the built binary into the per-revision root, and their reason is one this side had not considered: the shared slot's `~/.cargo/.crates.toml` entry is their established source for reading the full pinned SHA, and a second install would blur it — the per-rev root needs no ledger. They justified the copy from OUR design, citing that the hand-off verifies by `--version` and that the directory name is the pin string verbatim. Verified functionally afterwards: a different-revision build in their tree now prints the switch note and delegates, where the day before it refused.

★AND THE ROUTING QUEUE THIS SESSION KEPT QUOTING WAS WRONG, which the owner then asked to be swept properly — so all THIRTY-ONE drafts were audited against their recipients rather than the recent handful. Ten replies were described as awaiting routing, repeatedly. Checking the RECIPIENTS rather than our own directory shows five of the six to the external spec consumer were adopted hours ago, each with a commit naming the rounds, and the first consumer's reply was adopted too — their round moved the pin off the revision they had been holding, with "upstream closed both reported defects" in the commit body. The real queue is THREE of thirty-one. The rule being broken is one this side already holds in writing: a draft's presence in our tree says nothing about delivery, and only the recipient's own documents decide it. Recorded here because the error was in the judgement procedure, not in any one count.

THE SWEEP ALSO FOUND A CONVENTION THAT WAS TRIED AND ABANDONED. Two of the thirty-one carry an in-file marker saying they were sent — one frozen, one annotated as edited AFTER sending. The other twenty-nine carry nothing, so the marker cannot be the index, and the audit has to go to the recipients every time. A fourth consumer's draft turned out to be not merely delivered but CLOSED: their own document records our option (A) as wrong, which nothing on this side had noticed.

WHAT REMAINS, so the next session does not re-derive it: three drafts unrouted (one to the spec consumer, two to the narrative consumer), and the scope fork the owner has now deferred twice — the map arc or the north-star return.

Round 872.publishable_decision_summary:
R872 (DOCS — the notices landed, a consumer repaired us better than our own advice, and the routing queue this session kept quoting was wrong by a factor of three). Code 0. This entry exists because the whole round-trip lives nowhere else: two consumers adopted, one of them found something the notice had not said, and the follow-up advice this side gave first would have broken them.

THE UNSOLICITED NOTICE WAS ADOPTED IN FOUR HOURS. The consumer who never filed anything — green only because this machine's PATH binary predated Round 840 — declared `[tool] pin` at the current revision and moved the constant their CI installs from in the same commit. Their ledger cites Round 868 and Round 871 by number.

AND THEY FOUND WHAT THE NOTICE DID NOT SAY. Declaring the pin without moving `MNEMOSYNE_REV` would have red-ed every hosted job and killed the agent-session MCP server, because their CI installs from that constant and then validates with it, and the pre-`[tool]` build dies at TOML parse on the key. Our notice gave the install-verify-declare ORDER and never mentioned a second install site. They derived it, measured three revisions on an isolated copy to prove it, and disclosed the mechanism in their own ledger.

THE PATH BINARY MOVED WHILE THE NOTICE SAT UNROUTED, which is the argument the notice was making, happening to it. At 19:56 the machine-global binary was `25d30d16` (Round 807, pre-Round 840) and their workspace was green because the check did not exist; at 21:29 it was `be4c1647` (Round 869) and their workspace was green because the check existed and had been fixed. Same tree, same command, opposite reasons, nothing changed on their side. It also skipped the red window — Round 840 through Round 867, a range whose one measured point (`0c82ad73`) refuses their tree with five swallowed citations. That is field evidence, on our own machine, for the STANDING-PROPERTY framing Round 861 gave the consumer report: adoption order cannot reach a binary installed later.

★THE FOLLOW-UP ADVICE THIS SIDE GAVE FIRST WOULD HAVE BROKEN THEM. The gap was real — their pin had no per-revision root to delegate to, because their installer writes only to the shared cargo slot — and the repair looked like one line: swap `--force` for `--root`. Reading their hooks first showed that swap removes the binary from `PATH`, and their pre-commit, their pre-push and their own pin-verifier all resolve through `command -v`, with the two hooks hard-failing on absence. The follow-up said ADD, never swap, and said why.

THEY THEN REPAIRED IT BETTER THAN THE ADVICE. Instead of a second `cargo install --root`, they COPY the built binary into the per-revision root, and their reason is one this side had not considered: the shared slot's `~/.cargo/.crates.toml` entry is their established source for reading the full pinned SHA, and a second install would blur it — the per-rev root needs no ledger. They justified the copy from OUR design, citing that the hand-off verifies by `--version` and that the directory name is the pin string verbatim. Verified functionally afterwards: a different-revision build in their tree now prints the switch note and delegates, where the day before it refused.

★AND THE ROUTING QUEUE THIS SESSION KEPT QUOTING WAS WRONG, which the owner then asked to be swept properly — so all THIRTY-ONE drafts were audited against their recipients rather than the recent handful. Ten replies were described as awaiting routing, repeatedly. Checking the RECIPIENTS rather than our own directory shows five of the six to the external spec consumer were adopted hours ago, each with a commit naming the rounds, and the first consumer's reply was adopted too — their round moved the pin off the revision they had been holding, with "upstream closed both reported defects" in the commit body. The real queue is THREE of thirty-one. The rule being broken is one this side already holds in writing: a draft's presence in our tree says nothing about delivery, and only the recipient's own documents decide it. Recorded here because the error was in the judgement procedure, not in any one count.

THE SWEEP ALSO FOUND A CONVENTION THAT WAS TRIED AND ABANDONED. Two of the thirty-one carry an in-file marker saying they were sent — one frozen, one annotated as edited AFTER sending. The other twenty-nine carry nothing, so the marker cannot be the index, and the audit has to go to the recipients every time. A fourth consumer's draft turned out to be not merely delivered but CLOSED: their own document records our option (A) as wrong, which nothing on this side had noticed.

WHAT REMAINS, so the next session does not re-derive it: three drafts unrouted (one to the spec consumer, two to the narrative consumer), and the scope fork the owner has now deferred twice — the map arc or the north-star return.

Round 873.decision_summary:
R873 (BUILD — the authored map seam loads again, and nothing was watching it). The owner's cadence choice was the second of the two honest holes Round 857 recorded: the only store that ever AUTHORED quest-giver surfaces no longer loaded, so the map seam's end-to-end demonstration had no loadable fixture and the live consumer exercised the seam only through the derived canon-coordinate seat.

WHAT ROUND 857 RECORDED WAS ONE OF FOUR BREAKAGES, AND NOT THE LOAD-BEARING ONE. It named the R708 removals — 18 `{kind:value}` objects and 5 `object_kind:"scalar"` predicates. Rebuilding from the tracked manifests found a third, entity kind becoming a registry ref rather than free text (R732/R738), and then the one that matters: THE TRACKED AUDIT MANIFEST NEVER CARRIED A DISCLOSURE PLAN AT ALL. The blind author wrote its `delve` plan straight into its own store, so the 4 quest-giver surfaces — the seam's only authored instance anywhere — existed in two gitignored `*.atomic.json` files and nowhere else. The repo could not rebuild its deepest end-to-end demonstration even before R708 broke the wire; a `git clean -x` would have ended it.

★THE MIGRATION IS HALF THE REPAIR. The store rotted for ~150 rounds because nothing in the workspace ever loaded it, and a tracked-but-unloaded fixture rots again on the next removal. So the deliverable is a fixture PLUS the gate that loads it: `dnd_quest_map_seam_smoke.rs` rebuilds the store the way the experiment's runbook does and asserts what the ledger already published, which makes a change here a change to a published claim rather than a silent drift.

THE FIXTURE HAS ONE NEW FILE, DELIBERATELY. `sections.json` / `order.json` / `narrative-rules.json` needed no migration, so the test READS them out of the frozen experiment record instead of copying them: a byte-identical second home is free to drift, and the frozen record is exactly what reading is for. Only the migrated fact manifest is a maintained artifact, and it lives in the crate's test tree rather than beside the audit record, because `claudedocs/` is territory the docs gate deliberately excludes as never-retro-edited — a maintained fixture does not belong in a frozen-record directory.

THE TOKEN VOCABULARIES ARE DERIVED, NOT INVENTED. Each of the 5 migrated predicates declares the closed `object_tokens` set the author's own objects assert — a floor, not a claim about what the predicate may legally take. Two of the five vocabularies are stated verbatim in the predicate's own authored description (`hidden or exposed`; `walking, ended, bound, or commanded`), which is corroboration from a source the derivation did not read.

IT ALSO CLOSED THE OTHER HOLE, WHICH WAS NOT THE ASSIGNMENT. Round 857 recorded that the quest `open` verdict — the one a quest LOG renders — had no real-data instance anywhere: 117 done, 37 unknown, ZERO open across the live consumer's 22 quests x 7 worlds, because finished manuscripts are not save-states. This store yields open 5 / done 7 / unknown 4 over 4 quests x 4 world-lines. One migration retired both of the round's honest holes, and the second was free.

Round 874.decision_summary:
R874 (DEBT — the work-list was on the wrong wire, and typing the field is what put it on the right one). Round 873 migrated the dnd-quest manifest by hand and paid 23 round trips to do it: Round 708 built a NAMED migration work-list for a store carrying the removed `{kind:value}` object or `object_kind:"scalar"` predicate, but a migration EDITS THE MANIFEST, and that path answered with a bare serde "unknown variant" naming one line. The wire that actually gets re-authored was the one without the help.

THE FIX WAS NOT WHERE I EXPECTED, AND THE FIRST TEST I WROTE SAID SO. I added the manifest scan, asserted that a scalar-predicate-only manifest is named, and it FAILED: `PredicateImport.object_kind` was a `String`. A manifest declaring a shape removed 165 rounds ago DESERIALIZED, and the reject came row by row out of `build_predicate`. A work-list can only report what the parse can see, so typing the field is not an adjacent improvement — IT IS THE MECHANISM. This is the free-text machine slot R661 named and R708 closed on the store, still open on the manifest wire, and the whole reason the wire could not answer.

★SO THE ENUM TRAVELS ALL THE WAY OUT. `PredicateImport.object_kind`, `add_predicate`, `set_predicate`, and both MCP argument structs now take `PredicateObjectKind`. 25 Rust sites, compiler-driven. The MCP tools' JSON Schema now CARRIES the closed set, so a client cannot spell a removed tag and learn of it only from a write-time reject; and the string-to-enum parse survives at exactly one place — the argv boundary, where a shell genuinely hands over text.

AND THE MESSAGE THAT SENT PEOPLE TO A SHAPE THAT NO LONGER EXISTS. `build_predicate`'s hand-written "expected one of: entity, scalar, token, quantity, fact" still offered `scalar` — a tag Round 708 deleted from the enum, in the fail-loud message of the very function that enforces the removal. Nothing caught it because nothing derived it. `PredicateObjectKind` now has `ALL` + `vocabulary()` (the Round 870 shape), the argv message interpolates it, and the Round 870 usage-line check is generalised from `--expectation` to any enum-valued flag so the two `--object-kind` usage lines are pinned too. They happened to be correct — which is a measurement, not a property.

★TYPING A FIELD DELETES TESTS, AND THAT IS ONLY SAFE IF THE QUESTION MOVES. Four cases of the R658 add/set parity test — unknown tag, empty tag, padded tag, miscased tag — are no longer VALUES either writer can be handed. Unrepresentable beats rejected, but a deleted assertion is coverage lost unless the question is re-asked where the bad input can still arrive. So each moved and is asserted at its new home: argv (`predicate_object_kind_smoke.rs`, both verbs) and serde (the manifest test's own controls). Round 875.decision_summary: R875 BUILD (the map arc — the READ half of the map axis): `report-transition-map`, a CLI + MCP read that hands back, per transition rule, the map its `adjacency` predicate declares — nodes, edges (declaring fact id, endpoints, and the fact's frame/branch), and per edge the STORED side-table values `edge_costs` (R710) and `edge_guards` (R722/R723). THE FINDING THAT MADE IT: the map axis shipped WRITE-ONLY and nothing read it back. Measured on today's binary before writing any code — `report-entity` carries the `adjacent` typed fact but no cost and no guard; `report-playable-world` carries the typed fact, its disclosure and its locator, and no cost and no guard; `query --term` does not see narrative facts at all; `mnemosyne-engine`, the kernel a consumer links, contains ZERO occurrences of either identifier. THE MECHANISM IS A COLLAPSE OF TWO DIFFERENT READS INTO ONE: R710 filed its own review's LOW-4 (`edge_costs` write-only) as substrate-round LATENCY awaiting "the derived read"; R711 then established that THAT read — minutes-within-a-tide, `tide_budget − Σcost` — is BLOCKED on an owner-reserved number, and the owner afterwards corrected the framing further (`tide_budget` is a tide-domain concept; a core that knows it violates invariant 4), so the blocked read is not merely deferred, it is NOT OURS TO BUILD. The deferral's premise therefore evaporated, but the carry it justified was never re-examined: plain CARRIAGE of what the store already holds is a different read from a domain COMPUTATION over it, and collapsing the two left the carriage read never designed, never deferred on its merits, and invisible — including to the RESUME memory, which recorded the reassuring and FALSE "the consumer can just read it with query". THE FIELD COST, from the consumer's own source (read-only, the R668 discipline — read the program, not the data): the tide engine's `map.rs` records, dated 2026-07-26, that it authored 28 edges' costs and guards through `add-edge-cost`/`add-edge-guard`, found no read that returned them, and opened our store sidecar itself — 1.2 MB parsed per start, measured at 1,843 allocations / 1.79 MB — then on 2026-07-28 moved that parse to a build-time bake. Its own comment names the consequence ("스토어 꼴을 무는 자리가 둘이 됐고, 둘이면 어긋난다" — the store's shape is now bitten in TWO places on its side, and two will diverge) and names the swap point waiting on us ("읽기 API 가 오는 날 갈아 끼울 자리는 그 굽는 함수 하나"). This round is the precedent R371 set when SCE found `normative_excerpt` write-only: surface it on the read paths, do not leave a consumer parsing the store. SSOT: the edge derivation is EXTRACTED, not re-written — `transition_edges` is now the single "what is an edge" for both the continuity gate and the read, so the read cannot offer a step the gate rejects (the R699 divergence, in the other direction); collecting the node set moved with it, out of the gate arm where it had been write-only dead since R716 moved G2 to `scan_spatial_map`. HONEST BOUNDARIES, each stated in the report rather than assumed: `undirected` is REPORTED, never applied (a consumer symmetrizes because the declaration says to — R697's one-way-state-machine reason); a guard is never evaluated (R712 layering); the read is FLAT and un-scoped exactly as the gate evaluates the map, so each edge carries its fact's frame/branch and no branch-scoped resolution is performed (R696 review finding 6 stays deferred); and it takes NO canon order, because requiring one would assert a scoping this read does not do. WHAT A NAIVE BAKE WOULD LOSE IS NAMED, NOT DROPPED: self-loops (excluded from edges, as the gate excludes them) and side-table keys on a fact that is not an edge of any declared map (the read's echo of `EdgeCostNotAnEdge`/`EdgeGuardNotAnEdge`) each get their own list — an authored fact absent with no reason given reads as "never authored". `transition_rules: 0` is a THIRD state, not an empty map: with no rule there is no declared adjacency predicate and the store genuinely cannot know which facts are edges (invariant 4), and the human render says that sentence (the R864 three-state discipline). ALSO CORRECTED: `describe-schema`, which R874 established is the only authority for the narrative registries, was pointing `edge_costs.referenced_by` at "the future derived travel-time computation" — a read that R711 had already established will never be ours, so the one surface a consumer consults for this axis was telling it to wait for the wrong thing. Both side-table rows now name the read that exists.
changes_bullets: validate/continuity.rs: `transition_edges` EXTRACTED as the single edge derivation (edges + nodes + self-loops) both the continuity gate's transition arm and the new read call; the gate arm now consumes it and no longer collects the node set it had stopped using at R716. New pure read `transition_map(store, rules) -> TransitionMapReport` (maps / transition_rules / unattached_costs / unattached_guards), order-free, running the store-registry half of the gate's boundary so an orphaned or unit-invalid side-table entry still fails loud.

ops/lib.rs: `transition_map_report(root, sidecar, rules_override)` — resolves the same narrative-rules artifact as the gate (the rule is what DECLARES the adjacency predicate; core must not know it, invariant 4) and NO canon order.

cli/main.rs: `report-transition-map [--rules] [--sidecar] [--json]` + a human render that prints cost, guard (all / k-of-N), self-loops, unattached side-table keys, and the distinct no-transition-rule sentence. mcp/main.rs: `report_transition_map` tool + `ReportTransitionMapArgs`.

validate/schema.rs: `describe-schema` `edge_costs` / `edge_guards` `referenced_by` now name the read that exists; the `edge_costs` row previously pointed at "the future derived travel-time computation", which R711 had already established is the consumer's and not ours.

Round 877.decision_summary: R877 DOCS (the map arc — reading the consumer's gates, code 0): the R876 notice gains a section on two of the consumer's own map gates, and the arc's long-carried G1–G6 roster is retired as obsolete. WHAT PROMPTED IT: R876 said in prose that this read makes their G5 deletable; going back to read the gate itself showed G5 says so in its own doc comment — "이 게이트가 죽는 날은 커널이 이 축에 읽기를 내주는 날이다 — 그때 파서는 하나가 된다" — which is now quoted verbatim rather than paraphrased. Reading the neighbours found two more things. FIRST, their G1 ("every edge costs something") judges by a SENTINEL: it looks for `minutes == 0`, but `minutes` is built with `unwrap_or(0)`, and our write path rejects a non-positive cost, so a stored zero cannot exist — the only case that gate can ever fire on is an edge with NO cost authored, expressed as though it were a zero one. The report omits the `cost` key entirely when none was authored, so the same gate can now be written as what it means. SECOND, and the sharper one: their G2 ("the map is undirected") appears UNABLE TO FAIL. Both constructors — `from_edges` and `from_json` — insert the same `Edge` into `(a,b)` AND `(b,a)` unconditionally, so `edge(b,a)` exists with equal `minutes` whenever `edge(a,b)` does; even a store holding both directions with different costs ends symmetric, because the later `Edge` overwrites both cells. That is a gate asserting a property its own constructor guarantees — the vacuous-pass class, which is why it is worth saying rather than leaving. The concern G2 aims at is real and is already detected on OUR side: `adjacency_reverse_duplicate` (R698) flags a store holding both directions under an undirected rule, and `adjacency_self_loop` flags `adjacent(a,a)`, which their bake does not check for at all. BOTH findings are marked in the notice as read-not-run: our read-only discipline forbids executing anything in their tree, so a wrong claim is our misreading and we say so. ALSO RETIRED: the G1–G6 roster this arc has carried since R668 as "the specification" and "the ONLY durable copy" — captured verbatim out of `build-map.py` before that file evaporated — no longer describes anything. The file is gone (R875 confirmed: deleted, untracked, no git history), and the gates that stand in its place are a DIFFERENT SET with a different character: not spec gates (nodes are registered places / every place is on the map / positive cost / connectivity / derived rules fresh / every character placed) but GAME-DESIGN gates (no free edge / undirected / the first day is connected / the first day does NOT fit the budget, so choosing is real / the baked table and the store agree). The memory that pointed future sessions at the old roster now says the roster is history and names the current five, so no later round reopens a port against a specification that no longer exists.

Round 878.decision_summary: R878 MEASUREMENT (code 0, no fixture): how many of the tracked `claudedocs/phase1-*` experiment kits can be rebuilt from their OWN tracked inputs, against today's binary. R873 found that ONE kit (dnd-quest) could not — 21 schema generations behind, and its disclosure plan present only in a gitignored file. That was never established as a CLASS. It is one. THE ANSWER: of 19 tracked kits, ONE rebuilds with real content, ONE rebuilds vacuously, FOURTEEN cannot rebuild a single arm, and THREE ship no store input at all. Per arm (an arm = a section manifest + a facts manifest, seeded into an empty workspace and imported through the real binary): 34 arms tested, 2 rebuild with substance (`2d-projection/v1/extract-vn`, 66 facts / 23 typed; `2d-projection/v1/extract-tsukuru`, 103 facts / 54 typed), 1 rebuilds only because it is EMPTY of the thing that breaks (`causes-poc`: 4 facts, 0 typed claims, 0 predicates — it cannot fail the wall because it never reaches it, and counting it as a success would be counting thinness as health), and 31 fail. ONE MECHANISM ACCOUNTS FOR 30 OF THE 31: R708's removal of the `value`/`scalar` object shape. Every kit authored before it carries `{kind:value}` objects or `object_kind=scalar` predicates, and there is NO migration arm — deliberately, because what a free-text value MEANT is an authorial re-decision (token? quantity? a fact ref? or prose that belongs in the claim), not a mechanical rewrite. The error is not a mystery, though: it names every offending fact id and predicate id and states the four ways out, which is R874's work-list arriving at exactly the wire this census walks. THE 31st IS A DIFFERENT AND SHARPER CLASS: `2d-projection/v1/author` dies on R752's widening of a disclosure override's `first_at` from a single coordinate to a coordinate SET. The old form is a pair `["together", "tg-14"]`, and serde deserializes a JSON array into a struct POSITIONALLY — so `branch` binds fine and the failure lands on `coords` wanting a sequence and finding a string. Had the widened field stayed a `String`, the removed shape would have imported SILENTLY. This is the R874 class again (a removed shape passing deserialization) and it was caught here only because the field's TYPE changed, not because anything checks the shape. Stores got a migration arm for this exact change (`migrate_disclosure_first_at_to_reveal`, v38 to v39); the manifest wire did not. AND THE STORE WIRE IS NOT A WAY AROUND R708: the one kit that ships a full store snapshot (`disclosure-craft/v3/authored.atomic.json`, schema_version 22, 52 facts) fails to LOAD with the same R708 message, so a widening gets a migration and a removal is a wall on both wires. TWO ERRORS OF MY OWN, both caught before reporting and both the same class — a rule that answers "broken" for something that works. My first pass keyed the census on the filenames `sections.json` / `facts.json`, which (a) reported `2d-projection/v1/extract-tsukuru` as broken when it ships `.norm.json` siblings that import cleanly — the arm is FINE and my first number for it was wrong — and (b) would have reported four kits (`causes-poc`, `factsfirst-poc`, `rung3-poc`, `selfextract-poc`) as having no input at all, when they simply name their manifests differently. Both were found by asking what else the directory holds rather than by trusting the rule, the R871 discipline. NO REPAIR IS PROPOSED HERE and none was performed: what to migrate, what to re-author, and what to let die is the owner's call, and the useful thing this round produces is that the question now has a number and a named cause per arm instead of one anecdote.

Round 880.decision_summary: R880 BUILD (the feasibility measurement the owner asked for, proved by a TEST rather than by reading): an old revision still builds, and it still reads its own evidence unmodified. THE QUESTION AND WHY IT MATTERED: asked whether re-typing the 30 R708-stale experiment manifests is the long-term-correct repair with cost set aside, the answer was NO, and on a correctness ground rather than an effort one — every kit's `deterministic_pins` is a pre-committed claim about what the BLIND AUTHOR produced ("the author CONVERGES to a base that imports with 0 errors"), so editing the author's output until it imports re-establishes the pin by editing the very thing the pin measures, which is the R469 contamination bound this repo already imposes on its experiments. The alternative offered was to leave the record byte-identical and move the TOOL instead: a kit is a workspace validated by one revision, which is exactly what `[tool] pin` (R826, hardened R861/R863) already expresses for consumers — we told them to pin the tool and never did it for our own evidence. That design rested on ONE unmeasured assumption, and it was named as the load-bearing unknown when the answer was given: that an old revision still builds and still eats the original bytes. MEASURED, ON THE OLDEST STALE KIT (`phase1-factsfirst-poc`, manifest added 2026-06-13): the authoring revision is DERIVED, not declared — the commit that first added the manifest, `7d95e68`, obtained from git history. That tree extracts, builds `mnemosyne-cli` in 12 seconds, and imports the ORIGINAL section and facts manifests with zero errors: 3 sections, then 2 frames + 0 branches + 2 entities + 1 predicate + 3 facts. Today's binary, handed the SAME BYTES, refuses with the R708 message naming all three offending facts and the one scalar predicate. Same file, same content, different revision — the revision is the whole difference, and re-checkability is recoverable without touching a byte of the record. THE PROOF IS A TEST, not a session measurement: `pinned_revision_rechecks_evidence_smoke.rs` derives the revision, extracts that tree with `git archive` (NOT a worktree, which would register state in `.git` and leak on panic), asserts the manifests are byte-identical between then and now so the test is demonstrably reading the original, builds the CLI into its own target dir, and asserts BOTH halves — the old binary's exact import counts, and today's binary refusing the same bytes for the R708 reason. It is `#[ignore]`d because it compiles a second copy of the workspace, and it names that cost in its own doc rather than hiding behind a fast green. WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT SETTLE: it settles that the pin-the-revision design is feasible at seven weeks and several hundred rounds of distance, which is the fact the design was blocked on. It does not settle that every kit's revision builds — one was measured, the oldest, deliberately. And the derivation is an UPPER BOUND: the add-commit is the tree state at commit time, which is at or after the run; a kit whose adding commit also moved the schema could be off by one, not observed here and stated as a limit rather than dismissed.

Round 881.decision_summary: R881 BUILD (the determinism measurement the record-as-a-triple design was blocked on, plus the gap it exposed): byte comparison IS sound for the store and the read reports, and it is sound STRUCTURALLY rather than by luck — but the one place it is guarded by convention instead of by structure had no test that could tell, and now does. THE QUESTION: R880 established that a kit's authoring revision still builds and still reads the original bytes. The design that rests on it — a record is (input, revision, expected output), re-checked by running the recorded revision against the untouched input — needs the expected output to be COMPARABLE, and this repo has been bitten there before: R852 found a generator whose emitted file was correct in content and different in bytes on every process, because a `HashMap` iteration order is seeded per process. So determinism was named as the load-bearing unknown before any of it was built. MEASURED, at real size and across processes: the 2D-projection author arm (20 sections, 59 facts, 21 entities) imported in six separate processes yields ONE distinct store hash (35 KB), ONE distinct `report-playable-world --json` (65 KB), and ONE distinct `validate-continuity --json`; the tsukuru arm (103 facts, 54 typed) likewise yields one store hash across six; and the R880 kit on its own pinned June binary yields one store hash and one stdout across five. A positive control confirms the comparison discriminates at all — one run given an extra frame produces a different hash. THE STRUCTURAL REASON, not just the count: `AtomicStore` holds 17 `BTreeMap`s and one `BTreeSet` and ZERO hash-ordered containers, and a sweep of every `Serialize` type in the workspace finds exactly ONE holding a `HashMap`/`HashSet` — `mnemosyne_engine::Interactivity`. So byte-comparison is safe by construction on the axes the design uses. THE GAP THAT SWEEP EXPOSED: `Interactivity` is rendered into GENERATED RUST SOURCE by this crate, which is exactly where R852 was bitten, and `render::interactivity` does sort both containers — but nothing asserted it. Injecting the removal of BOTH sorts left the entire 1332-test workspace GREEN. That silence was NOT evidence of a missing gate, and it was not reported as one: the only non-empty `Interactivity` the renderer had ever seen was a ONE-entry map from `build.rs`, where sorting is a no-op, so the injection could not have reddened anything either way — the R868 mis-aim class, caught by asking what fixture the injected line actually takes before drawing a conclusion. THE FIX IS THE FIXTURE: `the_interactive_layer_comes_out_in_sorted_order` gives this leg the outside assertion R852 gave the pool ("asserts it from OUTSIDE, where a later round that reaches for the map cannot quietly be right"), with five entries per leg inserted in neither sorted nor reversed order, comparing the emitted sequence against sorted rather than chaining pairwise checks. Five is a deliberate dial and the round says so: a dropped sort escapes only if hash order happens to BE sorted, which is 1 chance in 120 per leg where three entries would have left 1 in 6. The gate is a probability and the fixture size is how it is set.
changes_bullets: crates/mnemosyne-engine-build/src/lib.rs: new `the_interactive_layer_comes_out_in_sorted_order` — the sibling of R852's pool gate for the other hash-ordered container this generator serializes, with a fixture large enough for a dropped sort to show.

Round 881.publishable_decision_summary: R881 BUILD (the determinism measurement the record-as-a-triple design was blocked on, plus the gap it exposed): byte comparison IS sound for the store and the read reports, and it is sound STRUCTURALLY rather than by luck — but the one place it is guarded by convention instead of by structure had no test that could tell, and now does. THE QUESTION: R880 established that a kit's authoring revision still builds and still reads the original bytes. The design that rests on it — a record is (input, revision, expected output), re-checked by running the recorded revision against the untouched input — needs the expected output to be COMPARABLE, and this repo has been bitten there before: R852 found a generator whose emitted file was correct in content and different in bytes on every process, because a `HashMap` iteration order is seeded per process. So determinism was named as the load-bearing unknown before any of it was built. MEASURED, at real size and across processes: the 2D-projection author arm (20 sections, 59 facts, 21 entities) imported in six separate processes yields ONE distinct store hash (35 KB), ONE distinct `report-playable-world --json` (65 KB), and ONE distinct `validate-continuity --json`; the tsukuru arm (103 facts, 54 typed) likewise yields one store hash across six; and the R880 kit on its own pinned June binary yields one store hash and one stdout across five. A positive control confirms the comparison discriminates at all — one run given an extra frame produces a different hash. THE STRUCTURAL REASON, not just the count: `AtomicStore` holds 17 `BTreeMap`s and one `BTreeSet` and ZERO hash-ordered containers, and a sweep of every `Serialize` type in the workspace finds exactly ONE holding a `HashMap`/`HashSet` — `mnemosyne_engine::Interactivity`. So byte-comparison is safe by construction on the axes the design uses. THE GAP THAT SWEEP EXPOSED: `Interactivity` is rendered into GENERATED RUST SOURCE by this crate, which is exactly where R852 was bitten, and `render::interactivity` does sort both containers — but nothing asserted it. Injecting the removal of BOTH sorts left the entire 1332-test workspace GREEN. That silence was NOT evidence of a missing gate, and it was not reported as one: the only non-empty `Interactivity` the renderer had ever seen was a ONE-entry map from `build.rs`, where sorting is a no-op, so the injection could not have reddened anything either way — the R868 mis-aim class, caught by asking what fixture the injected line actually takes before drawing a conclusion. THE FIX IS THE FIXTURE: `the_interactive_layer_comes_out_in_sorted_order` gives this leg the outside assertion R852 gave the pool ("asserts it from OUTSIDE, where a later round that reaches for the map cannot quietly be right"), with five entries per leg inserted in neither sorted nor reversed order, comparing the emitted sequence against sorted rather than chaining pairwise checks. Five is a deliberate dial and the round says so: a dropped sort escapes only if hash order happens to BE sorted, which is 1 chance in 120 per leg where three entries would have left 1 in 6. The gate is a probability and the fixture size is how it is set.

Round 882.decision_summary: R882 BUILD (wiring the record-as-a-triple design, first half): every tracked experiment manifest now DECLARES the revision that can read it, and a gate keeps the declaration from drifting away from git history. R878 measured that 31 of 35 tracked manifests no longer import; R880 proved a kit's authoring revision still builds and still reads the original bytes; R881 proved the resulting comparison is sound by construction. The design those settled — a record is (input, revision, expected output), re-checked by running the recorded revision against the UNTOUCHED input, never by editing the input to suit a later tool — needed the revision written down. It now is: 23 `replay.json` files, one per replay unit, covering all 36 tracked manifests. WHAT A DECLARATION HOLDS, and why each field earns its place: the schema tag; a `revision_provenance` that is `derived-upper-bound` or `declared-at-run`, because a pin recovered from history and a pin recorded by the run that produced it are not equally strong and a reader must be able to tell; the derivation spelled out in the file itself (`git log --diff-filter=A -1`, the commit that first added the manifest, which is AT OR AFTER the run); and per manifest the SECTIONS/FACTS PAIRING plus its own revision. THE PAIRING IS NOT DECORATION — it is the datum this session got wrong twice by inferring it from filenames: a census keyed on `sections.json`/`facts.json` reported a working arm as broken because that kit ships `.norm.json` siblings, and would have reported four more kits as having no input at all because they name their manifests differently. Recorded, that class cannot recur. THE UNIT IS THE COMMIT, NOT THE DIRECTORY: the obvious grouping — one pin per version directory — was measured before it was adopted and it is WRONG for one unit. `continuity-stress/v1` holds a re-extraction added in a later commit than the game arm beside it, so a per-directory pin would have quietly attributed one manifest to a tree that never produced it. Each manifest therefore carries its own revision, and the file groups without aggregating. A ROLE IS RECORDED TOO — `replay-input` or `raw-agent-output` — because one kit tracks both its agent's raw output and the normalized form, and a reader that cannot tell them apart draws the wrong conclusion from the raw one, which is exactly what happened. THE GATE IS A TEST, NOT A `validate-workspace` CHECK, and that is a decision rather than convenience: this is a property of THIS repo's evidence, and a consumer running Mnemosyne has no `claudedocs/phase1-*` kits, so putting it in the validator every consumer runs would export a repo-local rule into the product. It asserts coverage in BOTH directions (no tracked manifest undeclared, no declared manifest missing), that every revision resolves to a real commit, and that every DERIVED pin still equals what the derivation yields — so a pin that has silently drifted is caught rather than sending a future re-check to the wrong tree. What it deliberately does NOT assert is that the revision still builds or that replay reproduces anything; that is R880's test, which compiles a second workspace and is ignored by default. Cheap always-on half here, expensive deliberate half there.

Round 883.decision_summary: R883 BUILD (replaying every declared unit at its own revision — and the mechanism immediately caught two of our own errors, one of them mine from four rounds earlier): every one of the 23 declared revisions still BUILDS, 32 of the 35 replay-input manifests import cleanly at the revision that authored them, and every single successful replay is DETERMINISTIC across two separate processes. R880 measured one revision, deliberately the oldest; this measures all of them. Build times are 12-15 seconds each. So the pin-the-revision design is not feasible at a sample — it is feasible at the whole corpus, today. THE THREE FAILURES ARE THE ROUND. The first is OURS AND IT IS MINE: `2d-projection/v1/run/author/facts.json` failed at `14d7a1e0`, THE REVISION THAT PRODUCED IT, because R879 edited that manifest in place to make it readable by today's binary. R879 argued the edit was safe because the transcription provably preserved content — the (telling, fact, branch, coords) triples were compared before and after and were identical — and that argument was RIGHT and the conclusion was WRONG. Measured here: the original bytes import at `14d7a1e0` cleanly (20 sections, 59 facts, 7 disclosure overrides); the edited bytes do not. The edit bought readability by today's tool at the price of readability by its own, which is the whole property the record exists to have. The rule R879 wrote for itself — "provable transcription in place, model re-decision as a derived copy" — has no exception for transcriptions, and R873 had it right from the start: the record is never edited, and a shape today's tool needs lives in a derived copy. So the record is back to its authored bytes, the migrated version now lives at `tests/fixtures/projection-2d-author/` beside a README that says why, and the R879 smoke test reads its facts from there while still reading sections, order and rules straight out of the record. Both halves verified: the restored record replays at `14d7a1e0`, and the derived copy still passes the R879 gate. THE OTHER TWO ARE A FORMAT FINDING, not a data one: `disclosure-craft`'s A and B facts manifests fail with `frame 'ground' not present in the frames registry`, and reading them shows why — they declare only `entities`, `facts`, `predicates`, so the frames their facts reference were registered by an earlier step the kit's runbook performed and R882's declaration does not record. The pairing is not wrong, it is INSUFFICIENT: a replay unit is not always (sections, facts), and `kit-replay/v1` can express a pair but not a sequence. That is the next increment of the schema and it is named rather than hacked around. WHAT THIS ROUND ESTABLISHES: the expected-output leg of the triple is now buildable — 32 digests were computed and each was confirmed by running its revision twice — but they are NOT written into the declarations yet, deliberately, because writing digests for a corpus with two known-incomplete units would record a completeness the corpus does not have.

Round 884.decision_summary: The record could say which pair, not in what order, and its census recognised an input by filename
changes_bullets: Widened the evidence record from `kit-replay/v1` pairs to `kit-replay/v2`: an `inputs` list (path + role, one home per file) plus `replays`, each an ORDERED list of `{verb, input, expect}` steps. R883 measured why a pair is the wrong unit — `disclosure-craft` feeds six manifests through four verbs, and `continuity-stress` ends with three `propose-verdict` probes that must be REJECTED. All 23 manifests converted; 36 replays, 81 declared inputs (was 68).

Replaced the coverage oracle. R882 recognised an input by matching its basename against a `FACTS_NAMES` const — a hand-list, which is a copy of the class it was built to kill — and it passed green while 14 tracked inputs sat undeclared, among them a whole re-extraction arm (`unattended-loop/v1/run/extract/reextracted.manifest.json`, 54 facts, a second replay unit nobody had enumerated). The oracle now asks the bytes: sections by `section_id`, proposals by their schema string (hoisted to `TYPING_PROPOSALS_SCHEMA` / `EDGE_PROPOSALS_SCHEMA` so the gate cannot keep a second copy of the literal), facts by whether any `FactsManifest` array — the key set taken FROM the type, via an all-default parse re-serialized — is non-empty.

Shape and parseability are two questions, and the first cut of the new oracle asked only the second, which silently dropped 6 of the 14. Measured on identical state: parse-based finds 8, shape-based finds all 14. The gap is R878's population — 39 of the 81 inputs predate the R708 `{kind:value}` removal, so today's binary rejects the bytes with a migration work-list. This is the same reasoning that DERIVED the `disclosure-craft` order rather than reading it off the runbook prose: its one `-facts-add` fact is the target of a typing proposal and a succession edge, so it must land between the base facts and the proposals.

Round 885.decision_summary: The record now says what its evidence rebuilds to, and replaying it found the negative control was not controlling
changes_bullets: Built the replay runner and recorded the third of the triple. For each of the 23 declared revisions it extracts that tree (`git archive`, not a worktree — a worktree registers state in `.git` and leaks on panic), builds `mnemosyne-cli` into an isolated target dir, and feeds the untouched inputs through the declared steps in order. 34 of 36 replays reproduce; the 2 declared blocked fail exactly as declared. Every digest was taken twice in separate processes and adopted only on agreement, then re-verified on a third full run before being written and a fourth after.

Determinism is measured per replay, not inherited. R881 established it structurally (BTreeMap 17 / BTreeSet 1 / hash-order 0) and sampled it; a digest taken from a single run could pin a hash map's iteration order and start rejecting the same evidence tomorrow. The runner takes each one twice and refuses to record a hash the second run did not agree with.

`blocked` is now enforced, not annotated. A replay declared blocked must actually fail at its revision — a stale note is worse than none, because it tells readers not to look. Both disclosure-craft arms fail with the exact diagnosis R884 wrote from reading the manifest: `frame 'ground' not present in the frames registry`. The reason was derived from the bytes and is now confirmed by the machine at the pinned revision.

A replay may declare the `mnemosyne.toml` the run worked under, and the runner copies it in with the rest of its directory rather than parsing the toml to chase its relative paths — a second parser there would be free to disagree with the config crate's. 4 replays declare one; only continuity-stress's is load-bearing.
verification_bullets: 1339 green (unchanged — the runner is `#[ignore]`d), clippy -D warnings clean, fmt clean, validate-workspace clean. The runner run: 36 replays across 23 revisions, 272s, exit 0.

The record was WRONG about its own negative control, and the runner is what found it. R884 declared continuity-stress's three `propose-verdict` probes as `expect: reject` on the strength of the run's recorded PIN-2 output. Replayed, the first probe APPLIED. Cause: the probes only violate a rule when the canon order and the narrative rules are loaded, and those are named by the kit's own tracked `mnemosyne.toml`, which the runner's bare seed workspace did not use. A negative control that passes because nothing was checked is the vacuous-pass class this repo keeps finding, and it was one commit old.

Injections, self-reported, three in one run — each names its own replay in the failure list, so attribution needs no separate runs. J-A (one character of a declared digest) reported record-vs-produced with both hashes. J-B (delete a real `blocked`) reported the replay failing, carrying the R708/frame-registry payload. J-C (declare a working replay blocked) reported that it ran, which is the stale-note direction.

The config's load-bearingness is a measurement, not a claim: the run WITHOUT it applied probe-exclusive, the run WITH it rolled all three back and produced a store. Same replay, same revision, one declaration apart.
Not injected: the then-vs-now byte check on inputs. Producing a discriminating case means editing a record, which this design forbids; R880 already asserts that class on one kit from the other side.
carry_forward_bullets: The runner is `#[ignore]`d and nothing runs it on a cadence. That is the same shape R873 named as the reason evidence rots for ~150 rounds — tracked but never loaded — and it is only half-answered here: the cheap always-on tests now load the declarations every `cargo test`, but the 23 builds (272s) do not. Where that runs is unsettled.

34 digests are `derived-upper-bound` pins, not `declared-at-run` ones. Nothing writes a pin at run time yet, so a future kit inherits an upper bound unless its runbook records the exact revision it ran under.

The digests were taken on one machine. Nothing yet proves a path or an environment value does not leak into the store bytes, so a disagreement on other hardware would be a finding about the digest, not about the evidence.

`narrative-rules.json` and `canon-order.json` files are still outside the coverage claim: they are read by report and validate verbs, not by a store-construction verb, so the shape oracle does not classify them and no gate requires them to be declared. The `config` field reaches the three that matter, by way of the directory they sit in, rather than naming them.

Round 886.decision_summary: The replay had no clock; the two things that can break it run on different ones
changes_bullets: New workflow `.github/workflows/evidence-replay.yml` runs the R885 replay runner on GitHub. R885 left it `#[ignore]`d and unrun, which is the shape R873 named as the reason evidence rots — tracked, and nothing loads it. This closes the other half.

Two triggers, because the two failure modes run on different clocks. A digest can only change if an input, a step, or the runner changes, so `push` / `pull_request` are path-filtered to `claudedocs/phase1-*/**` plus the test file. The filter is tight BY CONSTRUCTION, not by guesswork: a digest is produced by the binary built at the kit's own pinned revision, so no change under `crates/` can move it. A pinned revision that stops BUILDING is the world moving instead — a yanked crate, a registry that stops serving an old lockfile — and no commit of ours triggers that, so it gets a weekly `schedule` plus `workflow_dispatch`.

Separate workflow rather than a job in `mnemosyne-validate`: that one runs on every push and all PRs, and paying 5 minutes there for a result our own code cannot change would be the wrong trade. Only the cargo registry is cached, not `target` — each replay builds into a throwaway target dir, so there is nothing there to reuse; what repays caching is the crate sources for 23 historical lockfiles.
verification_bullets: `fetch-depth: 0` is measured, not assumed. Cloned this repo at `--depth 1` and asked it for a pinned revision: `git archive 7d95e688` exits 128, `not a valid object name`. The runner extracts 23 historical commits, so checkout's default shallow clone would fail every one of them for a reason with nothing to do with the evidence.

Cost measured before recommending, not after: all 23 pinned revisions declare toolchain 1.94.1 — one toolchain, no per-revision download — and one cold isolated build is 12.8s, which is where the 272s full run comes from. `timeout-minutes: 45` leaves margin for a cold dependency cache, which this job pays more often than most.

Both workflow files parse, checked with a YAML parser rather than by eye: triggers and jobs enumerate as intended and the new checkout carries `fetch-depth: 0`. R583 is why this is checked at all — this repo has already shipped a malformed workflow that left CI silently non-running.
The declaration-gates step was run locally with `--locked` (6 passed) so the job cannot fail on a lockfile mismatch before it reaches the work.

NOT verified, and only a push can: that GitHub accepts the schedule, that the hosted runner's checkout behaves as the local shallow-clone experiment predicts, and that 23 historical lockfiles still resolve against crates.io from a hosted runner. That last one is the residual risk R880 recorded as UNOBSERVED — this workflow exists partly to observe it, and until it runs once the observation has not been made.
carry_forward_bullets: Nothing prevents a malformed workflow YAML from landing. R583's failure was silent — the CI simply did not run — and the check above was a one-off run of a parser this repo does not carry: there is no YAML crate anywhere in the dependency tree, and pulling one in for a single test assertion was declined rather than done quietly. A future round that wants this gated should decide the dependency deliberately.

The weekly schedule is a guess at a cadence, not a measurement. A yanked dependency has no known arrival rate here; weekly was chosen because the job is 5 minutes and the failure it looks for is slow-moving.
GitHub disables scheduled workflows on repositories with no activity for 60 days. If this repo goes quiet, the cadence stops silently — the same class of silence R583 was.
